Other functions also equal (n-1)! at the integers. \Gamma is singled out as the only log-convex solution of f(x+1)=xf(x) with f(1)=1 on (0,\infty) (the Bohr-Mollerup theorem).

Theorem 3.16 \Gamma satisfies a recursion, is meromorphic with simple poles at the nonpositive integers, and \Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi
  1. \Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s) for \Re s>0.
  2. \Gamma extends to a meromorphic function on \CC whose poles are the points 0,-1,-2,\dots. They are simple, and the residue at -n is (-1)^n/n!.
  3. \Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi.
Proof

For part 1, integrate by parts: \int_0^\infty e^{-x}x^{s}\,\dd x=\bigl[-e^{-x}x^s\bigr]_0^\infty+s\int_0^\infty e^{-x}x^{s-1}\,\dd x, and the boundary term is 0 for \Re s>0.

For part 2, iterate part 1 to get

\Gamma(s)=\frac{\Gamma(s+n+1)}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n)}.

The right side is meromorphic on \Re s>-n-1 and agrees with \Gamma on \Re s>0, so it is the continuation there; let n grow. The only possible poles are at s=0,-1,\dots,-n. At s=-n the numerator is \Gamma(1)=1 and the factors other than s+n give (-n)(-n+1)\cdots(-1)=(-1)^nn!, so the residue is 1/((-1)^nn!)=(-1)^n/n!.

For part 3, substitute x=u^2: \Gamma(\tfrac12)=\int_0^\infty e^{-x}x^{-1/2}\dd x=2\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}\dd u=\sqrt\pi.

Example

The recursion gives \Gamma at half-integers beyond the integral: \Gamma(-\tfrac12)=\Gamma(\tfrac12)/(-\tfrac12)=-2\sqrt\pi=-3.5449 and \Gamma(-\tfrac32)=\Gamma(-\tfrac12)/(-\tfrac32)=\tfrac43\sqrt\pi=2.3633. At an integer to the left, say s=-2, the function has a pole with residue 1/2!=\tfrac12.

Recall

The Gaussian integral. \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2}\,\dd u=\sqrt\pi. Substituting u=\sqrt\pi\,x gives the form used below: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\pi x^2}\,\dd x=1.

Two more facts about \Gamma will be used without proof. First, \Gamma has no zeros, so 1/\Gamma is entire. This follows from the reflection formula \Gamma(s)\Gamma(1-s)=\pi/\sin\pi s [15, Chapter 6]. Second, Stirling’s formula tells us how fast \Gamma grows. For each fixed \delta>0, as \abs s\to\infty with \abs{\arg s}\le\pi-\delta,

\log\Gamma(s)=\Bigl(s-\tfrac12\Bigr)\log s-s+\tfrac12\log2\pi+O\!\left(\frac1{\abs s}\right).
(3.4)

For a feel of the accuracy, at s=10 we have \Gamma(10)=362{,}880 and the right side exponentiates to 359{,}870, a ratio of 1.0084, close to the next correction 1+1/(12\cdot10) [16, Chapter 5].

Used later
  • The factor \Gamma(s/2) is part of the completed zeta function in Riemann’s integral, and its poles produce the trivial zeros of \zeta in Theorem 4.14.
  • Stirling’s formula controls the growth of \Gamma(s/2) along vertical lines, and so the count of zeros up to height T in The zeros and the hypothesis.

3.9The Fourier transform and the Gaussian#

Definition 3.17 Schwartz class

The Schwartz class \mathcal S(\RR) is the set of infinitely differentiable functions f:\RR\to\CC such that \sup_x\abs{x}^a\abs{f^{(b)}(x)}<\infty for all integers a,b\ge0. In words, f and every derivative decay faster than any power of x. It contains the Gaussians and every smooth function with bounded support. It is much smaller than the set of integrable functions: \mathcal S(\RR) is a space of well-behaved test functions that is closed under differentiation, products, and the Fourier transform.

Definition 3.18 Fourier transform

For f\in\mathcal S(\RR) the Fourier transform is

\hat f(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,e^{-2\pi ixy}\,\dd x.

It measures how much of the pure wave e^{2\pi ixy} of frequency y is contained in f. It is again in \mathcal S(\RR) and it is invertible: f(x)=\int\hat f(y)e^{2\pi ixy}\,\dd y [17, Chapter 5].

Take the one function we can transform by hand.

Theorem 3.19 The Gaussian is its own Fourier transform

For f(x)=e^{-\pi x^2}, \hat f(y)=e^{-\pi y^2}.

Proof

Let g(y)=\int e^{-\pi x^2}e^{-2\pi ixy}\,\dd x. Differentiating under the integral and noting -2\pi i x\,e^{-\pi x^2}=i\,\frac{\dd}{\dd x}e^{-\pi x^2}, we get

g'(y)=i\int\Bigl(\tfrac{\dd}{\dd x}e^{-\pi x^2}\Bigr)e^{-2\pi ixy}\,\dd x=-i\int e^{-\pi x^2}\,\tfrac{\dd}{\dd x}e^{-2\pi ixy}\,\dd x=-2\pi y\,g(y),

where the middle step integrates by parts with no boundary term. This differential equation has the solution g(y)=g(0)e^{-\pi y^2}, and g(0)=\int e^{-\pi x^2}\dd x=1.

Squeezing the Gaussian in x spreads it in y. For t>0, substitute x=u/\sqrt t:

\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\pi tx^2}e^{-2\pi ixy}\,\dd x=\frac1{\sqrt t}\,e^{-\pi y^2/t}.
(3.5)

A Gaussian of width about 1/\sqrt t has a transform of width about \sqrt t, and the factor t^{-1/2} keeps the total mass in balance. As a check, at t=2 and y=0.7 both sides equal 0.3275 when the left side is integrated numerically.

Used later
  • The theta function of The theta function is a sum of such Gaussians, and its symmetry t\mapsto1/t is Equation (3.5) summed over the integers.
  • Test functions in the explicit formula of Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion are taken from this class.

3.10Poisson summation#

Theorem 3.20

The sum of a Schwartz function over the integers equals the sum of its Fourier transform over the integers

Statement

For every f\in\mathcal S(\RR),

\sum_{n\in\ZZ}f(n)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ}\hat f(n).
(3.6)
In plain terms

Add up the values of a function at the whole numbers, and you get the same answer as adding up the values of its Fourier transform at the whole numbers. A sum over points equals a sum over frequencies.

Why it is needed

Our zeta function is a sum over integers, \sum n^{-s}. If we can write it as a sum over the integers of something that also has a Fourier transform, Poisson summation will swap the sum for a different sum. That swap, applied to Gaussians, is the source of the symmetry s\leftrightarrow1-s.

Idea

Make f periodic by adding up all its shifts by integers. A periodic function is its own Fourier series. The Fourier coefficients of the periodized function are exactly the values \hat f(k), and evaluating the series at 0 gives the formula.

Proof

Set F(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ}f(x+n). Because f and f' decay faster than any power, the sums converge uniformly on [0,1] together with their derivatives, so F is smooth, and F(x+1)=F(x). Its Fourier coefficients are

c_k=\int_0^1F(x)e^{-2\pi ikx}\,\dd x=\sum_n\int_0^1f(x+n)e^{-2\pi ik(x+n)}\,\dd x=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)e^{-2\pi ikx}\,\dd x=\hat f(k),

using e^{-2\pi ikn}=1 and joining the intervals [n,n+1]. A smooth periodic function equals its Fourier series at every point [17, Chapter 3], so F(0)=\sum_kc_k. That says \sum_nf(n)=\sum_k\hat f(k).

Example

Apply it to f(x)=e^{-2\pi x^2}, whose transform is 2^{-1/2}e^{-\pi y^2/2} by Equation (3.5) with t=2. The left side is \sum_ne^{-2\pi n^2}=1.0037349. The right side is 2^{-1/2}\sum_ne^{-\pi n^2/2}=1.4194955/1.4142136=1.0037349. The two sums agree to every digit shown, though one converges at a rate e^{-2\pi n^2} and the other at e^{-\pi n^2/2}.

Used in
  • With f(x)=e^{-\pi tx^2} for all t>0 this is the symmetry \theta(1/t)=\sqrt t\,\theta(t): Theorem 4.9.
  • The explicit formula of The explicit formula: each zero is a wave and the positivity criterion of Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion are duality statements of the same shape: a sum over primes on one side, a sum over zeros on the other.

3.11The Mellin transform#

The Fourier transform is built for the additive group \RR, where the building blocks are the waves e^{2\pi ixy}. Zeta lives on the multiplicative group of positive reals, where numbers multiply and the building blocks are the powers x^{it}.

Definition 3.21 Mellin transform

For a function f on (0,\infty) that decays fast enough at 0 and at \infty, its Mellin transform is

(\mathcal Mf)(s)=\int_0^\infty f(x)\,x^{s}\,\frac{\dd x}{x}.

It is a function of the complex variable s, defined where the integral converges, usually on a vertical strip. The measure \dd x/x is the one that does not change when x is rescaled to ax, just as \dd x does not change under translation. The powers x^{it} are the characters of the multiplicative group, since (xy)^{it}=x^{it}y^{it}, as e^{2\pi ixy} are for addition.

Substituting x=e^u shows that this is the Fourier transform in disguise:

(\mathcal Mf)(\sigma+it)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\bigl(f(e^u)e^{\sigma u}\bigr)e^{itu}\,\dd u.

With g(u)=f(e^u)e^{\sigma u} this reads (\mathcal Mf)(\sigma+it)=\hat g\bigl(-t/(2\pi)\bigr): the Fourier transform of g, with the frequency rescaled by 2\pi and reflected. The real part \sigma tilts the function by an exponential so that the integral converges. The same \sigma will decide where \sum n^{-s} converges.

Example

The model computation. For a>0 substitute y=ax in the Mellin transform of e^{-ax}:

\int_0^\infty e^{-ax}x^{s}\,\frac{\dd x}{x}=a^{-s}\int_0^\infty e^{-y}y^{s}\,\frac{\dd y}{y}=a^{-s}\,\Gamma(s).

So the Gamma function is the Mellin transform of e^{-x}, and the power a^{-s} appears. Now sum over a=n=1,2,3,\dots using \sum_{n\ge1}e^{-nx}=1/(e^x-1):

\int_0^\infty\frac{x^{s-1}}{e^x-1}\,\dd x=\Gamma(s)\,\zeta(s),\qquad\Re s>1.

At s=2 the left side, evaluated numerically, is 1.6449340668, and \Gamma(2)\zeta(2)=\pi^2/6=1.6449340668. An exponential sum has become the Dirichlet series \sum n^{-s} times \Gamma. Chapter 4 does the same with Gaussians.

The Fourier transform can be undone, so the Mellin transform can be too: the values of \mathcal Mf on one vertical line determine f. Write \int_{(c)} for the integral up the line \Re s=c.

Theorem 3.22 Mellin inversion recovers f from its transform on a vertical line [17]

Let c be real, and let f be a function on (0,\infty) for which u\mapsto f(e^u)e^{cu} is in \mathcal S(\RR). Then for every x>0,

f(x)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{(c)}(\mathcal Mf)(s)\,x^{-s}\,\dd s.
(3.7)
Proof

Put g(u)=f(e^u)e^{cu}, so that (\mathcal Mf)(c+it)=\hat g(-t/2\pi). Fourier inversion for g\in\mathcal S(\RR) [17, Chapter 5], with the substitution y=-t/2\pi, gives g(u)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty(\mathcal Mf)(c+it)\,e^{-itu}\,\dd t. Multiply by e^{-cu}, put x=e^u and s=c+it, so that \dd s=i\,\dd t and e^{-cu}e^{-itu}=x^{-s}.

Test it on f(x)=e^{-x} with c=1, where \mathcal Mf=\Gamma: the formula says e^{-x}=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{(1)}\Gamma(s)x^{-s}\,\dd s, and at x=1 numerical integration up the line gives 0.3678794=e^{-1}.

Compact support gives an entire transform#

Part III of this page works with test functions \varphi that are smooth on (0,\infty) and vanish outside a closed interval [1/Y,Y], that is, with compact support in \log t. For those, the Mellin transform is far better behaved than a general one: it is defined on the whole plane, and on every vertical strip it decays faster than any power. This is the idea behind the Paley and Wiener theorem. We need one general fact first, the one that makes an integral of holomorphic functions holomorphic.

Lemma 3.23 An integral of holomorphic functions, dominated on compact sets, is holomorphic [15]

Let U\subseteq\CC be open, let I\subseteq\RR be an interval, and let F(t,s) be continuous on I\times U and holomorphic in s for each t. Suppose that for each compact K\subset U there is an integrable h_K on I with \abs{F(t,s)}\le h_K(t) for all s\in K. Then s\mapsto\int_IF(t,s)\,\dd t is holomorphic on U.

Proof sketch [15, Chapter 2]

Over a closed bounded subinterval of I the integral is holomorphic: it is continuous, and its integral around every small triangle vanishes by Fubini and Cauchy’s theorem, so Morera’s theorem applies. The bound h_K makes these truncated integrals converge uniformly on K as the subinterval grows to I, and a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic.

Proposition 3.24 A smooth function with compact support in (0,\infty) has an entire Mellin transform that decays fast on every vertical strip

Let Y>1 and let \varphi be smooth on (0,\infty) with \varphi(t)=0 outside [1/Y,Y]. Then (\mathcal M\varphi)(z)=\int_{1/Y}^{Y}\varphi(t)\,t^{z}\,\dd t/t is an entire function of z, and for every integer k\ge0

\abs{z}^k\,\abs{(\mathcal M\varphi)(z)}\le Y^{\abs{\Re z}}\int_0^\infty\Bigl\lvert\Bigl(t\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\Bigr)^k\varphi(t)\Bigr\rvert\,\frac{\dd t}t.
(3.8)

So on each strip \abs{\Re z}\le a the transform decays faster than any power of \abs{\Im z}, Mellin inversion holds on every vertical line, and the line of integration can be moved freely.

Proof

The integrand \varphi(t)t^{z-1} is continuous, entire in z, and zero outside [1/Y,Y], where \abs{t^{z}}=t^{\Re z}\le Y^{\abs{\Re z}}. So Lemma 3.23 applies and \mathcal M\varphi is entire, and the case k=0 of the bound is the same estimate. For k\ge1, integrate by parts: \int_0^\infty t\varphi'(t)\,t^{z}\,\frac{\dd t}t=\int_0^\infty\varphi'(t)\,t^z\,\dd t=-z\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{z}\,\frac{\dd t}t, with no boundary terms because \varphi vanishes near 1/Y and Y. So the operator t\frac{\dd}{\dd t} becomes multiplication by -z, and k applications give (-z)^k(\mathcal M\varphi)(z)=\bigl(\mathcal M(t\tfrac{\dd}{\dd t})^k\varphi\bigr)(z), which the case k=0 bounds. For inversion, u\mapsto\varphi(e^u)e^{cu} is smooth and vanishes outside [-\log Y,\log Y], so it is in \mathcal S(\RR) for every c, and Theorem 3.22 applies on every line. To move the line from \Re z=c_1 to \Re z=c_2, apply Cauchy’s theorem to the rectangle with corners c_1\pm iT and c_2\pm iT: the transform has no poles, and its horizontal sides tend to 0 as T\to\infty by Equation (3.8).

The smallest case shows what each hypothesis buys. Drop smoothness and take \varphi to be 1 on [1/Y,Y] and 0 elsewhere. Then (\mathcal M\varphi)(z)=\int_{1/Y}^Yt^{z-1}\,\dd t=(Y^z-Y^{-z})/z. It is still entire, because the zero of the denominator at z=0 is canceled and the value there is 2\log Y. It grows like Y^{\abs{\Re z}} to the left and right, as the bound says. But on a vertical line it decays only like 1/\abs z: with Y=2, the value at z=1 is 1.5, and at z=10i it is \sin(10\log2)/5=0.1208. The jumps of \varphi at 1/2 and 2 cost the fast decay; smoothing them restores it. Compact support is what makes the transform entire; smoothness is what makes it decay.

The converse also holds: an entire function with bounds of the shape Equation (3.8) is the Mellin transform of a smooth function that vanishes outside [1/Y,Y]. In Fourier language this is the Paley and Wiener theorem [15, Chapter 4], and Part III uses it only in the direction proved here.

The Mellin transform also turns multiplicative convolution into multiplication, as the Fourier transform does for ordinary convolution. If (\varphi\star f)(x)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,f(x/t)\,\dd t/t, then substituting x=ty in the double integral gives

\mathcal M(\varphi\star f)(z)=(\mathcal M\varphi)(z)\,(\mathcal Mf)(z)

wherever both transforms converge absolutely.

Used later
  • Riemann’s integral for \zeta in Riemann’s integral is the Mellin transform of a sum of Gaussians, and Lemma 3.23 makes its continuation entire in Theorem 4.12.
  • Perron’s formula in The explicit formula: each zero is a wave is the same inversion applied to the step function that jumps at x=1. That function is not smooth, so The explicit formula: each zero is a wave proves the version it needs directly.
  • The test functions of Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion and of Part III have compact support in \log t, so their transforms are entire and decay on strips by Proposition 3.24. Part III writes M\varphi(z) for (\mathcal M\varphi)(z), and its convolution operator A(\varphi) is f\mapsto\varphi\star f.
Recap

You now have the following tools, and where each one is used.

  • The arrow n^{-s}=n^{-\sigma}e^{-it\log n} and its multiplicativity: the series for \zeta in Zeta on the whole plane, and the Euler product throughout.
  • Holomorphic functions, domain coloring, and the order of a zero: reading pictures of \xi and \zeta.
  • The identity theorem and uniqueness of analytic continuation: every extension of \zeta is the same function.
  • Cauchy’s theorem and formula, residues, and the residue theorem: the pole of \zeta at 1 and, in The explicit formula: each zero is a wave, the sum over zeros.
  • The logarithmic derivative and the argument principle: counting zeros in The zeros and the hypothesis.
  • The Gamma function, with its poles, its lack of zeros, and Stirling’s formula: the completion factor of \xi and the trivial zeros.
  • The Fourier transform, the self-dual Gaussian, Poisson summation, and the Mellin transform: the theta function and Riemann’s integral in the next chapter.
  • Mellin inversion, holomorphic integrals, and the entire, fast-decaying transforms of compactly supported test functions: Riemann’s integral, Weil’s explicit formula in Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion, and Part III.
Previous2. Euler's product: primes inside one functionNext4. Zeta on the whole plane

Chapter 4

Zeta on the whole plane

After this chapter you can state and prove the continuation of zeta to the whole complex plane and its functional equation, and you know where the trivial zeros and the pole come from.

Builds on 3. The complex analysis we need

In plain terms

The zeta function starts life as a sum that only makes sense when the real part of s is larger than 1. Riemann rewrote that sum as an integral of the theta function, a sum of Gaussians, and the integral makes sense for every s except 1. The same step reveals a hidden symmetry: the function looks the same when s is replaced by 1-s. That symmetry explains the trivial zeros and confines all other zeros to a vertical strip.

The Euler product turned primes into a function, but only on the half-plane where the series converges. The primes will be read off the zeros of that function, and the zeros we care about sit at real part between 0 and 1, outside the half-plane. So this chapter is where the object of the whole page is built. Everything here uses the tools of The complex analysis we need: the arrow n^{-s}, uniqueness of continuation, the Gamma function, the Fourier transform, Poisson summation, and the Mellin transform.

4.1Where the series converges#

Definition 4.1 the Riemann zeta function on the right half-plane

For s=\sigma+it with \sigma>1 put

\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}.

So far this is a function on the half-plane \{\sigma>1\} and nowhere else. It is a Dirichlet series, a sum of the arrows n^{-s} of Equation (3.1), and it agrees with the real-variable function of Euler's product: primes inside one function when t=0. It is not yet a function on the plane, and a formula for it elsewhere is what this chapter supplies.

Theorem 4.2 The series converges absolutely for \sigma>1 and defines a holomorphic function there

For every \delta>0, the series \sum n^{-s} converges absolutely and uniformly on \{\sigma\ge1+\delta\}. Hence \zeta is holomorphic on \{\sigma>1\}, and \abs{\zeta(s)}\le\zeta(\sigma).

Proof

Since \abs{n^{-s}}=n^{-\sigma}\le n^{-1-\delta} and \sum_n n^{-1-\delta}\le1+\int_1^\infty x^{-1-\delta}\,\dd x=1+1/\delta<\infty, the Weierstrass M-test gives absolute and uniform convergence. A uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic [15, Chapter 2], and each term n^{-s}=e^{-s\log n} is entire. The bound is the triangle inequality: \abs{\sum n^{-s}}\le\sum n^{-\sigma}.

The Euler product also survives the passage from real to complex s, because its proof in Euler's product: primes inside one function used only two things: absolute convergence and the rule (mn)^{-s}=m^{-s}n^{-s}.

Theorem 4.3 The Euler product holds for \sigma>1, and \zeta has no zeros there

For \sigma>1,

\zeta(s)=\prod_p\frac1{1-p^{-s}},

the product converging absolutely, and \zeta(s)\neq0.

Proof

Fix \sigma>1 and a bound P. Each factor is a geometric series, \frac1{1-p^{-s}}=\sum_{k\ge0}p^{-ks}, with \abs{p^{-s}}<1. Multiplying the finitely many factors with p\le P and using unique factorization, the product equals \sum n^{-s} over the n whose prime factors are all at most P. Every n\le P is of that form, so

\Bigl\lvert\zeta(s)-\prod_{p\le P}\frac1{1-p^{-s}}\Bigr\rvert\le\sum_{n>P}n^{-\sigma}\xrightarrow[P\to\infty]{}0.

For the zeros: \sum_p\abs{p^{-s}}<\infty, so \prod_p(1-p^{-s}) converges to some L, and L\cdot\zeta(s)=\lim_P\prod_{p\le P}(1-p^{-s})\cdot\prod_{p\le P}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}=1. Since L\cdot\zeta(s)=1, \zeta(s)\ne0.

Test it on s=2+3i. The first thousand arrows added head to tail give 0.79834-0.11374i (the example in Complex numbers and the arrow n^{-s}), and \zeta(2+3i)=0.79802-0.11374i to the digits shown, with \abs{\zeta(2+3i)}=0.806\le\zeta(2)=1.645. The second theorem will matter immediately: it says no zero of \zeta lies to the right of the line \sigma=1.

4.2Where the series stops, and why the function does not#

At \sigma\le 0 the terms \abs{n^{-s}}=n^{-\sigma}\ge1 do not even tend to zero, so the sum cannot converge. At s=1 it is the harmonic series, which diverges. Approaching that edge from the right, the sum grows without bound but in an orderly way: \zeta(1.5)=2.6124, \zeta(1.1)=10.5844, and \zeta(1.01)=100.5779, close to 1/(\sigma-1) plus a constant near 0.58. The sum is announcing a pole, and a pole is a perfectly good point for a holomorphic function to have nearby. On 0<\sigma\le1 the arrows do shrink, but they shrink too slowly: Theorem 4.6 will show how the partial sums behave there. In every case the series fails.

A formula that stops working is a statement about the formula. The geometric series \sum z^k stops at \abs z=1, and the function 1/(1-z) it came from carries on, unaffected, for every z\ne1 (Analytic continuation). The same may be true of \zeta. By Theorem 3.7 there is at most one way to continue it, so the question is only whether a continuation exists and whether we can write it down. Riemann answered both in 1859 [18]. We follow his route in two stages: a quick step into the strip \sigma>0, then the theta function for the whole plane.

4.3The first step in: an alternating series#

Many of the arrows in \sum n^{-s} point in nearly the same direction, and their sum is large. Subtracting the even terms twice flips their sign, and the resulting arrows partly cancel.

Definition 4.4 the alternating zeta series

For \sigma>0 define

\eta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty(-1)^{n-1}n^{-s}=1-2^{-s}+3^{-s}-4^{-s}+\cdots.

It is a different function from \zeta, with a different series. It is related to \zeta by an exact formula where both converge, and it is the relation, and not equality, that gives the continuation.

For \sigma>1 both series converge absolutely, and removing the even terms twice gives

\eta(s)=\sum_n n^{-s}-2\sum_{n\ \mathrm{even}}n^{-s}=\zeta(s)-2\cdot2^{-s}\zeta(s)=(1-2^{1-s})\,\zeta(s).
(4.1)
Theorem 4.5

\zeta extends to the half-plane \sigma>0 with a single simple pole at s=1, of residue 1

Statement

The function \zeta has an analytic continuation to \{\sigma>0\} that is holomorphic except at s=1, where it has a simple pole of residue 1. Away from the points 1+2\pi ik/\log2 with k\in\ZZ, it is given there by \zeta(s)=\eta(s)/(1-2^{1-s}).

In plain terms

Alternating the signs makes the series converge a bit further left, all the way to the imaginary axis. Dividing by 1-2^{1-s} undoes the damage, and the one place where the division is by zero, s=1, is where \zeta blows up like 1/(s-1).

Why it is needed

The nontrivial zeros of \zeta lie at real part between 0 and 1. Before this step, the strip where they live is a region where \zeta is not even defined. After it, the right half of the strip is covered, and we see the pole at 1, which is the analytic form of the divergence of \sum 1/n and of the infinitude of the primes.

Idea

The series for \eta converges for \sigma>0 because its terms alternate and shrink. By Equation (4.1) the quotient \eta/(1-2^{1-s}) equals \zeta on \sigma>1, so by uniqueness it is the continuation. The only worry is the points where the denominator vanishes; a second identity, with 3 in place of 2, shows that they are harmless except at s=1.

Proof

The series for \eta converges and is holomorphic on \sigma>0. The partial sums of (-1)^{n-1} are 1,0,1,0,\dots, bounded. Also \abs{n^{-s}-(n+1)^{-s}}=\bigl\lvert s\int_n^{n+1}x^{-s-1}\,\dd x\bigr\rvert\le\abs s\,n^{-\sigma-1}, which is summable for \sigma>0, and n^{-s}\to0. By Dirichlet’s test, summation by parts, the series converges, uniformly on compact subsets of \{\sigma>0\}, so \eta is holomorphic there.

The quotient continues \zeta. The function \eta(s)/(1-2^{1-s}) is meromorphic on \sigma>0, with possible poles at the zeros of 1-2^{1-s}, which are s_k=1+2\pi ik/\log2 for k\in\ZZ. By Equation (4.1) it equals \zeta on \sigma>1, so by Theorem 3.7 it is the continuation of \zeta wherever it is holomorphic.

No pole at s_k for k\ne0. Remove the multiples of 3 three times: (1-3^{1-s})\zeta(s)=\sum_nb_nn^{-s} on \sigma>1, where b_n=1 if 3\nmid n and b_n=-2 if 3\mid n. The partial sums of b_n are 1,2,0,1,2,0,\dots, bounded, so the same test shows this series converges on \sigma>0. Hence \zeta also equals \sum b_nn^{-s}/(1-3^{1-s}), with possible poles only at s'_{k'}=1+2\pi ik'/\log3. A point in both lists satisfies k\log3=k'\log2, that is 3^k=2^{k'}, which by unique factorization forces k=k'=0. So at each s_k with k\ne0 one of the two expressions is holomorphic, and \zeta has no pole there.

The pole at s=1. Near s=1 the denominator is 1-2^{1-s}=(s-1)\log2+O((s-1)^2), and \eta(1)=1-\tfrac12+\tfrac13-\cdots=\log2. So \zeta(s)=\dfrac{\log 2+O(s-1)}{(s-1)\log2\,(1+O(s-1))}=\dfrac1{s-1}+O(1), a simple pole of residue 1.

Example

At s=\tfrac12: \eta(\tfrac12)=0.6048986 and 1-2^{1/2}=-0.4142136, so \zeta(\tfrac12)=-1.4603545. The real series \sum n^{-1/2} diverges to +\infty, but the continuation takes a negative value there. Near the pole, \zeta(1.001)=1000.5773=1/0.001+0.5773. The constant is Euler’s constant \gamma_E=\lim_N(1+\tfrac12+\dots+\tfrac1N-\log N)=0.5772157, the next term of the expansion \zeta(s)=\frac1{s-1}+\gamma_E+O(s-1), proved in Theorem 4.7 below.

Used in
  • The pole fixes the main term x in the count \psi(x)=x-\cdots of The explicit formula: each zero is a wave: the residue of \zeta at 1 is the origin of the “x”.
  • The full continuation, which this one is only the first step toward: Theorem 4.12.

The step cannot continue past \sigma=0 by this method. The alternating series genuinely diverges there, and each further correction costs another new identity.

What the partial sums do below the line#

Now that \zeta has a value at every s with \sigma>0, we can say exactly how the series fails there.

Theorem 4.6 For \sigma>0 the partial sums miss \zeta by a spiral of size N^{1-\sigma}

Let S_N(s)=\sum_{n\le N}n^{-s}. For \sigma>0 and s\ne1,

S_N(s)=\zeta(s)+\frac{N^{1-s}}{1-s}+O\!\left(N^{-\sigma}\right)
(4.2)

as N\to\infty, with the implied constant depending on s.

Proof

For \sigma>1, write \sum_{n>N}n^{-s}=\int_N^\infty x^{-s}\,\dd x+E_N(s) with E_N(s)=\sum_{n>N}\bigl(n^{-s}-\int_{n-1}^nx^{-s}\,\dd x\bigr), and \int_N^\infty x^{-s}\,\dd x=N^{1-s}/(s-1). For x\in[n-1,n] we have \abs{n^{-s}-x^{-s}}\le\abs s(n-x)(n-1)^{-\sigma-1}, so each term of E_N is at most \tfrac12\abs s(n-1)^{-\sigma-1}. Summing over n>N bounds \abs{E_N(s)} by \tfrac12\abs s\,(N^{-\sigma-1}+N^{-\sigma}/\sigma)=O(N^{-\sigma}), and the series defining E_N converges locally uniformly for all \sigma>0, so E_N is holomorphic there. Thus on \sigma>1

\zeta(s)=S_N(s)+\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}+E_N(s),

and the right side is holomorphic on \sigma>0 except for the pole at 1. By uniqueness of continuation it is the continuation of \zeta. Rearrange to get Equation (4.2).

Three cases follow, and the arrows show all of them. For \sigma>1 the extra term N^{1-s}/(1-s) has size N^{1-\sigma}/\abs{1-s}\to0, and the partial sums converge to \zeta(s). For \sigma=1 with t\ne0 its size is 1/\abs t forever: the partial sums circle \zeta(s) at a fixed radius, and never settle. For 0<\sigma<1 its size grows like N^{1-\sigma}, so the partial sums spiral outward and diverge.

Example

At s=1+i the distance \abs{S_N-\zeta(s)} is 1.0004,\ 1.000004,\ 1.00000004 for N=10,\,100,\,1000, and 1/\abs{1-s}=1. At s=\tfrac12 the partial sums are 5.02,\ 18.59,\ 61.80,\ 198.54 for N=10,\ 10^2,\ 10^3,\ 10^4, tracking 2\sqrt N+\zeta(\tfrac12), where \zeta(\tfrac12)=-1.46 is the value the continuation assigns. The sharpest case is a zero of the continued function, s=\tfrac12+14.1347i, where \zeta(s)=0. The partial sums have size 0.709,\ 2.236,\ 7.071,\ 22.36,\ 70.70 for N=10^2,\dots,10^6, growing by \sqrt{10} for each factor of 10 in N, in agreement with \sqrt N/\abs{1-s}=\sqrt N/14.14.

The same formula pins down the constant term at the pole, which Euler's product: primes inside one function left as a promise.

Theorem 4.7 The constant term of \zeta at its pole is Euler’s constant
\zeta(s)=\frac1{s-1}+\gamma_E+O(s-1)\qquad\text{as }s\to1,\qquad\gamma_E=\lim_{N\to\infty}\Bigl(\sum_{n\le N}\frac1n-\log N\Bigr).
Proof

Subtract \frac1{s-1} from \zeta(s)=S_N(s)+\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}+E_N(s) and let s\to1 with N fixed. The terms converge: S_N(s)\to H_N=\sum_{n\le N}\frac1n, then \frac{N^{1-s}-1}{s-1}\to-\log N, and E_N(s)\to E_N(1). So the constant term c of the Laurent expansion at 1 satisfies c=H_N-\log N+E_N(1) for every N. By the bound in the previous proof, \abs{E_N(1)}\le\tfrac12(N^{-2}+N^{-1})\to0. Letting N\to\infty gives c=\lim_N(H_N-\log N)=\gamma_E.

For example, H_{10000}-\log10000=0.5772657 against \gamma_E=0.5772157, and the gap 0.00005 is of the size \tfrac1{2N} that the bound allows.

4.4The theta function#

The alternating series reached only the half-plane \sigma>0. To go all the way we need an expression for \zeta that has the symmetry hidden inside it built in. It comes from a sum of Gaussians.

Definition 4.8 Jacobi theta function

For real t>0 the theta function is

\theta(t)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ}e^{-\pi n^2t}=1+2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\pi n^2t}.

It is a function of the real variable t, a sum of Gaussians centered at 0 and sampled at the integers. It is not a Dirichlet series: the exponent is n^2 and n is in the exponent of e, not in the base of a power. It is the sum of f(n) over the integers for the function f(x)=e^{-\pi tx^2} of The Fourier transform and the Gaussian.

Its values show two regimes. For large t only n=0,\pm1 matter: \theta(2)=1.0037349 and \theta(4)=1.0000070, both close to 1+2e^{-\pi t}. For small t the Gaussian is wide and many terms contribute: \theta(1)=1.0864348, and \theta(0.01)=10.0000000, where the direct sum needs \abs n up to about 50 before e^{-\pi n^2/100} falls below 10^{-34}. The ten in \theta(0.01)=10 is no accident.

Theorem 4.9

The theta function satisfies \theta(1/t)=\sqrt t\,\theta(t)

[17]
Statement

For every t>0,

\theta\!\left(\frac1t\right)=\sqrt t\,\theta(t).
(4.3)
In plain terms

Playing the sum of Gaussians at speed t is the same, up to a factor \sqrt t, as playing it at speed 1/t. A function that is very sharply peaked on the integers is very flat in frequency, and the symmetry says that the lattice of integers looks the same from both sides.

Why it is needed

This is the one new analytic input of the chapter. Everything else, the continuation to the plane, the functional equation, and the trivial zeros, follows by moving t\mapsto1/t through Riemann’s integral.

Idea

Poisson summation says that a sum over the integers equals the same sum for the Fourier transform. The Fourier transform of a Gaussian of width 1/\sqrt t is a Gaussian of width \sqrt t, and the sum of those is \theta(1/t) up to a constant.

Proof

Apply Theorem 3.20 to f(x)=e^{-\pi tx^2}\in\mathcal S(\RR). The left side is \sum_nf(n)=\theta(t). By Equation (3.5), \hat f(k)=t^{-1/2}e^{-\pi k^2/t}, so the right side is t^{-1/2}\sum_ke^{-\pi k^2/t}=t^{-1/2}\theta(1/t). Hence \theta(t)=t^{-1/2}\theta(1/t), which is Equation (4.3).

Example

At t=4 the identity says \theta(\tfrac14)=2\,\theta(4). Numerically \theta(\tfrac14)=2.0000139 and 2\theta(4)=2.0000139. At t=100 it says \theta(0.01)=10\,\theta(100)=10(1+2e^{-100\pi}), so \theta(0.01) differs from 10 by less than 10^{-135}. The symmetry replaced a sum of fifty terms by a single one.

Used in
  • Riemann’s integral and the functional equation: Riemann’s integral and Theorem 4.12.
  • The bridge to the 2026 proofs, where this step reappears on adeles: The bridge to the proofs.
Aside

In the variable \tau=it, the function \sum e^{\pi in^2\tau} is a modular form of weight \tfrac12 and t\mapsto1/t is the inversion \tau\mapsto-1/\tau restricted to the imaginary axis [15, Chapter 10]. Riemann used only the real symmetry, and that is all we need.

4.5Riemann’s integral#

Let \omega(t)=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\pi n^2t}=\tfrac12(\theta(t)-1), the theta function with the constant term removed. The number \omega(t) is small when t is large, about e^{-\pi t}.

We now build a Mellin transform of \omega and read off the zeta function. This is the model computation of The Mellin transform with Gaussians in place of exponentials. Put

\Phi(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac s2\right)\zeta(s).
Theorem 4.10 For \sigma>1, \Phi(s) is the Mellin transform of \omega at s/2 [18]

For \sigma>1,

\pi^{-s/2}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac s2\right)\zeta(s)=\int_0^\infty\omega(t)\,t^{s/2}\,\frac{\dd t}t.
(4.4)
Proof
  1. The Mellin transform of one Gaussian. By the example in The Mellin transform with a=\pi n^2 and s/2 in place of s, \int_0^\infty e^{-\pi n^2t}t^{s/2}\,\frac{\dd t}t=(\pi n^2)^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)=\pi^{-s/2}n^{-s}\Gamma(s/2).
  2. Sum over n. The sum of absolute values of the terms is \sum_n\pi^{-\sigma/2}n^{-\sigma}\Gamma(\sigma/2), finite exactly when \sigma>1. So sum and integral may be exchanged (Tonelli, then Fubini).
  3. Conclude. Exchanging them gives \int_0^\infty\omega(t)t^{s/2}\frac{\dd t}t=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\sum_nn^{-s}, which is the left side.

Why does the integral hold only for \sigma>1 and what is gained by writing it? A Mellin transform is a sum over scales: the number \omega(t) records how much of the lattice sum lives at scale t, and the weight t^{s/2} asks how much that scale matters. At large t the Gaussians are narrow and almost all vanish, and the contribution is exponentially small for any s. At small t there are many terms, and how fast they grow is what the weight must beat. The same computation with e^{-nx} in place of e^{-\pi n^2t} would give \Gamma(s)\zeta(s)=\int_0^\infty\frac{x^{s-1}}{e^x-1}\,\dd x, which also has a bad end at x=0, but it has no symmetry to exploit there. The Gaussian does, and that is why Riemann used it.

Test it at s=2. The left side is \pi^{-1}\Gamma(1)\zeta(2)=\pi/6=0.5235988, and numerical integration of the right side gives 0.5235988. At s=3 both sides are 0.1913133, and at s=4 both are 0.1096623.

The condition \sigma>1 is no coincidence. Near t=0 the symmetry Equation (4.3) gives \theta(t)\approx t^{-1/2}, so \omega(t)\approx\tfrac12t^{-1/2} and the integrand behaves like \tfrac12t^{(\sigma-3)/2}, which is integrable at 0 exactly when \sigma>1. The integral fails where the Dirichlet series fails. The difficulty has moved from a sum that diverges to an integral that diverges at one end, and at that end we have a tool, the symmetry t\mapsto1/t, which trades the end near 0 for the end near \infty.

4.6The functional equation#

Definition 4.11 the completed zeta function

The completed zeta function is

\xi(s)=\tfrac12\,s(s-1)\,\pi^{-s/2}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac s2\right)\zeta(s)=\tfrac12\,s(s-1)\,\Phi(s).

It is zeta multiplied by three factors: the polynomial \tfrac12s(s-1) cancels the poles at 0 (from \Gamma(s/2)) and 1 (from \zeta); the poles of the Gamma factor at -2,-4,\dots cancel the zeros of \zeta there; and \pi^{-s/2} is the factor that makes the symmetry exact. It is not \zeta, and what makes it better is that it is entire and symmetric. Its zeros are exactly the nontrivial zeros of \zeta, as Theorem 4.14 shows.

Theorem 4.12

\zeta continues to the whole plane, and its completion \xi is entire and symmetric under s\mapsto1-s

[18]
Statement
  1. The function \xi(s) extends to an entire function.
  2. \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) for all s\in\CC.
  3. Consequently \zeta(s)=\dfrac{2\pi^{s/2}\,\xi(s)}{s(s-1)\,\Gamma(s/2)} is meromorphic on \CC. Its only pole is a simple pole at s=1, of residue 1, and \zeta(0)=-\tfrac12.
In plain terms

Zeta, dressed with Gamma and a polynomial, is the same when you swap s and 1-s. Everything the function does on the right half of the plane is mirrored on the left half. The plane has no new corners to explore: knowing zeta for \sigma\ge\tfrac12 means knowing it everywhere.

Why it is needed

Two things need this theorem. The zeros of \zeta will be counted and located, and the symmetry cuts the work in half and makes the line \sigma=\tfrac12 special. And both 2026 proofs begin from generalizations of the theta-function step that produces it (The bridge to the proofs).

Idea

Riemann’s integral is a Mellin transform in t. Cut it at t=1. The piece \int_1^\infty is fine for all s because \omega decays like e^{-\pi t}. The piece \int_0^1 is turned, by t\mapsto1/t and the theta symmetry, into another \int_1^\infty, with s replaced by 1-s, and two elementary terms. Everything is then visibly symmetric.

Proof

Work with \sigma>1 and track each step. The first five steps turn the integral from 0 to 1 into an integral from 1 to \infty and two elementary terms.

Steps
  1. Cut the integral Equation (4.4) at t=1: \Phi(s)=\int_1^\infty\omega(t)t^{s/2}\frac{\dd t}t+\int_0^1\omega(t)t^{s/2}\frac{\dd t}t.
  2. Substitute t=1/u in the second piece: \int_0^1\omega(t)t^{s/2}\frac{\dd t}t=\int_1^\infty\omega(1/u)\,u^{-s/2}\frac{\dd u}u.
  3. Rewrite \omega(1/u) using Equation (4.3) and \theta=1+2\omega: \omega(1/u)=\tfrac12\bigl(\sqrt u\,\theta(u)-1\bigr)=\sqrt u\,\omega(u)+\tfrac12(\sqrt u-1).
  4. Insert it: the second piece becomes \int_1^\infty\omega(u)\,u^{(1-s)/2}\frac{\dd u}u+\tfrac12\int_1^\infty\bigl(u^{(1-s)/2}-u^{-s/2}\bigr)\frac{\dd u}u. The split is allowed because each integral converges on its own: the first because \omega(u) decays like e^{-\pi u} (step 6), the second because \sigma>1.
  5. Evaluate the elementary integral, using \int_1^\infty u^{-a-1}\,\dd u=1/a for \Re a>0 with a=(s-1)/2 and a=s/2: \tfrac12\bigl(\tfrac2{s-1}-\tfrac2s\bigr)=\tfrac1{s-1}-\tfrac1s.

Putting the steps together gives

\Phi(s)=\frac1{s-1}-\frac1s+\int_1^\infty\omega(t)\bigl(t^{s/2}+t^{(1-s)/2}\bigr)\frac{\dd t}t.
(4.5)
Steps
  1. The integral in Equation (4.5) is an entire function of s. For t\ge1, n^2\ge n gives \omega(t)\le\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\pi nt}=\frac{e^{-\pi t}}{1-e^{-\pi t}}\le1.05\,e^{-\pi t}. On a compact set of s with \abs\sigma\le R we have \abs{t^{s/2}}+\abs{t^{(1-s)/2}}\le2t^{(R+1)/2}, so the integrand is at most 2.1\,t^{(R+1)/2-1}e^{-\pi t}, an integrable function of t on [1,\infty) that does not depend on s. The integrand is continuous and entire in s, so Lemma 3.23 applies.
  2. Hence the right side of Equation (4.5) is meromorphic on \CC, with poles at most at 0 and 1. It agrees with \Phi on \sigma>1, so by Theorem 3.7 it is the continuation of \Phi, and \zeta(s)=\pi^{s/2}\Phi(s)/\Gamma(s/2) continues too.
  3. The right side of Equation (4.5) is unchanged under s\mapsto1-s: the first two terms go to \frac1{-s}-\frac1{1-s}=\frac1{s-1}-\frac1s, and the two terms t^{s/2},t^{(1-s)/2} swap. Hence \Phi(s)=\Phi(1-s).
  4. Multiply by \tfrac12s(s-1). The polynomial is unchanged under s\mapsto1-s because (1-s)(-s)=s(s-1), and it cancels the two poles, since s(s-1)\bigl(\frac1{s-1}-\frac1s\bigr)=s-(s-1)=1. So \xi(s)=\tfrac12+\tfrac12s(s-1)\int_1^\infty\omega(t)\bigl(t^{s/2}+t^{(1-s)/2}\bigr)\frac{\dd t}t, which is entire (part 1), and \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) (part 2).
  5. Solve for \zeta: \zeta(s)=2\pi^{s/2}\xi(s)/\bigl(s(s-1)\Gamma(s/2)\bigr). The function 1/\Gamma is entire (The Gamma function), and \xi is entire, so the only possible poles are the zeros of s(s-1).
  6. At s=0: \Gamma(s/2)\sim2/s, so s\,\Gamma(s/2)\to2 and \zeta(0)=\dfrac{2\cdot\xi(0)}{(-1)\cdot2}=-\tfrac12, using \xi(0)=\tfrac12, which is the formula of step 9 at s=0. There is no pole at 0.
  7. At s=1: \zeta(s)\sim\dfrac{2\pi^{1/2}\,\xi(1)}{(s-1)\,\Gamma(1/2)}=\dfrac{2\cdot\frac12\sqrt\pi}{\sqrt\pi\,(s-1)}=\dfrac1{s-1}, a simple pole of residue 1, using \xi(1)=\xi(0)=\tfrac12 and \Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi.
Example

Numerically, \xi(0)=\xi(1)=\tfrac12 and \xi(\tfrac12)=0.4971208. Take s=0.3+2i. Then \xi(s)=0.453449-0.008437i, and \xi(1-s)=\xi(0.7-2i) equals it to twenty digits. The integral formula in step 9 gives the same value of \xi(s), so the continuation agrees with \zeta computed independently. The residue at s=1 is the same 1 found in the strip theorem, as it must be by Theorem 3.7.

Used in
  • Zeros of \zeta in the strip and their symmetry: The symmetry as geometry and The zeros and the hypothesis.
  • The location of the trivial zeros: Theorem 4.14.
  • The explicit formula of The explicit formula: each zero is a wave needs \zeta'/\zeta on the whole plane, which this theorem provides.

Two independent continuations now exist on \sigma>0, one from the alternating series and one from Riemann’s integral, and by Theorem 3.7 they must agree. They do. At s=\tfrac12 the alternating series gave \zeta(\tfrac12)=-1.4603545. The formula of part 3 gives \zeta(\tfrac12)=\dfrac{2\pi^{1/4}\,\xi(\tfrac12)}{\tfrac12\cdot(-\tfrac12)\,\Gamma(\tfrac14)}=\dfrac{2(1.3313354)(0.4971208)}{-0.25\cdot3.6256099}=-1.4603545. Two different calculations, with different convergence regions and different ingredients, produce the same eight digits because there is only one holomorphic function to find.

The functional equation is often quoted in an asymmetric form, with \zeta(s) on one side and \zeta(1-s) on the other. Substituting the definition of \xi into \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) and using the duplication and reflection formulas for \Gamma gives

\zeta(s)=2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{\pi s}2\Bigr)\Gamma(1-s)\,\zeta(1-s),

which is the form in [19, §2.1]. At s=0.3+2i both sides equal 0.385310-0.282528i. We keep the symmetric form \xi(s)=\xi(1-s), which has no Gamma factors to carry.

Symbols
symbol what it is kind where it lives
\eta(s) the alternating series \sum(-1)^{n-1}n^{-s} function holomorphic on \sigma>0
S_N(s) the partial sum \sum_{n\le N}n^{-s} function entire
\gamma_E Euler’s constant 0.5772157\dots real number constant term of \zeta at s=1
\omega(t) \sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\pi n^2t}=\tfrac12(\theta(t)-1) function t>0

\xi(s) \tfrac12s(s-1)\Phi(s) function entire

4.7The symmetry as geometry#

What does \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) look like in the plane? The map s\mapsto1-s takes the point \sigma+it to (1-\sigma)-it. It is the half-turn about the point s=\tfrac12 on the real axis: a rotation by 180^\circ, and not a reflection in a line.

A second symmetry comes from the formula in step 9. The function \omega is real, and \overline{t^{s/2}}=t^{\bar s/2} for real t>0, so \xi(\bar s)=\overline{\xi(s)}. Combining the two,

\xi(1-\bar s)=\xi(\bar s)=\overline{\xi(s)},\qquad\text{so}\qquad\abs{\xi(1-\bar s)}=\abs{\xi(s)}.
(4.6)

The map s\mapsto1-\bar s is the reflection in the vertical line \sigma=\tfrac12: it fixes the line and swaps the sides. So \abs\xi is a mirror-symmetric landscape with the mirror at \sigma=\tfrac12, and a domain coloring of \xi is mirrored in the line with the hues reversed.

On the line itself, 1-\bar s=s. Taking s=\tfrac12+it in \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) gives \xi(\tfrac12+it)=\xi(\tfrac12-it)=\overline{\xi(\tfrac12+it)}, so \xi(\tfrac12+it) is a real number. As a check, \xi(\tfrac12+10i)=0.0379679, with imaginary part zero to 21 decimal places. A real function of one variable t changes sign at each simple zero, and so a sign change between two values of t proves a zero in between. That is how zeros on the line are caught numerically: the first one, at t=14.134725, is where \xi(\tfrac12+it) crosses 0. The symmetry also halves the work: knowing \xi on \sigma\ge\tfrac12 and t\ge0 gives it on the whole plane.

The symmetries also act on zeros. If \rho is a zero of \xi then so are 1-\rho, \bar\rho, and 1-\bar\rho. Off the line these four points are distinct (no zero is real, as The zeros and the hypothesis shows) and a zero comes with three partners. On the line, \bar\rho=1-\rho and the quadruple collapses to a pair, \rho and \bar\rho. The Riemann Hypothesis is the assertion that every quadruple collapses, and it is taken up in The zeros and the hypothesis.

4.8The trivial zeros#

The functional equation settles the zeros of \zeta outside a vertical band.

Definition 4.13 trivial and nontrivial zeros

The trivial zeros of \zeta are the points s=-2,-4,-6,\dots. Every other zero of \zeta is a nontrivial zero. Trivial means that the zero is accounted for by a known factor, here the Gamma function. It does not mean that the zero is uninteresting, only that it carries no arithmetic information.

Theorem 4.14 Outside the closed strip 0\le\sigma\le1, the only zeros of \zeta are the trivial zeros, and they are simple

\zeta(s)=0 for s=-2,-4,-6,\dots, each zero is simple, and \zeta(s)\ne0 for every other s with \sigma>1 or \sigma<0. Hence every nontrivial zero lies in the closed strip 0\le\sigma\le1.

Proof

For \sigma>1 there are no zeros by Theorem 4.3. Now let \sigma<0. By Theorem 4.12, \zeta(s)=2\pi^{s/2}\xi(s)/\bigl(s(s-1)\Gamma(s/2)\bigr) and \xi(s)=\xi(1-s). Write out \xi(1-s)=\tfrac12(1-s)(-s)\,\pi^{-(1-s)/2}\,\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{1-s}2\bigr)\,\zeta(1-s). Here \Re(1-s)>1, so \zeta(1-s)\neq0 by Theorem 4.3, \Gamma\bigl(\tfrac{1-s}2\bigr) is finite because its argument has positive real part and nonzero because \Gamma has no zeros (The Gamma function), and s\ne0,1. So \xi(s)\ne0 on \sigma<0, and the zeros of \zeta(s) there are exactly the zeros of 1/\Gamma(s/2). Those are at s/2=0,-1,-2,\dots, and s=0 is excluded since \sigma<0. Each is a simple zero because \Gamma has a simple pole there (Theorem 3.16).

Test it. The values \zeta(-2)=\zeta(-4)=0, while \zeta(-2.5)=0.0085169 is not zero. The first nontrivial zeros are at heights 14.134725, 21.022040, 25.010858, 30.424876, 32.935062 on the line \sigma=\tfrac12, and \zeta has exactly three zeros with 0<t\le30 (counted by the argument principle, as The zeros and the hypothesis will do). The theorem leaves open what happens inside the strip. The strip is the entire content of the Riemann Hypothesis, and The zeros and the hypothesis will show that no zero sits on \sigma=0 or \sigma=1.

4.9Values at negative integers, and what they do not mean#

The continuation has values at every integer. Some come from the formula by a short calculation.

Example

The value at 0. Step 11 of the proof gave \zeta(0)=-\tfrac12.

The value at -1. Use \xi(-1)=\xi(2)=\tfrac12\cdot2\cdot1\cdot\pi^{-1}\Gamma(1)\zeta(2)=\zeta(2)/\pi=\pi/6, where \zeta(2)=\pi^2/6=1.6449341 is Euler’s value. Then

\zeta(-1)=\frac{2\pi^{-1/2}\,\xi(-1)}{(-1)(-2)\,\Gamma(-\tfrac12)}=\frac{2\pi^{-1/2}\cdot\pi/6}{2\cdot(-2\sqrt\pi)}=-\frac1{12},

using \Gamma(-\tfrac12)=-2\sqrt\pi from Theorem 3.16.

The value at -3. The same computation with \xi(-3)=\xi(4)=\pi^2/15 and \Gamma(-\tfrac32)=\tfrac43\sqrt\pi gives \zeta(-3)=\tfrac1{120}. In general \zeta(1-2k)=-B_{2k}/(2k), with B_{2k} the Bernoulli numbers [9]. Every one of these was checked numerically: \zeta(-1)=-0.0833333, \zeta(-3)=0.0083333, \zeta(-5)=-0.0039683.

A common misreading

“1+2+3+\cdots=-\tfrac1{12}” does not say what it seems to say. What is true is that the unique continuation of \sum n^{-s} takes the value -\tfrac1{12} at s=-1. At s=-1 the series itself is 1+2+3+\cdots, with partial sums N(N+1)/2 that diverge to +\infty. So:

  • It is not a statement that the partial sums approach -\tfrac1{12}, or that the sum is -\tfrac1{12} in the usual sense. The partial sums go to infinity.
  • It is not the Abel sum or the Cesàro sum. Abel summation (the limit of \sum nx^n as x\to1^-) and Cesàro summation both diverge to +\infty here.
  • It is the same kind of statement as 1+2+4+8+\cdots=-1, which is \tfrac1{1-z} at z=2 in Analytic continuation: the value of a function at a point where its defining series diverges.
  • It is forced, by Theorem 3.7: any holomorphic function equal to \sum n^{-s} on \sigma>1 has the value -\tfrac1{12} at -1.
  • It does have a sum-like meaning with a cutoff. With the smooth cutoff e^{-\varepsilon n}, \sum ne^{-\varepsilon n}=1/\varepsilon^2-\tfrac1{12}+O(\varepsilon^2). For \varepsilon=0.1 this is 99.916708 against 100-\tfrac1{12}=99.916667. The divergent part 1/\varepsilon^2 is what the cutoff throws away, and -\tfrac1{12} is the finite part left over.

4.10The bridge to the proofs#

Look back at where the symmetry came from. Not from the Dirichlet series, and not from the Euler product, which sees only the primes. It came from the theta function, a sum over the integers, and from Poisson summation, which says that the integers are their own dual. The Gamma factor \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2) is the price of turning that sum into a Mellin transform, and it plays the role of an Euler factor for a “prime at infinity”.

Both 2026 proofs begin from far-reaching generalizations of exactly this step. Masullo’s proof generalizes the single sum over \ZZ to adelic theta functions, which is Tate’s thesis carried out in families. The proof of Alpoge with Claude generalizes it to theta lifts between totally definite unitary groups. Parts III and IV of this page return to those objects. For now the point is that the function whose zeros encode the primes, and its symmetry, have the same source: a Gaussian sum over a lattice, and its Fourier transform.

Recap

You now have the following, and where each is used.

  • \zeta(s)=\sum n^{-s} is holomorphic on \sigma>1, equals the Euler product there, and has no zeros there (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3): used for the zero-free half-plane in The zeros and the hypothesis.
  • The series fails at \sigma\le1, and the partial sums spiral around \zeta(s) by N^{1-s}/(1-s) (Theorem 4.6).
  • \zeta continues to \sigma>0 with a simple pole of residue 1 at s=1 (Theorem 4.5): the main term in The explicit formula: each zero is a wave.
  • The theta symmetry \theta(1/t)=\sqrt t\,\theta(t) is Poisson summation on a Gaussian (Theorem 4.9).
  • Riemann’s integral and the functional equation: \xi is entire and \xi(s)=\xi(1-s), and \zeta is meromorphic on \CC (Theorem 4.12).
  • The symmetry is a half-turn about \tfrac12; \abs\xi is mirrored in the line \sigma=\tfrac12; \xi is real on it; zeros come in quadruples (The symmetry as geometry).
  • The trivial zeros are at -2,-4,\dots, and all other zeros lie in the closed strip (Theorem 4.14).
  • \zeta(0)=-\tfrac12 and \zeta(-1)=-\tfrac1{12} are values of a continuation and not sums (Values at negative integers, and what they do not mean).

Chapter 5

The zeros and the hypothesis

Locate every zero of zeta to within a strip, see the symmetry that pairs them, count them, and state exactly what the Riemann Hypothesis says about where in the strip they sit.

Builds on 4. Zeta on the whole plane

In plain terms

The function \zeta vanishes at infinitely many points that are not the obvious ones, and all of them lie in a vertical strip of width 1. They come in mirror-image pairs, they get denser as you climb, and the first one sits at height 14.1347\ldots. The Riemann Hypothesis says that every one of them lies exactly on the center line of the strip.

The previous chapters built the machine. \zeta is a function on the whole plane, it has one pole at s=1, it obeys the functional equation \xi(s)=\xi(1-s), and it vanishes at -2,-4,-6,\dots for a reason that the Gamma function explains. What the machine does not yet tell us is where else it vanishes, and that is the question the rest of the page depends on. Chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave will show that each zero is one wave in the count of primes, so the position of the zeros is the position of the waves, and the size of the primes’ fluctuations is decided by how far to the right of the center line a zero can sit. This chapter locates the zeros as far as classical methods can, shows that the center line is the natural place for them, and then states the hypothesis in one sentence.

5.1Where a zero cannot be#

We start with the easiest region, the half plane where the Euler product converges. Chapter Euler's product: primes inside one function showed that for \sigma>1 the product over primes converges to \zeta(s), and the plan is to turn that product into an exponential of a series, because an exponential is never zero. For \sigma>1 and each prime p we have \lvert p^{-s}\rvert = p^{-\sigma}<1, so the Taylor series of the logarithm applies to each factor,

-\log\bigl(1-p^{-s}\bigr) = \sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{p^{-ks}}{k}.

Exponentiating and multiplying over p turns the Euler product into

\zeta(s)=\exp\Bigl(\sum_{p}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{p^{-ks}}{k}\Bigr)\qquad(\sigma>1).
(5.1)

The double series converges absolutely, because its absolute value is at most \sum_p\sum_k p^{-k\sigma}/k\le\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-\sigma}=\zeta(\sigma)<\infty, where the middle inequality holds since every pair (p,k) gives a different integer n=p^k. A convergent exponential is a nonzero complex number, so \zeta(s)\neq0 whenever \sigma>1.

The same argument gives a quantitative statement that we will use again. Taking absolute values in the Euler product and using \lvert 1-p^{-s}\rvert\le 1+p^{-\sigma} gives \lvert\zeta(s)\rvert\ge\prod_p(1+p^{-\sigma})^{-1}, and since (1+p^{-\sigma})^{-1}=(1-p^{-\sigma})/(1-p^{-2\sigma}) the right side telescopes into a ratio of zeta values,

\lvert\zeta(s)\rvert\ \ge\ \frac{\zeta(2\sigma)}{\zeta(\sigma)}\qquad(\sigma>1).

At s=2+14.1347i the bound says \lvert\zeta(s)\rvert\ge\zeta(4)/\zeta(2)=0.6580, and the true value is 0.6908, so the bound is tight when \sigma is as large as 2. It becomes weak as \sigma\to1, because \zeta(\sigma)\to\infty while the true value stays finite. At s=1.1+14.1347i the bound gives 0.1408 against a true value of 0.3771.

Next we transfer the statement to the left half plane, using the functional equation as a mirror. Recall \xi(s)=\tfrac12 s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s), an entire function with \xi(s)=\xi(1-s). For \sigma>1 every factor of \xi is nonzero, because \Gamma has no zeros, s(s-1)\ne0 there, and \zeta(s)\ne0 by the previous paragraph, so \xi has no zero with \sigma>1. If \sigma<0 then 1-s has real part greater than 1, so \xi(s)=\xi(1-s)\ne0 as well. Together these facts say that every zero of \xi has 0\le\sigma\le1. The zeros of \zeta outside that strip are exactly the ones in the factor 1/\Gamma(s/2), namely the trivial zeros at -2,-4,-6,\dots from the previous chapter.

Definition 5.1 Nontrivial zero, critical strip, critical line

A nontrivial zero of \zeta is a zero of the entire function \xi. It is a complex number \rho=\beta+i\gamma at which \zeta(\rho)=0 and which is not one of -2,-4,-6,\dots. The critical strip is the set of s=\sigma+it with 0\le\sigma\le1, and the critical line is the vertical line \sigma=\tfrac12 through its middle. A nontrivial zero is counted with multiplicity, meaning the order m of vanishing, so that \xi(s)=(s-\rho)^m h(s) with h(\rho)\ne0.

Nontrivial is a name and not a claim about difficulty, and the word “zero” here never means a zero of \zeta on the negative real axis. Whether a nontrivial zero can have \beta\ne\tfrac12 is exactly what the Riemann Hypothesis addresses.

5.2The four mirror images of a zero#

Two symmetries of \xi act on the set of zeros, and together they force a four-fold pattern. The first symmetry is the functional equation \xi(s)=\xi(1-s), which reflects the plane in the point s=\tfrac12 and therefore sends \rho=\beta+i\gamma to 1-\rho=(1-\beta)-i\gamma. The second comes from the fact that \zeta(s) is real for real s and is given by series with real coefficients. The Schwarz reflection principle then gives \xi(\bar s)=\overline{\xi(s)}, so \rho is a zero exactly when its conjugate \bar\rho=\beta-i\gamma is, with the same multiplicity. Composing the two gives the third image, 1-\bar\rho=(1-\beta)+i\gamma, which is the reflection of \rho in the critical line.

\rho=\beta+i\gamma,\qquad \bar\rho=\beta-i\gamma,\qquad 1-\rho=(1-\beta)-i\gamma,\qquad 1-\bar\rho=(1-\beta)+i\gamma .
(5.2)

A zero on the critical line is its own reflection in that line, because \beta=\tfrac12 makes 1-\bar\rho=\rho, so there the four images collapse to the two points \tfrac12\pm i\gamma. A hypothetical zero off the line would come with three companions. If \zeta vanished at 0.7+14.1347i, it would also vanish at 0.7-14.1347i, at 0.3+14.1347i, and at 0.3-14.1347i, forming the corners of a rectangle straddling the critical line. This is the first reason the critical line is natural, because it is the only vertical line that the symmetry maps to itself. If a zero is on that line, it needs no partner to the left or right.

One more fact about zeros fixes where the pairs sit vertically. For real \sigma between 0 and 1 the alternating series from chapter Zeta on the whole plane shows that (1-2^{1-\sigma})\zeta(\sigma)=\eta(\sigma)>0, while 1-2^{1-\sigma}<0 on that interval, so \zeta(\sigma)<0 there. For instance \zeta(\tfrac12)=-1.4603545\ldots. Hence no zero has \gamma=0, every nontrivial zero comes with a conjugate on the other side of the real axis, and it suffices to list the zeros with \gamma>0 in increasing order.

5.3The first ten zeros#

Before saying anything about all zeros it helps to hold a few of them. The ten smallest ordinates, computed to six decimals with the arbitrary-precision zero finder in mpmath, are listed below together with the gap to the previous one.

n \gamma_n gap
1 14.134725
2 21.022040 6.887315
3 25.010858 3.988818
4 30.424876 5.414018
5 32.935062 2.510186
6 37.586178 4.651116
7 40.918719 3.332541
8 43.327073 2.408354
9 48.005151 4.678078
10 49.773832 1.768681

The average gap over these ten zeros is (49.7738-14.1347)/9=3.96, and we will see in a moment that the expected spacing near height 30 is 2\pi/\log(30/2\pi)=4.02, so the numbers are typical of what the theory predicts. The gaps are far from regular, ranging from 1.77 to 6.89 in the table, and the first zero is the lowest of all, so the strip is free of zeros below height 14.13. In the language of the previous section, these are the points \tfrac12\pm i\gamma_n.

Why a zero on the line is one real equation, not two#

To find a zero of an arbitrary complex function at a point s one has to solve two real equations, \Re\zeta=0 and \Im\zeta=0, in two unknowns \sigma and t, and that is a codimension two coincidence that gives no help from the intermediate value theorem. On the critical line the situation is much better, and the reason is the symmetry of the previous section. For real t the functional equation gives \xi(\tfrac12+it)=\xi(\tfrac12-it) and the reflection principle gives \xi(\tfrac12-it)=\overline{\xi(\tfrac12+it)}, so \xi(\tfrac12+it) equals its own conjugate and is a real number. Since \zeta(s) is \xi(s) times the factor 2\pi^{s/2}/(s(s-1)\Gamma(s/2)), which has no zero or pole on the critical line, the value \zeta(\tfrac12+it) is a real number times a unit complex number that rotates slowly with t. The rotation is recorded by the Riemann-Siegel theta function, a real phase that has nothing to do with Jacobi’s theta function \theta(t) of chapter Zeta on the whole plane or with Chebyshev’s function \vartheta(x) of chapter Counting primes, so we give it its own subscript,

\theta_{\mathrm{RS}}(t)=\Im\log\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac14+\tfrac{it}{2}\bigr)-\tfrac{t}{2}\log\pi ,
(5.3)

and the real function that remains after undoing the rotation is the Hardy function Z(t)=e^{i\theta_{\mathrm{RS}}(t)}\zeta(\tfrac12+it).

Definition 5.2 Hardy’s Z function

Z(t)=e^{i\theta_{\mathrm{RS}}(t)}\zeta(\tfrac12+it) for real t is a real-valued function of one real variable with \lvert Z(t)\rvert=\lvert\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\rvert. It is a rotated copy of \zeta along the critical line, not a new function with different zeros, and its zeros are exactly the ordinates of the nontrivial zeros of \zeta that lie on the critical line.

A sign change of Z forces a zero by the intermediate value theorem, and this is how zeros on the line are certified. At t=14.0 we get Z(14.0)=-0.1056 and at t=14.3 we get Z(14.3)=+0.1328, so there is a zero in between, and it is the first one at 14.134725. Likewise Z(20.9)=+0.1395 and Z(21.2)=-0.2000 bracket the second zero at 21.022040. The picture to keep in mind is the path t\mapsto\zeta(\tfrac12+it) in the plane. Because the value is always a real multiple of a rotating unit vector, the path passes through the origin exactly at the zeros on the critical line, and at a simple zero it passes straight through, because Z changes sign there.

5.4How many zeros are there below height T?#

We want to know how fast the zeros accumulate, because the formula of chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave sums a wave for every one of them, and whether that sum behaves depends on how many there are. Riemann stated the answer without proof in 1859 and von Mangoldt proved it in 1905. Here N(T) is the number of nontrivial zeros \rho with 0<\gamma\le T, counted with multiplicity.

Theorem 5.3

The number of zeros up to height T is about \frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}-\frac{T}{2\pi}

[20]
Statement

For T\ge2 not equal to the ordinate of a zero,

N(T)=\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{RS}}(T)}{\pi}+1+E_N(T),\qquad E_N(T)=\frac1\pi\arg\zeta\bigl(\tfrac12+iT\bigr)=O(\log T),
(5.4)

where \arg\zeta(\tfrac12+iT) is defined by continuous change of argument along the path from 2 to 2+iT to \tfrac12+iT. Most texts write S(T) for the remainder E_N(T); this page keeps the letter S for the smoothed sum of chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations. Since \theta_{\mathrm{RS}}(T)=\tfrac T2\log\tfrac T{2\pi}-\tfrac T2-\tfrac\pi8+O(1/T), this gives

N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}-\frac{T}{2\pi}+O(\log T).
(5.5)
In plain terms

Up to height T there are about \frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi} zeros, a little fewer once the correction -\frac{T}{2\pi} is applied, and the true count never strays from that smooth curve by more than a constant times \log T. The zeros therefore get denser as you climb, with an average gap of 2\pi/\log(T/2\pi) near height T.

Why it is needed

Chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave adds a wave for each zero, and it needs to know that the sum of 1/\lvert\rho\rvert over zeros up to T grows only like \log^2T. That fact follows from this count by partial summation, and it is the reason the explicit formula can be truncated and controlled.

Idea

The argument principle says that N equals the winding number of \xi around a large rectangle. The symmetries of the previous section make the four quarters of the boundary contribute equally, and on the one quarter that matters the change in the argument of \xi is dominated by the argument of the Gamma factor, which Stirling’s formula evaluates. What remains is the argument of \zeta itself, which is small because \zeta cannot wind around the origin many times on a segment where it has few zeros of its real part.

Proof sketch

[20]

Apply the argument principle from chapter The complex analysis we need to \xi on the rectangle with corners 2\pm iT and -1\pm iT, which contains exactly the nontrivial zeros with \lvert\gamma\rvert<T. By \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) and \xi(\bar s)=\overline{\xi(s)} the change of \arg\xi along each of the four quarters of the boundary is the same, so 2N(T)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot4\Delta, that is N(T)=\Delta/\pi, where \Delta is the change of \arg\xi along the path 2\to2+iT\to\tfrac12+iT. Write \xi(s)=\tfrac12 s(s-1)\cdot\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\cdot\zeta(s) and add the three changes. The factor s(s-1) turns from the positive number 2 to the negative number -(\tfrac14+T^2) and so contributes \pi, which is the “+1” in the theorem. The middle factor contributes exactly \theta_{\mathrm{RS}}(T), because it starts at the positive number \pi^{-1}\Gamma(1) at s=2 and its argument at s=\tfrac12+iT is \Im\log\Gamma(\tfrac14+\tfrac{iT}2)-\tfrac T2\log\pi. For the last factor, \arg\zeta is bounded on 2\to2+iT because \zeta is close to 1 there, and on the horizontal segment from 2+iT to \tfrac12+iT one shows that the change of \arg\zeta is O(\log T) by bounding the number of zeros of \Re\zeta(\sigma+iT) with a Jensen-type estimate. The expansion of \theta_{\mathrm{RS}} is Stirling’s formula for \Gamma(\tfrac14+\tfrac{iT}2). The full argument is in Davenport [6] and Titchmarsh [19], and Edwards [9] follows von Mangoldt’s original route.

Example

The formula can be tested against exact counts, which mpmath produces by evaluating the argument principle numerically. The columns give the true count N(T), the smooth part \frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac T{2\pi}-\frac T{2\pi}, and the exact main term \theta_{\mathrm{RS}}(T)/\pi+1 of Equation (5.4), whose difference from N(T) is E_N(T).

T N(T) \frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac T{2\pi}-\frac T{2\pi} \theta_{\mathrm{RS}}(T)/\pi+1 E_N(T)
20 1 0.502 1.378 -0.378
50 10 8.548 9.423 +0.577
100 29 28.127 29.002 -0.002
200 79 78.318 79.193 -0.193
500 269 268.712 269.587 -0.587
1000 649 647.741 648.616 +0.384

The exact main term exceeds the smooth part by 0.875 in every row, which is the constant \tfrac78 in the refinement N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}+\tfrac78+E_N(T)+O(1/T). After that constant is added the remaining error is E_N(T), which stays between -0.6 and +0.6 in the table, much smaller than the bound O(\log T) would allow. At T=1000 the average gap is 2\pi/\log(1000/2\pi)=1.24.

Used in

Chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave uses this count to bound the sum of 1/\lvert\rho\rvert and to control the truncation of the explicit formula, and chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations uses it to turn the explicit formula into the bound \psi(x)=x+O(\sqrt x\log^2x).

5.5The zeros determine the function#

A polynomial is determined, up to a constant, by its zeros, and the Hadamard product says that the same holds for \xi even though it has infinitely many. We want this statement because it makes the zeros the complete description of the function, so that facts about \zeta can be turned into facts about its zeros, which is exactly what the explicit formula does. The theorem uses the fact that \xi is entire of order 1, which means \lvert\xi(s)\rvert\le\exp(C\lvert s\rvert\log\lvert s\rvert), and that fact comes from Stirling’s estimate for \Gamma.

Theorem 5.4

The function \xi is the product of its zeros

[21]
Statement

With the nontrivial zeros \rho listed with multiplicity,

\xi(s)=\xi(0)\prod_{\rho}\Bigl(1-\frac{s}{\rho}\Bigr),\qquad \xi(0)=\tfrac12 ,
(5.6)

where the product is taken in pairs of zeros \rho,\,1-\rho (or in the order of increasing \lvert\gamma\rvert), and then converges for every s.

In plain terms

Knowing the location of every nontrivial zero is enough to rebuild \xi exactly, and hence \zeta, because the only constant needed is the value \tfrac12 at the origin. The function carries no information beyond its zeros.

Why it is needed

The explicit formula is obtained by taking the logarithmic derivative of \zeta, and Hadamard’s product turns that logarithmic derivative into a sum over zeros, which is how the zeros enter the count of primes.

Idea

An entire function of order 1 differs from the product over its zeros only by a factor e^{A+Bs}, and the functional equation \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) forces the linear term to cancel when zeros are grouped in the pairs \rho,\,1-\rho, leaving the constant \xi(0).

Proof sketch

[21]

Hadamard’s factorization theorem for entire functions of order 1 gives \xi(s)=e^{A+Bs}\prod_\rho(1-s/\rho)e^{s/\rho} with \sum_\rho\lvert\rho\rvert^{-1-\varepsilon}<\infty for each \varepsilon>0. Setting s=0 gives e^{A}=\xi(0)=\tfrac12. The symmetry of \xi then shows that B=-\sum_\rho\Re(1/\rho)=-\sum_\rho 1/\rho with the zeros paired as \rho,\bar\rho so that the imaginary parts cancel, and hence the exponential factors e^{Bs}\prod_\rho e^{s/\rho} multiply to 1, which leaves the product in Equation (5.6). The details are in Davenport [6] and Edwards [9].

Example

Two numerical tests of the product. First, take logarithmic derivatives of Equation (5.6) at s=0 to get \xi'(0)/\xi(0)=-\sum_\rho 1/\rho. The functional equation gives \xi'(0)/\xi(0)=-\xi'(1)/\xi(1), and from the definition of \xi one computes \xi'(1)/\xi(1)=1+\gamma_E+\tfrac12\bigl(\tfrac{\Gamma'}{\Gamma}(\tfrac12)\bigr)-\tfrac12\log\pi. Here the logarithmic derivative of \xi is \frac1s+\frac1{s-1}-\frac12\log\pi+\frac12\frac{\Gamma'}{\Gamma}(\frac s2)+\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s); at s=1 the term \frac1s gives the 1, and \frac1{s-1}+\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)\to\gamma_E, where \gamma_E=0.5772\ldots is Euler’s constant, the constant term of the Laurent series \zeta(s)=\frac1{s-1}+\gamma_E+\cdots at the pole. Finally \Gamma'(\tfrac12)/\Gamma(\tfrac12)=-\gamma_E-2\log2. Therefore

\sum_\rho\frac1\rho=1+\frac{\gamma_E}{2}-\frac12\log(4\pi)=0.0230957\ldots ,
(5.7)

where the sum is over all nontrivial zeros, paired. A pair \tfrac12\pm i\gamma contributes \frac{1}{1/2+i\gamma}+\frac1{1/2-i\gamma}=\frac{1}{1/4+\gamma^2}, so for zeros on the line the total is \sum_{\gamma>0}1/(\tfrac14+\gamma^2). The ten zeros of the table above contribute 0.01354, which is 58.6% of the total, the first 100 zeros give 0.01998 (86.5%), and the first 1000 zeros, which reach height 1419.42, give 0.02238 (96.9%). The convergence is slow because the tail beyond height T is about (\log(T/2\pi)+1)/(2\pi T), which is 0.0007 at T=1419 and brings the partial sum to 0.0231. Second, at s=2 the definition gives \xi(2)=\zeta(2)/\pi=\pi/6=0.52360, while the pairs \tfrac12\pm i\gamma_n give factors 1+2/(\tfrac14+\gamma_n^2) in Equation (5.6), and \tfrac12\prod_{n\le N}\bigl(1+2/(\tfrac14+\gamma_n^2)\bigr) equals 0.51368 for N=10, 0.52035 for N=100, and 0.52285 for N=1000, which is within 0.15\% of \pi/6. The product rebuilds a value of \xi that was never used as an input.

Used in

Chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave differentiates this product to write \zeta'/\zeta as a sum over zeros. Chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations uses the number 0.0462=2\sum_\rho\Re(1/\rho) to state the smoothed explicit formula with an explicit constant.

5.6No zeros on the line \sigma=1#

Everything so far leaves open whether a zero could sit on the boundary of the strip, at \sigma=1 or \sigma=0, and this is the first place where a real argument is needed, since the Euler product no longer converges there. The statement matters because it is the input that proves the prime number theorem, as Hadamard [5] and de la Vallée Poussin [7] showed independently in 1896, and the argument below is the standard textbook one. It uses a trick of positivity. The Euler product tells us about \log\lvert\zeta\rvert as a sum with cosines, and a particular nonnegative combination of three cosines beats a hypothetical zero.

Theorem 5.5

\zeta has no zero on the line \sigma=1

[7]
Statement

\zeta(1+it)\ne0 for every real t\ne0, and consequently \xi has no zero on the lines \sigma=1 and \sigma=0, so every nontrivial zero lies in the open strip 0<\beta<1.

In plain terms

Zeta cannot vanish on the right edge of the critical strip. The proof shows that if it did, three sizes that the Euler product ties together would multiply to something smaller than 1, which they are forbidden to do.

Why it is needed

Without this theorem the zeros could lie on the boundary of the strip, and the explicit formula would then contain a term as large as x itself, destroying the asymptotic \psi(x)\sim x. The prime number theorem is exactly the statement that no such term exists.

Idea

The Euler product writes \log\lvert\zeta(\sigma+it)\rvert as \sum_{p,k}\frac{p^{-k\sigma}}{k}\cos(kt\log p). A zero on \sigma=1 would make this very negative as \sigma\downarrow1, while at t=0 the pole makes it very positive. The weights 3,4,1 are chosen so that the combination of cosines is never negative, which forbids a zero at 1+it because 4 times the zero’s order of vanishing would outweigh the pole of order 3 by 4-3=1.

Proof

Fix \sigma>1 and real t. Taking the real part of the exponent in Equation (5.1) gives

\log\lvert\zeta(\sigma+it)\rvert=\sum_p\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{p^{-k\sigma}}{k}\cos\bigl(kt\log p\bigr),

because p^{-ks}=p^{-k\sigma}e^{-ikt\log p} has real part p^{-k\sigma}\cos(kt\log p). Write \theta=kt\log p. The trigonometric identity \cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1 gives

3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta=2+4\cos\theta+2\cos^2\theta=2(1+\cos\theta)^2\ \ge\ 0.
(5.8)

Form the combination 3\log\zeta(\sigma)+4\log\lvert\zeta(\sigma+it)\rvert+\log\lvert\zeta(\sigma+2it)\rvert of the three sums with t replaced by 0, t, and 2t. The cosine arguments are 0, \theta, and 2\theta, so the combination equals

\sum_p\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{p^{-k\sigma}}{k}\bigl(3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta\bigr)\ \ge\ 0 ,

and exponentiating gives the inequality

\zeta(\sigma)^3\,\lvert\zeta(\sigma+it)\rvert^4\,\lvert\zeta(\sigma+2it)\rvert\ \ge\ 1\qquad(\sigma>1,\ t\in\RR).
(5.9)

Now suppose \zeta(1+it_0)=0 for some real t_0\neq0, and let \sigma\downarrow1 with t=t_0. The factor \zeta(\sigma)\sim1/(\sigma-1) has a simple pole, so \zeta(\sigma)^3 is of size (\sigma-1)^{-3}. Since \zeta is differentiable at 1+it_0 and vanishes there, \lvert\zeta(\sigma+it_0)\rvert\le C(\sigma-1) for some constant C and \sigma near 1, so the fourth power is of size at most (\sigma-1)^4. The remaining factor \lvert\zeta(\sigma+2it_0)\rvert stays bounded, because 2t_0\ne0 and \zeta is analytic at 1+2it_0. The left side of Equation (5.9) is therefore at most a constant times (\sigma-1)^{-3+4}=(\sigma-1), which tends to 0 and contradicts being at least 1. Hence \zeta(1+it_0)\ne0.

For the left edge, \xi(it)=\xi(1-it)=\xi(1+(-t)i) and \xi(1+iu)\neq0 for u\ne0 by what we just proved together with the nonvanishing of the factors of \xi away from s=0,1, while \xi(0)=\xi(1)=\tfrac12\ne0. So there are no zeros of \xi on \sigma=0 or \sigma=1.

Example

Take \sigma=1.1 and t=14.134725, the height of the first zero. Then \zeta(\sigma)^3\lvert\zeta(\sigma+it)\rvert^4\lvert\zeta(\sigma+2it)\rvert=44.35, comfortably above 1. Moving \sigma toward 1 at the same t gives 2.38\times10^4 at \sigma=1.01 and 2.22\times10^7 at \sigma=1.001, so the left side blows up like (\sigma-1)^{-3} because \zeta(1+14.13i) is not zero. A hypothetical zero would have made it shrink instead. Other points confirm that the bound holds with room to spare. At \sigma=2 and t=0.5 the value is 27.19, at \sigma=1.1 and t=1 it is 1485.6, and at \sigma=1.01 and t=3 it is 156{,}187. The polynomial in Equation (5.8) vanishes only at \theta=\pi modulo 2\pi, so a term of the double series is zero only for a prime power p^k with kt\log p an odd multiple of \pi, and no choice of t can arrange this for every prime at once.

Used in

This theorem puts the zeros strictly inside the strip, so in the explicit formula of chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave every zero term has size at most x^{\beta} with \beta<1, and chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations measures how much smaller than x the zero terms can be.

5.7The statement of the hypothesis#

We have now fenced the zeros in. They lie in the open strip 0<\sigma<1, they come in symmetric sets of two or four, they are denser and denser as one climbs, and everything we computed lies on one vertical line, the line that the symmetry maps to itself. Riemann wrote in 1859 that it is very probable that all the roots of \xi are real in his variable t, which in our variable s=\tfrac12+it says the same thing, and that he had not proved this after a few brief attempts because it was not needed for his immediate aim [18]. The statement has carried his name ever since, and the 2026 proofs are the subject of Parts III and IV of this page.

Theorem 5.6

Every nontrivial zero of \zeta has real part \tfrac12

[18]
Statement

Let \rho=\beta+i\gamma be a nontrivial zero of \zeta. Then \beta=\tfrac12. Equivalently, every zero of \xi lies on the critical line, and the supremum \Theta of the real parts of the nontrivial zeros equals \tfrac12.

In plain terms

All the interesting zeros of the zeta function sit on one straight line, the center of the critical strip. The statement is Riemann’s guess of 1859, and the proofs that make it a theorem are the subject of Parts III and IV.

Why it is needed

The real part of a zero sets the size of the wave it contributes to the count of primes, as chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave shows, so the hypothesis is the statement that primes fluctuate as little as the functional equation allows. Everything in Parts II to V is organized around what this one sentence means and how it is proved.

Idea

The symmetries of this chapter permit a zero at \beta+i\gamma only together with 1-\beta+i\gamma, so \beta=\tfrac12 is the single position that needs no partner. The theorem says that every zero takes that position, and that the four-fold orbits of the symmetry never occur.

Proof sketch

[1]

This chapter does not prove the statement. Its proofs are the subject of Parts III and IV, which follow two routes that both pass through Weil’s explicit formula, introduced in chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion. Part III follows Masullo [1], who proves the hypothesis for the L-functions of all unitary Hecke characters of all number fields, of which \zeta is the simplest. Part IV follows Alpoge with Claude [2; 3], who prove it for \zeta and for the Dirichlet L-functions of chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations. What this chapter does show is that the zeros lie in the open strip, that the symmetries pair them, and that their number below height T is given by Equation (5.5).

Used in

Chapters The explicit formula: each zero is a wave and What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations read the statement as a bound on how far the prime counts can stray from their smooth estimates. Chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion rewrites it as a positivity statement about primes.

The rest of this chapter records what was known about the hypothesis before 2026, because that record shows what the proofs had to be consistent with. Hardy proved in 1914 that infinitely many zeros lie on the critical line [22], by showing that Z(t) changes sign somewhere beyond every height. Selberg showed in 1942 that a positive proportion of zeros lie on the line, Levinson showed in 1974 that more than a third do, and Conrey showed in 1989 that at least two fifths do. On the computational side, Platt and Trudgian verified in 2021 that every zero with 0<\gamma\le3\cdot10^{12} lies on the line, by a rigorous computation of the kind described in the section on Hardy’s function, which compares the number of sign changes with the count N(T) [23]. A zero off the line would have appeared as a four-fold set of counterexamples, and none was ever found.

A common misreading

The count N(T) in Equation (5.5) counts all nontrivial zeros, on the line or not, so it cannot by itself rule out a zero off the line. The numerical verifications work by showing that the number of sign changes of Z on [0,T] equals N(T), and the equality leaves no room for any other zero. That certifies a finite range, which is why the record stops at a height while the statement does not.

Recap

The reader now has the following.

  • Zeta has no zero with \sigma>1, by writing it as an exponential, and no zero with \sigma<0 except the trivial ones, by the functional equation. Together with the 3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta argument for \sigma=1, this puts every nontrivial zero in the open strip 0<\sigma<1.
  • The zero set is symmetric under \rho\mapsto\bar\rho and \rho\mapsto1-\rho, so zeros come in pairs on the critical line and in quadruples off it. On the critical line a zero is one real equation for the real function Z(t).
