  • The first ten zeros begin at 14.134725, and N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac T{2\pi}-\frac{T}{2\pi}+O(\log T), with average gap 2\pi/\log(T/2\pi).
  • The product \xi(s)=\tfrac12\prod_\rho(1-s/\rho) says the zeros determine the function, and the number \sum_\rho1/\rho=0.0230957\ldots is an exact check of it.
  • The Riemann Hypothesis, \beta=\tfrac12 for every nontrivial zero.

Chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave uses the Hadamard product and the count N(T) to show how each zero becomes a wave in the staircase of the primes.

Previous4. Zeta on the whole planeNext6. The explicit formula: each zero is a wave

Chapter 6

The explicit formula: each zero is a wave

Derive von Mangoldt’s exact formula for the prime-power staircase \psi(x), and read each pair of zeros of zeta as one wave in \log x.

Builds on 5. The zeros and the hypothesis

In plain terms

The count of primes can be written exactly as a smooth main term plus a sum with one term for every zero of the zeta function. Each pair of zeros contributes a single wave, whose speed is the height of the zero and whose size grows like a power of x set by the zero’s real part. Adding the waves one pair at a time turns a smooth line into the jagged staircase of the primes.

Chapter The zeros and the hypothesis located the zeros, and chapter Counting primes set the question, which is how far the staircase \psi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n) strays from the line y=x. This chapter connects the two. The tool is a short chain of ideas. A contour integral can act as a switch that turns terms of a Dirichlet series on and off, the series -\zeta'/\zeta(s)=\sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-s} from chapter Euler's product: primes inside one function has the primes built into its coefficients, and moving the integration contour to the left collects the poles of \zeta'/\zeta, which are the zeros. The result, von Mangoldt’s explicit formula, is the hinge between the arithmetic of primes and the analysis of zeros, and every later result on this page, including both proofs, is an application of some version of it.

6.1The goal: an exact formula for \psi#

We want an identity, not an estimate. Chapter Counting primes introduced \psi(x) as the sum of \Lambda(n) over n\le x, which jumps by \log p at each prime power p^k and is flat in between. For instance \psi(7)=\log2+\log3+\log2+\log5+\log7=6.0403 counts the prime powers 2,3,4,5,7, and at x=8 it jumps by \log2 to \psi(8)=6.7334. The staircase is discontinuous, and a formula built out of waves is continuous at every finite stage, so exact agreement at a jump is impossible and the natural statement is that the formula takes the midpoint of the jump.

Definition 6.1 The midpoint value of the staircase

For x>1 let \psi_0(x) be \psi(x) when x is not a prime power, and \psi(x)-\tfrac12\Lambda(x) when x is a prime power, so that \psi_0(x)=\tfrac12\bigl(\psi(x^-)+\psi(x^+)\bigr). It is the same staircase with the value at each jump replaced by the midpoint of the jump, not a different function, and it agrees with \psi at every x that is not a prime power.

At x=8 the left limit is \psi(8^-)=6.0403 and the right value is \psi(8)=6.7334, so \psi_0(8)=6.3868. At x=10, which is not a prime power, \psi_0(10)=\psi(10)=7.8320. These two numbers will be our test cases.

6.2Perron’s switch#

The Dirichlet series \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-s} knows about every prime power, but it does not know about the cutoff n\le x, and we need a device that reads off the partial sums. The device is the following integral, which takes the value 1 when its parameter y is larger than 1 and the value 0 when y is smaller. Applied to y=x/n it equals 1 exactly when n<x.

Definition 6.2 The Perron switch

For c>0, y>0, and T>0 define

I_T(y)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{c-iT}^{c+iT}\frac{y^s}{s}\,\dd s ,
(6.1)

the integral along the vertical segment \Re s=c from height -T to height T. It is a smooth function of y that, as T\to\infty, approaches the step function that is 1 for y>1, \tfrac12 for y=1, and 0 for 0<y<1. It is not itself a step function for any finite T, and its limit does not depend on c.

The idea

The integrand y^s/s is analytic except for a simple pole at s=0 with residue 1. If y>1 then \lvert y^s\rvert=y^{\sigma} decays as \sigma\to-\infty, so we can push the contour far to the left and pick up the residue 1 from the pole at 0. If y<1 then y^\sigma decays as \sigma\to+\infty, so the contour can be pushed to the right, where it meets no pole and the integral is 0. The switch is the statement that the pole at s=0 is on the left of the contour, and y decides which way the integral can be closed.

Lemma 6.3

The truncated Perron integral is within y^c/(\pi T\lvert\log y\rvert) of the step function

[6]
Statement

For c>0, T>0, and y>0 with y\ne1,

\Bigl\lvert I_T(y)-\mathbf 1_{y>1}\Bigr\rvert\le\frac{y^c}{\pi T\lvert\log y\rvert},
(6.2)

and I_T(1)=\frac1\pi\arctan(T/c)\to\tfrac12 as T\to\infty.

In plain terms

The sharp edge of a step function can be produced by integrating y^s/s along a long vertical line, and the error shrinks like 1/T except right next to the step, where y is close to 1.

Why it is needed

Sums with the cutoff n\le x are what we want, and Dirichlet series have no cutoff. The switch converts one into the other, and the bound says how long a segment is needed to simulate it, which later becomes the error term of the explicit formula.

Idea

Close the segment into a rectangle in the direction where y^\sigma decays, and bound the two horizontal sides, whose integrand is small because \lvert1/s\rvert\le1/T there.

Proof

Suppose first y>1. Take the rectangle with corners c\pm iT and -U\pm iT for a large number U>0. The only pole inside is s=0 with residue y^0=1, so the integral over the full boundary is 2\pi i. On the two horizontal sides \lvert y^s/s\rvert\le y^\sigma/T, and \int_{-U}^{c}y^\sigma\,\dd\sigma\le y^c/\log y, so those sides together contribute at most \frac1{2\pi}\cdot2\cdot\frac{y^c}{T\log y}=\frac{y^c}{\pi T\log y}. On the left side \lvert s\rvert\ge U and \lvert y^s\rvert=y^{-U}, so that side contributes at most \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot2T\cdot y^{-U}/U, which tends to 0 as U\to\infty because y>1. Letting U\to\infty gives \lvert I_T(y)-1\rvert\le y^c/(\pi T\log y).

If 0<y<1 close the rectangle to the right instead, with corners c\pm iT and U\pm iT. There is no pole inside, so the full boundary integral is 0, the horizontal sides contribute at most \frac1{2\pi}\cdot2\cdot\frac{y^c}{T\lvert\log y\rvert} because \int_c^Uy^\sigma\,\dd\sigma\le y^c/\lvert\log y\rvert, and the right side tends to 0 as U\to\infty since y^U\to0. Hence \lvert I_T(y)\rvert\le y^c/(\pi T\lvert\log y\rvert). For y=1 the integrand is 1/s, and \frac1{2\pi i}\int_{-T}^{T}\frac{i\,\dd t}{c+it}=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-T}^T\frac{c\,\dd t}{c^2+t^2}=\frac1\pi\arctan\frac Tc, since the odd part cancels.

Example

Take c=1. For y=2 the true value of the switch is 1, and numerical integration gives I_{10}(2)=0.9261 and I_{100}(2)=0.9910, with errors 0.074 and 0.009 against the bounds 0.092 and 0.0092 from Equation (6.2). For y=\tfrac12 the true value is 0, and the integrals are 0.0201 at T=10 and 0.00226 at T=100, against the bounds 0.0230 and 0.00230. At y=1 the integral at T=100 is 0.49682, which equals \frac1\pi\arctan(100) and approaches \tfrac12.

Used in

Section Applying the switch to the primes applies the switch to every term \Lambda(n)(x/n)^s of the series for -\zeta'/\zeta, and chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations applies a version with kernel 1/(s(s-1)) in which the integral converges absolutely.

6.3Applying the switch to the primes#

We now have a way to turn the cutoff n\le x into an integral, and the series that knows the primes is -\zeta'/\zeta(s)=\sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-s}, which converges absolutely for \sigma>1. Choose c>1; any such c gives the identity below, and for the error estimate we take c=1+1/\log x, so that x^c=e\,x stays of size x. For each n we apply the switch with y=x/n, which is greater than 1 exactly when n<x, and the identity (x/n)^s=x^sn^{-s} lets us sum over n after the integral. Writing \mathbf 1_{n\le x} for the indicator of the cutoff, and treating n=x as the midpoint case,

\psi_0(x)=\sum_n\Lambda(n)\,\mathbf 1_{n\le x}\ \approx\ \sum_n\Lambda(n)\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{c-iT}^{c+iT}\Bigl(\frac xn\Bigr)^s\frac{\dd s}{s}=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{c-iT}^{c+iT}\Bigl(-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)\Bigr)\frac{x^s}{s}\,\dd s .
(6.3)

The sum and integral can be exchanged because on the line \sigma=c the sum \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-c}=-\zeta'/\zeta(c) converges absolutely and the segment has finite length. Combined with Equation (6.2), the difference between the two sides of Equation (6.3) is at most \sum_n\Lambda(n)(x/n)^c\min\bigl(1,\tfrac1{\pi T\lvert\log(x/n)\rvert}\bigr), which with c=1+1/\log x is of size O(x\log^2x/T+\log x) for large T, the last term coming from the prime powers closest to x (this estimate is carried out in Davenport [6]). So \psi_0(x) is the limit as T\to\infty of the integral on the right. The integral now involves only the function \zeta'/\zeta and the kernel x^s/s, which means that all arithmetic information about the primes sits in the poles and growth of \zeta'/\zeta.

6.4Moving the contour left#

An integral over a vertical line equals the sum of residues of everything between that line and another one, plus the integral over the new line, and the plan is to drag the line to the left as far as it will go. Fix x>1, take a large T that is not an ordinate of a zero, and take a large odd number U so that the line \sigma=-U avoids the trivial zeros. The rectangle with corners c\pm iT and -U\pm iT contains the singularities of the integrand F(s)=-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)\frac{x^s}{s}. The residues are the following, and they rest on the fact that \zeta'/\zeta has a simple pole with residue m at each zero of multiplicity m, a simple pole with residue -1 at s=1, and no other poles, so that -\zeta'/\zeta has residue -m at each zero and +1 at s=1.

Steps
  1. At s=1 the function -\zeta'/\zeta has a simple pole with residue +1, because \zeta(s)\sim1/(s-1) gives \zeta'/\zeta\sim-1/(s-1), so the residue of F is x^1/1=x.
  2. At each nontrivial zero \rho of multiplicity m the function -\zeta'/\zeta has residue -m, so F contributes -m\,x^\rho/\rho. Counting zeros with multiplicity, this is one term -x^\rho/\rho for every zero.
  3. At s=0 the factor 1/s has a pole. Since \zeta(0)=-\tfrac12 and \zeta'(0)=-\tfrac12\log2\pi, the value -\zeta'(0)/\zeta(0)=-\log2\pi is finite, so the residue of F is -\log2\pi.
  4. At each trivial zero s=-2k with k\ge1 the function -\zeta'/\zeta has residue -1, so F contributes -x^{-2k}/(-2k)=+x^{-2k}/(2k), and summing over k gives \sum_{k\ge1}\frac{x^{-2k}}{2k}=-\tfrac12\log(1-x^{-2}).

Adding the four contributions gives the sum of residues,

x-\sum_{\lvert\gamma\rvert<T}\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}-\log2\pi-\tfrac12\log\bigl(1-x^{-2}\bigr),

where the last term uses all the trivial zeros and the sum over \rho is over the zeros inside the rectangle. What remains is to show that the other three sides of the rectangle contribute something that disappears. The left side at \sigma=-U tends to 0 as U\to\infty because \lvert x^s\rvert=x^{-U}\to0 for x>1 while the logarithmic derivative of \zeta grows only like \log U there, by the functional equation. The two horizontal sides need more care, since \zeta'/\zeta is large near zeros. A standard estimate from Hadamard’s product, \frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)=\sum_{\lvert t-\gamma\rvert<1}\frac1{s-\rho}+O(\log\lvert t\rvert), shows that for each large T one can choose a height T' within 1 of T whose distance from every ordinate is at least a constant times 1/\log T, and on that height \lvert\zeta'/\zeta\rvert\ll\log^2T. The horizontal sides are then O\bigl(x\log^2(xT)/T\bigr), which tends to 0 as T\to\infty. We state what comes out.

Theorem 6.4

Each zero of \zeta is one wave in the count of primes

[24]
Statement

For every real x>1,

\psi_0(x)=x-\sum_{\rho}\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}-\log2\pi-\tfrac12\log\bigl(1-x^{-2}\bigr),
(6.4)

where the sum runs over all nontrivial zeros \rho with multiplicity and is understood as the limit

\sum_\rho\frac{x^\rho}\rho=\lim_{T\to\infty}\sum_{\lvert\gamma\rvert<T}\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}.
(6.5)

For x\ge2 and T\ge2 the truncated sum satisfies \psi(x)=x-\sum_{\lvert\gamma\rvert\le T}\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}+O\bigl(\tfrac xT\log^2(xT)+\log x\bigr).

In plain terms

The staircase of primes equals the line y=x, minus a correction with one term for each zero of zeta, minus a small constant and a small correction that fades as x grows. There is no approximation in the formula, only in how many terms one is willing to add.

Why it is needed

This is the first formula in which a statement about primes is exactly a statement about zeros. If every zero has real part \tfrac12, every term of the sum has size about \sqrt x/\lvert\rho\rvert, and the truncated version of the formula keeps the staircase within about \sqrt x\log^2x of the line. If some zero had real part larger than \tfrac12, its term would grow faster than \sqrt x and would eventually dominate. Chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations makes this precise.

Idea

The switch turns the partial sum into an integral of -\zeta'/\zeta\cdot x^s/s along a vertical line, and shifting the line left picks up a residue at every pole of \zeta'/\zeta, which are the zeros of \zeta. The pole at 1 gives the main term x, each nontrivial zero gives one term, and the pole of 1/s at the origin and the trivial zeros give the small corrections.

Proof sketch

[24]

This is the argument of the preceding sections. Apply Equation (6.3) with c>1, shift the contour to \sigma=-U collecting the four families of residues listed above, and estimate the horizontal and left sides as described, which gives Equation (6.4) in the limit and the truncated version at finite T. Von Mangoldt gave the first complete proof in 1895, for a formula of this kind that Riemann had announced for \pi(x) in 1859 [18; 24]. Textbook accounts are in Davenport [6], Ingham [25], and Edwards [9].

Example

We test Equation (6.4) with the first N zero pairs \tfrac12\pm i\gamma_n, computed with mpmath. A pair contributes -2\Re(x^\rho/\rho) to the right side, and the base value x-\log2\pi-\tfrac12\log(1-x^{-2}) is the right side with no zeros. The columns give the formula with N pairs of zeros, with the exact \psi_0 in the last column.

x N=0 N=1 N=10 N=100 N=1000 exact \psi_0(x)
8 6.1700 6.5356 6.3279 6.3442 6.3865 6.3868
10 8.1671 7.7561 7.7868 7.8265 7.8272 7.8320
100 98.1622 97.1042 95.0403 93.6700 94.0113 94.0453

At x=8, which is a jump of the staircase, the formula converges to the midpoint \psi_0(8)=6.3868 and not to either side, \psi(8^-)=6.0403 or \psi(8)=6.7334. At x=10, which is not a jump, the smooth part alone gives 8.167 while the truth is 7.832, and the first pair of zeros alone moves it to 7.756. The convergence is slow in the last column, as expected from the error term x\log^2(xT)/T, and one thousand pairs (all zeros up to height 1419) leave an error of 0.005 at x=10 and 0.034 at x=100.

Used in

Chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations turns the truncated version into a bound on \psi(x)-x in terms of \Theta, and chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion generalizes the formula from the kernel x^s/s to an arbitrary test function.

Two remarks on Equation (6.4) are needed before we read it. The last two terms, -\log2\pi-\tfrac12\log(1-x^{-2}), are the correction from the pole of 1/s and the trivial zeros, and they are small and almost constant, lying between -1.84 and -1.69 for x\ge2 and within 0.01 of -\log2\pi=-1.8379 once x\ge10, so the bulk of the structure sits in the sum over the nontrivial zeros. The second remark is about the sum itself, which converges only conditionally, and section What the sum over zeros means explains what that means.

6.5A dictionary from the plane to the real line#

Looking back over the four residues, the same pattern appears each time, and stating it once makes the whole formula easier to remember. Every singularity s_0 of -\zeta'/\zeta contributes a term proportional to x^{s_0}, and writing s_0=\sigma_0+it_0 turns that into x^{\sigma_0}e^{it_0\log x}. The real part \sigma_0 of the position sets how fast the term grows or decays as x increases, and the imaginary part t_0 sets how fast it oscillates in \log x. A position in the plane is therefore a pair of numbers, a growth rate and a frequency, and the formula reads each singularity as one behavior of the staircase.

singularity of -\zeta'/\zeta where term in \psi_0(x) growth frequency
the pole of \zeta s=1 +x x^1 0
a nontrivial zero s=\beta+i\gamma -x^\rho/\rho x^\beta \gamma
the pole of 1/s s=0 -\log2\pi constant 0
a trivial zero s=-2k +\dfrac{x^{-2k}}{2k} x^{-2k}, decaying 0

The table organizes the whole chapter. The pole at s=1 is the loudest component because it is the farthest to the right, and it is the line y=x that the staircase follows on average, which is the prime number theorem in this language. The nontrivial zeros sit strictly to its left, by the theorem of chapter The zeros and the hypothesis that no zero lies on \sigma=1, and so each has a wave that grows like x^\beta with \beta<1, which is smaller than x by the factor x^{\beta-1}. The prime number theorem \psi(x)\sim x therefore says that the sum of these waves is of smaller order than x, and the question of how much smaller is the question about \beta that the Riemann Hypothesis answers. The trivial zeros sit far to the left and have no oscillation, so they contribute decaying powers and not waves, which is why the formula treats them separately in the closed form -\tfrac12\log(1-x^{-2}).

The table also gives a way to see why the formula is exact and not approximate. We never discard a singularity, so every statement about \psi_0(x) is a statement about the complete list of singularities of \zeta'/\zeta, and conversely knowing \psi_0(x) for all x determines all of them. In the variable u=\log x the staircase is a sum of point masses of weight \Lambda(n) at the positions u=\log n, and its frequencies are the zeros, which is a Fourier-type duality between two lists of numbers, the logarithms of prime powers on one side and the ordinates of zeros on the other. Chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion makes the duality symmetric by replacing the sharp cutoff with an arbitrary test function.

6.6What the sum over zeros means#

The terms of \sum_\rho x^\rho/\rho do not decay fast enough for the series to converge absolutely, and the formula is true only because of cancellation among oscillating terms. A single term has absolute value x^\beta/\lvert\rho\rvert\approx x^{1/2}/\lvert\gamma\rvert, so the sum of absolute values is a constant times \sqrt x\sum1/\lvert\gamma\rvert, and that diverges because the zeros accumulate faster than 1/\gamma decays. By the count of chapter The zeros and the hypothesis there are about \frac{T}{2\pi}\log T zeros below height T, and the partial sums 2\sum_{n\le N}1/\lvert\rho_n\rvert over zeros of both signs equal 0.67 at N=10, 2.06 at N=100, and 4.64 at N=1000, so they keep growing like a constant times \log^2T.

Definition 6.5 Conditionally convergent series and symmetric truncation

A series is conditionally convergent when it converges but the series of absolute values diverges. Its value then depends on the order of summation, so a rule is needed. The symmetric truncation in Equation (6.5) adds all zeros with \lvert\gamma\rvert<T, in particular a zero and its conjugate together, and lets T\to\infty. It is a rule about the order of terms, and it is not a statement that the terms can be rearranged freely.

Pairing \rho with its conjugate \bar\rho makes every term real, since x^{\bar\rho}/\bar\rho=\overline{x^\rho/\rho}, so

\sum_{\lvert\gamma\rvert<T}\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}=2\sum_{0<\gamma<T}\Re\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}.

The partial sums settle down because the phases x^{i\gamma}=e^{i\gamma\log x} rotate at different speeds and the contributions of high zeros average out, much as the Fourier series of a step function converges although its coefficients decay only like 1/n. Near a jump of the staircase the convergence is slow and the partial sums overshoot, the Gibbs phenomenon familiar from Fourier series, and at the jump itself the series converges to the midpoint \psi_0, which is why the theorem is stated for \psi_0.

6.7One pair of zeros is one wave#

The formula becomes useful when we read its terms one pair at a time. Fix a zero \rho=\beta+i\gamma with \gamma>0. The two terms from \rho and \bar\rho are complex conjugates, so their sum is real, and writing x^\rho=x^\beta e^{i\gamma\log x} and \rho=\lvert\rho\rvert e^{i\arg\rho} gives

-\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}-\frac{x^{\bar\rho}}{\bar\rho}=-2\Re\frac{x^\rho}\rho=-\frac{2\,x^{\beta}}{\lvert\rho\rvert}\cos\bigl(\gamma\log x-\arg\rho\bigr).
(6.6)

This is a cosine in the variable u=\log x with three numbers attached. The frequency is \gamma, meaning that the wave repeats every 2\pi/\gamma units of \log x. The amplitude is 2x^\beta/\lvert\rho\rvert, which grows like the power x^\beta=e^{\beta u}. The phase is \arg\rho=\arctan(\gamma/\beta), which is within 0.04 of \pi/2 for every zero in our table.

Definition 6.6 The wave of a zero

For a nontrivial zero \rho=\beta+i\gamma with \gamma>0, its wave is the real function W_\rho(x)=-\frac{2x^\beta}{\lvert\rho\rvert}\cos(\gamma\log x-\arg\rho) of x>1, the sum of the terms of \rho and \bar\rho in Equation (6.4). It is the contribution of one zero to the count of primes, and it is a wave in \log x, not in x, so successive crests are spaced by a constant factor of x and not by a constant distance.

For the first zero, \rho_1=\tfrac12+14.134725i, the amplitude is 2x^{1/2}/\lvert\rho_1\rvert=0.1414\,\sqrt x since \lvert\rho_1\rvert=14.1436, the phase is \arg\rho_1=1.5354, and the period in \log x is 2\pi/14.134725=0.44452, so the crests are spaced by the factor e^{0.44452}=1.5597 in x. At x=10 the wave equals -0.4110, which is exactly the shift from 8.1671 to 7.7561 in the table of the previous section. To see this by hand, note that \log10=2.302585, so the argument of the cosine is 14.134725\times2.302585-1.5354=31.0110, which is 4.9355 turns of 2\pi and so, reduced modulo 2\pi, is the angle -0.4050 with cosine 0.9191. The amplitude at x=10 is 2\sqrt{10}/14.1436=0.4472, and -0.4472\times0.9191=-0.4110. The second zero, \rho_2=\tfrac12+21.022040i, has amplitude 0.09511\sqrt x and crests spaced by the factor 1.3484, and the third has 0.07995\sqrt x with spacing factor 1.2856. The weights 2/\lvert\rho_n\rvert of the first five zeros are 0.1414, 0.0951, 0.0799, 0.0657, and 0.0607, so they decay slowly, like 1/\gamma.

The importance of \beta appears when we compare the waves with \sqrt x. If \beta=\tfrac12 the wave oscillates with amplitude 2\sqrt x/\lvert\rho\rvert, a fixed multiple of \sqrt x that shrinks as \lvert\rho\rvert grows. If a zero had \beta=0.7, its amplitude would be 2x^{0.7}/\lvert\rho\rvert, which at x=10^{6} is already x^{0.2}=15.8 times larger than the same wave on the critical line, and the ratio keeps growing as x^{\beta-1/2}. A zero off the line always comes with its mirror 1-\beta+i\gamma from chapter The zeros and the hypothesis, whose wave has amplitude x^{1-\beta} and so is the smaller of the two, and the larger wave x^\beta is the one that would show. Dividing the formula by \sqrt x gives the cleanest way to see the hypothesis in this chapter. If all zeros are on the line,

\frac{\psi_0(x)-x}{\sqrt x}=-\sum_{\gamma>0}\frac{2}{\lvert\rho\rvert}\cos\bigl(\gamma\log x-\arg\rho\bigr)-\frac{\log2\pi+\tfrac12\log(1-x^{-2})}{\sqrt x},
(6.7)

a sum of cosines in u=\log x with fixed weights 2/\lvert\rho\rvert, summed in order of increasing \gamma, plus a term that decays like 1/\sqrt x. In the u variable the normalized error is therefore a superposition of cosines of different frequencies \gamma_n, which never settles down. It is typically of size about one, but it is not bounded: Littlewood proved in 1914 that (\psi(x)-x)/\sqrt x is larger than a constant times \log\log\log x in absolute value, with each sign, for arbitrarily large x [10]. The rare large excursions come from many waves briefly falling into phase.

6.8The primes as a chord#

Put the pieces together and the formula says that the staircase of primes is a sum of waves, one pair of zeros per wave, each with its own frequency \gamma_n and a volume that falls off slowly with \gamma_n. This is where the phrase “the music of the primes” becomes a literal statement. The frequencies are the heights of the zeros, which are not integer multiples of a fundamental, so the chord is not harmonic in the way a violin note is, and the notes are the list 14.134725, 21.022040, 25.010858, 30.424876, 32.935062, and so on, that we computed in chapter The zeros and the hypothesis. The pitch axis is \log x, and the staircase is the sound that those notes make. Reading from the lowest note upward, the first wave gives a slow rise and fall that repeats every factor of 1.56 in x, the second adds a faster ripple, and each further note sharpens the detail.

Definition 6.7 The spectrum of the primes

The spectrum of the primes is the multiset of frequencies \{\gamma\} with which the waves in Equation (6.6) oscillate in \log x, that is the ordinates of the nontrivial zeros, with the amplitude of each given by 2x^\beta/\lvert\rho\rvert. It is our name for the set of zeros read as a set of frequencies, and it is a statement about the explicit formula and not a separate theorem.

The picture explains why the formula needs infinitely many zeros. The staircase has a vertical jump of height \log p at each prime power, and a sum of finitely many cosines is smooth, so only the full infinite chord can make a jump. At x=p^k the waves must add up to a rise of \log p at once, and between prime powers they must cancel to leave a flat stretch. Adding zeros one pair at a time is like adding notes to a chord until the sound becomes a sharp click. The sharpness is limited by the highest note included. A wave of frequency \gamma cannot resolve features narrower than about 2\pi/\gamma in \log x, so with the first 200 zeros, whose highest ordinate is \gamma_{200}=396.38, the resolution is 2\pi/396.38=0.0159 in \log x, which at x=60 is a window of about 0.95 in x itself. That is why the figure below stops at x=60, where consecutive primes such as 59 and 61 are still just separated, and why it would take many more zeros to draw the staircase cleanly at x=10^6, where consecutive primes differ by a relative amount of about 10^{-5}.

The chord also explains the stakes of the next chapter. The loudness of a note is x^\beta/\lvert\rho\rvert. With every \beta=\tfrac12 each note grows like \sqrt x, and chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations shows that the whole chord then grows like \sqrt x up to a factor \log^2x, which is the quietest it can be given that the zeros exist at all. A zero with \beta>\tfrac12 would be a note whose volume grows faster than \sqrt x, a note that sooner or later outshouts all the others.

Aside

Riemann’s own formulation in 1859 was for \pi(x) and not for \psi(x). He defined J(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\pi(x^{1/n})/n, found J(x)=\operatorname{li}(x)-\sum_\rho\operatorname{li}(x^\rho)-\log2+\int_x^\infty\frac{\dd t}{t(t^2-1)\log t} for x>1, and recovered \pi(x) by Möbius inversion, so that his wave is the integral logarithm \operatorname{li}(x^\rho) in place of x^\rho/\rho. The two versions carry the same information, and the one for \psi is simpler because -\zeta'/\zeta already has \Lambda as its coefficients, which is why this page uses it. Edwards [9] follows Riemann’s route in detail.

Recap

The reader now has the following.

  • The switch \frac1{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}y^s\frac{\dd s}{s} equals 1 for y>1 and 0 for y<1, with a truncation error of y^c/(\pi T\lvert\log y\rvert).
  • Applied to -\zeta'/\zeta it gives \psi_0(x) as a contour integral, and moving the contour left collects residues at s=1, at each nontrivial zero, at s=0, and at the trivial zeros.
  • Von Mangoldt’s formula \psi_0(x)=x-\sum_\rho x^\rho/\rho-\log2\pi-\tfrac12\log(1-x^{-2}), with the sum read as a symmetric limit, was tested numerically at x=8, 10, and 100.
  • A pair of zeros is one real wave -\frac{2x^\beta}{\lvert\rho\rvert}\cos(\gamma\log x-\arg\rho) in \log x, of frequency \gamma and amplitude growing like x^\beta, so the position of the zeros decides how fast the waves can grow.

Chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations converts this picture into a theorem on the size of \psi(x)-x, and reads the hypothesis as the statement that the staircase is as quiet as it can be.

Previous5. The zeros and the hypothesisNext7. What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations

Chapter 7

What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations

Read the hypothesis as the statement that the primes fluctuate as little as they can, see the same statement for sums with a smooth cutoff, and meet the versions for Dirichlet characters, number fields, and Hecke characters.

Builds on 6. The explicit formula: each zero is a wave

In plain terms

The position of the zeros of the zeta function decides how far the primes can stray from their smooth average. If the zeros sit on the center line, the staircase of primes stays within about the square root of its height of the line it follows, which is exactly the size of the wobble of a long run of fair coin flips. The same statement is believed for the families of zeta-like functions attached to arithmetic progressions and to other number systems, and the Riemann Hypothesis is the first rung of that ladder.

Chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave showed that every zero contributes a wave to the count of primes, with amplitude x^\beta for a zero of real part \beta. This chapter turns that observation into two theorems, one saying that the largest real part of a zero fixes the size of the error exactly, and the other saying what the error is when every zero lies on the critical line. It then explains why the square root is the natural size, tests this on real numbers, introduces a smoothed version of the sum that Part IV will use, lists equivalent statements, and follows the same pattern into the Dirichlet characters, the number fields, and the Hecke characters. It is the logical center of Part I because it says what the hypothesis is for, and the later parts of the page are about how it is proved.

7.1The size of the error is decided by the farthest zero#

The explicit formula expresses the error \psi(x)-x as a sum of waves, and the loudest wave is the one with the largest real part. Write \Theta for the supremum of the real parts \beta of the nontrivial zeros. We know three things about it already. It is at most 1, since every zero lies in the open strip. It is at least \tfrac12, since zeros come in pairs \rho and 1-\bar\rho and so at least one of \beta and 1-\beta is at least \tfrac12. And the hypothesis is the statement \Theta=\tfrac12. The theorem below says that \Theta is exactly the exponent of the error, in both directions.

Theorem 7.1

The error in the count of primes has exponent exactly \Theta, the largest real part of a zero

[25]
Statement

Let \Theta be the supremum of the real parts of the nontrivial zeros of \zeta. Then \tfrac12\le\Theta\le1 and

\psi(x)=x+O\bigl(x^{\Theta}\log^2x\bigr).
(7.1)

Conversely, if \psi(x)=x+O(x^{\alpha}) for some \alpha<1, then every nontrivial zero has real part at most \alpha. Hence \Theta is the infimum of all exponents \alpha with \psi(x)-x=O(x^{\alpha}), and no exponent below \tfrac12 is possible.

In plain terms

How big the zeros’ real parts can be is exactly how big the error in counting primes can be. A zero at real part 0.7 would rule out every bound of the form x^{\alpha} with \alpha<0.7, and conversely an error bounded by x^{0.6} would push every zero to the left of 0.6. Because the symmetry of the zeros never allows \Theta<\tfrac12, the exponent \tfrac12 is the best that can ever be true.

Why it is needed

This is the dictionary between the two sides of the page. It says that the arithmetic question, how regularly the primes are distributed, and the analytic question, where the zeros sit, are the same question, so that proving the hypothesis is proving that the primes are as regular as the functional equation allows.

Idea

For the bound, apply the truncated explicit formula and replace every x^\beta by x^\Theta, which leaves a sum of 1/\lvert\rho\rvert that is only \log^2 large. For the converse, -\zeta'/\zeta(s) equals a Mellin transform of \psi(x)-x plus an explicit term, and a Mellin transform of something of size x^\alpha is analytic to the right of \alpha, which leaves no room for the poles that zeros create.

Proof
Show the proof

The bound. First we bound \sum_{\lvert\gamma\rvert\le T}1/\lvert\rho\rvert. Since \lvert\rho\rvert\ge\gamma and the zeros with \gamma<0 are conjugates of those with \gamma>0, the sum is at most 2\sum_{0<\gamma\le T}1/\gamma. By partial summation against N(t), this equals 2\bigl(N(T)/T+\int_{14}^{T}N(t)\,\dd t/t^2\bigr), and chapter The zeros and the hypothesis gives N(t)\ll t\log t, so the sum is \ll\log T+\int_{14}^T\frac{\log t}{t}\,\dd t\ll\log^2T. Next take T=x in the truncated formula of Theorem 6.4. Each term has \lvert x^\rho\rvert=x^\beta\le x^\Theta, so for x\ge2

\lvert\psi(x)-x\rvert\le x^\Theta\sum_{\lvert\gamma\rvert\le x}\frac1{\lvert\rho\rvert}+C\Bigl(\frac xx\log^2(x^2)+\log x\Bigr)\ \ll\ x^\Theta\log^2x,

where the last step uses x^\Theta\ge1.

The converse. For \sigma>1 partial summation gives -\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)=\sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-s}=s\int_1^\infty\psi(x)x^{-s-1}\,\dd x, and \frac{s}{s-1}=s\int_1^\infty x\cdot x^{-s-1}\,\dd x. Subtracting,

-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)-\frac{s}{s-1}=s\int_1^\infty\bigl(\psi(x)-x\bigr)x^{-s-1}\,\dd x\qquad(\sigma>1).
(7.2)

If \lvert\psi(x)-x\rvert\le Cx^\alpha, the integrand is at most Cx^{\alpha-\sigma-1}, so the integral on the right converges absolutely and defines an analytic function for every \sigma>\alpha. The left side is meromorphic on the plane and agrees with the right side for \sigma>1, so by uniqueness of continuation the left side is analytic on \sigma>\alpha; its pole at s=1 has been subtracted. But \zeta'/\zeta has a pole at every zero of \zeta, so no zero has \beta>\alpha.

The range. If \alpha<\tfrac12 were admissible, every zero would have \beta\le\alpha<\tfrac12, which contradicts the existence of a zero with \beta\ge\tfrac12 (take any \rho, and use \rho or 1-\bar\rho). Combining the bound with the converse, \Theta=\inf\{\alpha:\psi(x)-x=O(x^\alpha)\} because x^\Theta\log^2x=O(x^{\Theta+\varepsilon}) for each \varepsilon>0.

Example

At x=10^6 a hypothetical \Theta=0.6 would allow errors of size x^{0.6}=3981, which is 3.98 times \sqrt x=1000, while the actual error is \psi(10^6)-10^6=-413.4, which is 0.41\sqrt x. A single value of x cannot test a statement about exponents, but at this height the data sit comfortably at the exponent \tfrac12.

Used in

The next section specializes to \Theta=\tfrac12, and chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion reformulates the statement \Theta=\tfrac12 as the nonnegativity of a quadratic form.

7.2The hypothesis as square-root cancellation#

Setting \Theta=\tfrac12 gives the statement that is usually called the hypothesis in its arithmetic form. It was proved equivalent to Riemann’s statement about zeros by von Koch in 1901 [11].

Theorem 7.2

The Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to \pi(x)=\Li(x)+O(\sqrt x\log x)

[11]
Statement

The following three statements are equivalent.

  1. Every nontrivial zero of \zeta has real part \tfrac12.
  2. \psi(x)=x+O\bigl(\sqrt x\log^2x\bigr).
  3. \pi(x)=\mathrm{Li}(x)+O\bigl(\sqrt x\log x\bigr).

Under these statements, Schoenfeld showed that explicit constants are possible, namely \lvert\psi(x)-x\rvert<\frac{\sqrt x\log^2x}{8\pi} for x\ge74 and \lvert\pi(x)-\operatorname{li}(x)\rvert<\frac{\sqrt x\log x}{8\pi} for x\ge2657, where \operatorname{li}(x)=\mathrm{Li}(x)+\operatorname{li}(2) with \operatorname{li}(2)=1.0452 [26].

In plain terms

The count of primes up to x differs from the smooth estimate \mathrm{Li}(x) by no more than a constant times \sqrt x\log x exactly when the zeros are on the line.

Why it is needed

This is the form of the hypothesis that can be checked directly against a table of primes, and it is the form in which the hypothesis is most often quoted.

Idea

Statements 1 and 2 are the two halves of the previous theorem with \Theta=\tfrac12. Statements 2 and 3 are the same information at the two weights, \Lambda(n) and the indicator of primes, and move into each other by partial summation, which divides or multiplies by \log t.

Proof
Show the proof

1 and 2. If every zero has \beta=\tfrac12 then \Theta=\tfrac12 and the previous theorem gives 2. If 2 holds then \psi(x)=x+O(x^{1/2+\varepsilon}) for each \varepsilon>0, so the converse in the previous theorem gives \Theta\le\tfrac12+\varepsilon for each \varepsilon, hence \Theta\le\tfrac12, and together with \Theta\ge\tfrac12 and the symmetry \rho\mapsto1-\bar\rho every zero has \beta=\tfrac12.

2 and 3. Let \vartheta(x)=\sum_{p\le x}\log p. Since \psi(x)-\vartheta(x)=\sum_{k\ge2}\vartheta(x^{1/k}) and Chebyshev’s bound \vartheta(y)\le Cy gives \vartheta(x^{1/2})\le C\sqrt x and \vartheta(x^{1/k})\le Cx^{1/3} for k\ge3 with at most \log_2x values of k, we get \psi(x)-\vartheta(x)=O(\sqrt x). Now assume 2, so \vartheta(x)=x+O(\sqrt x\log^2x). Then

\pi(x)=\int_{2^-}^x\frac{\dd\vartheta(t)}{\log t}=\frac{\vartheta(x)}{\log x}+\int_2^x\frac{\vartheta(t)}{t\log^2t}\,\dd t.

Write \vartheta(t)=t+E(t) with E(t)=O(\sqrt t\log^2t). The terms in t give \frac{x}{\log x}+\int_2^x\frac{\dd t}{\log^2t}, and since \int_2^x\frac{\dd t}{\log^2t}=\mathrm{Li}(x)-\frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{2}{\log2} (integrate \int\dd t/\log t by parts), these add to \mathrm{Li}(x)+O(1). The error terms give O(\sqrt x\log x) from E(x)/\log x and \int_2^xO(t^{-1/2})\,\dd t=O(\sqrt x), so \pi(x)=\mathrm{Li}(x)+O(\sqrt x\log x), which is 3. Conversely assume 3 and write \pi(t)=\mathrm{Li}(t)+F(t) with F(t)=O(\sqrt t\log t). Partial summation the other way gives \vartheta(x)=\pi(x)\log x-\int_2^x\frac{\pi(t)}{t}\,\dd t, and since \int_2^x\log t\,\dd\mathrm{Li}(t)=x-2 we get \vartheta(x)=x-2+F(x)\log x-\int_2^x\frac{F(t)}{t}\,\dd t=x+O(\sqrt x\log^2x). Adding \psi-\vartheta=O(\sqrt x) gives 2.

Example

The bound can be tested against the sieve. At x=10^6 there are \pi(10^6)=78498 primes, \mathrm{Li}(10^6)=78626.50, and the error is -128.50. Against the scale \sqrt x\log x=13816 this is 0.0093. Schoenfeld’s bound uses \operatorname{li}, and \pi(10^6)-\operatorname{li}(10^6)=-129.55 is 0.24 of the allowed amount \sqrt x\log x/(8\pi)=549.7. For \psi, a sieve to 10^7 shows that \lvert\psi(x)-x\rvert is below Schoenfeld’s bound at every integer x from 74 to 10^7, and the largest ratio to the bound is 0.804, reached at x=96.

Used in

Section Why the square root is the natural size explains why the exponent \tfrac12 is natural, and the Dirichlet-character version later in this chapter repeats statement 2 for primes in arithmetic progressions.

The table below shows how the three quantities that RH controls behave at powers of ten. The columns give the error \psi(x)-x with its size relative to \sqrt x, the error \pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x), and the Mertens function M(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\mu(n) that we meet in the next section. Every number was computed by a sieve up to 10^7.

x \psi(x)-x (\psi(x)-x)/\sqrt x \pi(x)-\mathrm{Li}(x) M(x) M(x)/\sqrt x
10 -2.17 -0.686 -1.12 -1 -0.316
10^2 -5.95 -0.595 -4.08 1 0.100
10^3 -3.32 -0.105 -8.56 2 0.063
10^4 13.40 0.134 -16.09 -23 -0.230
10^5 51.56 0.163 -36.76 -48 -0.152
10^6 -413.40 -0.413 -128.50 212 0.212
10^7 -1460.60 -0.462 -338.36 1037 0.328

The relative error (\psi(x)-x)/\sqrt x stays between -0.69 and 0.16 in the table. At the integers 2\le x\le10^7 its largest absolute value is 0.924, at x=2, and for x\ge100 it never exceeds 0.777, which happens at x=1422. (Between integers it can be a little larger, just before a jump: it reaches 1.33 just below x=3 and 0.80 just below the prime 1423.) So in this range the factor \log^2x that the theorem allows, which is about 260 at x=10^7, is never used, and the error stays within one \sqrt x of the line. The data therefore suggest that the proved bound is not sharp in its logarithms, which is consistent with the theorem, because the converse pins down only the exponent and the logarithms enter through the method of proof.

7.3Why the square root is the natural size#

The exponent \tfrac12 is forced from below by the functional equation, but nothing so far says why anyone should expect the hypothesis to give exactly that. The reason is the behavior of random sums. If \varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_N are independent fair coins with values \pm1, then S_N=\sum\varepsilon_i has mean 0 and variance N, so its typical size is \sqrt N, and a deviation of three standard deviations has probability about 0.27\%. A sum of N terms of size 1 could be as large as N, but when the signs are unrelated almost all of it cancels and only the square root of the number of terms survives, which is called square-root cancellation.

The Möbius function gives the cleanest bridge from this idea to the zeta function. Recall that \mu(n) is 0 if n has a repeated prime factor and otherwise (-1)^k if n is a product of k distinct primes, and that \sum_n\mu(n)n^{-s}=1/\zeta(s). The partial sums M(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\mu(n) behave like a random walk if the signs of \mu are unrelated to each other, in which case M(x) would be of size \sqrt{x} up to a constant. About 6/\pi^2=61\% of the integers are squarefree, so the model walk has standard deviation \sqrt{0.61x}=0.78\sqrt x. The table gives M(x)/\sqrt x=-0.316, 0.100, 0.063, -0.230, -0.152, 0.212, and 0.328, all within half a standard deviation of the model, so the data look like coin flips. For x\ge100 the largest value of \lvert M(x)\rvert/\sqrt x up to 10^7 is 0.567, at x=199.

The link to the hypothesis is the following theorem of Littlewood from 1912 [27]. The hypothesis holds exactly when M(x)=O(x^{1/2+\varepsilon}) for every \varepsilon>0, which is again a statement about the zeros, because the Mellin transform of M(x) is 1/(s\zeta(s)) and 1/\zeta has poles at the zeros. The direction from the bound on M to the zeros is the same argument as the converse above. If M(x)=O(x^{\alpha}) then 1/\zeta(s)=s\int_1^\infty M(x)x^{-s-1}\,\dd x is analytic for \sigma>\alpha, which leaves no room for a zero there.

A common misreading

Square-root cancellation is a heuristic that explains why \tfrac12 is the natural exponent, and it proves nothing, because the signs of \mu(n) are not independent coins and share structure through common divisors. The conjecture of Mertens that \lvert M(x)\rvert<\sqrt x for all x>1 was disproved by Odlyzko and te Riele in 1985 [28], although every counterexample lies far beyond the range of the table, where \lvert M(x)\rvert/\sqrt x stays below 0.9. The coin model therefore captures the exponent and not the constant.

The explicit formula says which conspiracy would break the square root. A wave x^\beta\cos(\gamma\log x-\cdots) with \beta>\tfrac12 would be a systematic pattern in the primes whose strength grows faster than random noise, and a zero off the line is exactly such a pattern, so the hypothesis says that the primes hide no structure of that size.

7.4Smoothing the sum#

The sharp cutoff in \psi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n) makes the zero sum only conditionally convergent, because a jump needs infinitely many waves to build. Smoothing the cutoff turns jumps into kinks and lets the waves have faster decaying amplitudes. The simplest smoothing replaces the weight 1_{n\le X} by the continuous weight (X/n-1)_+, which vanishes for n\ge X and grows linearly as n decreases.

Definition 7.3 The smoothed sum

For real X>1 the smoothed sum is

S(X)=\sum_{n\le X}\Lambda(n)\Bigl(\frac Xn-1\Bigr).
(7.3)

It is a continuous, increasing, piecewise linear function of X with slope \sum_{n\le X}\Lambda(n)/n between prime powers, so it has no jumps. It is not the same as \psi(X), and the two are related by S(X)=X\int_1^X\psi(u)u^{-2}\,\dd u, so S(X)/X is the integral of \psi(u)/u against the measure \dd u/u on [1,X].

The relation to \psi follows from \frac{X}{n}-1=\int_n^X\frac{X}{u^2}\,\dd u for n\le X, and then exchanging the sum and the integral. As a check, S(10)=\Lambda(2)\cdot4+\Lambda(3)\cdot\tfrac73+\Lambda(4)\cdot\tfrac32+\Lambda(5)\cdot1+\Lambda(7)\cdot\tfrac37+\Lambda(8)\cdot\tfrac14+\Lambda(9)\cdot\tfrac19, which equals 9.114492. The kernel behind the smoothing is \frac1{2\pi i}\int_{(c)}y^s\frac{\dd s}{s(s-1)} for c>1, which equals (y-1)_+ and decays like \lvert s\rvert^{-2} instead of \lvert s\rvert^{-1}, so that the new integral converges absolutely. To see the value, shift the contour as in section Perron’s switch. For y>1 shift left and collect the residues y at s=1 and -1 at s=0, giving y-1, and for y<1 shift right and collect nothing.

Theorem 7.4

The smoothed prime sum equals X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X+\log2\pi minus an absolutely convergent sum over zeros

[24]
Statement

For every real X>1,

S(X)=X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X+\log2\pi-\sum_\rho\frac{X^\rho}{\rho(\rho-1)}-\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{X^{-2k}}{2k(2k+1)},
(7.4)

where \gamma_E=0.5772\ldots is Euler’s constant, and the sum over the nontrivial zeros \rho converges absolutely, so its order does not matter. Consequently S(X)=X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X+O(X^{\Theta}) with no logarithmic factor, and if every zero has real part \tfrac12 then \rho(\rho-1)=-\lvert\rho\rvert^2 and

\Bigl\lvert\sum_\rho\frac{X^\rho}{\rho(\rho-1)}\Bigr\rvert\le c_0\sqrt X,\qquad c_0=\sum_\rho\frac1{\lvert\rho\rvert^{2}}=2+\gamma_E-\log4\pi=0.0461914\ldots
(7.5)
In plain terms

Replace the sharp cutoff by a gentle ramp and the staircase of primes becomes a smooth curve with an explicit main term. The correction is a sum over zeros whose terms shrink like 1/\lvert\rho\rvert^2, so the sum converges absolutely and is controlled by one number, 0.0462, times \sqrt X.

Why it is needed

Every difficulty in the sum over zeros of chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave came from the slowly decaying weights 1/\rho. With the weights 1/(\rho(\rho-1)) the sum can be bounded and differentiated term by term, which is the control that positivity arguments need.

Idea

Repeat the previous chapter with the kernel 1/(s(s-1)) in place of 1/s. The weights 1/\rho become 1/(\rho(\rho-1)), and the pole at s=1 becomes double, which turns the main term x into X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X. The same formula also follows by integrating von Mangoldt’s formula against X\,\dd u/u^2 from 1 to X, and that route checks the constant: the terms -\log2\pi, \sum_\rho1/(\rho(\rho-1))=-2\sum_\rho1/\rho=-0.0461914, and \sum_k1/(2k(2k+1))=1-\log2=0.3068528 each contribute their value times X, and they add up to -1.5772157=-(1+\gamma_E), the coefficient of X.

Proof
Show the proof

For c>1 and X>1, the kernel identity above together with absolute convergence of \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-c} gives

S(X)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{(c)}\Bigl(-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)\Bigr)\frac{X^s}{s(s-1)}\,\dd s ,

an absolutely convergent integral because \lvert s(s-1)\rvert^{-1}\ll\lvert t\rvert^{-2}. Let F(s)=-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)\frac{X^s}{s(s-1)}. We shift the line to \sigma=-U with U odd and large, collecting the residues of F.

Steps
  1. At s=1 there is a double pole, because -\zeta'/\zeta has a simple pole with Laurent expansion \frac1{s-1}-\gamma_E+O(s-1) and the kernel has another factor \frac1{s-1}. The residue is the derivative of g(s)=X^s/s at s=1 plus -\gamma_E times g(1), that is X\log X-X-\gamma_EX=X(\log X-1-\gamma_E).
  2. At each nontrivial zero \rho the residue of -\zeta'/\zeta is -m for multiplicity m, so the contribution is -m\,X^\rho/(\rho(\rho-1)).
  3. At s=0 the kernel has a simple pole with residue \frac{X^0}{0-1}=-1 and -\zeta'/\zeta(0)=-\log2\pi is finite, so the contribution is +\log2\pi.
  4. At each trivial zero s=-2k the residue of -\zeta'/\zeta is -1 and the kernel equals \frac{X^{-2k}}{(-2k)(-2k-1)}=\frac{X^{-2k}}{2k(2k+1)}, so the contribution is -\frac{X^{-2k}}{2k(2k+1)}.

Summing the four contributions gives the right side of Equation (7.4). It remains to show that the integrals over the horizontal sides and over the left side vanish in the limit. On the horizontal sides at heights \pm T, chosen as in chapter The explicit formula: each zero is a wave so that \lvert\zeta'/\zeta\rvert\ll\log^2T there (and by the functional equation the same bound holds to the left of \sigma=-1), the integrand is at most X^\sigma\log^2T/T^2 in size, and \int_{-\infty}^cX^\sigma\,\dd\sigma=X^c/\log X, so the contribution tends to 0 as T\to\infty. On the left side, \lvert X^s\rvert=X^{-U} and \zeta'/\zeta grows at most like \log(U+\lvert t\rvert) by the functional equation, so that side tends to 0 as U\to\infty because X>1. The sum over \rho converges absolutely because \lvert\rho(\rho-1)\rvert\ge\lvert\rho\rvert^2/2 and \sum_\rho\lvert\rho\rvert^{-2}<\infty by the zero count of chapter The zeros and the hypothesis, and the bound by X^\Theta follows from \lvert X^\rho\rvert\le X^\Theta.

When every \beta=\tfrac12, we have \rho(\rho-1)=-\rho(1-\rho)=-\rho\bar\rho=-\lvert\rho\rvert^2 because 1-\rho=\bar\rho on the critical line. Since also \Re(1/\rho)=\beta/\lvert\rho\rvert^2=1/(2\lvert\rho\rvert^2), we get \sum_\rho\lvert\rho\rvert^{-2}=2\sum_\rho\Re(1/\rho)=2\sum_\rho1/\rho=2\bigl(1+\tfrac{\gamma_E}{2}-\tfrac12\log4\pi\bigr)=2+\gamma_E-\log4\pi by Equation (5.7).

Example

We test Equation (7.4) with the first N zero pairs. The table gives the exact S(X) and the error (formula minus truth) when the sum over zeros is cut after N pairs. For N=0 the formula keeps only the main term and the trivial-zero sum.

X S(X) error, N=0 N=10 N=100 N=1000 c_0\sqrt X
10 9.114492 -0.0246 +0.0039 +0.000025 +0.0000036 0.146
50 118.619882 -0.0417 -0.0102 -0.00053 -0.0000047 0.327
100 304.517139 +0.1162 -0.0015 -0.0030 -0.000063 0.462
1000 5332.070527 +0.3070 -0.0456 -0.0029 +0.0003 1.461

At X=1000 the main term with the constant, X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X+\log2\pi, is 5332.3775 against the truth 5332.0705, and the whole zero sum is only 0.307 in size, comfortably below the bound c_0\sqrt X=1.46 of Equation (7.5). Ten pairs of zeros bring the error down to 0.05 and a hundred to 0.003, which is far faster than for \psi in the previous chapter, where a thousand pairs still left errors of 0.005 at x=10 and 0.034 at x=100. The constant c_0=0.0461914 is consistent with the zeros as well, since the 1000 zero pairs below height 1419 already give \sum\lvert\rho\rvert^{-2}=0.04475, and the tail adds about 0.0014.

Used in

Chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion generalizes the smoothing from the kernel (y-1)_+ to an arbitrary test function, and Part IV works with this particular sum. The bound Equation (7.5) shows that under the hypothesis the smoothed sum is an almost periodic function of \log X with a controlled constant.

The Mellin argument of the previous theorem also works for S and gives an equivalent form of the hypothesis without logarithms. Since \int_1^\infty S(X)X^{-s-1}\,\dd X=-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)/(s(s-1)) for \sigma>1, the transform of the main term X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X is (s-1)^{-2}-(1+\gamma_E)(s-1)^{-1}, and the argument shows that S(X)=X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X+O(X^\alpha) for some \alpha<1 forces every zero to have \beta\le\alpha. Together with the formula above this gives the statement that the hypothesis holds exactly when S(X)=X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X+O(\sqrt X).

7.5Other statements equivalent to the hypothesis#

The earlier sections proved the equivalence of the hypothesis with three of its arithmetic forms, and several more exist that look nothing like a statement about zeros. The list below marks what is proved on this page and what is cited.

  1. \pi(x)=\mathrm{Li}(x)+O(\sqrt x\log x), von Koch 1901, proved above.
  2. \psi(x)=x+O(\sqrt x\log^2x), proved above.
  3. S(X)=X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X+O(\sqrt X), proved above (the converse by the Mellin argument just given).
  4. M(x)=O(x^{1/2+\varepsilon}) for every \varepsilon>0, Littlewood 1912, with the direction from the bound to the zeros proved above and the other direction cited [27; 19].
  5. \sigma(n)<e^{\gamma_E}n\log\log n for every integer n>5040, where \sigma(n) is the sum of the divisors of n (Robin 1984, cited [29]).
  6. The nonnegativity of Weil’s functional on test functions of the form f*\tilde f, which is the subject of chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion.

Statement 5 can be checked on small cases. The inequality fails for exactly 27 integers from 2 up to 5040, and 5040 is the last of them, with \sigma(5040)=19344 against e^{\gamma_E}\cdot5040\log\log5040=19237.06, so it fails by 0.56\%. For larger highly composite numbers it holds, with \sigma(n) equal to 0.9858 of the right side at n=10080 and 0.9833 at n=55440, and Gronwall’s theorem that \limsup\sigma(n)/(n\log\log n)=e^{\gamma_E} shows that the constant cannot be improved. Robin’s theorem says that if the hypothesis were false the inequality would fail for infinitely many n, and since it is true it holds for every n>5040.

7.6Dirichlet characters and the first generalization#

The proofs of this chapter used only an Euler product with \Lambda in its logarithmic derivative, a continuation to the plane, a functional equation, and a count of zeros, and these features hold for a much larger family. The smallest extension replaces all integers by the integers in a fixed residue class, so as to count primes in arithmetic progressions, and the answer is the template for everything that follows.

Definition 7.5 Dirichlet character

A Dirichlet character modulo q is a function \chi:\ZZ\to\CC obtained from a group homomorphism \chi:(\ZZ/q\ZZ)^\times\to\CC^\times by setting \chi(n)=\chi(n\bmod q) when \gcd(n,q)=1 and \chi(n)=0 otherwise. It is completely multiplicative, meaning \chi(mn)=\chi(m)\chi(n) for all integers, and periodic with period q. The principal character \chi_0 is the one with \chi_0(n)=1 for all n coprime to q. It is not identically 1, since it takes the value 0 at the multiples of the primes dividing q.

There are exactly \varphi(q) characters modulo q, where \varphi is Euler’s totient function. For q=4 the group (\ZZ/4\ZZ)^\times=\{1,3\} has two characters, the principal one and the character \chi_4 with \chi_4(1)=1 and \chi_4(3)=-1, which is 1,0,-1,0 on n\equiv1,2,3,0\bmod4. For q=5 the group (\ZZ/5\ZZ)^\times is cyclic of order 4 with generator 2, since 2,4,3,1 are its successive powers, so a character is fixed by the value \chi(2)\in\{1,i,-1,-i\}, which gives four characters, written \chi_{5,0},\chi_{5,1},\chi_{5,2},\chi_{5,3} below with \chi_{5,j}(2)=i^j.

n\bmod5 1 2 3 4
\chi_{5,0} 1 1 1 1
\chi_{5,1} 1 i -i -1
\chi_{5,2} 1 -1 -1 1
\chi_{5,3} 1 -i i -1

Characters separate the residue classes. For \gcd(a,q)=1 one has the orthogonality relation \frac1{\varphi(q)}\sum_\chi\overline{\chi(a)}\chi(n)=1 if n\equiv a\bmod q and 0 otherwise, where the sum is over all \varphi(q) characters. Therefore the sum \psi(x;q,a)=\sum_{n\le x,\,n\equiv a}\Lambda(n) satisfies

\psi(x;q,a)=\frac1{\varphi(q)}\sum_\chi\overline{\chi(a)}\,\psi(x,\chi),\qquad\psi(x,\chi)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)\chi(n).
(7.6)

For q=4 and a=1 this reads \psi(x;4,1)=\tfrac12\bigl(\psi(x,\chi_0)+\psi(x,\chi_4)\bigr), and at x=100 the numbers are \psi(100,\chi_0)=89.8864 and \psi(100,\chi_4)=-0.1126, giving \psi(100;4,1)=44.8869, while the same formula with a minus sign gives \psi(100;4,3)=44.9995, in agreement with direct summation. The principal character carries the main term, and every other character carries a sum that should be small.

Definition 7.6 Dirichlet L-function

For a Dirichlet character \chi the L-function is L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)n^{-s} for \sigma>1. It is a Dirichlet series with unit-size coefficients, and for \chi=\chi_0 it equals \zeta(s)\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-s}). It is not a new kind of object for q=1, where it is \zeta itself.

Because \chi is completely multiplicative, the proof of the Euler product in chapter Euler's product: primes inside one function goes through unchanged and gives L(s,\chi)=\prod_p(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1} for \sigma>1, and taking the logarithmic derivative gives -\frac{L'}{L}(s,\chi)=\sum_n\Lambda(n)\chi(n)n^{-s}. The same Perron argument then expresses \psi(x,\chi) as a sum over the zeros of L(s,\chi). For \chi_4 the series is the alternating Leibniz series L(s,\chi_4)=1-3^{-s}+5^{-s}-7^{-s}+\cdots, with L(1,\chi_4)=\pi/4=0.785398, and the Euler product with all primes up to 2\times10^5 gives L(2,\chi_4)=0.9159655948, against the true value (Catalan’s constant) 0.9159655942. For the quadratic character \chi_{5,2} modulo 5, L(1,\chi_{5,2})=\frac{2}{\sqrt5}\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}=0.43041.

The analytic properties repeat those of \zeta with small changes. For a nonprincipal character L(s,\chi) has no pole, so it is entire. Chapter Zeta on the whole plane derived the functional equation of \zeta from Poisson summation applied to a theta function, and the same method applied to a theta function twisted by \chi gives the following statement, which we cite. Call \chi primitive if it is not induced by a character of a smaller modulus, and write a=0 if \chi(-1)=1 (an even character) and a=1 if \chi(-1)=-1 (an odd character).

Proposition 7.7

A primitive L-function has a completed form that is symmetric under s\mapsto1-s

[6]
Statement

Let \chi be a primitive character modulo q>1 with parity a\in\{0,1\}. The completed function

\xi(s,\chi)=\Bigl(\frac q\pi\Bigr)^{(s+a)/2}\Gamma\Bigl(\frac{s+a}2\Bigr)L(s,\chi)
(7.7)

is entire and satisfies \xi(s,\chi)=\varepsilon(\chi)\xi(1-s,\bar\chi) with \lvert\varepsilon(\chi)\rvert=1, where \bar\chi is the conjugate character and \varepsilon(\chi)=1 when \chi is real. The zeros of L(s,\chi) outside the critical strip are the trivial zeros s=-a-2k for k\ge0.

In plain terms

The L-function of a primitive character has the same kind of mirror symmetry as zeta, with the line \sigma=\tfrac12 as the mirror. The only changes are a factor depending on the modulus and a small shift in the Gamma function that depends on whether the character is even or odd.

Why it is needed

The mirror symmetry is what makes the critical line special, exactly as for \zeta, and so the generalized hypothesis is stated with the same line.

Idea

The proof repeats the one for \zeta with a theta function whose terms carry \chi(n). Poisson summation turns \sum\chi(n)n^ae^{-\pi n^2t/q} into a sum over the Fourier transform of \chi, which is a Gauss sum times \bar\chi.

Proof sketch

[6]

Davenport proves this from the theta functions \sum_n\chi(n)n^ae^{-\pi n^2t/q} and the Gauss sum \tau(\chi)=\sum_{m\bmod q}\chi(m)e^{2\pi im/q}, with \varepsilon(\chi)=\tau(\chi)/(i^a\sqrt q) [6]. We use only the statement.

Example

For \chi_4 (odd, so a=1, and q=4) the claim is that \xi(s,\chi_4)=(4/\pi)^{(s+1)/2}\Gamma(\tfrac{s+1}2)L(s,\chi_4) equals \xi(1-s,\chi_4). Numerically \xi(0.3+2i,\chi_4)=0.7132035-0.0468964i and \xi(0.7-2i,\chi_4) is the same number to 15 digits, and the same holds at 0.7-5.5i, where both sides equal 0.0308394-0.0158398i. The trivial zeros of L(s,\chi_4) are -1,-3,-5,\ldots.

Used in

The statement of the generalized hypothesis below uses the critical line \sigma=\tfrac12 that this symmetry singles out.

The nontrivial zeros of L(s,\chi) lie in the same strip and are counted the same way, with the asymptotic count \frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{qT}{2\pi e} for the zeros of a real character with 0<\gamma\le T (Davenport [6]). The first zeros of L(s,\chi_4) are \tfrac12+i\gamma with \gamma=6.020949, 10.243770, 12.988098, 16.342607, and 18.291993, and those of the quadratic character modulo 5 are 6.648453, 9.831444, 11.958846, 16.033821, and 17.566994, each found as a sign change of \xi(\tfrac12+it,\chi), which for these two real characters is a real function of t because \varepsilon(\chi)=1. For T=45 the count formula gives 16.9 zeros of L(s,\chi_4) with 0<\gamma\le45, and the sign changes number 17. For a complex character the zeros are not symmetric about the real axis, since \rho is a zero of L(s,\chi) exactly when \bar\rho is a zero of L(s,\bar\chi), but the functional equation still makes them symmetric about the critical line, in the form \rho\mapsto1-\bar\rho.

Definition 7.8 The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet characters

The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) for Dirichlet characters is the statement that for every primitive Dirichlet character \chi, every nontrivial zero of L(s,\chi) has real part \tfrac12. It is the Riemann Hypothesis for the whole family L(s,\chi) at once, and it is not implied by the case of \zeta alone, which is the case q=1 of the family. Imprimitive characters follow because their L-functions differ from the primitive ones by finitely many Euler factors, whose zeros lie on the line \sigma=0.

The proofs of GRH are the subject of Parts III and IV. Part III proves the hypothesis for the L-functions of all unitary Hecke characters of all number fields, which include the Dirichlet L-functions, following Masullo [1], and Part IV proves it for \zeta and the Dirichlet L-functions, following Alpoge with Claude [2; 3]. For the arithmetic consequences we use the statement.

Theorem 7.9

Primes in a progression are equidistributed to within the square root, when every L-function obeys the hypothesis

[6]
Statement

Assume GRH for Dirichlet characters. For each modulus q and each a coprime to q,

\psi(x;q,a)=\frac{x}{\varphi(q)}+O\bigl(\sqrt x\log^2x\bigr),\qquad\pi(x;q,a)=\frac{\mathrm{Li}(x)}{\varphi(q)}+O\bigl(\sqrt x\log x\bigr),
(7.8)

where the implied constants may depend on q.

In plain terms

Each of the \varphi(q) admissible residue classes receives its fair share 1/\varphi(q) of the primes, and the departure from a fair share is of size \sqrt x up to logarithms.

Why it is needed

Dirichlet proved in 1837 that every class that can contain infinitely many primes does contain infinitely many [30], and the prime number theorem for progressions gives the density 1/\varphi(q), but only the generalized hypothesis gives an error that small.

Idea

By Equation (7.6) the sum \psi(x;q,a) splits into \psi(x,\chi) over characters. The principal character gives x by the explicit formula for \zeta, and each other character has no pole at s=1 and so contributes only a sum over its zeros, with no main term. If every zero is on the line, each such sum is at most \sqrt x\log^2x by the same argument as for \zeta.

Proof sketch

[6]

For primitive \chi\ne\chi_0 the explicit formula reads \psi_0(x,\chi)=-\sum_\rho\frac{x^\rho}{\rho}+O(\log x), with no main term because L(s,\chi) is entire. The truncation and the bound \sum_{\lvert\gamma\rvert\le T}1/\lvert\rho\rvert\ll\log^2(qT) go through as for \zeta, and with T=x and all \beta=\tfrac12 one gets \psi(x,\chi)\ll\sqrt x\log^2x. Summing over the \varphi(q) characters in Equation (7.6) gives the first claim, and partial summation as in the proof of Theorem 7.2 gives the second. The imprimitive characters differ from primitive ones by O(\log x). See Davenport [6] and Montgomery and Vaughan [14].

Example

At x=10^6 the primes 1\bmod4 number 39175 and the primes 3\bmod4 number 39322, and for \psi the deviations from x/2 are \psi(10^6;4,1)-500000=-631.2 and \psi(10^6;4,3)-500000=+204.6, which are -0.63\sqrt x and +0.20\sqrt x. For the modulus 5 the four classes 1,2,3,4 contain 19617, 19622, 19665, and 19593 primes up to 10^6 (plus the single prime 5 itself), against the fair share 78497/4=19624.25, so the deviations are -7, -2, +41, and -31. All of them are smaller than \sqrt x/\log x\approx72.

Used in

The race of the next paragraphs is a consequence of this explicit formula. The same template is used in the number field setting at the end of the chapter.

The explicit formula for \chi_4 explains a famous asymmetry. The primes 3\bmod4 are ahead of the primes 1\bmod4 at every power of ten, and the difference \Delta(x)=\pi(x;4,3)-\pi(x;4,1) equals 1,2,7,10,25,147,218 at x=10^k for k=1,\ldots,7. The first x at which the primes 1\bmod4 pull ahead is 26861, and among the integers up to 10^7 they lead at only 0.034\%. The source of the bias is visible in the explicit formula. Under the hypothesis for L(s,\chi_4), the sum \psi(x,\chi_4)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)\chi_4(n) is a sum of waves with no main term, so it oscillates around 0. But the square of every odd prime is 1\bmod4, so the prime squares contribute +\sum_{3\le p\le\sqrt x}\log p\approx\sqrt x to it with no sign changes, and the primes alone must therefore carry a sum \sum_{p\le x}\chi_4(p)\log p that oscillates around -\sqrt x. Dividing by \log x to count primes, this pushes \Delta(x) up by about \sqrt x/\log x, which is 10.9,\,27.5,\,72.4,\,196.2 at x=10^4,\ldots,10^7, close to the observed 10,\,25,\,147,\,218 except at 10^6, where the oscillating terms from the zeros of L(s,\chi_4) add about 75. The race is thus governed by the zeros \tfrac12+6.020949i,\,\tfrac12+10.243770i,\ldots of L(s,\chi_4), in the same way that the staircase of primes is governed by the zeros of \zeta.

7.7Number fields and the Dedekind zeta function#

Dirichlet characters generalize by changing the question from “which residue class is p in” to “how does p behave in a larger number system”. A number field is a finite extension K of \QQ, such as \QQ(i), the field of numbers a+bi with a,b rational. Its integers form a ring \mathcal O_K, which for \QQ(i) is the ring \ZZ[i] of Gaussian integers, and instead of numbers n one counts ideals. The role of the integer n is played by an ideal \mathfrak a and its norm N\mathfrak a, which is the number of elements of \mathcal O_K/\mathfrak a.

Definition 7.10 Dedekind zeta function

For a number field K the Dedekind zeta function is \zeta_K(s)=\sum_{\mathfrak a}N\mathfrak a^{-s}, where \mathfrak a runs over the nonzero ideals of \mathcal O_K, convergent for \sigma>1. It has the Euler product \zeta_K(s)=\prod_{\mathfrak p}(1-N\mathfrak p^{-s})^{-1} over the prime ideals \mathfrak p. It is not \zeta(s) of K viewed as a field of numbers, and for K=\QQ it equals \zeta(s).

For K=\QQ(i) the prime ideals can be described by how a rational prime p factors in \ZZ[i]. The prime 2 is ramified, 2=-i(1+i)^2, and has one prime ideal of norm 2. Primes p\equiv1\bmod4 split into two distinct prime ideals of norm p, as 5=(2+i)(2-i). Primes p\equiv3\bmod4 stay prime (they are inert), giving one prime ideal of norm p^2. Matching the local factors, a split prime contributes (1-p^{-s})^{-2}, an inert prime contributes (1-p^{-2s})^{-1}=(1-p^{-s})^{-1}(1+p^{-s})^{-1}, and 2 contributes (1-2^{-s})^{-1}. These are exactly the local factors of \zeta(s)L(s,\chi_4), since \chi_4(p)=1,-1,0 for the three cases, and so

\zeta_{\QQ(i)}(s)=\zeta(s)\,L(s,\chi_4).
(7.9)

The coefficient of n^{-s}, which counts the ideals of norm n, is a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\chi_4(d), and it equals r_2(n)/4 where r_2(n) is the number of ways to write n as a sum of two squares, because the four units \pm1,\pm i generate the same ideal. For example a(5)=2 and r_2(5)=8, a(3)=0 and r_2(3)=0, a(25)=3 and r_2(25)=12, and a(65)=4 and r_2(65)=16, all confirmed by direct count. The residue of \zeta_{\QQ(i)} at s=1 is L(1,\chi_4)=\pi/4, which agrees with the class number formula \frac{2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2}hR}{w\sqrt{\lvert d_K\rvert}}=\frac{2\pi}{4\cdot2} for r_1=0, r_2=1, h=1, R=1, w=4, d_K=-4 [31].

Equation Equation (7.9) shows that the zeros of the Dedekind zeta function of \QQ(i) are the zeros of \zeta together with the zeros of L(s,\chi_4). This is a general pattern, since the Dedekind zeta function of any abelian extension of \QQ factors into the Dirichlet L-functions of the characters of the extension, and for nonabelian extensions it factors into more general Artin L-functions. For the real quadratic field \QQ(\sqrt5), for instance, the same matching, with p\equiv\pm1\bmod5 split, p\equiv\pm2\bmod5 inert, and 5 ramified, gives \zeta_{\QQ(\sqrt5)}(s)=\zeta(s)\,L(s,\chi_{5,2}). The functional equation also holds. With \Gamma_{\RR}(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2) and \Gamma_{\CC}(s)=2(2\pi)^{-s}\Gamma(s), if K has r_1 real and r_2 complex places and discriminant d_K, the function \xi_K(s)=\lvert d_K\rvert^{s/2}\Gamma_{\RR}(s)^{r_1}\Gamma_{\CC}(s)^{r_2}\zeta_K(s) satisfies \xi_K(s)=\xi_K(1-s) [31]. Unlike \xi, this completed function keeps the simple poles at s=0 and s=1, because it has no factor s(s-1). For \QQ(i) (r_1=0, r_2=1, d_K=-4) this says 4^{s/2}\cdot2(2\pi)^{-s}\Gamma(s)\zeta(s)L(s,\chi_4) is symmetric under s\mapsto1-s, and numerically its value is -0.0728610+0.0203257i at both s=0.3+2i and s=0.7-2i.

Hecke characters generalize Dirichlet characters from \QQ to K. A Dirichlet character modulo q is a character of a ray class group of \QQ, meaning the group of positive fractions whose numerator and denominator are prime to q, taken modulo those that are 1\bmod q, and a Hecke character is a character of a generalized ideal class group in which, in addition, one may remember an angle at each infinite place. The finite-order ones are the characters of ray class groups, the direct analogue of Dirichlet characters, and the others are the Grössencharaktere of Hecke [32]. On \QQ(i) an example is \chi^{(k)}\bigl((\alpha)\bigr)=(\alpha/\lvert\alpha\rvert)^{4k} for the ideal generated by \alpha, which depends only on the ideal because a unit multiplies \alpha/\lvert\alpha\rvert by a fourth root of unity, and that becomes 1 after the power 4k. Its L-function L(s,\chi^{(k)})=\sum_{\mathfrak a}\chi^{(k)}(\mathfrak a)N\mathfrak a^{-s} has an Euler product, a continuation, and a functional equation like the ones above, and \chi^{(0)} gives \zeta_{\QQ(i)} back. Characters with values on the unit circle, like these, are called unitary, and they are the ones for which the critical line is \sigma=\tfrac12.

Definition 7.11 The extended Riemann Hypothesis

The extended Riemann Hypothesis for a family of L-functions is the statement that every nontrivial zero of every function in the family has real part \tfrac12. It is used for the family of Dedekind zeta functions \zeta_K of all number fields K, and in its widest form for the L-functions L(s,\chi) of all unitary Hecke characters \chi of all number fields. It is a statement about each function in the family separately and is not a statement about the sum or product of functions, and nothing in it depends on a normalization other than the unitary one. Terminology varies, and many authors call the Dirichlet case, the Dedekind case, and the Hecke case all “the generalized Riemann Hypothesis”.

For counting primes, the extended hypothesis gives for number fields what the generalized hypothesis gives for progressions. Under the hypothesis for \zeta_K the number of prime ideals of norm at most x is \mathrm{Li}(x) plus an error of size about \sqrt x times logarithms of x and of the discriminant d_K, and the Chebotarev density theorem, which says how primes split in Galois extensions, acquires a similar error term (see Iwaniec and Kowalski [33]).

7.8The three hypotheses side by side#

The ladder can now be summarized. Each rung covers a larger class of functions, all with an Euler product, a completed form with a functional equation, and zeros inside a critical strip, and each statement is the same sentence, “the nontrivial zeros have real part \tfrac12”, about a bigger family.

statement functions covered Euler product over symmetry trivial zeros proved on this page in
Riemann Hypothesis \zeta(s) primes p \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) -2,-4,-6,\dots Parts III and IV
Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (Dirichlet) L(s,\chi) for all primitive \chi of all moduli q primes p, with \chi(p) \xi(s,\chi)=\varepsilon\,\xi(1-s,\bar\chi) -a-2k Parts III and IV
Extended Riemann Hypothesis (Dedekind) \zeta_K(s) for all number fields K prime ideals \mathfrak p, with N\mathfrak p \xi_K(s)=\xi_K(1-s) at s=0,-1,-2,\dots with orders set by r_1,r_2 Part III
Hecke version (unitary) L(s,\chi) for all unitary Hecke characters \chi of all number fields prime ideals, with \chi(\mathfrak p) \xi(s,\chi)=\varepsilon\,\xi(1-s,\bar\chi) from the infinite type Part III

Each line contains the previous ones, since \zeta is the case q=1 of the Dirichlet family, a Dirichlet L-function is a factor of the Dedekind zeta function of a cyclotomic field (for \QQ(i), the factor L(s,\chi_4)), and a Dedekind zeta function is the Hecke L-function of the trivial character. The last column records how far each proof reaches. Part III, following Masullo [1], proves the last line, and with it every line above. Part IV, following Alpoge with Claude [2], proves the first two lines.

Recap

The reader now has the following.

  • The exponent of the error in the count of primes is exactly \Theta, the largest real part of a zero, so the hypothesis is equivalent to \psi(x)=x+O(\sqrt x\log^2x) and to \pi(x)=\mathrm{Li}(x)+O(\sqrt x\log x).
  • Square-root cancellation, the behavior of a sum of fair coins, explains why \tfrac12 is the natural exponent, and a sieve to 10^7 shows \lvert\psi(x)-x\rvert/\sqrt x and \lvert M(x)\rvert/\sqrt x below 1 at every integer x\ge2.
  • The smoothed sum S(X)=\sum_{n\le X}\Lambda(n)(X/n-1) has an explicit formula with an absolutely convergent zero sum, verified numerically and bounded by 0.0462\sqrt X under the hypothesis.
  • Equivalent forms (Littlewood’s bound on M(x), Robin’s divisor inequality, and Weil’s positivity in the next chapter).
  • The generalizations to Dirichlet characters, number fields, and Hecke characters, with \zeta_{\QQ(i)}=\zeta\cdot L(s,\chi_4) as the example and a table that lines up the three hypotheses.

Part II takes the explicit formula as its starting point. Chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion replaces the sharp cutoff and the smoothed ramp by an arbitrary test function, so that the formula becomes a duality between the primes and the zeros, and it shows that the hypothesis is a statement that a certain quadratic form is nonnegative. Chapters The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields and Stepanov's proof then turn to the one world in which the analogue was proved long ago, curves over finite fields, and explain what that proof used that the integers lack, which is where Parts III and IV begin.
