Chapter 10

Stepanov's proof

Follow Stepanov’s method in Bombieri’s form from the auxiliary function to the Riemann Hypothesis for curves, and name the four ingredients, Frobenius, cheap multiplicity, Riemann and Roch, and the Galois trick, that the integers do not supply directly.

Builds on 9. The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields, 8. Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion

In plain terms

To show that an equation has few solutions, build a polynomial that vanishes at every solution, many times over, while keeping its degree small. A polynomial cannot vanish more times than its degree, so the solutions must be few. Over a finite field this trick is cheap, because raising to the power p makes a function vanish p times at once, and it proves the Riemann Hypothesis for curves with nothing more than linear algebra and a count of dimensions.

The note behind the second proof of 2026 calls its argument a descendant of Stepanov’s. It says that Stepanov’s argument uses multiplicity, that multiplicity is what is hard to find over the integers, and it lists a “Stepanov determinant” in its timeline [2]. This chapter gives the function-field argument completely, in the form Bombieri gave Stepanov’s method in 1973, so that every later use of the words “auxiliary function”, “multiplicity”, and “Stepanov determinant” refers to something the reader has seen work [54; 50]. A textbook account of the same proof is the appendix of Rosen’s book [47, appendix]. Each step is shown in parallel on the curve y^2 = x^3 + x + 1, the elliptic curve of The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields.

10.1The idea: vanish too often#

The whole method rests on the fact that a nonzero polynomial cannot have more roots than its degree, counted with multiplicity.

Definition 10.1 Order of vanishing

A polynomial R vanishes to order at least m at a point r when (x - r)^m divides R, equivalently when R and its first m - 1 derivatives vanish at r in characteristic 0. On a curve, the order \ord_P(h) of a function h at a point P is the exponent of a local parameter in h: positive at a zero, negative at a pole, and 0 otherwise. It is an integer attached to a point, not a value of the function.

Theorem 10.2 A nonzero polynomial of degree D that vanishes to order at least m at N distinct points satisfies mN\le D

If R \ne 0 has degree D and (x - r_i)^m divides R for N distinct r_1, \dots, r_N, then mN \le D.

Proof

The factors (x - r_i)^m are pairwise coprime, so their product, of degree mN, divides R.

On its own this bounds the number of roots of R, which is useless if the set we care about is described by a polynomial of large degree. Stepanov’s point is to bound a set S by building, for the occasion, an auxiliary R that vanishes on S to high order m while its degree D grows more slowly than m times the true size of S. Then \abs S \le D/m, and the art is to make D/m close to the truth.

Example

Count the x \in \FF_{101} for which f(x) = x^3 + x + 1 is a nonzero square. They are the roots of f(x)^{50} - 1, since by Euler’s criterion a^{50} = 1 exactly for nonzero squares in \FF_{101}. That polynomial has degree 150, so the obvious bound is 150, while the true count is 52 (and the curve has N_1 = 2\cdot 52 + 1 = 105 points, as f has no root modulo 101). The expected count is about p/2 = 50.5. Stepanov’s elementary argument builds an auxiliary polynomial of the shape

R(x) = f(x)^K \sum_{j} \bigl( r_j(x) + s_j(x)\, f(x)^{(p-1)/2} \bigr) x^{jp}

with unknown polynomials r_j, s_j of small degree, and imposes vanishing to order K at every x in the set. The factor x^{jp} is invisible to the first p - 1 derivatives, because \frac{\dd}{\dd x} x^{jp} = jp\,x^{jp-1} = 0 in characteristic p, and on the set itself x^p = x and f(x)^{(p-1)/2} = 1. So the vanishing conditions become conditions on the few coefficients of the r_j and s_j alone, a small linear system, and the result is a bound p/2 + O(\sqrt p), with the implied constant depending only on \deg f [33, §11.6; 55, ch. I].

The rest of the chapter replaces polynomials in x by functions on a curve, which removes all special features of y^2 = f(x), and replaces derivatives by p-th powers, which removes the need to compute any derivative at all.

10.2Functions on a curve and the Riemann and Roch count#

On a curve the role of the degree is played by the poles. A rational function on C is a quotient of polynomials in the coordinates, taken modulo the equation of C. These functions form a field \FF_q(C), the function field of C, and every nonzero h in it has finitely many zeros and poles.

Theorem 10.3 A nonzero rational function on a smooth projective curve has as many zeros as poles, counted with multiplicity [51]

For h \in \FF_q(C) nonzero, \sum_P \ord_P(h) = 0, the sum running over the points of C over \overline{\FF}_q.

This is the curve version of Theorem 10.2. A polynomial of degree D in x, seen as a function on the projective line, has a pole of order D at infinity and nowhere else, so it has D zeros counted with multiplicity [51, ch. II, §6]. On a curve, a function whose only pole is at one point P_0, of order at most k, has at most k zeros counted with multiplicity. So the space of such functions is the space of “polynomials of degree at most k” on C, and we need its dimension.

Definition 10.4 Riemann and Roch space

For a point P_0 \in C(\FF_q) and an integer k \ge 0, L(kP_0) is the set of h \in \FF_q(C) that are regular everywhere except possibly at P_0, where the pole has order at most k, together with h = 0. It is a finite-dimensional vector space over \FF_q, and \ell(k) = \dim L(kP_0). It is not a ring, since products add pole orders, and it is not the space of all functions with poles bounded by k somewhere. More generally, for a formal sum D = \sum n_P P of points, L(D) is the space of h with \ord_P(h) \ge -n_P at every P.

Theorem 10.5

Functions with a single pole of order at most k form a space of dimension at least k+1-g, with equality once k\ge2g-1

[51]
Statement

Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g over \FF_q, P_0 \in C(\FF_q), and D a divisor of degree d defined over \FF_q. Then \ell(D) \le d + 1 when d \ge 0, \ell(D) \ge d + 1 - g, and \ell(D) = d + 1 - g when d \ge 2g - 1. For D = kP_0 the spaces are nested, L((k-1)P_0) \subseteq L(kP_0), with \ell(k) - \ell(k-1) \in \{0, 1\}, so L(kP_0) has a basis of functions with pairwise distinct pole orders at P_0.

In plain terms

On a curve of genus g there are about as many functions with a pole of order at most k at one point as there are polynomials of degree at most k, minus g, and the shortfall of exactly g is reached once k reaches 2g - 1.

Why it is needed

Stepanov’s argument creates an auxiliary function by solving a linear system whose unknowns and equations are dimensions of such spaces. Without this count there is no way to know that unknowns outnumber equations.

Idea

The genus measures how many pole orders are missing. Each step k - 1 \to k either adds a function with a pole of exact order k or adds nothing, and the theorem says that exactly g steps add nothing, all of them at k \le 2g - 1. The equality comes from the full Riemann and Roch theorem, \ell(D) - \ell(K - D) = d + 1 - g with K a canonical divisor of degree 2g - 2, since \ell(K - D) = 0 once d > 2g - 2.

Proof sketch

[51, ch. IV, §1]

The Riemann and Roch theorem and its consequences listed here are in Hartshorne [51, ch. IV, §1]. The nesting statement follows because a function in L(kP_0) is determined modulo L((k-1)P_0) by one coefficient, its leading term in a local parameter at P_0. Choosing one function at each step where the dimension rises gives the basis with distinct pole orders.

Example

For y^2 = f(x) with f squarefree of odd degree 2g + 1 and P_\infty the point at infinity, x has a pole of order 2 at P_\infty and y a pole of order 2g + 1, and neither has other poles. The functions x^i (pole order 2i) and x^i y (pole order 2i + 2g + 1) have distinct pole orders, hence are linearly independent. The orders reached are every even number and every odd number from 2g + 1 on, so the missing orders, the gaps, are 1, 3, \dots, 2g - 1, exactly g of them. This agrees with the theorem and confirms the genus g = \lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor claimed in The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields. For the elliptic curve y^2 = x^3 + x + 1 (g = 1):

k 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
new basis function 1 none x y x^2 xy x^3 x^2y
\ell(k) 1 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
k + 1 - g 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7

From k = 1 = 2g - 1 on, \ell(k) = k + 1 - g exactly.

Used in

The counts enter Lemma 10.8 and the choice of parameters in Theorem 10.9.

10.3Frobenius turns being rational into an equation#

The set Stepanov counts, C(\FF_q), must be described by an equation that the auxiliary function can use. Frobenius provides it. A function h \in \FF_q(C) has coefficients in \FF_q, and a^q = a for those coefficients, so raising h to the power q raises its arguments instead,

h(P)^q = h\bigl(\Frob(P)\bigr) \qquad \text{for every point } P \text{ at which } h \text{ is regular},
(10.1)

where \Frob raises each coordinate of P to the power q. At a rational point \Frob(P) = P, so h(P)^q = h(P). Being a rational point, a property defined by which field the coordinates lie in, becomes an identity between the function h^q and the function h that holds at those points.

Example

On y^2 = x^3 + x + 1 over \FF_q, at every rational affine point x^q = x and y^q = y. As functions on the curve x^q and x differ, but y^q = y\cdot(y^2)^{(q-1)/2} = y\, f(x)^{(q-1)/2}, so the condition y^q = y at a point with y \ne 0 says f(x)^{(q-1)/2} = 1, the Euler criterion of the example in The idea: vanish too often. Frobenius has turned “f(x) is a square in \FF_q” into a polynomial identity at the point.

The second gift of characteristic p is that p-th powers vanish deeply. Because (a + b)^p = a^p + b^p, the map h \mapsto h^{p^\mu} respects sums, and orders of vanishing multiply: \ord_P(h^{p^\mu}) = p^\mu \ord_P(h). So if h is regular at P and h(P) = 0, then h^{p^\mu} vanishes at P to order at least p^\mu. In the language of derivatives, \frac{\dd}{\dd x}\bigl(h^{p}\bigr) = p\,h^{p-1}h' = 0, so a p-th power has vanishing derivative everywhere and any zero of it is automatically a multiple zero. Multiplicity, which in characteristic 0 costs one linear condition per derivative, is free.

10.4The auxiliary function#

Fix from now on a smooth projective curve C of genus g over \FF_q with q = p^{2\mu} a square, so \sqrt q = p^\mu, and a rational point P_0 \in C(\FF_q) (if there is none, N_1 = 0 and there is nothing to bound). Fix integers A, B \ge 0, and let e_1, \dots, e_r be a basis of L(AP_0) with distinct pole orders, as in Theorem 10.5, so r = \ell(A). The auxiliary function will be

F = \sum_{i=1}^{r} e_i^{p^\mu}\, b_i^{q}, \qquad b_1, \dots, b_r \in L(BP_0),
(10.2)

with the b_i chosen so that the companion function \sum_i e_i^{p^\mu} b_i, in which b_i^q is replaced by b_i, vanishes identically. Three lemmas say that F then vanishes to order p^\mu at every rational point other than P_0, that F is not zero, and that such b_i exist.

Lemma 10.6

If the companion sum \sum_i e_i^{p^\mu}b_i is identically zero, then F vanishes to order at least p^\mu at every rational point other than P_0

[50]
Statement

If b_1, \dots, b_r \in L(BP_0) satisfy \sum_{i} e_i^{p^\mu} b_i = 0 in \FF_q(C), then the function F of Equation (10.2) lies in L\bigl((Ap^\mu + Bq)P_0\bigr), it equals \bigl(\sum_i e_i\, b_i^{p^\mu}\bigr)^{p^\mu}, and \ord_P(F) \ge p^\mu for every P \in C(\FF_q) with P \ne P_0.

In plain terms

Replace b_i^q by b_i and the sum becomes zero by construction. At a rational point the replacement changes nothing, so F is zero there, and because F is a p^\mu-th power, it is zero there p^\mu times over.

Why it is needed

This is where the count of rational points enters: every one of them is forced to be a deep zero of one function with a bounded pole.

Idea

Frobenius makes b_i^q and b_i agree at rational points, so F agrees there with the companion sum, which is zero. The power structure gives the multiplicity.

Proof

Each e_i^{p^\mu} has a pole of order at most Ap^\mu at P_0 and each b_i^q one of order at most Bq, with no other poles, so F \in L((Ap^\mu + Bq)P_0). Since q = p^\mu \cdot p^\mu, we have b_i^q = (b_i^{p^\mu})^{p^\mu}, and h \mapsto h^{p^\mu} respects sums, so F = \bigl(\sum_i e_i b_i^{p^\mu}\bigr)^{p^\mu}. Let P \ne P_0 be rational. All e_i and b_i are regular at P, and by Equation (10.1) b_i(P)^q = b_i(P). Hence

F(P) = \sum_i e_i(P)^{p^\mu}\, b_i(P)^q = \sum_i e_i(P)^{p^\mu}\, b_i(P) = \Bigl(\sum_i e_i^{p^\mu} b_i\Bigr)(P) = 0.

So h = \sum_i e_i b_i^{p^\mu} satisfies h(P)^{p^\mu} = F(P) = 0, hence h(P) = 0, \ord_P(h) \ge 1, and \ord_P(F) = p^\mu \ord_P(h) \ge p^\mu.

Used in

Combined with Lemma 10.7 and Theorem 10.3 it gives the bound of Theorem 10.9.

The function F might still be zero, and then the lemma says nothing. The next lemma excludes this when A is small, by looking at pole orders at P_0.

Lemma 10.7

If A<p^\mu and some b_i is nonzero, then the auxiliary function is not zero

[50]
Statement

Suppose A < p^\mu. If b_1, \dots, b_r \in \FF_q(C) are not all zero, then \sum_i e_i\, b_i^{p^\mu} \ne 0, and therefore F \ne 0.

In plain terms

The basis functions e_i have different pole orders, all smaller than p^\mu, while p^\mu-th powers have pole orders divisible by p^\mu. The terms of the sum therefore have different pole orders and cannot cancel.

Why it is needed

Without it the auxiliary function could vanish identically and bound nothing. It is the only place where the size of A is restricted, and it is what forces q to be a square.

Idea

Look at the order of each term at P_0. Two integers -n_i + p^\mu k and -n_j + p^\mu k' with 0 \le n_i \ne n_j < p^\mu are never equal, so at most one term attains the smallest order, and a sum whose terms have distinct orders has the smallest of them as its order.

Proof

Let n_i be the pole order of e_i at P_0, so \ord_{P_0}(e_i) = -n_i with 0 \le n_i \le A < p^\mu, and the n_i are distinct. For b_i \ne 0, \ord_{P_0}(e_i b_i^{p^\mu}) = -n_i + p^\mu \ord_{P_0}(b_i) \equiv -n_i \pmod{p^\mu}. The nonzero terms therefore have pairwise distinct orders at P_0. For functions with distinct orders at a point, the order of the sum is the minimum of the orders, which is finite, so the sum is not zero. Then F = (\sum_i e_i b_i^{p^\mu})^{p^\mu} \ne 0.

Used in

Used in Theorem 10.9 and in the twisted counts of Theorem 10.12.

It remains to find b_i, not all zero, with \sum_i e_i^{p^\mu} b_i = 0. This is linear algebra over \FF_q.

Lemma 10.8

When the product of the dimensions of L(AP_0) and L(BP_0) exceeds the dimension of L((Ap^\mu+B)P_0), the auxiliary function exists

[50]
Statement

If \ell(A)\,\ell(B) > \ell(Ap^\mu + B), there are b_1, \dots, b_r \in L(BP_0), not all zero, with \sum_i e_i^{p^\mu} b_i = 0.

In plain terms

There are more unknown coefficients than conditions, so a nonzero solution exists.

Why it is needed

This is where Riemann and Roch is used, and the inequality decides how large q must be compared with g.

Idea

The map (b_1, \dots, b_r) \mapsto \sum_i e_i^{p^\mu} b_i is linear over \FF_q, from a space of dimension \ell(A)\ell(B) into L((Ap^\mu + B)P_0).

Proof

For fixed e_i the map b \mapsto e_i^{p^\mu} b is \FF_q-linear, so \Phi(b_1, \dots, b_r) = \sum_i e_i^{p^\mu} b_i is a linear map from L(BP_0)^r, of dimension r\,\ell(B) = \ell(A)\ell(B), to \FF_q(C). Each term has poles only at P_0, of order at most Ap^\mu + B, so \Phi takes values in L((Ap^\mu + B)P_0), of dimension \ell(Ap^\mu + B). A linear map from a larger space to a smaller one has a nonzero kernel.

Example

For E: y^2 = x^3 + x + 1 over \FF_{25} (so p = 5, \mu = 1, p^\mu = 5, g = 1), take A = 4 and B = 7, with e_1, \dots, e_4 = 1, x, y, x^2 and L(7P_\infty) spanned by 1, x, y, x^2, xy, x^3, x^2y. There are 4 \cdot 7 = 28 unknown coefficients, and \Phi lands in L(27P_\infty), of dimension 27. Solving the 27 \times 28 system over \FF_{25} (we used \FF_{25} = \FF_5(t) with t^2 = 3) gives a kernel of dimension exactly 1. The system has coefficients in \FF_5, so the kernel is spanned by a solution with coefficients in \FF_5:

b_1 = 2 + x + 2x^2 + x^3,\quad b_2 = 2x + 4x^2 + 3x^3,\quad b_3 = (3 + 4x^2)\,y,\quad b_4 = x.

The identity b_1 + x^5 b_2 + y^5 b_3 + x^{10} b_4 = 0 holds in \FF_5[x, y]/(y^2 - x^3 - x - 1): with y^6 = (x^3 + x + 1)^3 it becomes a polynomial identity in x modulo 5, which we checked. The function h = \sum_i e_i b_i^5 is then a polynomial in x alone of degree 19, so its pole order at P_\infty is 38 \le A + B\sqrt q = 39, and it vanishes at all 26 affine points of E(\FF_{25}), as Lemma 10.6 predicts. The auxiliary function is F = h^5.

Used in

The inequality is checked for the chosen A and B in Theorem 10.9.

10.5The upper bound#

The three lemmas combine into a bound once A and B are chosen. The choice A = \sqrt q - 1 is the largest that Lemma 10.7 allows, and B = \sqrt q + 2g is the smallest that makes the dimension count work for large q.

Theorem 10.9

A curve of genus g over a square field with q>(g+1)^4 has at most q+1+(2g+1)\sqrt q rational points

[50]
Statement

Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g over \FF_q, with q a square and q > (g+1)^4. Then

N_1 \le q + (2g + 1)\sqrt q \;\le\; q + 1 + (2g+1)\sqrt q.
(10.3)
In plain terms

On a curve of genus g over a large enough field, the number of points exceeds q by at most 2g + 1 square roots of q.

Why it is needed

This is the upper half of the Riemann Hypothesis for curves, with a constant 2g + 1 instead of 2g, which Lemma 9.7 shows is good enough.

Idea

The auxiliary function has a pole of order at most A\sqrt q + Bq at P_0, and a zero of order at least \sqrt q at each of the other N_1 - 1 rational points. Dividing by \sqrt q gives N_1 - 1 \le A + B\sqrt q, which is about q + 2g\sqrt q.

Proof
Steps
  1. Set the parameters A = \sqrt q - 1 and B = \sqrt q + 2g, so that A < p^\mu = \sqrt q, as Lemma 10.7 requires. Both B and Ap^\mu + B are at least 2g - 1, so Theorem 10.5 gives their dimensions exactly, and A + 1 - g = \sqrt q - g > 0 because \sqrt q > (g+1)^2.
A\sqrt q + B = q - \sqrt q + \sqrt q + 2g = q + 2g.
  1. Count dimensions with Theorem 10.5: \ell(A) \ge A + 1 - g = \sqrt q - g, \ell(B) = B + 1 - g = \sqrt q + g + 1, and \ell(A\sqrt q + B) = q + g + 1.
\ell(A)\ell(B) - \ell(A\sqrt q + B) \ge (\sqrt q - g)(\sqrt q + g + 1) - (q + g + 1) = \sqrt q - (g+1)^2 > 0.
  1. By Lemma 10.8 there are b_i \in L(BP_0), not all zero, with \sum_i e_i^{p^\mu}b_i = 0. By Lemma 10.7 the function F of Equation (10.2) is not zero, and by Lemma 10.6 it has order at least \sqrt q at each of the N_1 - 1 rational points P \ne P_0 and a pole only at P_0, of order at most A\sqrt q + Bq.
\sqrt q\,(N_1 - 1) \le \sum_{P \ne P_0} \ord_P(F) \le A\sqrt q + Bq,

where the second inequality is Theorem 10.3: the zeros of F, counted with multiplicity, number at most its poles. 4. Divide by \sqrt q and insert the parameters.

N_1 \le 1 + A + B\sqrt q = 1 + (\sqrt q - 1) + (q + 2g\sqrt q) = q + (2g+1)\sqrt q.
Example

For E over \FF_{25}, g = 1 and q = 25 > 16 = (g+1)^4. The parameters are A = 4 and B = 7, as in the example of Lemma 10.8, with 28 > 27, and the bound is N_1 \le 25 + 3 \cdot 5 = 40. The true count is 27, and Hasse’s bound is 26 + 2\cdot 5 = 36. At q = 16 the count gives \ell(3)\ell(6) = 18 against \ell(18) = 18, no strict inequality, and at q = 9 it gives 10 against 11: the method genuinely needs \sqrt q > (g+1)^2. Over \FF_{25^n} the bound is 25^n + 3\cdot 5^n, which is q^n + O(q^{n/2}), the shape the Riemann Hypothesis needs.

Used in

Applied over every field \FF_{q^n} in Theorem 10.13, and to twisted counts in Theorem 10.12.

A common misreading

The bound N_1 \le q + (2g+1)\sqrt q is weaker than Weil’s q + 1 + 2g\sqrt q for a single field, and it says nothing when q \le (g+1)^4. Neither matters. The theorem is applied to \FF_{q^n} for all large n, where both conditions hold, and Lemma 9.7 converts any constant into the exact statement \abs{\alpha_i} = \sqrt q, from which Weil’s bound for every n follows.

10.6The lower bound through a Galois cover#

An auxiliary function can only bound a count from above, because it shows that zeros cannot be too many. To bound N_1 from below, Bombieri counted the points that a curve misses and showed that they are themselves the rational points of other curves, to which the upper bound applies [50]. The hyperelliptic case shows the whole idea with no Galois theory.

Example

Let d \in \FF_q be a nonsquare and let E'\colon d\,y^2 = f(x) be the quadratic twist of E\colon y^2 = f(x), with \deg f odd and q odd. Each x \in \FF_q with f(x) = 0 gives one point on each curve. Each x with f(x) a nonzero square gives two points on E and none on E', and each x with f(x) a nonsquare gives none on E and two on E', since then f(x)/d is a square. With one point at infinity on each,

N_1(E) + N_1(E') = 2q + 2.

So the upper bound for E' is a lower bound for E: N_1(E) \ge 2q + 2 - \bigl(q + (2g+1)\sqrt q\bigr) = q + 2 - (2g+1)\sqrt q. For y^2 = x^3 + x + 1 over \FF_5 the twist 2y^2 = x^3 + x + 1 has 3 points and 9 + 3 = 12, and over \FF_7 the twist 3y^2 = x^3 + x + 1 has 11 points and 5 + 11 = 16.

In the language of Frobenius the twist counts points P of E over \overline{\FF}_q with \Frob(P) = \iota(P), where \iota(x, y) = (x, -y): such a point has x \in \FF_q and y^q = -y, so y \notin \FF_q unless y = 0, while y^2 = f(x) \in \FF_q. The two curves share the map x to the projective line, whose group of symmetries is \{1, \iota\}, and every rational point of the line lifts to points fixed by either \Frob or \iota^{-1}\Frob. The general argument replaces \{1, \iota\} by the Galois group of a cover.

Definition 10.10 Twisted point count

Let C' be a curve over \FF_q and \sigma an automorphism of C' defined over \FF_q, so that \sigma commutes with \Frob. The twisted count is

N_\sigma = \#\{P \in C'(\overline{\FF}_q) : \Frob(P) = \sigma(P)\}.

For \sigma = 1 it is N_1(C'). It is a count of points of C' over \overline{\FF}_q, not of points over \FF_q, and it is the number of rational points of the twist of C' by \sigma, a curve of the same genus.

Lemma 10.11

Every twisted count obeys the same upper bound as the curve itself, up to one extra point

[50]
Statement

Let C' have genus g' and a point P_0 \in C'(\FF_q), with q a square and q > (g'+1)^4. For every automorphism \sigma of C' defined over \FF_q,

N_\sigma \le q + 1 + (2g'+1)\sqrt q.
In plain terms

Points that Frobenius moves by a symmetry instead of fixing are no more numerous than the fixed ones could be.

Why it is needed

The lower bound for C subtracts these counts from a total, so each needs an upper bound of the same quality.

Idea

Run the same argument with b_i \circ \sigma in place of b_i in the companion sum. At a point with \Frob(P) = \sigma(P), Equation (10.1) gives b_i(P)^q = b_i(\sigma P), which is what the companion sum evaluates.

Proof

Take e_i, A, B as in Theorem 10.9, and replace the companion condition by G_\sigma = \sum_i e_i^{p^\mu}\,(b_i\circ\sigma) = 0. The point \sigma^{-1}(P_0) is rational because \sigma commutes with \Frob, so G_\sigma lies in L(D) with D = Ap^\mu P_0 + B\,\sigma^{-1}(P_0), a divisor over \FF_q of degree Ap^\mu + B, and the dimension count of Theorem 10.9 goes through unchanged. If \Frob(P) = \sigma(P) and P \ne P_0, \sigma(P) \ne P_0, then F(P) = \sum_i e_i(P)^{p^\mu}b_i(\sigma P) = G_\sigma(P) = 0, and F \ne 0 by Lemma 10.7, which does not involve \sigma. Counting zeros as before, with at most two excluded points, gives N_\sigma \le 2 + A + B\sqrt q = q + 1 + (2g'+1)\sqrt q.

Used in

Used in Theorem 10.12.

Theorem 10.12

A curve has at least q minus a constant times \sqrt q rational points, by counting the points that its Galois twists catch

[50]
Statement

Let C be a smooth projective curve over \FF_q and x\colon C \to \mathbb P^1 a nonconstant separable function of degree d. Let C' \to \mathbb P^1 be the Galois closure, with group G, and H \subseteq G the subgroup with C = C'/H, so d = \abs G/\abs H. Assume \FF_q is algebraically closed in the function field of C', that C' has a rational point, and that q is a square with q > (g'+1)^4, where g' is the genus of C'. If r is the number of branch points of C' \to \mathbb P^1 over \overline{\FF}_q, then

N_1(C) \ge q + 1 - d\,r - (d - 1)(2g'+1)\sqrt q.
In plain terms

Every rational point of the line has rational points above it on exactly one of several twisted copies of the curve. The copies together have as many points as they should, and each copy has at most its share plus a square root, so no copy, including C itself, can have much less than its share.

Why it is needed

The upper bound alone cannot locate the zeros. The lower bound, with any constant, completes the two-sided estimate that Lemma 9.7 needs.

Idea

Over an unramified rational point t of the line, the \abs G points of C' form one orbit of G, and \Frob maps the orbit to itself, so it acts on each point as some \sigma \in G. Summing N_\sigma over all \sigma \in G counts the line’s points \abs G times, while the sum over \sigma \in H counts the points of C at most \abs H times. Subtract.

Proof
Show the proof

Write \pi\colon C' \to \mathbb P^1 and \varrho\colon C' \to C for the quotient maps, both defined over \FF_q, with \pi\circ\sigma = \pi for \sigma \in G and \varrho\circ\sigma = \varrho for \sigma \in H.

Steps
  1. The sum over G counts the line. Let t \in \mathbb P^1(\FF_q) not be a branch point. Its fiber \pi^{-1}(t) has \abs G points permuted simply transitively by G, and \Frob preserves it because \pi(\Frob P) = \Frob(\pi P) = t. So each P in the fiber satisfies \Frob(P) = \sigma(P) for exactly one \sigma \in G, and the fiber contributes exactly \abs G to the sum below. At most r rational points of the line are branch points.
\sum_{\sigma \in G} N_\sigma \ge \abs G\,(q + 1 - r).
  1. The sum over H counts C. If \Frob(P) = \sigma(P) with \sigma \in H, then Q = \varrho(P) satisfies \Frob(Q) = \varrho(\sigma P) = Q, so Q \in C(\FF_q). The fiber \varrho^{-1}(Q) is one H-orbit, and for P in it the set of \sigma \in H with \Frob(P) = \sigma(P) is empty or a coset of the stabilizer of P. Since the fiber size times the stabilizer size is \abs H, each Q contributes at most \abs H.
\sum_{\sigma \in H} N_\sigma \le \abs H\, N_1(C).
  1. The other twists are bounded above. By Lemma 10.11, N_\sigma \le q + 1 + (2g'+1)\sqrt q for each of the \abs G - \abs H elements \sigma \notin H. Combining with steps 1 and 2,
\abs H\, N_1(C) \ge \abs G(q + 1 - r) - (\abs G - \abs H)\bigl(q + 1 + (2g'+1)\sqrt q\bigr).
  1. Divide by \abs H and use d = \abs G/\abs H.
N_1(C) \ge q + 1 - d\,r - (d-1)(2g'+1)\sqrt q.

For y^2 = f(x) and the function x, C' = C, G = \{1, \iota\}, H = \{1\}, and d = 2, and step 1 holds with equality including the ramified points, which gives the exact identity of the example above.

Used in

Used in Theorem 10.13.

10.7From the bounds to the zeros#

The two bounds hold over every large enough field, and Lemma 9.7 turns them into the statement about zeros.

Theorem 10.13

Every inverse root of the zeta function of a curve over \FF_q has absolute value \sqrt q

[48]
Statement

For every smooth projective curve C of genus g over \FF_q, the inverse roots of Z(C, u) satisfy \abs{\alpha_i} = \sqrt q, and \abs{N_n - q^n - 1} \le 2g\,q^{n/2} for every n \ge 1.

In plain terms

The Riemann Hypothesis holds for every curve over every finite field.

Why it is needed

This is the statement Theorem 9.6 announced, now with a complete proof that uses only linear algebra on the curve, Frobenius, and the Riemann and Roch count.

Idea

Pass to a field \FF_{q^{n_0}} over which every hypothesis of the two bounds holds, apply them over all its extensions, and let Lemma 9.7 convert the two-sided bound into the location of the inverse roots.

Proof
Steps
  1. Choose a separating function x on C (one exists because \FF_q is perfect), and let C' be the Galois closure of C \to \mathbb P^1, with genus g'. Its field of constants is a finite extension \FF_{q^{k}}, and C' has a point over some \FF_{q^{j}}. Let n_0 be a common multiple of 2, k, and j. Over \FF_{q^{n_0 m}} for every m \ge 1, the field size is a square, C' is a curve with a rational point and constant field the base field, and for m \ge m_0 the size exceeds (g'+1)^4 \ge (g+1)^4.
Q_m = q^{n_0 m}, \qquad \sqrt{Q_m} = q^{n_0 m/2}.
  1. Over \FF_{Q_m}, Theorem 10.9 (which holds trivially if C has no rational point there) and Theorem 10.12 give, for m \ge m_0,
-d\,r - (d-1)(2g'+1)\sqrt{Q_m} \le N_{n_0 m} - Q_m - 1 \le (2g+1)\sqrt{Q_m}.
  1. Hence \abs{N_{n_0 m} - Q_m - 1} \le c\,Q_m^{1/2} for a constant c and all m \ge m_0. By Equation (9.9), N_{n_0 m} = Q_m + 1 - \sum_i (\alpha_i^{n_0})^m, so the numbers \beta_i = \alpha_i^{n_0} are the inverse roots of C over \FF_{q^{n_0}}, and they satisfy the functional equation with q^{n_0} in place of q. By Lemma 9.7 applied over \FF_{q^{n_0}}, \abs{\alpha_i^{n_0}} = q^{n_0/2}.
\abs{\alpha_i} = \sqrt q.
  1. The bound \abs{N_n - q^n - 1} = \abs{\sum_i \alpha_i^n} \le 2g\,q^{n/2} follows from the triangle inequality.
Used in

This completes Theorem 9.6. Part IV adapts the shape of the argument to the integers.

Aside

Weil’s own proofs of 1948 went differently, and they connect this chapter to Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion. In the first, the graph \Gamma of Frobenius and the diagonal \Delta are curves on the surface C \times C, their intersection number \Gamma\cdot\Delta is N_1, and the Castelnuovo and Severi inequality, a positivity statement for intersection numbers on a surface, applied to combinations a\Gamma + b\Delta, makes a certain quadratic form in a and b nonnegative. Its discriminant condition is exactly \abs{N_1 - q - 1} \le 2g\sqrt q [48; 51, ch. V, ex. 1.10]. The second proof uses the positivity of the Rosati involution on endomorphisms of the Jacobian. In both, the Riemann Hypothesis for curves is the nonnegativity of a quadratic form, which is the shape of Theorem 8.9. Stepanov’s method avoids the surface entirely and bounds the counts directly, which is why it, and not Weil’s geometry, is the model for an argument over the integers, where no surface \mathrm{Spec}\,\ZZ \times \mathrm{Spec}\,\ZZ with the needed intersection theory is known.

10.8What the proof used#

Four ingredients did the work. For each, the integers offer something and lack something. The note behind the second proof of 2026 names integer substitutes for some of them, and this section records the ingredients in the vocabulary Part IV uses. The comparisons with the integers below are our reading except where the note is quoted.

Frobenius. The identity h(P)^q = h(\Frob P) turned “the coordinates of P lie in \FF_q” into the algebraic statement b^q = b at P, which a function can be built to exploit. The integers have no such map. The only ring endomorphism of \ZZ is the identity, and modulo a prime p the Frobenius a \mapsto a^p is the identity of \FF_p by Fermat’s theorem, so it cuts out nothing. In Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion the absence appears as the missing operator of the Hilbert and Polya idea: over a curve the zeros are eigenvalues of Frobenius, and over \ZZ there is no known operator with the zeros as spectrum.

Derivatives and p-th powers. Vanishing to order m was free, because a p^\mu-th power that vanishes at a point vanishes there to order p^\mu, and in Stepanov’s elementary version because x^{jp} is invisible to derivatives of order below p. Over the integers the natural notion of “vanishing to order m at p” is divisibility by p^m, and there is no derivative to detect it: every additive map \delta\colon\ZZ\to\ZZ with \delta(ab) = a\delta(b) + b\delta(a) is zero, because \delta(1) = \delta(1\cdot 1) = 2\delta(1) forces \delta(1) = 0 and then \delta(n) = n\delta(1) = 0. The note behind the second proof describes the difficulty in these terms, saying that over the integers multiplicity corresponds to “something like differentiating whole numbers” [2]. One partial substitute is Buium’s theory of arithmetic derivatives, in which the Fermat quotient n \mapsto (n - n^p)/p plays the role of a derivative with respect to p [56]. The note takes a different route, a chain of theta lifts, “each mimicking multiplicity”, with about \sqrt X lifts for the von Mangoldt sum of length X [2]. Part IV describes it.

Riemann and Roch. The count \ell(D) = \deg D + 1 - g guaranteed that unknowns outnumbered equations. Over the integers, “functions with bounded poles” become integers or lattice vectors of bounded size, and the count becomes a count of lattice points. Its standard form for linear systems is Siegel’s lemma: a system of M linear equations in K > M unknowns with integer coefficients of absolute value at most H has a nonzero integer solution with every entry at most (KH)^{M/(K-M)} in absolute value [57]. Arakelov geometry refines such counts into an arithmetic Riemann and Roch theory, and one of its tools, Bost’s slope inequality, appears in the timeline of the second proof [58; 2].

The Galois trick. The lower bound came from summing over twists: the twisted counts N_\sigma over all \sigma \in G add up to a known total, so upper bounds for all but one give a lower bound for the last. Over the integers the analog of summing over twists is summing over characters, as in the orthogonality relation for Dirichlet characters in What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations, which recovers primes in one progression from sums over all characters. This analogy is ours.

The method can also be phrased with determinants, the form in which the integer version is built. Choose points P_1, \dots, P_K and functions \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_K, and form the K\times K matrix \bigl(\varphi_j(P_i)\bigr). Its determinant \Delta vanishes exactly when some nonzero combination \sum_j c_j\varphi_j vanishes at every P_i, that is, exactly when an auxiliary function through the points exists. Here each point imposes one condition, vanishing, and we say the argument has multiplicity one. To demand vanishing to order m, each point contributes m rows, its value and m - 1 derivatives (or, in characteristic p, the condition is absorbed by p-th powers as above), and the argument has multiplicity m. Stepanov’s gain is entirely in the multiplicity: with multiplicity one the same count only shows that N_1 is at most the degree of an auxiliary function, which gives nothing better than the trivial bound.

Over \ZZ, with integer points and integer-valued \varphi_j, the determinant \Delta is an integer, and a nonzero integer has absolute value at least 1. So if one can show that \Delta is divisible by a large power p^e (because the points agree modulo p, which is the arithmetic form of high multiplicity) and also that \abs\Delta < p^e (an analytic size estimate), then \Delta = 0 and the auxiliary function exists. This is the determinant method of Bombieri and Pila, in its real form, and of Heath-Brown, in its p-adic form [59; 60]. The timeline in the note behind the second proof lists a “Stepanov determinant” as its first item, and it describes a step that proves “W(1_S) \ge 0 via a determinant”, with W Weil’s functional of Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion and 1_S the indicator of a set S, as “Stepanov with multiplicity one again” [2]. In the terms of this section, and as our reading rather than the note’s words, the first is an auxiliary-function determinant of the kind just described, and the second is an argument of this shape in which each point imposes a single condition.

Symbols
Symbol What it is Kind Where it lives
\ord_P(h) order of vanishing of h at P integer Definition 10.1
\FF_q(C) function field of C field Functions on a curve and the Riemann and Roch count
L(D), \ell(D) functions with poles bounded by D, and its dimension vector space, integer Definition 10.4
P_0 a fixed rational point point of C The auxiliary function
p^\mu \sqrt q, with q = p^{2\mu} integer The auxiliary function
A, B pole bounds of the e_i and b_i integers Theorem 10.9
e_i, b_i, F basis of L(AP_0), unknowns, auxiliary function functions on C Equation (10.2)
N_\sigma twisted count integer Definition 10.10
G, H, d, r Galois group, subgroup, degree, branch points group, integers Theorem 10.12
Recap
  • An auxiliary function that vanishes to order m at N points and has degree, or pole order, D forces mN \le D (Theorem 10.2, Theorem 10.3).
  • Frobenius makes rational points satisfy b^q = b, and p-th powers make vanishing automatically deep (Lemma 10.6), pole orders at P_0 keep F nonzero (Lemma 10.7), and Riemann and Roch gives enough unknowns (Lemma 10.8).
  • With A = \sqrt q - 1 and B = \sqrt q + 2g, the bound is N_1 \le q + (2g+1)\sqrt q for square q > (g+1)^4 (Theorem 10.9).
  • Twisted counts over a Galois cover give the lower bound (Theorem 10.12), and Lemma 9.7 turns the two-sided bound into \abs{\alpha_i} = \sqrt q (Theorem 10.13).
  • The integers lack a Frobenius and a derivative, and offer Siegel’s lemma for Riemann and Roch and characters for twists. Over \ZZ an auxiliary determinant is an integer, which vanishes once it is divisible by a large prime power yet smaller than it. Parts III and IV take it from here.
