Part IIIRoute one: a trace formula on the idele class group

Chapter 11

The adeles: all completions at once

After this chapter you can compute the p-adic size of a rational number, integrate over the p-adic numbers, describe the adeles, the ideles, and the idele class group of Q, and say why a function on that class group with trivial character is a function of one positive real variable.

Builds on 2. Euler's product: primes inside one function, 3. The complex analysis we need, 4. Zeta on the whole plane

In plain terms

A fraction has an ordinary size, and it also has one size for every prime: a number divisible by a high power of 3 counts as small for the prime 3. These sizes are tied together by one rule, that their product is always 1. The adeles are the space that records all of these sizes at once. The proof in this part of the page lives there, because it removes the primes from a sum one at a time, and the adeles are where “one prime at a time” has a precise meaning.

Part III follows the proof of A. M. Masullo [1]. Its objects are sums like Riemann’s theta function, and its main move is to delete from such a sum all terms divisible by one prime p, look at what the deletion lost, and repeat for the next prime. Over \QQ every object can be written as a function of one positive real variable, and that is how chapters Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions to From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis will write them. But the deletion step, and the reason it changes the Mellin transform by exactly one Euler factor, is clearest in a space where each prime has its own coordinate. That space is the adele ring. This chapter builds it over \QQ and keeps only what Part III uses: the p-adic numbers with their measure and Fourier transform, the adeles and ideles, the idele class group C_\QQ\cong\RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times, the functions g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}, and Poisson summation on \AA/\QQ.

There is a short way to see why the adeles are forced on us. In Zeta on the whole plane the completed zeta function was a product of the Gamma factor \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2) and the Euler factors (1-p^{-s})^{-1}, and the chapter called the Gamma factor the Euler factor of a “prime at infinity”. By the end of this chapter each of these factors will be the same kind of integral, taken over a different completion of \QQ: the Gamma factor over \RR, and the factor at p over the p-adic numbers \QQ_p. A product of integrals over all completions is one integral over their product, and that product is the adeles.

11.1A second way to measure size#

The ordinary absolute value measures how far a number is from 0 on the line. A prime gives a different notion of nearness: two integers are close for the prime p when their difference is divisible by a high power of p. This is the notion behind congruences, and it has an absolute value of its own.

Definition 11.1 p-adic valuation and p-adic absolute value

Fix a prime p. Every nonzero rational number can be written uniquely as x=p^{m}\,a/b with m\in\ZZ and integers a,b not divisible by p. The exponent m is the p-adic valuation v_p(x), and the p-adic absolute value is

\abs{x}_p=p^{-v_p(x)},\qquad \abs{0}_p=0.

It is a function from \QQ to the nonnegative rationals. It is not a distance along the line: \abs{x}_p is small when x is divisible by a high power of p, whatever the ordinary size of x. We write \abs{x}_\infty for the ordinary absolute value, so that “v” can range over the symbols \infty,2,3,5,\dots and \abs{x}_v means the matching size.

Test it on 600=2^3\cdot3\cdot5^2. Its sizes are \abs{600}_\infty=600, \abs{600}_2=\tfrac18, \abs{600}_3=\tfrac13, \abs{600}_5=\tfrac1{25}, and \abs{600}_p=1 for every other prime. A fraction can be large at a prime: \abs{7/12}_2=4 and \abs{7/12}_3=3, because the denominator holds 2^2 and 3.

Two properties make \abs{\cdot}_p an absolute value. It is multiplicative, \abs{xy}_p=\abs x_p\abs y_p, because valuations add. And it satisfies a strong form of the triangle inequality,

\abs{x+y}_p\le\max\bigl(\abs x_p,\abs y_p\bigr),
(11.1)

because if p^m divides both x and y (in the sense of valuations), it divides their sum. This ultrametric inequality has a geometric consequence that will matter below: a ball \{x:\abs{x-a}_p\le r\} has every one of its points as a center, and two balls are either nested or disjoint.

Are there other sizes? Ostrowski’s theorem says no. Every absolute value on \QQ that is not trivial is a positive power of either the ordinary one or one of the \abs{\cdot}_p [61]. So the list \infty,2,3,5,7,\dots is complete. These are called the places of \QQ.

The sizes of one rational number are not independent of each other. They are bound by a single identity.

Theorem 11.2 The product of all the sizes of a nonzero rational number is 1

For every x\in\QQ with x\ne0,

\abs{x}_\infty\prod_p\abs{x}_p=1,
(11.2)

where all but finitely many factors of the product are equal to 1.

Proof

Write x=\pm\prod_p p^{v_p(x)}, which is unique factorization. Then \abs x_\infty=\prod_pp^{v_p(x)} and \prod_p\abs x_p=\prod_pp^{-v_p(x)}, and the two products are inverse to each other. Only the primes dividing the numerator or the denominator give factors other than 1.

Test it on x=-45/28. The sizes are \abs x_\infty=\tfrac{45}{28}, \abs x_2=4, \abs x_3=\tfrac19, \abs x_5=\tfrac15, \abs x_7=7, and the product is \tfrac{45\cdot4\cdot7}{28\cdot9\cdot5}=\tfrac{1260}{1260}=1. The formula is unique factorization written as a balance: every prime that makes x large at infinity makes it small at that prime by exactly the same factor. This is the same unique factorization that gave the Euler product in Euler's product: primes inside one function, and it will reappear as the statement that the rational numbers have size 1 in the adeles.

11.2Completing: the p-adic numbers#

The real numbers are what you get by adding to \QQ the limits of all sequences that are Cauchy for \abs\cdot_\infty. Doing the same with \abs\cdot_p gives a new field.

Definition 11.3 the p-adic numbers and the p-adic integers

The field \QQ_p of p-adic numbers is the completion of \QQ for \abs\cdot_p: its elements are equivalence classes of sequences of rationals that are Cauchy for \abs\cdot_p, and \abs\cdot_p and v_p extend to it. Every x\in\QQ_p with x\ne0 has a unique expansion

x=\sum_{k\ge m}a_kp^k,\qquad a_k\in\{0,1,\dots,p-1\},\ a_m\ne0,
(11.3)

which converges for \abs\cdot_p, and then v_p(x)=m. The ring of p-adic integers is the closed unit ball \ZZ_p=\{x:\abs x_p\le1\}, the expansions with m\ge0, and its units are \ZZ_p^\times=\{x:\abs x_p=1\}, the expansions with a_0\ne0. \QQ_p is not a subset of \RR or of \CC, and the expansion runs to the left, toward higher powers, not to the right as a decimal does.

The expansion is the digits of a number in base p, allowed to continue forever toward the high powers. Ordinary integers are the finite expansions with m\ge0. Some familiar numbers have infinite ones. In \ZZ_5,

-1=4+4\cdot5+4\cdot5^2+4\cdot5^3+\cdots,

because adding 1 makes every digit carry: the partial sums are 5^k-1, and \abs{(5^k-1)-(-1)}_5=5^{-k}\to0. In \ZZ_2 the fraction \tfrac13 has digits 1,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,\dots from 2^0 upward: its last k digits are the inverse of 3 modulo 2^k, for example 43 modulo 64, and 3\cdot43=129\equiv1 modulo 64. So a rational number lies in \ZZ_p exactly when p does not divide its denominator.

That last sentence is the fact this part of the page uses most, so we record it with its global form.

Lemma 11.4 A rational number is an integer exactly when it is a p-adic integer for every prime p

For x\in\QQ: x\in\ZZ_p if and only if p does not divide the denominator of x in lowest terms. Hence x\in\ZZ if and only if x\in\ZZ_p for every prime p, and x\in\ZZ with p\nmid x if and only if x\in\ZZ_p^\times and x\in\ZZ_\ell for every prime \ell\ne p.

Proof

\abs x_p\le1 means v_p(x)\ge0, which means no power of p in the denominator. An integer is a rational with no prime in its denominator. For the last claim, x\in\ZZ_p^\times adds the condition v_p(x)=0, which for an integer means p\nmid x.

Every nonzero x\in\QQ_p factors uniquely as x=p^{v_p(x)}u with u\in\ZZ_p^\times, by pulling the lowest power out of Equation (11.3). So \QQ_p^\times is a disjoint union of shells,

\QQ_p^\times=\bigsqcup_{m\in\ZZ}p^m\ZZ_p^\times.
(11.4)

This decomposition is the p-adic counterpart of writing a nonzero real number as a sign times a positive number, and it is how every integral over \QQ_p^\times below is computed: one shell at a time.

The topology of \ZZ_p is that of a tree. The ball a+p^k\ZZ_p is the set of p-adic integers whose last k digits agree with those of a; it splits into p smaller balls according to the next digit. So \ZZ_p is the set of infinite paths down a tree in which every node has p children, and \ZZ_p\cong\varprojlim_k\ZZ/p^k\ZZ, a compatible choice of residue modulo every power of p. Each ball is both open and closed, and \ZZ_p is compact: a sequence of paths always has a subsequence that agrees on longer and longer initial segments. Compactness of \ZZ_p is what will make the adeles locally compact.

11.3Measuring sets and integrating in \QQ_p#

To write Euler factors as integrals we need a way to integrate over \QQ_p. On \RR the length \dd x is singled out by one property: it does not change when sets are translated. The same property singles out a measure on \QQ_p.

Definition 11.5 Haar measure on \QQ_p and on its multiplicative group

The additive Haar measure \dd x on \QQ_p is the unique translation-invariant measure with \int_{\ZZ_p}\dd x=1 [62]. The multiplicative Haar measure on \QQ_p^\times is

\dd^\times x=\frac{p}{p-1}\,\frac{\dd x}{\abs x_p},
(11.5)

normalized so that \int_{\ZZ_p^\times}\dd^\times x=1; this is the normalization of the source [1, p. 127 and Definition A.3.2.2] and of Tate [63]. On \RR^\times the multiplicative measure is \dd x/\abs x. Neither is a probability measure on all of \QQ_p or \QQ_p^\times: both give the whole space infinite mass.

Every value of \dd x follows from translation invariance and the normalization. The ball \ZZ_p is the disjoint union of the p^k translates a+p^k\ZZ_p, 0\le a<p^k, which all have the same measure, so

\int_{a+p^k\ZZ_p}\dd x=p^{-k}=\abs{p^k}_p.

More generally, \int_{aB}\dd x=\abs a_p\int_B\dd x for any a\in\QQ_p^\times and measurable B [1, Lemma A.3.1.4, p. 556]: the p-adic absolute value is exactly the factor by which multiplication changes volume, as \abs a_\infty is on \RR. The units are \ZZ_p minus p\ZZ_p, so \int_{\ZZ_p^\times}\dd x=1-\tfrac1p, which explains the factor \tfrac p{p-1} in Equation (11.5). On each shell of Equation (11.4) the factor 1/\abs x_p is constant, so every shell p^m\ZZ_p^\times has multiplicative measure exactly 1.

Now the computation that motivates everything. Integrate \abs x_p^s against \dd^\times x over the p-adic integers, one shell at a time:

Proposition 11.6 The integral of \abs x_p^s over the nonzero p-adic integers is the Euler factor at p, and over the units it is 1 [63]

For \Re s>0,

\int_{\QQ_p^\times}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}(x)\,\abs x_p^{s}\,\dd^\times x=\frac1{1-p^{-s}},\qquad\int_{\QQ_p^\times}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times}(x)\,\abs x_p^{s}\,\dd^\times x=1.
(11.6)

At the real place, for the Gaussian, \int_{\RR^\times}e^{-\pi x^2}\abs x^s\,\dd x/\abs x=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2) for \Re s>0.

Proof

By Equation (11.4), \ZZ_p\setminus\{0\}=\bigsqcup_{m\ge0}p^m\ZZ_p^\times. On the shell p^m\ZZ_p^\times the integrand is the constant p^{-ms} and the shell has measure 1, so the first integral is \sum_{m\ge0}p^{-ms}=(1-p^{-s})^{-1}, a geometric series that converges for \Re s>0. The second integral keeps only the shell m=0. For the real integral, the integrand is even, so it is 2\int_0^\infty e^{-\pi x^2}x^{s}\,\dd x/x, and the substitution u=\pi x^2 turns it into \pi^{-s/2}\int_0^\infty e^{-u}u^{s/2}\,\dd u/u=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2).

At s=2 the three factors for p=2,3,5 are \tfrac43, \tfrac98, and \tfrac{25}{24}, and the product of the factors for p\le13 is 1.61792, on its way to \zeta(2)=1.64493. The Gaussian integral at s=2 is \pi^{-1}\Gamma(1)=0.318310, which a numerical quadrature reproduces to every digit shown. So both kinds of factor in Riemann’s \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s) are integrals of the same shape: a nice function on a completion of \QQ, times \abs x_v^s, against the multiplicative Haar measure.

The second integral in Equation (11.6) is the seed of the method of Part III. The function \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} gives the Euler factor at p. Replacing it by \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times}=\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}-\mathbf 1_{p\ZZ_p} gives 1, so the replacement divides by that Euler factor, that is, it multiplies by 1-p^{-s}. Chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions reads the same replacement as “delete the multiples of p from a sum over integers”, and chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces measures what the deletion loses.

11.4Characters and the Fourier transform on \QQ_p#

Poisson summation on \RR needed the waves e^{2\pi ixy}, which are the continuous homomorphisms from the additive group \RR to the unit circle. \QQ_p has waves too.

Definition 11.7 the p-adic fractional part and the standard character

For x\in\QQ_p with expansion Equation (11.3), the p-adic fractional part is \{x\}_p=\sum_{k<0}a_kp^k, the part of the expansion with negative powers. It is a rational number in [0,1) whose denominator is a power of p, and x-\{x\}_p\in\ZZ_p. The standard characters are

\mathbf e_p(x)=e^{2\pi i\{x\}_p}\quad(x\in\QQ_p),\qquad\mathbf e_\infty(x)=e^{-2\pi ix}\quad(x\in\RR).
(11.7)

Each is a continuous homomorphism from the additive group to the unit circle. \mathbf e_p is equal to 1 on all of \ZZ_p and is not identically 1 on p^{-1}\ZZ_p. The opposite signs at p and at \infty are Tate’s convention [63]; they are chosen so that the product over all places is trivial on \QQ (Lemma 11.11).

The Fourier transform on \QQ_p is \hat f(y)=\int_{\QQ_p}f(x)\,\mathbf e_p(xy)\,\dd x, and on \RR it is \hat f(y)=\int f(x)\mathbf e_\infty(xy)\,\dd x=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ixy}\,\dd x, the transform of The complex analysis we need. The functions it acts on at p are the Schwartz-Bruhat functions on \QQ_p: the locally constant functions with compact support, which are the finite linear combinations of indicators of balls \mathbf 1_{a+p^k\ZZ_p}. They play the role of the Schwartz functions on \RR.

Proposition 11.8 The indicator of the p-adic integers is its own Fourier transform [63]

\widehat{\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}}=\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}, and more generally \widehat{\mathbf 1_{p^k\ZZ_p}}=p^{-k}\,\mathbf 1_{p^{-k}\ZZ_p} for k\in\ZZ.

Proof

\widehat{\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}}(y)=\int_{\ZZ_p}\mathbf e_p(xy)\,\dd x. If y\in\ZZ_p then xy\in\ZZ_p for every x\in\ZZ_p, the integrand is 1, and the integral is \int_{\ZZ_p}\dd x=1. If y\notin\ZZ_p, then x\mapsto\mathbf e_p(xy) is a character of the compact group \ZZ_p that is not identically 1, since at x=1 it equals e^{2\pi i\{y\}_p} with \{y\}_p\in(0,1). Pick x_0 with \mathbf e_p(x_0y)\ne1. Translation invariance gives I=\int\mathbf e_p((x+x_0)y)\,\dd x=\mathbf e_p(x_0y)I, so I=0. The general case follows by the substitution x\mapsto p^kx, which multiplies \dd x by p^{-k} [1, Example A.3.1.6, p. 557].

So \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} is to \QQ_p what the Gaussian e^{-\pi x^2} is to \RR: it is self-dual, and by Proposition 11.6 its multiplicative integral is the local Euler factor. This parallel, which Tate made the organizing principle of his thesis [63], is the reason the Gaussian and the indicators appear side by side in the next section. The units do not share it: from the proposition, \widehat{\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times}}=\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}-p^{-1}\mathbf 1_{p^{-1}\ZZ_p}, which is not supported in \ZZ_p.

11.5All sizes at once: the adeles#

A rational number x has all of its sizes \abs x_\infty,\abs x_2,\abs x_3,\dots at once. So it is natural to look at the vector (x,x,x,\dots) with one coordinate in each completion, \RR,\QQ_2,\QQ_3,\dots, and at the space of all such vectors. The full product \RR\times\prod_p\QQ_p is too big: it is not locally compact, so it has no Haar measure and no Fourier analysis. A rational number has only finitely many primes in its denominator, so its vector lies in \ZZ_p at all but finitely many places. Keeping exactly this condition gives the right space.

Definition 11.9 the adeles of \QQ

The adele ring of \QQ is

\AA=\Bigl\{x=(x_\infty,x_2,x_3,x_5,\dots)\in\RR\times\prod_p\QQ_p:\ x_p\in\ZZ_p\text{ for all but finitely many }p\Bigr\},

with componentwise addition and multiplication. Its topology is the restricted product topology: a basic open set is U_\infty\times\prod_{p\in S}U_p\times\prod_{p\notin S}\ZZ_p, with S a finite set of primes and U_v open in \QQ_v. With it, \AA is a locally compact ring [1, Lemma A.1.1.2, p. 539]. The rationals sit inside by the diagonal embedding \xi\mapsto(\xi,\xi,\xi,\dots). We write \hat\ZZ=\prod_p\ZZ_p, a compact ring, so that \RR\times\hat\ZZ is an open subring of \AA. The adeles are not a field and not a vector space over \RR; \AA is not the product topology restricted from \RR\times\prod_p\QQ_p either, since \prod_p\ZZ_p is open in \AA but not in the full product.

The rationals are discrete in \AA, and they fill it up to a compact piece. This is the adelic form of the familiar facts that \ZZ is discrete in \RR with quotient a circle.

Theorem 11.10 Every adele is a rational number plus a unique element of [0,1) times the profinite integers

\QQ is a discrete subgroup of \AA, and every x\in\AA can be written uniquely as x=\xi+y with \xi\in\QQ and y\in[0,1)\times\hat\ZZ. Hence \AA/\QQ is compact, and [0,1)\times\hat\ZZ is a fundamental domain for it [1, Example A.2.1.3, p. 545].

Proof

Existence. Only finitely many components x_p lie outside \ZZ_p. Let r=\sum_p\{x_p\}_p, a finite sum of rationals. For each prime p, x_p-\{x_p\}_p\in\ZZ_p, and each other term \{x_\ell\}_\ell with \ell\ne p has only powers of \ell in its denominator, so lies in \ZZ_p. Hence x_p-r\in\ZZ_p for every p. Now subtract the integer n=\lfloor x_\infty-r\rfloor, which lies in every \ZZ_p. With \xi=r+n, the adele y=x-\xi has y_\infty\in[0,1) and y_p\in\ZZ_p for all p.

Uniqueness and discreteness. If \xi+y=\xi'+y', then \xi-\xi'\in\QQ lies in every \ZZ_p, so it is an integer by Lemma 11.4, and it lies in (-1,1), so it is 0. The same argument shows that the open set (-1,1)\times\hat\ZZ meets \QQ only in 0, which is discreteness.

Try it on x=(\tfrac{8}{3},\ \tfrac{1}{4},\ \tfrac{1}{3},\ 0,0,\dots), with components at \infty, 2, 3, and 0 elsewhere. Here \{x_2\}_2=\tfrac14 and \{x_3\}_3=\tfrac13, so r=\tfrac7{12}, and x_\infty-r=\tfrac{8}{3}-\tfrac{7}{12}=\tfrac{25}{12}, so n=2 and \xi=\tfrac{31}{12}. Then y_\infty=\tfrac1{12}, y_2=\tfrac14-\tfrac{31}{12}=-\tfrac73\in\ZZ_2, and y_3=\tfrac13-\tfrac{31}{12}=-\tfrac94\in\ZZ_3, as promised.

The additive Haar measure on \AA is the product \dd x=\dd x_\infty\prod_p\dd x_p of the measures above. It gives the fundamental domain [0,1)\times\hat\ZZ the volume 1\cdot\prod_p1=1, so

\operatorname{vol}(\AA/\QQ)=1.
(11.8)

The source fixes its measures by exactly this condition, which removes all volume factors from the formulas of the next chapter [1, Remark 2.2.3.3, p. 82].

The characters at each place multiply to a character of \AA, \mathbf e(x)=\mathbf e_\infty(x_\infty)\prod_p\mathbf e_p(x_p), a finite product because \mathbf e_p=1 on \ZZ_p.

Lemma 11.11 The standard character of the adeles is equal to 1 on the rational numbers

For every \xi\in\QQ, \mathbf e(\xi)=1.

Proof

Let r=\sum_p\{\xi\}_p. As in the proof of Theorem 11.10, \xi-r lies in every \ZZ_p, so it is an integer. Then \mathbf e(\xi)=e^{-2\pi i\xi}\prod_pe^{2\pi i\{\xi\}_p}=e^{2\pi i(r-\xi)}=1.

Test it on \xi=\tfrac7{12}. The partial fraction decomposition \tfrac7{12}=\tfrac14+\tfrac13 gives \{\xi\}_2=\tfrac14 and \{\xi\}_3=\tfrac13, and \mathbf e(\xi)=e^{-2\pi i\cdot7/12}e^{2\pi i/4}e^{2\pi i/3}=1. The lemma is partial fractions: every rational number is an integer plus a sum of fractions with prime-power denominators, one per prime.

The functions Part III uses#

Definition 11.12 Schwartz-Bruhat functions on the adeles

A Schwartz-Bruhat function on \AA is a finite linear combination of products

f(x)=f_\infty(x_\infty)\prod_pf_p(x_p),

written f=f_\infty\otimes\bigotimes_pf_p, where f_\infty is a Schwartz function on \RR, each f_p is a Schwartz-Bruhat function on \QQ_p, and f_p=\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} for all but finitely many p, so that the product is finite at every adele. These are the adelic test functions. A Schwartz-Bruhat function is not a function on \QQ, although it can be restricted to \QQ, and that restriction is how it enters the sums of the next chapter.

Over \QQ with the trivial character, only one kind of product will be needed:

f=g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p},\qquad f(x)=g(x_\infty)\,\mathbf 1_{\hat\ZZ}\bigl((x_p)_p\bigr),
(11.9)

with g an even Schwartz function on \RR. By Lemma 11.4, its restriction to the rationals is

f(\xi)=\begin{cases}g(\xi),&\xi\in\ZZ,\\0,&\xi\in\QQ\setminus\ZZ.\end{cases}
(11.10)

The indicators at the primes act as a filter: each \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} removes the rationals with p in the denominator, and all of them together leave exactly the integers. Changing one factor to \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times} also removes the integers divisible by p. By Proposition 11.8 the Fourier transform of Equation (11.9) is \hat f=\hat g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}, another function of the same kind.

Poisson summation on \AA/\QQ#

The last fact this chapter hands on is Poisson summation, now with \QQ in place of \ZZ and \AA in place of \RR. It holds for the same reason: \QQ is discrete in \AA, the quotient is compact with volume 1 by Equation (11.8), and the characters of \AA that are trivial on \QQ are exactly x\mapsto\mathbf e(\xi x) with \xi\in\QQ, so \QQ is its own dual lattice.

Theorem 11.13

The sum of a Schwartz-Bruhat function over the rationals equals the sum of its Fourier transform over the rationals

[63]
Statement

Let f be a Schwartz-Bruhat function on \AA and \hat f(y)=\int_\AA f(x)\mathbf e(xy)\,\dd x its Fourier transform. Then

\sum_{\xi\in\QQ}f(\xi)=\sum_{\xi\in\QQ}\hat f(\xi).
(11.11)

Applied to x\mapsto f(ax) for an idele a (defined in the next section), it gives \sum_{\xi\in\QQ}f(\xi a)=\abs a^{-1}\sum_{\xi\in\QQ}\hat f(\xi a^{-1}).

In plain terms

Adding up an adelic function over all fractions gives the same total as adding up its Fourier transform over all fractions. For the functions of this page, both sums reduce to sums over the ordinary integers, and the statement becomes the Poisson summation of The complex analysis we need.

Why it is needed

Riemann’s functional equation came from Poisson summation for the integers inside the reals. Tate’s version of that proof, which the next chapter follows, uses Poisson summation for the rationals inside the adeles, and its scaled form is the “adelic Riemann-Roch theorem” [1, Theorem 2.2.3.2, p. 82]. Without it there is no symmetry t\mapsto1/t for the theta sums of Part III, and so no control of their decay at 0.

Idea

Periodize f over \QQ to get a function on the compact group \AA/\QQ, expand it in the characters of that group, which are the \mathbf e(\xi\,\cdot) with \xi\in\QQ, and evaluate at 0. The coefficients are the values \hat f(\xi), exactly as on the circle \RR/\ZZ.

Proof sketch

[63, Chapter XV, §4.2]

The three inputs are the discreteness and cocompactness of \QQ (Theorem 11.10), \operatorname{vol}(\AA/\QQ)=1, and the identification of the characters of \AA trivial on \QQ with \QQ itself through \mathbf e. With these, the proof is the one on the circle, with Fourier series on \AA/\QQ. For the function f=g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} one can check the statement by hand: by Equation (11.10) the left side is \sum_{n\in\ZZ}g(n), and since \hat f=\hat g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} the right side is \sum_{n\in\ZZ}\hat g(n). These agree by Poisson summation on \RR.

Example

Take g(x)=e^{-\pi x^2}, which equals its own transform. Both sides of Equation (11.11) are \sum_ne^{-\pi n^2}=1.0864348. Scale by the idele a with a_\infty=2 and a_p=1 for all p, which has \abs a=2: the left side is \sum_ne^{-4\pi n^2}=1.0000070, and the right side is \tfrac12\sum_ne^{-\pi n^2/4}=\tfrac12\cdot2.0000139=1.0000070. This is the theta symmetry of Zeta on the whole plane at t=4.

Used in
  • The adelic Riemann-Roch identity for theta sums and their decay: Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions.
  • The S-local Fourier transform in Connes’s computation of the local terms: The local trace and the Trace Formula.

11.6Ideles and the idele class group#

The sums of Part III are not over additive translates \xi+x but over multiplicative ones \xi x, and the Mellin transform is an integral over a multiplicative group. So we need the invertible adeles.

Definition 11.14 the ideles of \QQ and their norm

The idele group \AA^\times is the group of invertible adeles: tuples x=(x_v)_v with every x_v\ne0 and x_p\in\ZZ_p^\times for all but finitely many p. It carries the restricted product topology of the pairs (\QQ_p^\times,\ZZ_p^\times), in which \RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times, with \hat\ZZ^\times=\prod_p\ZZ_p^\times, is an open subgroup. The norm of an idele is

\abs x=\abs{x_\infty}_\infty\prod_p\abs{x_p}_p,
(11.12)

a finite product, and \abs\cdot:\AA^\times\to\RR_{>0} is a continuous homomorphism. The rationals \QQ^\times sit in \AA^\times diagonally, and by the product formula Theorem 11.2 every one of them has norm 1. The ideles are a group under multiplication, not a ring.

A common misreading

The idele topology is not the topology that \AA^\times inherits from \AA. Let p_k be the k-th prime and let x^{(k)} be the idele with component p_k at p_k and 1 at every other place. In \AA the sequence converges to 1, because x^{(k)}-1 is 0 except at p_k, where it is p_k-1\in\ZZ_{p_k}, and so it lies in every basic neighborhood of 0 once p_k is outside the finite set S. But the inverses have component 1/p_k\notin\ZZ_{p_k}, so they do not converge to 1 in \AA. In the subspace topology inversion would not be continuous. The restricted product topology of the pairs (\QQ_p^\times,\ZZ_p^\times) repairs this, and in it x^{(k)} does not converge at all [1, Definition A.1.3.1, p. 541].

Since every rational has norm 1, the norm passes to the quotient by \QQ^\times. Over \QQ this quotient has a very simple shape.

Definition 11.15 the idele class group

The idele class group of \QQ is the quotient C_\QQ=\AA^\times/\QQ^\times, a locally compact abelian group. The norm defines a continuous surjective homomorphism \abs\cdot:C_\QQ\to\RR_{>0}, whose kernel C_\QQ^1 is compact. C_\QQ is a group of classes of ideles, not a group of numbers, and it is not a subgroup of \AA^\times.

Theorem 11.16

The idele class group of \QQ is the positive reals times the units of the profinite integers, and the norm is the projection to the positive reals

[1]
Statement

Every idele x can be written uniquely as x=\xi\cdot(t,u) with \xi\in\QQ^\times, t\in\RR_{>0} at the real place, and u\in\hat\ZZ^\times at the finite places. Hence

C_\QQ\cong\RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times,\qquad\abs{x}=t,\qquad C_\QQ^1\cong\hat\ZZ^\times.
(11.13)
In plain terms

Any idele can be moved, by multiplying with one well-chosen fraction, to a positive real number at infinity and a unit at every prime. That fraction is unique, so an idele class is just a positive real number and a compatible list of units. The positive real number is the norm.

Why it is needed

This is the identification that lets every chapter of Part III work on \RR_{>0} with \dd t/t. A function on C_\QQ that does not depend on the unit part u is a function of the single variable t=\abs x, and the Mellin transform on \RR_{>0} is the Fourier analysis of C_\QQ in that variable.

Idea

The rational \xi is read off from the idele: its sign is the sign of x_\infty, and its power of p is the valuation of x_p. Dividing by it removes all the valuations at once. Uniqueness is Lemma 11.4 again: a rational number that is a unit at every prime and positive is 1.

Proof sketch

[1, (A.2.2.1) to (A.2.2.3), p. 546]

Existence. Put \xi=\operatorname{sgn}(x_\infty)\prod_pp^{v_p(x_p)}, a finite product since v_p(x_p)=0 for almost all p. Then \xi^{-1}x has a positive real component, and at each p its component \xi^{-1}x_p has valuation v_p(x_p)-v_p(\xi)=0, so it is a unit. Uniqueness. If \xi(t,u)=\xi'(t',u'), then \xi/\xi' is a rational number that is a unit at every p, so it is \pm1 by Lemma 11.4, and positive at the real place, so it is 1. Norm. \abs{\xi(t,u)}=\abs\xi\cdot t\cdot\prod_p\abs{u_p}_p=1\cdot t\cdot1=t by the product formula. Topology. The map (t,u)\mapsto class of (t,u) is a continuous bijective homomorphism from \RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times onto C_\QQ, and it is open because \RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times is open in \AA^\times and meets each class once.

Example

Take the idele with x_\infty=-3.5, x_2=12, x_3=\tfrac59, x_5=\tfrac15, and x_p=1 for p\ge7. The recipe gives \xi=-2^{2}\cdot3^{-2}\cdot5^{-1}=-\tfrac4{45}. Dividing, the real component becomes t=3.5\cdot\tfrac{45}4=\tfrac{315}8=39.375, and the finite components become -135 at 2, -\tfrac{25}4 at 3, -\tfrac94 at 5, and -\tfrac{45}4 at every p\ge7, each a unit at its prime. The norm computed directly is \abs x=3.5\cdot\tfrac14\cdot9\cdot5=39.375=t.

Used in
  • Every function of Part III with trivial character is a function of t=\abs x\in\RR_{>0}: Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions onward.
  • The idelic lift of the kernel and its stratification by “unit at the first k primes” live on \AA^\times, not on C_\QQ: Cutting the kernel along the primes.

Characters of the class group#

A character of C_\QQ is a continuous homomorphism to the unit circle. On \RR_{>0} these are t\mapsto t^{i\tau} with \tau\in\RR, the waves of the Mellin transform. On \hat\ZZ^\times a continuous character has an open kernel, because a small enough neighborhood of 1 in the circle contains no subgroup but \{1\}, and an open subgroup of \hat\ZZ^\times contains all units congruent to 1 modulo some integer q. So the character factors through \hat\ZZ^\times\to(\ZZ/q\ZZ)^\times, and it is a Dirichlet character modulo q in the sense of What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations. Every character of C_\QQ is therefore (t,u)\mapsto t^{i\tau}\chi(u) with \chi a Dirichlet character. This is how the Dirichlet L-functions enter the adelic picture.

For the Riemann zeta function, \chi is trivial. A function on C_\QQ that is invariant under \hat\ZZ^\times is a function of t alone, and the Haar measure of C_\QQ, the product of \dd t/t with the probability measure on \hat\ZZ^\times, becomes \dd t/t. This is the sense in which the source’s statements on C_F, specialized to F=\QQ and the trivial character, become statements on \RR_{>0} [1, p. 127].

11.7What changes in general#

For a number field F the construction is the same with more places. The places of F are the prime ideals \mathfrak p of its ring of integers \mathcal O_F and the real and complex embeddings of F. Each finite place v has a completion F_v, a finite extension of some \QQ_p, with its ring of integers \mathcal O_{F_v}, a uniformizer \pi_v that plays the role of p, and a residue field of size q_v=N\mathfrak p. The normalized absolute values satisfy the product formula, the adeles \AA_F are the restricted product of the (F_v,\mathcal O_{F_v}), and the ideles are the restricted product of the (F_v^\times,\mathcal O_{F_v}^\times) [1, p. 7 and Appendix A.1].

Two things become harder. First, the class group C_F=\AA_F^\times/F^\times still maps onto \RR_{>0} with compact kernel C_F^1, but C_F^1 is no longer just a product of local units: it remembers the units of \mathcal O_F and the ideal class group of F. A function on C_F splits into isotypes, one for each character of C_F^1, and each isotype is again a space of functions of one positive real variable. Second, the characters of C_F are the Hecke characters of What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations, so the trivial isotype gives the Dedekind zeta function of F, and the others give Hecke L-functions. Masullo’s theorem covers all of them [1, p. 6], and the chapters of Part III each end by naming what this costs.

Recap

You now have the following, and where each is used.

  • The p-adic absolute value, the places \infty,2,3,5,\dots of \QQ, and the product formula \abs x_\infty\prod_p\abs x_p=1 (Theorem 11.2): used for the norm of ideles and in the next chapter’s symmetry.
  • \QQ_p, \ZZ_p, \ZZ_p^\times, the shells p^m\ZZ_p^\times, and the fact that a rational number is an integer exactly when it is in every \ZZ_p (Lemma 11.4): the filter that turns sums over \QQ into sums over \ZZ.
  • Haar measure on \QQ_p and \QQ_p^\times, and the local integrals \int\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}\abs x_p^s\,\dd^\times x=(1-p^{-s})^{-1} and \int\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times}\abs x_p^s\,\dd^\times x=1 (Proposition 11.6): the reason that removing a prime multiplies by 1-p^{-s} in Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions and Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces.
  • The characters \mathbf e_v, the Fourier transform, and \widehat{\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}}=\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} (Proposition 11.8).
  • The adeles, the fundamental domain [0,1)\times\hat\ZZ, \operatorname{vol}(\AA/\QQ)=1, and the functions g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} (Definition 11.12).
  • Poisson summation on \AA/\QQ (Theorem 11.13): the adelic Riemann-Roch identity of Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions.
  • The ideles, their norm, and C_\QQ\cong\RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times with \abs x=t (Theorem 11.16): why every object of Part III is a function on \RR_{>0} with \dd t/t, and where the lift to the ideles of Cutting the kernel along the primes takes place.
Previous10. Stepanov's proofNext12. Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions

Chapter 12

Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions

After this chapter you can build a theta sum from any even Schwartz function, compute its Mellin transform as zeta times a factor, say exactly which functions on the positive reals are theta sums, and read the quotient of all functions by the theta sums as the list of jets of Mellin transforms at the zeros of zeta.

Builds on 11. The adeles: all completions at once, 4. Zeta on the whole plane, 8. Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion

In plain terms

Riemann proved his functional equation by adding up a Gaussian over the integers. Nothing in that proof needs the Gaussian: any even, rapidly decreasing function gives a sum with the same symmetry, and its Mellin transform is the zeta function times a simple factor. Collect all of these sums into one space. A function on the positive reals belongs to that space exactly when its Mellin transform vanishes at every zero of zeta, so what remains of a function after the theta sums are removed is precisely its behavior at the zeros.

This chapter opens Route M, the proof of A. M. Masullo [1]. Its plan is to compute one trace in two ways. The trace is that of a convolution operator acting on “all functions modulo theta sums”, a space whose only content, as this chapter shows, is one number (or a few numbers) for each zero of \zeta. Computed through the zeros, the trace is a sum over zeros; computed through the primes, it is the prime side of Weil’s explicit formula. Chapters Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces to From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis change the space so that zeros off the critical line drop out of the first computation and not of the second. Here we build the space, in its original, fine form, and see that in that form the two computations give back Weil’s explicit formula of Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion and nothing more.

Everything is over \QQ with the trivial character, on the half-line \RR_{>0} with the measure \dd t/t. By Theorem 11.16, that is the idele class group C_\QQ seen through the norm. The adeles of The adeles: all completions at once appear for one purpose: to explain why the operations used here are the natural ones.

12.1Riemann’s proof, read again#

Recall the proof in Zeta on the whole plane. Riemann summed the Gaussian e^{-\pi n^2 t} over n\in\ZZ to get the theta function \theta(t), used Poisson summation to prove \theta(1/t)=\sqrt t\,\theta(t), took the Mellin transform of \omega(t)=\tfrac12(\theta(t)-1) to get \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s), cut the integral at t=1, and used the symmetry to turn the part near 0 into a second integral near \infty. The result was an entire \xi(s) with \xi(s)=\xi(1-s).

Change the variable from t to t^2, so that the Gaussian is evaluated at nt instead of n\sqrt t:

\theta(t^2)-1=\sum_{n\ne0}e^{-\pi(nt)^2}.
(12.1)

In this form the proof used exactly three properties of g(x)=e^{-\pi x^2}. It is even and decays rapidly, so the sum converges and its Mellin transform factors as \zeta(s) times the Mellin transform of g. Its Fourier transform is again a rapidly decaying function, here g itself, so Poisson summation relates the sum at t to a sum at 1/t. And the Mellin transform of g is a known function, \tfrac12\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2). The first two hold for every even Schwartz function, and the third is a convenience. So the proof is one member of a family, indexed by the function g, and the family is the object of this chapter.

12.2Theta sums#

Definition 12.1 the theta sum of an even Schwartz function

Let g be an even Schwartz function on \RR. Its theta sum is the function of t>0

\Theta_g(t)=\sum_{n\ne0}g(nt)=2\sum_{n\ge1}g(nt).

It is a smooth function on \RR_{>0}, a sum of the values of g on the lattice t\ZZ\setminus\{0\}. It is not a modular form, and it is not a theta lift: it is a periodization over the multiplicative group \QQ^\times, as the adelic description below shows. For g(x)=e^{-\pi x^2} it is \theta(t^2)-1. We write Mg(s)=\int_0^\infty g(t)\,t^s\,\dd t/t for the Mellin transform of g restricted to (0,\infty); it converges for \Re s>0.

Three functions will serve as examples throughout. The Gaussian g_0(x)=e^{-\pi x^2} is Riemann’s. The function

g_\star(x)=\bigl(4\pi^2x^4-6\pi x^2\bigr)e^{-\pi x^2}
(12.2)

is obtained from g_0 by the differential operator (x\tfrac{\dd}{\dd x})(x\tfrac{\dd}{\dd x}+1), and the reason for that choice appears in The two conditions, and the decay they buy. The third is compactly supported. Start from the standard bump function \operatorname{bump}(x)=e^{-1/(1-x^2)} for \abs x<1 and \operatorname{bump}(x)=0 otherwise, and apply the same operator:

g_c(x)=\frac{2x^2\,(x^4+4x^2-3)}{(1-x^2)^4}\,e^{-1/(1-x^2)}\quad(\abs x<1),\qquad g_c(x)=0\quad(\abs x\ge1).
(12.3)

It is smooth and even, it vanishes outside (-1,1), and its largest absolute value is 5.78, near x=0.90. Because g_c(nt)=0 as soon as nt\ge1, the theta sum \Theta_{g_c}(t) is a finite sum, and it is identically 0 for t\ge1.

The symmetry#

The theta function’s symmetry came from Poisson summation on \ZZ. The same step works for every g, with two correction terms that come from the missing term n=0.

Theorem 12.2 The theta sum at t equals the theta sum of the Fourier transform at 1/t, divided by t, up to two constant terms [63]

For every even Schwartz function g and every t>0,

\Theta_g(t)=\frac1t\,\Theta_{\hat g}\!\left(\frac1t\right)+\frac{\hat g(0)}t-g(0).
(12.4)

This is the adelic Riemann-Roch theorem of Tate [63, Chapter XV, Theorem 4.2.1] for the adelic function g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} and the idele (t,1,1,\dots), in the form of [1, Theorem 2.2.3.2, p. 82].

Proof

Apply Poisson summation Theorem 11.13 (on \RR, it is the theorem of The complex analysis we need) to x\mapsto g(tx), whose Fourier transform is y\mapsto t^{-1}\hat g(y/t). It gives \sum_{n\in\ZZ}g(nt)=t^{-1}\sum_{k\in\ZZ}\hat g(k/t). Remove the term n=0 on the left, which is g(0), and the term k=0 on the right, which is t^{-1}\hat g(0).

For the Gaussian, \hat g_0=g_0 and g_0(0)=\hat g_0(0)=1, and the identity is \theta(t^2)-1=t^{-1}(\theta(t^{-2})-1)+t^{-1}-1, which is Jacobi’s \theta(1/u)=\sqrt u\,\theta(u) at u=t^2. At t=\tfrac12 both sides equal 1.0000139. Adelically the identity is a statement about \QQ inside \AA, and over \QQ it reduces to a statement about \ZZ inside \RR because, by Lemma 11.4, the indicators \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} cut the sum over \QQ down to \ZZ.

The Mellin transform#

Theorem 12.3 The Mellin transform of a theta sum is twice \zeta times the Mellin transform of g [63]

For \Re s>1,

\int_0^\infty\Theta_g(t)\,t^s\,\frac{\dd t}t=2\,\zeta(s)\,Mg(s).
(12.5)

For g=g_0 the right side is \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s) [1, Theorem 3.2.2.1, p. 124].

Proof

Substitute u=nt in each term: \int_0^\infty g(nt)t^s\,\dd t/t=n^{-s}Mg(s), because \dd t/t=\dd u/u. The sum over n\ge1 of the absolute values is \sum_nn^{-\sigma}\int_0^\infty\abs{g(u)}u^\sigma\,\dd u/u<\infty for \sigma>1, so sum and integral can be exchanged, and the factor 2 counts \pm n. For the Gaussian, Mg_0(s)=\tfrac12\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2) by Proposition 11.6.

Write Z_g(s)=2\zeta(s)Mg(s) for this function. The same cut at t=1 that proved the functional equation of \zeta proves one for every Z_g.

Theorem 12.4 Every Z_g continues to the plane with at most two simple poles and satisfies Z_g(s)=Z_{\hat g}(1-s) [63]

Z_g extends to a meromorphic function on \CC whose only possible poles are simple poles at s=1, with residue \hat g(0), and at s=0, with residue -g(0). For all s,

Z_g(s)=Z_{\hat g}(1-s).
(12.6)
Proof

For \Re s>1, split the integral Equation (12.5) at t=1 and substitute t=1/u in the part over (0,1). By Equation (12.4) at 1/u, \Theta_g(1/u)=u\,\Theta_{\hat g}(u)+u\,\hat g(0)-g(0). The two constant terms integrate against u^{-s}\,\dd u/u over (1,\infty) to \hat g(0)/(s-1) and -g(0)/s. Hence

Z_g(s)=\int_1^\infty\Theta_g(t)\,t^{s}\frac{\dd t}t+\int_1^\infty\Theta_{\hat g}(t)\,t^{1-s}\frac{\dd t}t+\frac{\hat g(0)}{s-1}-\frac{g(0)}s.
(12.7)

Both integrals converge for every s, locally uniformly, because \Theta_g and \Theta_{\hat g} decay faster than any power as t\to\infty. So the right side is the meromorphic continuation, with the stated poles. Writing the same formula for Z_{\hat g}(1-s) and using \hat{\hat g}=g (since g is even) swaps the two integrals, and its two fractions g(0)/((1-s)-1)-\hat g(0)/(1-s)=\hat g(0)/(s-1)-g(0)/s are the same two fractions, which proves Equation (12.6).

For g_0 this is the proof of Zeta on the whole plane, with the residues 1 and -1 of the function called \Phi there. The theorem says more than Riemann’s, though, because g is arbitrary: the functional equation of \zeta is now a property of an entire family of Mellin transforms.

The same computation, on the adeles#

Why should \zeta(s) appear as a factor, independently of g? The adeles give the answer, and it is the content of Tate’s thesis over \QQ. Take the adelic function f=g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} of Equation (11.9) and an idele class represented by (t,u)\in\RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times. The adelic theta function of f is

\Phi(f)(t,u)=\sum_{\xi\in\QQ^\times}f\bigl(\xi\cdot(t,u)\bigr)=\sum_{\xi\in\QQ^\times}g(\xi t)\prod_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}(\xi u_p)=\sum_{n\ne0}g(nt)=\Theta_g(t),
(12.8)

because \xi u_p\in\ZZ_p for every p exactly when \xi\in\ZZ (Lemma 11.4), and the result does not depend on u. This is the definition of the global adelic theta function in the source [1, Definition 2.2.3.1, p. 81], specialized to \QQ.

Now compute Tate’s zeta integral \int_{\AA^\times}f(x)\abs x^s\,\dd^\times x in two ways. As a product over places, it is \int_{\RR^\times}g(x)\abs x^s\,\dd x/\abs x times the local integrals \int\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}\abs x_p^s\,\dd^\times x=(1-p^{-s})^{-1} of Proposition 11.6, which is 2Mg(s)\,\zeta(s) by the Euler product. As an integral over the class group, fold the sum over \QQ^\times: by Theorem 11.16, \RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times is a fundamental domain for \QQ^\times in \AA^\times, with measure \dd t/t times the probability measure on \hat\ZZ^\times, so the integral is \int_0^\infty\Theta_g(t)\,t^s\,\dd t/t. The two answers are Equation (12.5). So the Euler product is the zeta integral unfolded over the places, the theta sum is the same integral folded over \QQ^\times, and \zeta(s) is the contribution of the indicators \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}, whatever g is.

Is every adelic theta function of trivial character a theta sum? The source’s Fifth Structure Theorem says yes: because every ideal of \ZZ is principal, the set of places S=\{\infty\} is already large enough, and every global theta function in the trivial isotype has the form \Phi(f_\infty\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}) [1, Theorem 6.2.1.1, p. 295, and p. 44]. Symmetrizing f_\infty changes nothing in the sum, so it is \Theta_g for an even g. Over \QQ, then, the family \{\Theta_g\} is the whole space of theta functions with trivial character, and nothing is lost by working with it.

12.3Removing one prime#

The adelic picture also says what it means to remove a prime. Replace the factor \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} by \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times}. By Lemma 11.4, the sum Equation (12.8) then runs over the integers prime to p, and by Proposition 11.6 the local integral at p becomes 1 instead of (1-p^{-s})^{-1}. On \RR_{>0} the replacement is a simple operator.

Definition 12.5 the operator that deletes the multiples of p

For a prime p and a function u on \RR_{>0}, put

(D_pu)(t)=u(t)-u(pt).

D_p is a linear operator on functions of one positive real variable. It is not a difference quotient and not a projection: applied twice, it gives u(t)-2u(pt)+u(p^2t). In the source it is Weil’s principal value operator \mathrm{PV}_p, f(x)\mapsto f(x)-f(\pi_p^{-1}x), acting on the factor at p [1, §5.3, p. 240, and p. 18].

Proposition 12.6 Deleting the multiples of p from a theta sum multiplies its Mellin transform by 1-p^{-s} [1]

For every even Schwartz g,

D_p\Theta_g(t)=\sum_{p\nmid n}g(nt)=\Phi\Bigl(g\otimes\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times}\otimes\bigotimes_{\ell\ne p}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_\ell}\Bigr)(t),
(12.9)

and, for any u whose Mellin transform converges at s, \int_0^\infty(D_pu)(t)\,t^s\,\dd t/t=(1-p^{-s})\int_0^\infty u(t)\,t^s\,\dd t/t. In particular the Mellin transform of D_p\Theta_g is 2(1-p^{-s})\zeta(s)Mg(s). This is Weil’s identity [1, Theorem 3.4.1.1, p. 143, and (1.8.1.3), p. 41], in our notation.

Proof

\Theta_g(pt)=\sum_{n\ne0}g(npt) is the part of \Theta_g(t) over the multiples of p, so the difference keeps the n prime to p, which is the adelic sum with \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times} at p by Lemma 11.4. For the Mellin transform, substitute t\mapsto t/p in \int u(pt)t^s\,\dd t/t, which gives p^{-s}\int u(t)t^s\,\dd t/t.

Test it at t=0.4 and p=3 with the Gaussian: \Theta_{g_0}(0.4)-\Theta_{g_0}(1.2)=1.478307, and 2\sum_{3\nmid n}e^{-\pi(0.4n)^2}=1.478307. On the weighted sums V_g(t)=t^{1/2}\Theta_g(t) of the next section, the same deletion reads V_g(t)-p^{-1/2}V_g(pt), and its Mellin factor in the variable z=s-\tfrac12 is 1-p^{-1/2-z}. The zeros of 1-p^{-s} are the points s=2\pi im/\log p, m\in\ZZ, evenly spaced on the imaginary axis with gap 2\pi/\log p. Chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces shows that the theta sums modulo the image of D_p are functions on a circle of length \log p, and that these zeros are its Fourier frequencies.

12.4The two conditions, and the decay they buy#

The poles of Z_g at 0 and 1 come from the constant terms \hat g(0)/t and -g(0) in Equation (12.4). Those terms also stop \Theta_g from decaying as t\to0: for the Gaussian, \Theta_{g_0}(t)\approx1/t-1 for small t. Both problems disappear together when the two constants are 0.

Proposition 12.7 If g(0)=0 and the integral of g is 0, the theta sum decays faster than any power of t at both ends [1]

Let g be even and Schwartz with g(0)=0 and \int_\RR g=\hat g(0)=0. Then for every N there is C_N with

\abs{\Theta_g(t)}\le C_N\,e^{-N\abs{\log t}}\qquad(t>0),
(12.10)

and the same holds for (t\tfrac{\dd}{\dd t})^k\Theta_g for every k. Equivalently \Theta_g(t)=O(t^N) as t\to0 and O(t^{-N}) as t\to\infty, for every N [1, Theorem 2.2.3.4(3), p. 83]. Then Z_g is entire.

Proof

For t\ge1, \abs{\Theta_g(t)}\le2\sum_{n\ge1}\abs{g(nt)}\le2C\sum_n(nt)^{-N-2}\le C't^{-N} since g is Schwartz. For t\le1, Equation (12.4) with g(0)=\hat g(0)=0 reads \Theta_g(t)=t^{-1}\Theta_{\hat g}(1/t), and the bound for t\ge1 applied to \hat g, which is again even and Schwartz, gives \abs{\Theta_g(t)}\le C't^{-1}t^{N+1}. For derivatives, (t\tfrac{\dd}{\dd t})\Theta_g=\Theta_{xg'}, and xg' is even and Schwartz with value 0 at 0 and \int xg'(x)\,\dd x=-\int g=0, so the same argument applies. Finally, Equation (12.7) has no fractions left, and its integrals are entire.

The decay is in \abs{\log t}, which is the natural size on the multiplicative line: e^{-N\abs{\log t}}=\min(t^N,t^{-N}). The compactly supported example shows it in numbers. \Theta_{g_c}(t) is exactly 0 for t\ge1, and as t decreases it is a sum of more and more terms that cancel:

t 0.1 0.05 0.03 0.02 0.015 0.01 0.005
terms 9 19 33 49 66 99 199
\Theta_{g_c}(t) 2.19 -0.469 -0.0361 -0.00587 -9.7\times10^{-5} -8.7\times10^{-6} -1.2\times10^{-9}

The cancellation has a plain meaning: t\,\Theta_{g_c}(t) is a Riemann sum for \int g_c=0 with step t, and Poisson summation says its error is \sum_{k\ne0}\hat g_c(k/t), which is smaller than any power of t. The decay sets in late because g_c is steep near \pm1, so \hat g_c decays slowly at first: \hat g_c(5)=-0.51. By Equation (12.4) there is a mirror statement: \Theta_{\hat g_c}(u)=u^{-1}\Theta_{g_c}(1/u), so the theta sum of \hat g_c vanishes identically for u\le1, although \hat g_c itself has no compact support.

Where the operator in g_\star comes from#

The conditions g(0)=0 and \int g=0 are the vanishing of the residues of Mg at s=0 and of Mg(1)=\tfrac12\int g. A differential operator can impose both. Integration by parts gives M\bigl(x\tfrac{\dd}{\dd x}g\bigr)(s)=-s\,Mg(s), so

M\Bigl(\bigl(x\tfrac{\dd}{\dd x}\bigr)\bigl(x\tfrac{\dd}{\dd x}+1\bigr)g\Bigr)(s)=s(s-1)\,Mg(s).
(12.11)

Applied to the Gaussian this gives g_\star of Equation (12.2), with Mg_\star(s)=\tfrac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2), and then Z_{g_\star}(s)=s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)=2\xi(s). So Riemann’s polynomial factor \tfrac12s(s-1) in \xi, which cancels the poles, is the Mellin image of the operator that enforces the two conditions. The same operator applied to \operatorname{bump} gives g_c, with Mg_c(s)=s(s-1)M\operatorname{bump}(s). One can check that \hat g_\star=g_\star: the Fourier transform turns x\tfrac{\dd}{\dd x} into -(y\tfrac{\dd}{\dd y}+1), so it swaps the two factors of the operator, and \hat g_0=g_0.

The weight t^{1/2} and the space of rapidly decaying functions#

The functional equation Equation (12.6) is symmetric about s=\tfrac12. Shifting by \tfrac12 puts the center at 0, which is the shifted variable z=s-\tfrac12 used throughout Part III, with the critical line at \Re z=0. On the function side the shift is multiplication by t^{1/2}:

V_g(t)=t^{1/2}\,\Theta_g(t),\qquad\int_0^\infty V_g(t)\,t^z\,\frac{\dd t}t=Z_g\!\left(z+\tfrac12\right).
(12.12)

With g(0)=\hat g(0)=0, Equation (12.4) becomes V_g(1/t)=V_{\hat g}(t), and Equation (12.6) becomes MV_g(z)=MV_{\hat g}(-z). For the self-dual g_\star, V_{g_\star}(1/t)=V_{g_\star}(t): the values are V_{g_\star}(1)=1.786788, V_{g_\star}(1.25)=V_{g_\star}(0.8)=1.104776, and V_{g_\star}(2)=V_{g_\star}(\tfrac12)=0.005487. Its Mellin transform is MV_{g_\star}(z)=2\xi(z+\tfrac12), which a direct numerical integration confirms: at z=0 both are 0.9942416, at z=0.3+2i both are 0.9077698+0.0253361i, and at z=14.134725i, the first zero, the integral is 0 to the working precision.

The weighted theta sums live in a space of functions that decay exponentially in \abs{\log t}, and the Mellin transform sends that space onto a space of entire functions.

Definition 12.8 exponentially decaying functions and the Schwartz-Bergman space

S_E(\RR_{>0}) is the space of smooth functions u on \RR_{>0} such that for all integers k,N\ge0,

\sup_{t>0}\,e^{N\abs{\log t}}\,\Bigl\lvert\bigl(t\tfrac{\dd}{\dd t}\bigr)^ku(t)\Bigr\rvert<\infty.

AS(\CC) is the space of entire functions F such that for every b>0 and every N, (1+\abs z)^N\abs{F(z)} is bounded on the vertical strip \abs{\Re z}\le b. The source calls S_E the exponentially decaying Schwartz-Bruhat functions and AS(\CC) the Schwartz-Bergman space [1, p. 40 and Definition D.3.1.3]. Neither is a Hilbert space: their topologies are given by the infinitely many bounds above, which makes them fine. Chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see replaces them by a coarser Hilbert space, and that replacement is the new idea of Route M.

Theorem 12.9 The Mellin transform is a bijection from the exponentially decaying functions onto the Schwartz-Bergman space [1]

The map u\mapsto Mu, Mu(z)=\int_0^\infty u(t)t^z\,\dd t/t, is a linear bijection from S_E(\RR_{>0}) onto AS(\CC), continuous in both directions, with inverse u(t)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}Mu(z)\,t^{-z}\,\dd z for any real c [1, Example 1.8.1.1, p. 40, and Appendix D.3].

Proof sketch [1, Appendix D.3]

With t=e^v, u\in S_E means that v\mapsto u(e^v)e^{xv} is a Schwartz function of v for every real x, and Mu(x+iy) is its Fourier transform in v. A Schwartz function has a Schwartz transform, uniformly for x in a bounded interval, and (t\tfrac{\dd}{\dd t})^ku goes to (-z)^kMu. The inverse is Mellin inversion of The complex analysis we need, and the line of integration can be moved freely because Mu is entire and decays on strips.

By Proposition 12.7, every V_g with g(0)=\hat g(0)=0 lies in S_E(\RR_{>0}).

Definition 12.10 the space of weighted theta sums
\mathcal V=\bigl\{V_g=t^{1/2}\Theta_g\ :\ g\text{ even Schwartz},\ g(0)=0,\ \textstyle\int_\RR g=0\bigr\}\subset S_E(\RR_{>0}).

It is a linear subspace, the source’s \lvert\cdot\rvert^{1/2}H_{0,\mathrm{cont}}(F^\times,\mathcal S_0(\AA_F)) for F=\QQ and the trivial character [1, p. 13]. It is not all of S_E: the next theorem says exactly which functions it contains.

12.5Which functions are theta sums?#

The weighted theta sum V_{g_\star} has Mellin transform 2\xi(z+\tfrac12), which vanishes at every point \rho-\tfrac12 with \rho a nontrivial zero of \zeta. Every other V_g does too, because its Mellin transform contains the factor \zeta(s). The converse is the first new viewpoint of Route M: vanishing at those points is the only condition.

Theorem 12.11

A function in S_E is a weighted theta sum exactly when its Mellin transform is \xi(z+\tfrac12) times an entire function

[1]
Statement

The Mellin transform maps \mathcal V onto

M(\mathcal V)=\xi\!\left(z+\tfrac12\right)\mathcal O(\CC)\,\cap\,AS(\CC),
(12.13)

where \mathcal O(\CC) is the space of entire functions. In words: u\in S_E(\RR_{>0}) is a weighted theta sum V_g if and only if Mu(z)/\xi(z+\tfrac12) is entire. This is the Global Converse Theorem [1, Theorem 6.3.2.1, p. 304] for F=\QQ and the trivial character, combined with the Fifth Structure Theorem (p. 295). The proof below is ours, written directly over \QQ: it uses the same analytic input as the source’s proof, horizontal segments on which 1/\zeta grows at most polynomially, but not the source’s S-local spaces.

In plain terms

Every theta sum has a Mellin transform that is zero at every zero of zeta, because the zeta function sits inside it as a factor. Conversely, any rapidly decaying function whose Mellin transform is zero at all those points, as often as zeta is, is a theta sum of some even function g. Nothing else distinguishes theta sums from other functions.

Why it is needed

This theorem turns a question about zeros into a question about a subspace. The next card reads off from it that the quotient of all functions by the theta sums is a list of numbers, one block per zero. Every later chapter computes the trace of an operator on that quotient, and the trace is a sum over zeros only because of this theorem.

Idea

One direction is the factorization MV_g(z)=2\zeta(s)Mg(s) with s=z+\tfrac12: rewrite 2\zeta through \xi, and check that the leftover factor has no poles. The other direction runs backward: given F, divide by 2\zeta to get a candidate for Mg, check that it decays on vertical lines, and invert the Mellin transform. The only difficulty is that 1/\zeta is not controlled everywhere in the critical strip, and it is handled by horizontal segments on which it is.

Proof
Show the proof

Write s=z+\tfrac12 throughout.

Theta sums have the factor. Let V_g\in\mathcal V. By Equation (12.12) and Theorem 12.3, MV_g(z)=2\zeta(s)Mg(s), and by the definition of \xi,

MV_g(z)=\xi(s)\,h(z),\qquad h(z)=\frac{4\,\pi^{s/2}\,Mg(s)}{s(s-1)\,\Gamma(s/2)}.

We show that h is entire. Because g is even and smooth, its Taylor expansion at 0 has only even powers, and splitting \int_0^\infty at 1 shows that Mg is meromorphic on \CC with at most simple poles at s=0,-2,-4,\dots, of residue g^{(2k)}(0)/(2k)! at s=-2k. The factor 1/\Gamma(s/2) is entire with simple zeros exactly at s=0,-2,-4,\dots, so Mg(s)/\Gamma(s/2) is entire. At s=0 the residue of Mg is g(0)=0, so Mg is regular there and Mg(s)/\Gamma(s/2) vanishes at 0, which cancels the factor s. At s=1, Mg(1)=\int_0^\infty g=\tfrac12\int_\RR g=0, which cancels s-1. So h is entire, and MV_g\in AS(\CC) by Proposition 12.7 and Theorem 12.9.

Every such function is a theta sum. Let F\in AS(\CC) with F(z)=\xi(s)h(z), h entire. Define

G(s)=\frac{F(s-\tfrac12)}{2\,\zeta(s)}=\tfrac14\,s(s-1)\,\pi^{-s/2}\,\Gamma(s/2)\,h\!\left(s-\tfrac12\right).
  1. Poles. By the second expression, G is meromorphic with at most simple poles at s=-2,-4,\dots (the pole of \Gamma(s/2) at 0 is canceled by s), it is regular at 0, and G(1)=0.
  2. Decay on vertical strips. We show that (1+\abs s)^N\abs{G(s)} is bounded on every vertical strip, away from small discs around the poles. Fix 0<\delta<1. By the first expression it suffices to bound 1/\zeta polynomially in \abs{\Im s}, since F decays faster than any power. On \Re s\ge1+\delta, \abs{1/\zeta(s)}\le\zeta(1+\delta) from the Euler product. On \Re s\le-\delta, write \zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)\cdot(\text{Gamma factors}) by the functional equation: \abs{1/\zeta(1-s)}\le\zeta(1+\delta), and Stirling’s formula bounds the reciprocal of the Gamma factors by a power of \abs{\Im s} for \abs{\Im s}\ge1, uniformly on bounded strips [1, Appendix B.1]. In the band -\delta\le\Re s\le1+\delta the zeros of \zeta prevent any such bound everywhere, and the classical substitute is this: there are heights T_n\to\pm\infty, at least one in every interval of length 1, with \abs{1/\zeta(\sigma+iT_n)}\le C\abs{T_n}^A for all \sigma in the band, for constants C and A [19, §9.7] [1, Corollary B.6.1.8, p. 643]. Take two consecutive heights T_n<T_{n+1} and the rectangle they cut from the band. G is holomorphic on it, because its poles -2,-4,\dots lie outside the band. On the two horizontal sides \abs G\le\abs F\cdot C\abs{T_n}^A/2, and on the two vertical sides the bounds of the previous sentences apply; since T_{n+1}-T_n\le2, every boundary point has \abs{\Im s} within 2 of \abs{T_n}, so \abs G\le C_N\abs{T_n}^{A'-N} on the whole boundary, with A' independent of N. By the maximum modulus principle the same bound holds inside, and N is arbitrary.
  3. Inverse Mellin transform. Define g(t)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}G(s)t^{-s}\,\dd s for t>0 and any c>0; by step 2 the integral converges absolutely and does not depend on c. Moving c to the right shows g(t)=O(t^{-c}) as t\to\infty for every c. Moving it to the left past the poles gives an expansion g(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_kt^{2k}+O(t^{2K+1}) as t\to0, with r_k the residue at -2k and no constant term because G is regular at 0. The same holds for (t\tfrac{\dd}{\dd t})^mg, whose Mellin transform is (-s)^mG(s), with the same powers t^{2k}. Since t^j\tfrac{\dd^j}{\dd t^j} is a polynomial in t\tfrac{\dd}{\dd t}, the remainder R_K=g-\sum_{k\le K}r_kt^{2k} satisfies \tfrac{\dd^j}{\dd t^j}R_K(t)=O(t^{2K+1-j}) for j\le2K. So the even extension of g to \RR is C^{2K} at 0 for every K, hence smooth, with g(0)=0; and the bounds at \infty give the decay of every derivative, so g is Schwartz.
  4. Conclusion. Mg=G by Mellin inversion, \int_\RR g=2Mg(1)=2G(1)=0, and MV_g(z)=2\zeta(s)G(s)=F(z). By Theorem 12.9, the function with Mellin transform F is V_g\in\mathcal V.

The source proves the general statement through its S-local spaces and the Asymptotic Residue Theorem along the same horizontal segments [1, pp. 305 to 309].

Example

For g_\star the factor is the constant h=2, so MV_{g_\star}=2\xi(z+\tfrac12) generates the whole image in the sense that every other image is \xi times an entire function. For the compact example, h_c(z)=4\pi^{s/2}M\operatorname{bump}(s)/\Gamma(s/2) with M\operatorname{bump}(\tfrac12)=0.561542, so h_c(0)=0.824800 and MV_{g_c}(0)=\xi(\tfrac12)h_c(0)=0.410025; a direct numerical integration of \int_0^1t^{1/2}\Theta_{g_c}(t)\,\dd t/t gives 0.410025. At z=0.25+3i the formula and the integral both give 0.594810+0.185073i. At z=14.134725i the formula gives 8\times10^{-16}, zero to the working precision, as it must.

Used in
  • The divisor exact sequence, next: Theorem 12.13.
  • The image of D_p on theta sums and the orbital quotient at p: Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces.
  • The closure of \mathcal V in a Hilbert norm, which keeps only the zeros in a strip: Choosing the topology: what a strip can see.

12.6The divisor exact sequence#

If membership in \mathcal V is decided by values at the zeros, then the quotient S_E/\mathcal V should be the list of those values. A zero of multiplicity m needs more than a value: the factor \xi vanishes to order m there, so a function is divisible by it only if its first m Taylor coefficients vanish.

Definition 12.12 the jet of a function at a zero

Let \rho be a nontrivial zero of \zeta with multiplicity m_\rho. The jet of u\in S_E(\RR_{>0}) at \rho is the vector

J_\rho(u)=\Bigl(\partial_z^{\,j}Mu\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr)\Bigr)_{0\le j<m_\rho}=\Bigl(\int_0^\infty u(t)\,t^{\rho-1/2}(\log t)^j\,\frac{\dd t}t\Bigr)_{0\le j<m_\rho}\in\CC^{m_\rho}.

Each coordinate is a continuous linear functional on S_E, integration against t^{\rho-1/2}(\log t)^j. A jet is a finite list of numbers attached to one zero; it is not a function. The zeros listed in The zeros and the hypothesis are simple, and for a simple zero J_\rho(u) is the single number Mu(\rho-\tfrac12); nothing here assumes that every zero is simple.

Theorem 12.13

Functions modulo theta sums are the jets of their Mellin transforms at the zeros of \zeta

[1]
Statement

The sequence

0\longrightarrow\mathcal V\longrightarrow S_E(\RR_{>0})\xrightarrow{\ J\ }\prod_\rho\CC^{m_\rho},\qquad J(u)=\bigl(J_\rho(u)\bigr)_\rho,
(12.14)

with the product over the nontrivial zeros \rho of \zeta, is exact: the kernel of J is exactly \mathcal V. Every jet sequence with finitely many nonzero entries is J(u) for some u. Hence the quotient \mathcal H=S_E(\RR_{>0})/\mathcal V is identified, by J, with a space of jet sequences at the points z=\rho-\tfrac12: two functions are the same point of \mathcal H exactly when they have the same jets at every zero. Under the Mellin transform the kernel statement reads: an element of AS(\CC) lies in \xi(z+\tfrac12)\mathcal O(\CC)\cap AS(\CC) exactly when its jets at all the points \rho-\tfrac12 vanish. This is the source’s Fundamental Divisor Exact Sequence [1, (1.8.3.2), p. 45, and p. 13] for F=\QQ, with the dual description of Theorem 7.1.4.2 (p. 326).

In plain terms

Take any rapidly decaying function on the positive reals and forget everything about it that a theta sum could account for. What is left is a short list of numbers for each zero of zeta: the value of its Mellin transform there, and, at a multiple zero, a few derivatives. Any finite list can occur. So “all functions modulo theta sums” is a space whose coordinates are the zeros.

Why it is needed

A trace of an operator on \mathcal H is now a sum over the coordinates of \mathcal H, that is, over the zeros. This is how the zeros enter the trace formula of Route M. Masullo names the sequence after the algebraic-geometry sequence 0\to\mathcal O_X(-D)\to\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal O_D\to0 for the divisor D of \xi(z+\tfrac12) on X=\CC: functions vanishing on D, all functions, and functions on D [1, p. 45]. The idea of using this quotient goes back to Connes, who worked in L^2 [43]; the source’s version uses the spaces S_E and AS instead.

Idea

Exactness in the middle is Theorem 12.11 read through jets: a function of AS whose jets at all zeros vanish is divisible by \xi(z+\tfrac12), and divisibility is what characterizes theta sums. That finitely many jets can be prescribed freely is an interpolation problem for entire functions that decay on strips.

Proof

\mathcal V maps to 0. If u=V_g, then Mu=\xi(z+\tfrac12)h with h entire, and \xi(z+\tfrac12) vanishes to order m_\rho at \rho-\tfrac12, so the first m_\rho derivatives of Mu vanish there.

The kernel of J is \mathcal V. If J(u)=0, then Mu vanishes at each \rho-\tfrac12 to order at least m_\rho. The zeros of \xi(z+\tfrac12) are exactly these points with exactly these orders, because \xi is entire and its zeros are the nontrivial zeros of \zeta (Zeta on the whole plane). So h=Mu/\xi(z+\tfrac12) has only removable singularities and is entire, and Mu\in AS(\CC) by Theorem 12.9. By Theorem 12.11, u\in\mathcal V.

Finite jet lists are attained. Fix finitely many points z_k=\rho_k-\tfrac12, with multiplicities m_k, and a target jet at each; all other jets are to be 0. Put F_0(z)=\xi(z+\tfrac12)\prod_k(z-z_k)^{-m_k}e^{z^2}. It is entire, it vanishes to full order at every other zero, and F_0(z_k)\ne0, so its jet at z_k is invertible in the ring of jets. Hermite interpolation gives a polynomial P whose jet at each z_k is the target jet divided by that of F_0, and then F=PF_0 has the target jets at the z_k and zero jets at every other zero. On a vertical strip \xi grows at most polynomially (the Gamma factor decays and \zeta grows polynomially), while \abs{e^{(x+iy)^2}}=e^{x^2-y^2}, so F\in AS(\CC), and u=M^{-1}F has the prescribed jets by Theorem 12.9.

Example

Take the log-Gaussian u_\sigma(t)=e^{-(\log t)^2/(2\sigma^2)}/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}), which lies in S_E and is not a theta sum. Its Mellin transform is Mu_\sigma(z)=e^{\sigma^2z^2/2}, so with \sigma=0.1 its first three coordinates in \mathcal H are Mu_\sigma(i\gamma)=e^{-\gamma^2/200}=0.36827, 0.10974, and 0.04382 at \gamma=14.134725, 21.022040, and 25.010858 (and their conjugates at -\gamma). Adding 5V_{g_\star} to u_\sigma changes the function by an amount comparable to its size, since V_{g_\star}(1)=1.787, but leaves all three numbers unchanged, because MV_{g_\star}=2\xi(z+\tfrac12) vanishes at every i\gamma. In \mathcal H the two functions are the same point.

Used in
  • The convolution operator acts on \mathcal H with eigenvalues M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12): Theorem 12.14.
  • In the Hilbert completion of Choosing the topology: what a strip can see the same quotient keeps only the jets at zeros with \abs{\Re\rho-\tfrac12}<a.
A common misreading

Not every infinite list of jets occurs. An element of AS(\CC) decays faster than any power on the strip \abs{\Re z}\le\tfrac12, which contains every point \rho-\tfrac12, so the jets J_\rho(u) of a single function tend to 0 faster than any power of \abs\gamma. The constant sequence 1,1,1,\dots is not J(u) for any u. The source writes the right end of its sequence as the full product \prod\CC^{N(z)} “forgetting about the uniformly Schwartz condition” [1, p. 13], and in its precise form (1.8.3.2) the right end is a quotient space with a Schauder basis whose dual basis is the jets at the zeros (p. 45).

12.7Convolution acts on the quotient#

The group \RR_{>0} acts on functions by dilation, and averaging the dilations against a test function \varphi gives the convolution operator of the whole route,

\bigl(A(\varphi)u\bigr)(x)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,u(x/t)\,\frac{\dd t}t,

for \varphi smooth with compact support in (0,\infty). It is multiplicative convolution, and the Mellin transform turns it into multiplication: substituting x=ty,

M\bigl(A(\varphi)u\bigr)(z)=M\varphi(z)\,Mu(z).
(12.15)
Theorem 12.14

Convolution by a test function preserves theta sums and acts on the quotient with one eigenvalue M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) for each zero, repeated m_\rho times

[1]
Statement

Let \varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty)).

  1. A(\varphi) maps S_E(\RR_{>0}) to itself and \mathcal V to itself: A(\varphi)V_g=V_{g_\varphi} with g_\varphi(y)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{-1/2}\,g(y/t)\,\dd t/t.
  2. On \mathcal H=S_E/\mathcal V, in the jet coordinates of Theorem 12.13, A(\varphi) acts on the jet at \rho by the lower triangular matrix with entries \binom ji(M\varphi)^{(j-i)}(\rho-\tfrac12), 0\le i\le j<m_\rho. Its eigenvalue on that block is M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12), with multiplicity m_\rho.
  3. A(\varphi) is nuclear on \mathcal H, and its trace is
\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(A(\varphi)\mid\mathcal H\bigr)=\sum_\rho m_\rho\,M\varphi\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr),
(12.16)

an absolutely convergent sum over all nontrivial zeros [1, (1.8.3.4), pp. 46 to 47, and Lemma B.4.4.9, p. 624].

In plain terms

Smearing a function by dilations does not turn a theta sum into anything else, so the operation makes sense on functions modulo theta sums. There it acts on each zero’s coordinates separately, by multiplying by the Mellin transform of the test function at that zero. Its trace is the sum of those multipliers over all zeros.

Why it is needed

This is the spectral side of a trace formula: an operator whose eigenvalues are indexed by the zeros of \zeta. Connes proposed such a spectral realization of the zeros in 1999 [43]. The whole of Route M consists in computing the same trace a second time, through the primes, in a space where the answer is not just Weil’s formula again.

Idea

On the Mellin side, A(\varphi) is multiplication by the entire function M\varphi. Multiplication by an entire function keeps the ideal of multiples of \xi(z+\tfrac12), and on Taylor coefficients at a point it acts by the Leibniz rule, a triangular matrix whose diagonal is the value at that point.

Proof
  1. M\varphi is entire, and on every vertical strip it decays faster than any power because \varphi is smooth with compact support in (0,\infty) (integrate by parts in \log t). So by Equation (12.15) A(\varphi) maps AS(\CC) to itself and multiples of \xi(z+\tfrac12) to multiples of it, hence S_E to S_E and \mathcal V to \mathcal V by Theorem 12.11. Directly: A(\varphi)V_g(x)=\int\varphi(t)(x/t)^{1/2}\sum_{n\ne0}g(nx/t)\,\dd t/t=x^{1/2}\Theta_{g_\varphi}(x). The function g_\varphi is even and Schwartz, g_\varphi(0)=g(0)\int\varphi(t)t^{-1/2}\,\dd t/t=0, and \int g_\varphi=\int g\cdot\int\varphi(t)t^{1/2}\,\dd t/t=0.
  2. By the Leibniz rule, \partial^j(M\varphi\cdot Mu)=\sum_{i\le j}\binom ji(M\varphi)^{(j-i)}(Mu)^{(i)}, evaluated at \rho-\tfrac12.
  3. The diagonal entries sum to the right side of Equation (12.16). The sum converges absolutely because M\varphi(i\gamma) decays faster than any power of \gamma while the number of zeros up to height T grows like T\log T (The zeros and the hypothesis). That the operator is nuclear in the source’s topology on \mathcal H, so that this sum is its trace, is proved in the source with Schauder bases [1, p. 46 and Chapter 7].
Used in
  • Weil’s explicit formula as this trace in the fine topology: Theorem 12.15.
  • The trace on the orbital quotient at p, which is a circle: Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces.
  • The same operator on the Hilbert quotient, whose trace keeps only zeros in a strip: Choosing the topology: what a strip can see and Cutting the kernel along the primes.

In this topology, the trace formula is Weil’s formula#

How would one compute the trace Equation (12.16) without knowing the zeros? Weil’s explicit formula of Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion already does it: it expresses the sum over zeros through primes and an archimedean integral. In the multiplicative notation of this part, and for \varphi(1)=0, it reads as follows.

Theorem 12.15

For a test function vanishing at 1, the sum over all zeros of M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) is given by the poles, the primes, and one archimedean integral

[35]
Statement

For \varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty)) with \varphi(1)=0,

\sum_\rho m_\rho\,M\varphi\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr)=M\varphi\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)+M\varphi\bigl(-\tfrac12\bigr)-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}\bigl(\varphi(n)+\varphi(1/n)\bigr)-\frac12\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac1{\abs{1-t}}+\frac1{1+t}\Bigr)\frac{\dd t}t.
(12.17)

This is the source’s idelic form of Weil’s explicit formula [1, Theorem B.4.4.7, p. 623] for F=\QQ; the specialization of its local terms to \RR_{>0} is ours. The integral converges absolutely because \varphi(1)=0.

In plain terms

The sum of the eigenvalues over all zeros can be computed without finding a single zero: it is two easy terms from the pole of zeta, minus a sum over prime powers, minus one integral that comes from the Gamma factor.

Why it is needed

It shows what the fine topology of this chapter can and cannot do. Every jet at every zero is a continuous functional on S_E, so every zero contributes to the trace, and the trace formula for A(\varphi) on \mathcal H is Weil’s formula and nothing more [1, pp. 39 and 46 to 47]. To learn where the zeros are, Route M must change the topology so that some jets stop being continuous while the prime side survives intact. That is chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see.

Idea

Integrate M\varphi(z) against \xi'/\xi(z+\tfrac12) around a tall rectangle. Inside, the residues are the zeros. On the boundary, write \xi'/\xi as the sum of the logarithmic derivatives of its factors: the pole terms give M\varphi(\pm\tfrac12), the Euler product gives the prime sum, and the Gamma factor gives the integral. The two kernels in the integral come from the two halves t>0 and t<0 of \RR^\times, the real completion of The adeles: all completions at once.

Proof sketch

[35]

The classical proof is Weil’s [35]; the idelic version with Weil’s local principal values at every place is [1, Theorem B.4.4.7, p. 623]. At a prime p the local term is \log p\int_{\QQ_p^\times}\varphi(\abs x_p)\abs x_p^{1/2}/\abs{1-x}_p\,\dd^\times x; on the shell p^m\ZZ_p^\times with m\ne0 the integrand is p^{-\abs m/2}\varphi(p^{-m}), and the units contribute nothing when \varphi(1)=0, which gives \log p\sum_{m\ge1}p^{-m/2}(\varphi(p^m)+\varphi(p^{-m})), the terms n=p^m of the prime sum. At the real place, with weight \tfrac12, the integral over \RR^\times splits into x>0 and x<0, which gives the two kernels.

Example

Take \varphi(t)=\operatorname{bump}\bigl((\log t-1)/0.6\bigr), with \operatorname{bump} the bump of Equation (12.3), so that \varphi is supported on 1.49<t<4.95 and \varphi(1)=0. Then M\varphi(\tfrac12)=0.442346, M\varphi(-\tfrac12)=0.162730, the prime terms (n=2,3,4) total 0.416292, and the integral term is 0.195324, so the right side of Equation (12.17) is -0.00653943. Summing 2\Re M\varphi(i\gamma) over the first 200 zeros with \gamma>0 (up to \gamma=396.38), computed with mpmath, gives -0.00653944. The agreement to about 10^{-8} checks the constants of the integral term. The individual zero terms are small (-2.6\times10^{-5} for the first zero) and of both signs, and after 100 zeros the partial sum -0.0065396 already agrees to five digits.

Used in
  • The geometric side of the Trace Formula, which is this same right side: The local trace and the Trace Formula.
  • The endgame compares the Trace Formula with this formula: From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis.

12.8What changes in general#

For a number field F and a Schwartz-Bruhat function f on \AA_F, the global theta function is \Phi_F(f)(g)=\sum_{\xi\in F^\times}f(\xi g) on C_F, and the adelic Riemann-Roch identity reads \Phi_F(f)(g)=\abs g^{-1}\Phi_F(\hat f)(g^{-1})+\abs g^{-1}\hat f(0)-f(0) [1, Theorem 2.2.3.2, p. 82]. Its Mellin transform along a character \chi\abs\cdot^s of C_F is Tate’s zeta integral Z(f,\chi\abs\cdot^s), which is the Hecke L-function L(s,\chi) times an entire factor [1, Theorem 3.2.2.1, p. 124]. Functions on C_F split into isotypes, one for each character of the compact group C_F^1, and each isotype is studied separately.

Three points need more care than over \QQ. First, the class group of F may be nontrivial, so the source enlarges the finite set of places S until the ring of S-integers has class number one, and then every theta function of a given isotype is \Phi_F(f_S\otimes\bigotimes_{v\notin S}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal O_{F_v}}) [1, Theorem 6.2.1.1, p. 295]. Its S-local version sums over the S-units instead of F^\times; over \QQ with S=\{\infty\} the S-units are \pm1, and the S-local theta function of f_\infty is just f_\infty(t)+f_\infty(-t) [1, p. 12]. Second, the converse theorem has the factor L(s,\chi) for a nontrivial isotype and (s+it_0)(1-s-it_0)L(s,\chi) for the trivial one, and the divisor exact sequence becomes jets at the zeros of L(z+\tfrac12,\chi) [1, Theorem 6.3.2.1, p. 304]. Third, D_p becomes \mathrm{PV}_v at a place v, with Mellin factor 1-\chi(\mathfrak p_v)q_v^{-s} in place of 1-p^{-s} [1, (1.8.1.2), p. 39].

Recap

You now have the following, and where each is used.

  • The theta sum \Theta_g(t)=\sum_{n\ne0}g(nt) of an even Schwartz g, which is the adelic theta function of g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} (Definition 12.1, Equation (12.8)); over \QQ every theta function with trivial character is of this form.
  • Its symmetry, adelic Riemann-Roch equals Poisson summation (Theorem 12.2), its Mellin transform 2\zeta(s)Mg(s) (Theorem 12.3), and the functional equation Z_g(s)=Z_{\hat g}(1-s) (Theorem 12.4).
  • The operator D_p, which deletes the multiples of p and multiplies the Mellin transform by 1-p^{-s} (Proposition 12.6): the orbital quotients of Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces and the sieve of Cutting the kernel along the primes.
  • The conditions g(0)=0 and \int g=0, the decay e^{-N\abs{\log t}} they give, and the space S_E(\RR_{>0}) with its Mellin image AS(\CC) (Proposition 12.7, Theorem 12.9).
  • The converse theorem: Mellin transforms of weighted theta sums are exactly \xi(z+\tfrac12) times entire functions in AS(\CC) (Theorem 12.11).
  • The divisor exact sequence: functions modulo theta sums are jets at the points \rho-\tfrac12 (Theorem 12.13): the spectral side in Choosing the topology: what a strip can see.
  • The operator A(\varphi) on the quotient, with eigenvalues M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) and trace \sum_\rho m_\rho M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) (Theorem 12.14), and the fact that in this fine topology the trace formula is Weil’s explicit formula (Theorem 12.15): the reason Choosing the topology: what a strip can see changes the topology.
