Chapter 13

Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces

After this chapter you can compute the trace of a convolution operator on a circle of length log p in two ways, show by Poisson summation that the two answers agree, and see why the answer is zero for every prime beyond the support of the test function.

Builds on 12. Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions

In plain terms

Wrap the positive real line around a circle so that the numbers 1, p, p^2, p^3, \dots all land on the same point. Smoothing along that circle by a test function is an infinite matrix in the basis of waves on the circle, and its trace, the sum of the diagonal entries, can be read off in two ways: as a sum over the waves, or as a sum over the powers of p. The two answers agree, and when the test function is too short to stretch from 1 to p the trace is exactly zero. Deleting the multiples of a prime from a theta sum produces exactly this circle, so every prime larger than the test function’s reach contributes nothing.

The previous chapter turned the zeros of \zeta into the spectrum of an operator: on the quotient of all functions by the weighted theta sums, convolution by \varphi acts with eigenvalues M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12). That is one side of a trace formula. The other side has to come from the primes, and the proof gets it by taking the theta sums apart one prime at a time. This chapter computes what one such step contributes. The answer is a trace on a circle of length \log p, and the fact that this trace vanishes once p is large is the mechanism the whole route turns on: it lets Cutting the kernel along the primes throw away every prime beyond a finite set. The source calls these bases “the crux of the matter” [1, §1.4.9, p. 31].

13.1A circle on the multiplicative line#

Everything in this chapter lives on \RR_{>0} with the measure \dd t/t, the measure that does not change when t is rescaled. Fix a number \lambda>1, think of it as a prime p, and declare two positive reals equivalent when their ratio is a power of \lambda.

Definition 13.1 the toy circle of length \log\lambda

The toy circle is the quotient group \RR_{>0}/\lambda^{\ZZ}, in which x and \lambda^kx are the same point for every k\in\ZZ. Every point has exactly one representative in [1,\lambda). The measure \dd t/t on [1,\lambda) gives it total length

\int_1^\lambda\frac{\dd t}{t}=\log\lambda .

In the coordinate u=\log t it is the circle \RR/(\log\lambda)\ZZ. A function on the toy circle is the same thing as a function \psi on \RR_{>0} with \psi(\lambda x)=\psi(x) for all x. It is not a subset of \RR_{>0}, and its functions do not decay: they repeat forever in both directions.

The way to make a periodic function out of an ordinary one is to add up all its rescaled copies, exactly as Poisson summation periodizes a function on \RR by adding its translates.

Definition 13.2 periodization over powers of \lambda

For a function \psi on \RR_{>0} that decays faster than every power of t at 0 and at \infty (the space S_E(\RR_{>0}) of Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions), its periodization is

\Phi_\lambda\psi(x)=\sum_{k\in\ZZ}\psi(\lambda^kx).

The sum converges with all derivatives, and \Phi_\lambda\psi(\lambda x)=\Phi_\lambda\psi(x), so \Phi_\lambda\psi is a smooth function on the toy circle. The operator \Phi_\lambda is the source’s “monogenic periodization” [1, Definition 4.2.1.1, p. 162].

Two different functions can have the same periodization, and the difference between them is what the circle forgets. The simplest function the circle cannot see is \psi(x)-\psi(\lambda x), because its periodization telescopes: the copy \psi(\lambda^kx) is added once and subtracted once.

Proposition 13.3 Periodization forgets exactly the differences \psi(x)-\psi(\lambda x), which on the Mellin side are the multiples of 1-\lambda^{-s} [1, Lemma 4.2.1.5, p. 165; Example 1.8.1.1, pp. 40 to 41]

The map \Phi_\lambda from S_E(\RR_{>0}) onto the smooth functions on the toy circle is continuous, surjective, and open, and its kernel is the closure of the span of the functions x\mapsto\psi(x)-\psi(\lambda x). Under the Mellin transform M\psi(s)=\int_0^\infty\psi(t)t^s\,\dd t/t the function \psi(x)-\psi(\lambda x) becomes

(1-\lambda^{-s})\,M\psi(s),

so the circle is the quotient “entire functions modulo multiples of 1-\lambda^{-s}”, and such a quotient is described by the values at the zeros s=2\pi im/\log\lambda of 1-\lambda^{-s}.

The Mellin identity is the substitution t\mapsto t/\lambda: \int_0^\infty\psi(\lambda t)t^s\,\dd t/t=\lambda^{-s}M\psi(s). The source remarks that 1-\lambda^{-s} “is reminiscent of a reciprocal Euler factor” [1, p. 41], and with \lambda=p it is one: \prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}=\zeta(s).

The points s=2\pi im/\log\lambda deserve a name, because they index everything that follows.

Symbols
Symbol What it is Kind Where it lives
z_m 2\pi im/\log\lambda, the mth zero of 1-\lambda^{-s} a point on the imaginary axis m\in\ZZ
e_m e_m(t)=t^{z_m}=e^{2\pi im\log t/\log\lambda} a function on the toy circle the exponential basis
c_m(\psi) \frac1{\log\lambda}\int_1^\lambda\psi(t)\,t^{-z_m}\,\frac{\dd t}t a number, the mth Fourier coefficient a linear functional on circle functions
\Phi_\lambda periodization \psi\mapsto\sum_k\psi(\lambda^k\,\cdot) an operator S_E(\RR_{>0})\to circle functions

Each e_m is \lambda-periodic because \lambda^{z_m}=e^{2\pi im}=1. In the coordinate u=\log t the functions e_m are the waves e^{2\pi imu/\log\lambda} and c_m is the usual Fourier coefficient, so a smooth circle function is its Fourier series, \psi=\sum_mc_m(\psi)\,e_m, with coefficients that decay faster than any power of m [17, Chapter 3]. The coefficients of a periodization are values of a Mellin transform: unfolding the integral over [1,\lambda) into an integral over \RR_{>0},

c_m(\Phi_\lambda\psi)=\frac1{\log\lambda}\sum_{k\in\ZZ}\int_1^\lambda\psi(\lambda^kt)\,t^{-z_m}\,\frac{\dd t}t=\frac1{\log\lambda}\int_0^\infty\psi(t)\,t^{-z_m}\,\frac{\dd t}t=\frac{M\psi(-z_m)}{\log\lambda},
(13.1)

where each substitution t\mapsto\lambda^{-k}t leaves t^{-z_m} unchanged because \lambda^{kz_m}=1. This is the concrete content of Proposition 13.3: \Phi_\lambda\psi=0 exactly when M\psi vanishes at every z_m.

13.2What a Schauder basis buys#

In finite dimensions the trace of a linear map is the sum of the diagonal entries of its matrix in any basis. The circle functions form an infinite-dimensional space, and the proof needs the same bookkeeping there, so it needs a basis in a sense that survives infinite sums.

Definition 13.4 Schauder basis

A Schauder basis of a topological vector space E is a sequence (x_m) in E together with continuous linear functionals (f_m), the coefficient functionals, with f_m(x_n)=1 if m=n and 0 otherwise, such that every u\in E is the convergent sum u=\sum_mf_m(u)\,x_m. It is absolute when these sums converge absolutely for every continuous seminorm. A Schauder basis is not a Hamel basis: infinite sums are allowed, and the coefficient functionals must be continuous. It need not be orthonormal, and the space need not carry an inner product.

Continuity of the coefficient functionals is the whole point: a functional that is not continuous cannot be passed through a limit, and every computation below is a limit. Once a basis with continuous coefficients exists, an operator A has a matrix with entries f_m(Ax_n), and for the operators that matter here (nuclear operators, the analog of trace-class operators on spaces such as S_E) the trace equals the sum of the diagonal entries \sum_mf_m(Ax_m). The source quotes this from Litvinov and builds all of its trace computations on it [1, §4.1.1, p. 158, Theorem 7.4.2.1, p. 367]. So an explicit basis lets a trace be computed like the trace of a matrix, and a basis in which the operator is diagonal makes the trace a sum of eigenvalues. Our reference for Schauder bases in locally convex spaces is Jarchow [64, Chapter 14].

Theorem 13.5 The waves t^{z_m} form an absolute Schauder basis of the smooth functions on the toy circle, with the Fourier coefficients as coefficient functionals [1, Lemma 4.2.1.2, p. 162]

For every \lambda>1 the functions e_m(t)=t^{2\pi im/\log\lambda}, m\in\ZZ, with coefficient functionals c_m, form an absolute Schauder basis of the space of smooth functions on \RR_{>0}/\lambda^\ZZ.

Proof sketch [1, Lemma 4.2.1.2, p. 162; §4.1.1, p. 157]

In the coordinate u=\log t this is the classical statement that a smooth periodic function equals its Fourier series, with coefficients decaying faster than every power of m, so the series converges absolutely in every derivative. The source calls the result “well known” and calls the basis the exponential system.

13.3The trace on the circle, computed twice#

Convolution A(\varphi)\psi(x)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\psi(x/t)\,\dd t/t, for \varphi smooth and compactly supported on \RR_{>0}, averages rescaled copies of \psi. Rescaling commutes with the identification x\sim\lambda x, so A(\varphi) maps \lambda-periodic functions to \lambda-periodic functions and commutes with \Phi_\lambda. It therefore acts on the toy circle, and there it can be computed in two ways, which we now do.

The first computation uses the basis. Apply A(\varphi) to a wave:

A(\varphi)e_m(x)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\Bigl(\frac xt\Bigr)^{z_m}\frac{\dd t}t=x^{z_m}\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{-z_m}\,\frac{\dd t}t=M\varphi(-z_m)\,e_m(x).

Every wave is an eigenvector, so the matrix of A(\varphi) in the exponential basis is diagonal with entries M\varphi(-z_m). As m runs over \ZZ so does -m, and the sum of the diagonal is \sum_mM\varphi(z_m). In the source’s words, the trace “is the sum of the eigenvalues” [1, p. 41].

The second computation uses the points. Write A(\varphi) as an integral over the circle: substitute y=x/t, so that \dd t/t=\dd y/y, and fold \RR_{>0} onto [1,\lambda) using the periodicity of \psi,

A(\varphi)\psi(x)=\int_0^\infty\varphi\Bigl(\frac xy\Bigr)\psi(y)\,\frac{\dd y}y=\int_1^\lambda k_\lambda(x,y)\,\psi(y)\,\frac{\dd y}y,\qquad k_\lambda(x,y)=\sum_{k\in\ZZ}\varphi\Bigl(\lambda^k\frac xy\Bigr).

The function k_\lambda is the integral kernel of A(\varphi) on the circle, the continuous analog of a matrix with rows indexed by x and columns by y, and the analog of the diagonal sum is the integral of the kernel along the diagonal y=x. On the diagonal k_\lambda(x,x)=\sum_k\varphi(\lambda^k) does not depend on x, so its integral over a circle of length \log\lambda is \log\lambda\sum_k\varphi(\lambda^k). The points \lambda^k have a geometric meaning: moving a point x of the circle by the factor t brings it back to itself exactly when t\in\lambda^\ZZ, so \lambda^k is the closed orbit that winds k times around the circle, and \varphi(\lambda^k) is how much the test function weighs that orbit.

Nothing so far says that the diagonal sum of the matrix and the diagonal mass of the kernel agree. For a finite matrix they are the same number by definition, but here one is a sum over frequencies and the other a sum over orbit points, and the identity between them is Poisson summation.

Theorem 13.6

The trace of convolution on a circle of length \log\lambda is the sum of the Mellin transform over the zeros of 1-\lambda^{-s}, and equals \log\lambda times the sum of \varphi over the powers of \lambda

[1, Example 1.8.1.1, pp. 40 to 41]
Statement

Let \lambda>1, z_m=2\pi im/\log\lambda, and \varphi smooth with compact support in \RR_{>0}. On the smooth functions on \RR_{>0}/\lambda^\ZZ the operator A(\varphi) is diagonal in the exponential basis with eigenvalues M\varphi(-z_m), these are absolutely summable, and

\operatorname{Tr}A(\varphi)=\sum_{m\in\ZZ}M\varphi\Bigl(\frac{2\pi im}{\log\lambda}\Bigr)=\log\lambda\sum_{k\in\ZZ}\varphi(\lambda^k)=\int_1^\lambda k_\lambda(x,x)\,\frac{\dd x}x.
(13.2)
In plain terms

The trace of smoothing along a circle can be counted by frequencies or by laps. Counting by frequencies adds up how much each wave is amplified. Counting by laps adds up how much the test function weighs each whole number of trips around the circle, times the length of the circle. Both counts give the same number.

Why it is needed

Every orbital trace in Cutting the kernel along the primes is this identity with \lambda=p. The left side is what the basis gives, and it is the side that exists inside the function spaces of the proof. The right side is what makes the answer computable and, for large p, zero.

Idea

In the coordinate u=\log t the test function becomes f(u)=\varphi(e^u), an ordinary bump on \RR, the Mellin transform at z_m becomes its Fourier transform at the frequency m/\log\lambda, and the powers \lambda^k become the lattice points k\log\lambda. Poisson summation for the lattice (\log\lambda)\ZZ says that summing f over the lattice equals summing \hat f over the dual lattice, divided by the lattice spacing.

Proof

Step 1, eigenvalues. The computation before the statement gives A(\varphi)e_m=M\varphi(-z_m)\,e_m. Since the e_m form a basis with coefficient functionals c_m (Theorem 13.5), the diagonal entries of the matrix are c_m(A(\varphi)e_m)=M\varphi(-z_m).

Step 2, summability. Put f(u)=\varphi(e^u), a smooth function with compact support on \RR. Then M\varphi(iy)=\int_\RR f(u)e^{iyu}\,\dd u, and integrating by parts twice gives \abs{M\varphi(iy)}\le\norm{f''}_{L^1}/y^2 for y\ne0. So \sum_m\abs{M\varphi(z_m)}<\infty. An operator that is diagonal in a basis with absolutely summable eigenvalues is nuclear, and its trace is the sum of the eigenvalues. On the Hilbert space L^2 of the circle with the measure \dd t/(t\log\lambda), in which the e_m are orthonormal, this is the definition of a trace-class diagonal operator. The source states nuclearity on the smooth functions [1, p. 41]. Reindexing m\to-m, \operatorname{Tr}A(\varphi)=\sum_mM\varphi(z_m).

Step 3, Fourier transform. With \hat f(\eta)=\int_\RR f(u)e^{-2\pi iu\eta}\,\dd u as in The complex analysis we need,

M\varphi(-z_m)=\int_\RR f(u)\,e^{-2\pi imu/\log\lambda}\,\dd u=\hat f\Bigl(\frac m{\log\lambda}\Bigr).

Step 4, Poisson summation. Apply Poisson summation \sum_kF(k)=\sum_m\hat F(m) to the compactly supported smooth function F(x)=f(x\log\lambda), whose transform is \hat F(\eta)=\hat f(\eta/\log\lambda)/\log\lambda:

\sum_{k\in\ZZ}f(k\log\lambda)=\frac1{\log\lambda}\sum_{m\in\ZZ}\hat f\Bigl(\frac m{\log\lambda}\Bigr).

The left side is \sum_k\varphi(\lambda^k). By Step 3 the right side is \frac1{\log\lambda}\sum_mM\varphi(-z_m)=\frac1{\log\lambda}\sum_mM\varphi(z_m). Multiplying by \log\lambda gives the second equality of Equation (13.2).

Step 5, the kernel. The kernel computation before the statement gives k_\lambda(x,x)=\sum_k\varphi(\lambda^k) for every x, and \int_1^\lambda\dd x/x=\log\lambda, which is the third equality.

Example

Take \lambda=2 and the bump \varphi(t)=\operatorname{bump}\bigl((\log t-0.5)/0.6\bigr) with \operatorname{bump}(x)=e^{-1/(1-x^2)} for \abs x<1 and 0 otherwise, so \varphi lives on \log t\in(-0.1,1.1), that is on t\in(0.905,3.004). Two orbit points fall in the support, t=1 and t=2, with \varphi(1)=0.0379029 and \varphi(2)=0.3277162, so the right side is \log2\times0.3656191=0.2534278. On the left, the m=0 term is M\varphi(0)=0.2663963, and adding the pairs \pm m gives the partial sums

0.2712885,\ 0.2546214,\ 0.2548982,\ 0.2529194,\ 0.2532840,\ 0.2530149,\ 0.2532958,\ 0.2532840

for \abs m\le1,\dots,8, and the full sum over \abs m\le60 is 0.2534278, agreeing with the right side to nine digits. With \lambda=3 and the bump on \log t\in(-0.3,1.5) both sides are 0.4411483. (Computed with mpmath by quadrature of M\varphi on the imaginary axis.)

Used in
  • Corollary 13.7: the right side is zero when no orbit point meets the support.
  • Theorem 13.11: the same identity with \lambda=p on the quotient of theta sums at p.
  • Cutting the kernel along the primes: the diagonal mass of each slice of the sieve.

13.4When the trace vanishes#

The right side of Equation (13.2) only looks at \varphi on the orbit points \lambda^k, so a test function that misses all of them has trace zero, however large its individual eigenvalues are.

Corollary 13.7 The circle trace is zero when the support of \varphi contains no power of \lambda [1, Example 1.8.1.1, p. 41; pp. 17, 19]

If \operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset(1,\lambda), then \operatorname{Tr}A(\varphi)=0 on the toy circle. More generally, if \varphi(1)=0 and \operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset(1/Y,Y) with Y\le\lambda, then \operatorname{Tr}A(\varphi)=0.

Proof

In the first case no \lambda^k lies in (1,\lambda): \lambda^k\le1 for k\le0 and \lambda^k\ge\lambda for k\ge1. In the second case, \lambda^k\ge\lambda\ge Y for k\ge1 and \lambda^k\le1/\lambda\le1/Y for k\le-1, so these points lie outside the open interval (1/Y,Y) that contains the support, and the term k=0 is \varphi(1)=0. In both cases every term of \log\lambda\sum_k\varphi(\lambda^k) vanishes.

The source states the first form. The second is the form the proof uses, because the test functions of the trace formula vanish at 1 and have support in a window (1/Y,Y) around it (in our notation; the source writes T for Y). Read through the orbits it says something intuitive: a test function whose reach is shorter than one lap of the circle cannot see the circle close up, so it registers no closed orbit.

Example

Take \lambda=2 and the bump \varphi(t)=\operatorname{bump}\bigl((\log t-\tfrac12\log2)/0.3\bigr), supported on t\in(1.047,1.910)\subset(1,2). The eigenvalue sum starts with M\varphi(0)=0.1331981, and the pairs \pm1 contribute 2\Re M\varphi(z_1)=-0.1395792, so after \abs m\le1 the partial sum is -0.0063811, and the next partial sums are -0.0200422, -0.0101432, -0.0012386, 0.0026308, 0.0028999. They oscillate toward 0, the value of the orbit side, while no single term is small. The trace vanishes by cancellation among the eigenvalues, not because any eigenvalue vanishes.

The proof will apply this to functions multiplied by the weight t^{1/2} of Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions, and the vanishing survives the weight. On functions \psi with t^{-c}\psi periodic, for a real c, the basis is t^{c+z_m}, the eigenvalues are M\varphi(-c-z_m), and the same five steps give (in our notation, by a computation of ours)

\sum_{m\in\ZZ}M\varphi(-c+z_m)=\log\lambda\sum_{k\in\ZZ}\lambda^{-ck}\varphi(\lambda^k).
(13.3)

Each orbit point now carries the factor \lambda^{-ck}, so the right side vanishes under the same conditions. For the first example above with c=\tfrac12 both sides equal \log2\,(\varphi(1)+2^{-1/2}\varphi(2))=0.1868955.

13.5Deleting the multiples of a prime#

The toy circle becomes arithmetic when \lambda=p and the periodized functions are theta sums. Recall from Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions the theta sum \Theta_g(t)=\sum_{n\ne0}g(nt) of an even Schwartz function g with g(0)=0 and \int_\RR g=0 (call such g admissible), its Mellin transform 2\zeta(s)Mg(s) with Mg(s)=\int_0^\infty g(t)t^s\,\dd t/t, and the operator D_p that deletes the multiples of p. The lemma below restates Proposition 12.6 in the form this chapter uses.

Lemma 13.8 Deleting the multiples of p from a theta sum is the difference of the sum and its rescaling by p, and multiplies the Mellin transform by 1-p^{-s}

For every prime p and every admissible g,

D_p\Theta_g(t)=\sum_{n\ne0,\ p\nmid n}g(nt)=\Theta_g(t)-\Theta_g(pt),\qquad M(D_p\Theta_g)(s)=(1-p^{-s})\,2\zeta(s)Mg(s).

In particular D_p\Theta_g=\Theta_{g-g(p\,\cdot)} is again a theta sum.

Proof

The integers n\ne0 divisible by p are exactly n=pn' with n'\ne0, so \sum_{p\mid n}g(nt)=\sum_{n'\ne0}g(n'pt)=\Theta_g(pt), and subtracting from \Theta_g(t) leaves the sum over p\nmid n. The Mellin identity is Proposition 13.3 with \lambda=p. The function g-g(p\,\cdot) is even and Schwartz, vanishes at 0, and has integral \int g-\tfrac1p\int g=0.

On the Mellin side the factor 1-p^{-s} removes the Euler factor at p from \zeta(s)=\prod_q(1-q^{-s})^{-1}, leaving \sum_{p\nmid n}n^{-s}. In adelic language, Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions showed that D_p replaces the indicator of \ZZ_p by the indicator of the units \ZZ_p^\times, which is the source’s Weil principal value operator \mathrm{PV}_p [1, §5.3, p. 240, p. 18].

A concrete theta sum makes every quantity checkable. Let

g_\star(x)=(4\pi^2x^4-6\pi x^2)\,e^{-\pi x^2}.

It is even and Schwartz, g_\star(0)=0, and \int_\RR g_\star=4\pi^2\cdot\tfrac3{4\pi^2}-6\pi\cdot\tfrac1{2\pi}=0. Its Mellin transform is \tfrac12\pi^{-s/2}\bigl(4\Gamma(\tfrac s2+2)-6\Gamma(\tfrac s2+1)\bigr)=\tfrac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac s2), so

M\Theta_{g_\star}(s)=2\zeta(s)\cdot\tfrac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac s2)=2\,\xi(s).
(13.4)

The function g_\star is our choice. At s=2 a numerical Mellin transform of \Theta_{g_\star} gives 1.0471976 and 2\xi(2)=\pi/3=1.0471976, and at s=0.3+2i both are 0.9068972-0.0168735i. The sum is concentrated near t=1: \Theta_{g_\star}(1)=1.7867876, \Theta_{g_\star}(2)=0.0038797, \Theta_{g_\star}(0.2)=1.9\times10^{-29} (by Theorem 12.2 it equals 5\,\Theta_{g_\star}(5)). Deleting the even terms, at t=0.4 both \Theta_{g_\star}(0.4)-\Theta_{g_\star}(0.8) and \sum_{2\nmid n}g_\star(0.4n) equal -1.2351560.

Definition 13.9 orbital quotient at p

The orbital quotient at p is the quotient vector space

E_p=\{\Theta_g\}\big/\{D_p\Theta_g\}

of the space of theta sums by the image of D_p, with the quotient topology. It is a space of equivalence classes, not of functions: two theta sums are identified when their difference is a theta sum with the multiples of p already deleted. It is the source’s p-primary orbital quotient, written there for a number field and a character [1, Definition 7.3.1.3, p. 343, Theorem 7.4.2.1, p. 367].

The periodization \Phi_p is defined on theta sums, because they decay faster than every power at both ends, and by the telescoping argument it kills D_p\Theta_g=\Theta_g-\Theta_g(p\,\cdot). So it induces a map from E_p to the smooth functions on the circle \RR_{>0}/p^\ZZ of length \log p. The theorem below says that nothing is lost: the quotient of theta sums at p is the circle, exactly as the quotient of all functions is.

Theorem 13.10

The orbital quotient of theta sums at p is the space of smooth functions on a circle of length \log p

[1]
Statement

Periodization over p^\ZZ induces an isomorphism of topological vector spaces

E_p=\{\Theta_g\}\big/\{D_p\Theta_g\}\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ S_E(\RR_{>0})\big/\ker\Phi_p\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ C^\infty(\RR_{>0}/p^\ZZ),

which commutes with every convolution A(\varphi). On the Mellin side it says that the multiples of \xi(s), modulo the multiples of (1-p^{-s})\xi(s), are the same as all functions modulo the multiples of 1-p^{-s}.

In plain terms

A theta sum is a very special function, built from a single g sampled at all the integers. Once the multiples of p are thrown out of it, what is left over can still be any smooth function on the circle of length \log p. The theta sums are rich enough that the circle sees them as it sees everything.

Why it is needed

The trace of Theorem 13.6 is a statement about the circle. The proof needs it for the orbital quotient of theta sums, because the pieces of the sieve in Cutting the kernel along the primes act on theta sums. This theorem is the bridge.

Idea

By Equation (13.1) the circle image of \Theta_g has Fourier coefficients M\Theta_g(-z_m)/\log p, and M\Theta_g is \xi(s) times an entire function. The points -z_m lie on the imaginary axis \Re s=0, which the functional equation \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) reflects onto the line \Re s=1, where \zeta has no zeros (The zeros and the hypothesis). So \xi never vanishes at the points the circle looks at, multiplying by \xi loses nothing there, and the circle sees a theta sum as freely as it sees an arbitrary function.

Proof sketch

[1, Theorem 7.5.0.1, p. 374; Corollary 7.5.0.3, p. 379; Lemma 4.2.1.5, p. 165]

The second isomorphism is Proposition 13.3. For the first, the source proves injectivity by showing that the coefficient functionals of the circle, pulled back to theta sums, are the evaluations of the Mellin transform at the zeros of 1-p^{-s}, and that these remain independent on E_p because the matrix relating them to the jets of M\Theta_g there is triangular with diagonal entries a power of L(1-s_c), nonzero by the non-vanishing of L on the line \Re s=1. Over \mathbb Q every zero of 1-p^{-s} is simple, so each matrix is 1\times1, and its entry is a value of \zeta on the line \Re s=1 times local factors that do not vanish there. Surjectivity uses the S-local orbital bases of Theorem 7.3.1.6 together with the polynomial growth of 1/\zeta(1+it) and of the derivatives of \zeta on vertical lines, which control the size of the inverse matrices so that the lifted basis still converges. A corollary is a quantitative coprimality: every \phi in the Mellin image of S_E is \xi(s)u(s)+(1-p^{-s})v(s) with \xi u and v in the same class. The source notes that this theorem is not logically needed for the main trace computation, which works with the orbital bases directly, and uses it to explain the structure behind them [1, §7.5, p. 374].

Example

For g_\star and p=2, the circle image \Phi_2\Theta_{g_\star} takes the values 1.79843, 1.20469, 1.18159, 1.65519 at x=1,1.25,1.5,1.75. By Equation (13.1) and Equation (13.4) its Fourier coefficients are c_m=\frac2{\log 2}\,\xi(-z_m)=\frac2{\log2}\,\xi(1+z_m). Numerically integrating the circle function gives c_0=1.4426950=1/\log2, c_1=0.178620+0.045832i, and c_2=-0.000753-0.000294i, matching \frac2{\log2}\xi(1+z_m) to five digits. For p=3 the same computation gives c_0=0.9102392=1/\log3, c_1=0.4146724+0.0584580i, and c_2=0.0245002+0.0101804i. None of these is zero, and none can be, because \zeta(1+it)\ne0.

Used in
  • Theorem 13.11: the trace on E_p is the circle trace with \lambda=p.
  • Cutting the kernel along the primes: each slice of the sieve acts on a copy of E_p.

13.6The orbital trace and why large primes vanish#

Everything is now in place for the statement that Cutting the kernel along the primes uses for every prime outside a finite set.

Theorem 13.11

Convolution by \varphi on the orbital quotient at p has trace \log p times the sum of \varphi over the powers of p, which is zero for every prime p\ge Y

[1]
Statement

Let \varphi be smooth with compact support in \RR_{>0}. Then A(\varphi) maps the image of D_p into itself, so it acts on E_p, the action is nuclear, and

\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(A(\varphi)\big|_{E_p}\bigr)=\sum_{m\in\ZZ}M\varphi\Bigl(\frac{2\pi im}{\log p}\Bigr)=\log p\sum_{k\in\ZZ}\varphi(p^k).
(13.5)

If moreover \varphi(1)=0 and \operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset(1/Y,Y), this trace is 0 for every prime p\ge Y.

In plain terms

Each prime has its own circle, and the convolution’s trace on that circle counts how often the test function meets a power of the prime. A test function that only reaches up to Y never meets a power of a prime beyond Y, so all those primes contribute nothing.

Why it is needed

A sum over all primes can only be reduced to a finite computation if all but finitely many terms vanish. This theorem is where that happens: the geometric side of the trace formula, cut along the primes, collapses onto the primes below Y and the archimedean place, and the source calls it “a massive cancellation phenomenon” [1, §1.4.10, p. 32].

Idea

Convolution commutes with rescaling, so it commutes with D_p and descends to E_p. By Theorem 13.10 the quotient is the circle of length \log p, so the trace is the circle trace of Theorem 13.6 with \lambda=p, and its vanishing is Corollary 13.7.

Proof

Invariance. For a theta sum, A(\varphi)\Theta_g=\Theta_{g'} with g'(x)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)g(x/t)\,\dd t/t, which is even and Schwartz, satisfies g'(0)=0, and has \int_\RR g'=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t\,\dd t/t\cdot\int_\RR g=0. Since A(\varphi) commutes with \psi\mapsto\psi(p\,\cdot), it commutes with D_p: A(\varphi)D_p\Theta_g=D_pA(\varphi)\Theta_g, which lies in the image of D_p. So A(\varphi) induces an operator on E_p.

Transport. The isomorphism of Theorem 13.10 commutes with A(\varphi), so the operator on E_p is conjugate to A(\varphi) on the circle \RR_{>0}/p^\ZZ, and conjugate nuclear operators have equal traces. Pulled back to E_p, the exponential basis has coefficient functionals \Theta_g\mapsto M\Theta_g(-z_m)/\log p, the evaluations of the Mellin transform at the zeros of 1-p^{-s}. These are the source’s orbital Schauder basis, and the source computes the trace in this basis [1, Theorem 7.3.1.6, p. 344, Theorem 7.4.2.1, p. 367].

Value. Theorem 13.6 with \lambda=p gives Equation (13.5), and Corollary 13.7 with \lambda=p\ge Y gives 0.

Example

With Y=4.5 and the bump \varphi(t)=\operatorname{bump}(\log t/\log4.5), which is supported on (1/4.5,4.5) but has \varphi(1)=e^{-1}\ne0, the trace on E_5 is \log5\,\varphi(1)=0.5920791 (both sides of Equation (13.5) agree to nine digits). Only the k=0 term survives, because 5 and 1/5 lie outside the support. With a test function that also vanishes at 1, as the trace formula requires, the trace on E_5, E_7, E_{11},\dots is exactly zero, while on E_2 and E_3 the points 2,4,\tfrac12,\tfrac14 and 3,\tfrac13 can still contribute.

Used in
  • Cutting the kernel along the primes: each slice of the sieve at a prime p\ge Y has diagonal mass zero, so only the S-local kernel is left.
  • The local trace and the Trace Formula: the primes p<Y reappear there through Connes’s local computation, with the weights \log p\,p^{-m/2} of Weil’s explicit formula.

The source states the general version of Equation (13.5) for a number field, where the right side becomes \sum_{v\mid p}\frac{\log q_v}{\mu_v(\mathcal O_v^\times)}\sum_k\varphi(\pi_v^k) [1, pp. 18 to 19, 51 to 52]. The source states the same right side for the orbital slices of the weighted kernel of Cutting the kernel along the primes [1, Theorem 11.3.2.1, p. 495]. If instead the weight t^{1/2} is kept on the functions, as in the quotient of the weighted sums V_g(t)-p^{-1/2}V_g(pt), then Equation (13.3) with c=\tfrac12 multiplies the kth orbit term by p^{-k/2}. Either way every term with k\ne0 vanishes when p\ge Y, and the term k=0 is \varphi(1)=0. The source’s proof of that theorem evaluates at the weighted points \varepsilon_p-\tfrac12 [1, (11.3.2.5), p. 496], so chapters Cutting the kernel along the primes and The local trace and the Trace Formula print the weighted form, \log p\sum_kp^{-k/2}\varphi(p^k).

13.7Different primes do not interfere#

The sieve of Cutting the kernel along the primes removes primes one after another, so it needs more than one circle at a time. After deleting the multiples of p_1,\dots,p_k, the next step deletes the multiples of p_{k+1}, and on the Mellin side the slice between the two stages is

\frac{\prod_{i\le k}(1-p_i^{-s})\cdot\xi(s)\cdot(\text{entire})}{\prod_{i\le k+1}(1-p_i^{-s})\cdot\xi(s)\cdot(\text{entire})}.

It is described by the zeros of the new factor 1-p_{k+1}^{-s}, and it is a faithful copy of the circle at p_{k+1} provided the earlier factors do not vanish at those zeros. They almost never do.

Theorem 13.12 For distinct primes p and q the zero sets of 1-p^{-s} and 1-q^{-s} meet only at s=0 [1, Theorem 7.1.3.2(1), p. 324; Theorem 1.7.1.1, p. 35]

For distinct primes p\ne q,

\Bigl\{\frac{2\pi ik}{\log p}:k\in\ZZ\Bigr\}\cap\Bigl\{\frac{2\pi ik'}{\log q}:k'\in\ZZ\Bigr\}=\{0\},

and every zero of 1-p^{-s} is simple. So every zero of a finite product \prod_{p\in T}(1-p^{-s}) other than s=0 is simple.

Proof

A common zero has k/\log p=k'/\log q, that is k\log q=k'\log p, that is q^k=p^{k'}. If k>0 then k'>0 and unique factorization forces k=k'=0, a contradiction, and k<0 reduces to this by inverting both sides. So k=k'=0. The zeros are simple because the derivative of 1-p^{-s} is \log p\cdot p^{-s}\ne0. The statement is the \mathbb Q-linear independence of \log p and \log q, which is how the source phrases it.

The zeros can come close without meeting. The near equality 2^{19}=524288\approx531441=3^{12} puts the zero 2\pi i\cdot12/\log2=108.7766i of 1-2^{-s} within 0.1118 of the zero 2\pi i\cdot19/\log3=108.6648i of 1-3^{-s}, and better rational approximations of \log3/\log2 give closer pairs, but Theorem 13.12 says no pair ever coincides. Part of the proof of Zeta on the whole plane used the same fact with 2 and 3.

What this buys can be said in our own words, as our illustration of the source’s bookkeeping. At a zero w\ne0 of 1-p_{k+1}^{-s} the earlier factors are nonzero, so the slice has one coefficient functional there, the value at w divided by \prod_{i\le k}(1-p_i^{-w}), and convolution multiplies it by M\varphi(w), exactly as on the circle of p_{k+1} alone. At s=0 all the factors vanish, so the slice remembers the kth derivative at 0 instead of the value, and convolution still multiplies it by M\varphi(0), because (M\varphi\cdot F)^{(k)}(0)=M\varphi(0)F^{(k)}(0) when F vanishes to order k at 0. So the list of eigenvalues on each slice is the list of the circle of the new prime, and its trace is \log p_{k+1}\sum_j\varphi(p_{k+1}^j) again. The one shared point s=0 is where the order of vanishing piles up as more primes are removed, and the letter names this “infinitely repeated pole” as the obstruction to the degenerate case a=0 of Choosing the topology: what a strip can see [1, pp. 36 to 37]. Away from that one point the circles of different primes are independent.

Over a function field the picture breaks. Every residue field there has q^d elements for a fixed q, so every zero 2\pi ik/\log q of 1-q^{-s} is also a zero of 1-q^{-ds}, and the Euler factors share infinitely many zeros. The source identifies this as one reason the method gives only Weil’s explicit formula there and not the Riemann hypothesis, which for curves was proved by other means (The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields) [1, §14.2, pp. 534 to 535].

Aside

The source gives the circles a geometric home that fulfills a prediction of Deninger [65]. The dual basis elements of the orbital quotient at p are distributions supported on a locus of the S-adeles whose quotient by the units is a loop of length \log p, a “periodic orbit”, and the corresponding objects at the archimedean place are “fixed points” of the flow by \RR_{>1} [1, §1.2.11, pp. 20 to 21, Theorem 8.1.0.1, p. 382]. The orbital traces are then Deninger’s local traces. The source is explicit that the picture helps organize the computation but is not logically needed, and that “there is no 3-manifold, nor foliation, nor foliated cohomology theory” [1, p. 16, p. 33].

13.8What changes in general#

For a number field F and a Hecke character \chi the same story runs with heavier notation [1, §1.2.9, pp. 17 to 19, §7.3 and §7.4]. The operator D_p becomes \mathrm{PV}_{S_p}, the composite of the operators f(x)\mapsto f(x)-f(\pi_v^{-1}x) over all places v above p, and on the Mellin side it multiplies by the product of reciprocal Euler factors \prod_{v\mid p}L_v(\chi_v\lvert\cdot\rvert_v^s)^{-1}. Each place v contributes a circle \RR_{>0}/q_v^\ZZ of length \log q_v, where q_v is the size of the residue field, and the exponential basis is twisted by the character, so the zeros sit at 2\pi ik/\log q_v-it_v. Several places above one p can share zeros, so multiplicities up to [F:\mathbb Q] appear, which is why the strata are taken over the whole set S_p of places above p at once. The orbital trace becomes \sum_{v\mid p}\frac{\log q_v}{\mu_v(\mathcal O_v^\times)}\sum_k\varphi(\pi_v^k), and it still vanishes once q_v exceeds the support. Theorem 13.12 holds for places of distinct residue characteristic with the same proof, and the shared point is the single point of the component that corresponds to s=0. Class groups force the finite set S to be large enough that \mathrm{Pic}(\mathcal O_{F,S})=1, and the strong coprimality of Theorem 13.10 uses the non-vanishing of L(s,\chi) on \Re s=1.

Recap

You now have the following, and where each is used.

  • The toy circle \RR_{>0}/\lambda^\ZZ of length \log\lambda, its exponential basis t^{2\pi im/\log\lambda}, and the periodization \Phi_\lambda, whose kernel is the multiples of 1-\lambda^{-s}: the model for every orbital quotient.
  • What a Schauder basis is and why it lets a trace be computed as a sum of diagonal entries: the method of every trace computation in Choosing the topology: what a strip can see and Cutting the kernel along the primes.
  • The circle trace \sum_mM\varphi(2\pi im/\log\lambda)=\log\lambda\sum_k\varphi(\lambda^k), proved by Poisson summation, with its weighted form, and its vanishing when no power of \lambda meets the support: the diagonal mass of each slice in Cutting the kernel along the primes.
  • The operator D_p, which deletes the multiples of p and multiplies the Mellin transform by 1-p^{-s}, and the orbital quotient E_p, which is the circle of length \log p because \zeta has no zeros on \Re s=1: the pieces of the sieve.
  • The orbital trace \log p\sum_k\varphi(p^k), zero for p\ge Y: why only the primes below Y survive into The local trace and the Trace Formula.
  • Independence of the \log p, so that different primes share only s=0: why the slices of the sieve are copies of single circles, and why the method needs a strip of positive width (Choosing the topology: what a strip can see).

Chapter 14

Choosing the topology: what a strip can see

After this chapter you can say which values of a Mellin transform a norm can see, prove that the Hardy-Sobolev norm of half-width a sees exactly the open strip of half-width a, and explain why the quotient by the theta sums then carries only the zeros inside that strip.

Builds on 12. Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions

In plain terms

A norm is a choice of what counts as small. Change the norm and some measurements stop making sense, because functions that the norm calls tiny can still give that measurement a large value. The proof measures functions with a norm under which the value of the Mellin transform at a point makes sense only inside a vertical strip around the critical line. Zeros of zeta outside that strip then leave no trace in the space, not because anything was assumed about them, but because the space has no way to see them.

Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions turned the zeros of \zeta into the spectrum of convolution on the quotient of all functions by the weighted theta sums. In the topology used there every zero is visible, and the trace of convolution is the zero side of Weil’s explicit formula, so computing it again by geometry can only give Weil’s explicit formula back. The new idea of this chapter is to change the topology before taking the quotient. In the Hardy-Sobolev space W_a the quotient remembers only the zeros \rho with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a, and the trace of convolution becomes a sum over those zeros. Cutting the kernel along the primes and The local trace and the Trace Formula then compute the same trace by geometry inside W_a and find Weil’s complete prime side, and From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis compares the two. The source calls the zeros outside the strip “victims” of the topology [1, p. 36].

14.1A norm decides which measurements exist#

In finite dimensions every linear functional is continuous, so every linear measurement of a vector is stable under small changes. In infinite dimensions this fails, and which measurements survive depends on the norm. The standard example is evaluation at a point. On continuous functions on [0,1] with the sup norm, f\mapsto f(\tfrac12) is continuous, since \abs{f(\tfrac12)}\le\sup\abs f. With the L^2 norm it is not: a tent of height 1 at \tfrac12 and width \eps has L^2 norm \sqrt{\eps/3}, which tends to 0, while its value at \tfrac12 stays 1.

Definition 14.1 continuous functional and its norm

A linear functional \ell on a normed space (E,\norm\cdot) is continuous when there is a constant C with \abs{\ell(u)}\le C\norm u for all u\in E. The least such C is its norm \norm\ell. A continuous functional on a dense subspace extends uniquely to the completion. A functional that is not continuous has no extension: there are u_n\to0 with \ell(u_n)=1, so in the completion the limit 0 would need two values.

The completion is where the consequence becomes structural. If a closed subspace is cut out by conditions \ell(u)=0, the quotient by it is described by those \ell. In a coarser norm some \ell are no longer continuous, the closure of the subspace grows, and the quotient shrinks. That is the whole mechanism of this chapter, applied to \ell= “a derivative of the Mellin transform at a zero of \zeta”.

14.2The Hardy-Sobolev space W_a#

Definition 14.2 the Hardy-Sobolev space W_a

For a>0, the space W_a is the completion of S_E(\RR_{>0}) in the norm

\norm\phi_a^2=\int_0^\infty\abs{\phi(t)}^2\max(t^{2a},t^{-2a})\,\frac{\dd t}t .

It is a Hilbert space of (classes of) functions on \RR_{>0}. Its elements need only decay slightly faster than t^{-a} at \infty and slightly faster than t^a at 0, in the square-mean sense, where elements of S_E decay faster than every power. It is not L^2(\RR_{>0},\dd t/t) unless a=0, and it is not a space of smooth functions. In the source it is W^{0,2}_{[-a,a]}(\RR_{>0}), the Hardy-Sobolev space of base [-a,a] and Sobolev degree 0 [1, §1.1.3, p. 11, §1.8.2.3, p. 44].

The source’s general space carries an extra factor (1+\abs{\log t}^2)^{\sigma_0/2} with a Sobolev degree \sigma_0\ge0. The introduction and the letter fix \sigma_0=0 and note that this suffices for the paper [1, p. 13, p. 46], and so does this page. The weight \max(t^{2a},t^{-2a})=e^{2a\abs{\log t}} penalizes mass far from t=1 in both directions, which is exactly what makes the Mellin transform holomorphic on a strip: after t=e^u, the Mellin transform at x+iy is the Fourier transform of \phi(e^u)e^{xu}, and the weight controls e^{xu} precisely when \abs x\le a.

Proposition 14.3 The Mellin transform identifies W_a with a Hardy space of holomorphic functions on the strip of half-width a, normed by the two edges [1, Proposition 9.2.2.4, p. 414; Lemma 9.2.2.2, p. 412]

For \phi\in S_E(\RR_{>0}),

\norm\phi_a^2\ \le\ \frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Bigl(\abs{M\phi(a+iy)}^2+\abs{M\phi(-a+iy)}^2\Bigr)\dd y\ \le\ 2\,\norm\phi_a^2 .
(14.1)

Consequently the Mellin transform extends from S_E to an isomorphism of W_a onto a Hilbert space of functions holomorphic on the open strip \lvert\Re z\rvert<a with square-integrable boundary values on its two edges.

Proof

For a real x, put h(u)=\phi(e^u)e^{xu}. Then M\phi(x+iy)=\int_\RR h(u)e^{iyu}\,\dd u=\hat h(-y/2\pi), and Plancherel’s theorem \int\abs{\hat h}^2=\int\abs h^2 [17, Chapter 5], after the change of variable y=2\pi\eta, gives

\frac1{2\pi}\int_\RR\abs{M\phi(x+iy)}^2\,\dd y=\int_0^\infty\abs{\phi(t)}^2\,t^{2x}\,\frac{\dd t}t .

Add the cases x=a and x=-a, and use \max(t^{2a},t^{-2a})\le t^{2a}+t^{-2a}\le2\max(t^{2a},t^{-2a}). The extension to W_a and holomorphy on the open strip follow from the evaluation bound of Theorem 14.4 below, which makes M\phi(z) continuous in \phi uniformly for z in compact subsets of the strip, so limits are locally uniform and therefore holomorphic. The source states the isomorphism for every Sobolev degree, and the inequality Equation (14.1) is our direct proof for degree 0.

Example

Take a=0.25 and \phi(t)=\operatorname{bump}(\log t-0.3) with \operatorname{bump}(x)=e^{-1/(1-x^2)} for \abs x<1. Numerically \norm\phi_a^2=0.161584 and the edge integral in Equation (14.1) is 0.273060, a ratio of 1.690, inside [1,2].

14.3Evaluation exists exactly inside the strip#

The functionals that describe the quotient of Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions are the evaluations of the Mellin transform and its derivatives at the points z=\rho-\tfrac12. The question for W_a is which of them stay continuous, and the answer is as clean as one could hope.

Theorem 14.4

In W_a the value of the Mellin transform at z_0, and each of its derivatives there, is a continuous functional exactly when z_0 lies in the open strip of half-width a

[1, Corollary 9.2.2.5, p. 414]
Statement

Let a>0, z_0=x_0+iy_0, and \delta^{(j)}_{z_0}(\phi)=(M\phi)^{(j)}(z_0)=\int_0^\infty\phi(t)(\log t)^jt^{z_0}\,\dd t/t on S_E(\RR_{>0}).

  1. If \abs{x_0}<a, every \delta^{(j)}_{z_0} is continuous for \norm\cdot_a, and for j=0 the norm is exactly
\norm{\delta_{z_0}}=\sqrt{\frac a{a^2-x_0^2}} .
(14.2)
  1. If \abs{x_0}\ge a, the functional \delta_{z_0} is not continuous: there are \phi_n\in S_E with M\phi_n(z_0)=1 for all n and \norm{\phi_n}_a\to0.
In plain terms

Inside the strip, the value of the Mellin transform at a point is controlled by the norm, with a constant that grows as the point nears an edge. On the edge and beyond it, there are functions as small as you like whose transform at that point is still 1, so the value at that point is not something the space can see.

Why it is needed

The quotient of W_a by the closure of the theta sums is described by the continuous functionals that vanish on the theta sums. This theorem says which zeros of \zeta can supply such functionals: those with z=\rho-\tfrac12 inside the strip, and no others. It is the step at which zeros outside the strip leave the trace.

Idea

Inside the strip, t^{z_0} is small enough at both ends to be paired with any element of W_a by Cauchy-Schwarz. Outside, push a bump far out toward t=\infty (or t=0) and tilt it by t^{-z_0}: the factor t^{z_0} in the Mellin integral undoes the tilt, so the value stays 1, while the norm, which grows only like t^{a}, sees an exponentially small function.

Proof

Inside. Write w(t)=\max(t^{2a},t^{-2a}). By Cauchy-Schwarz,

\abs{\delta^{(j)}_{z_0}(\phi)}\le\Bigl(\int_0^\infty\abs\phi^2w\,\frac{\dd t}t\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\int_0^\infty\frac{\abs{\log t}^{2j}t^{2x_0}}{w(t)}\,\frac{\dd t}t\Bigr)^{1/2}.

With u=\log t the second integral is \int_0^\infty u^{2j}\bigl(e^{-2(a-x_0)u}+e^{-2(a+x_0)u}\bigr)\dd u=(2j)!\bigl[(2(a-x_0))^{-2j-1}+(2(a+x_0))^{-2j-1}\bigr], finite because a\pm x_0>0. For j=0 it equals \frac1{2(a-x_0)}+\frac1{2(a+x_0)}=\frac a{a^2-x_0^2}. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz holds for \phi=\overline{t^{z_0}}/w, which lies in W_a and is approximated by elements of S_E, so the constant Equation (14.2) is the norm.

Right of the strip, x_0>a. Fix a smooth \operatorname{bump}_1\ge0 supported in (0,1) with \int\operatorname{bump}_1=1, and for n\ge1 put \phi_n(t)=t^{-z_0}\operatorname{bump}_1(\log t-n). Then

M\phi_n(z_0)=\int_0^\infty\operatorname{bump}_1(\log t-n)\,\frac{\dd t}t=\int_\RR\operatorname{bump}_1(u-n)\,\dd u=1,

while \phi_n lives on t\in(e^n,e^{n+1}), where w(t)=t^{2a}, so

\norm{\phi_n}_a^2=\int_\RR\operatorname{bump}_1(u-n)^2e^{-2(x_0-a)u}\,\dd u\le e^{-2(x_0-a)n}\int\operatorname{bump}_1^2\ \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\ 0 .

Left of the strip, x_0<-a. Use \phi_n(t)=t^{-z_0}\operatorname{bump}_1(-\log t-n), which lives on t\in(e^{-n-1},e^{-n}), and the same computation with u\mapsto-u.

On an edge, x_0=\pm a. The tilted bump now has norm independent of n, so spread it out. Take B_N smooth with 0\le B_N\le1, equal to 1 on [1,N-1] and supported in [0,N], and put \phi_N(t)=t^{-z_0}B_N(\pm\log t)/N, with the sign of x_0, so that \abs{t^{-z_0}}^2w(t)=1 on the support. Then M\phi_N(z_0)=\frac1N\int B_N\ge\frac{N-2}N and \norm{\phi_N}_a^2=\frac1{N^2}\int B_N^2\le\frac1N. Dividing \phi_N by M\phi_N(z_0) gives functions with transform 1 at z_0 and norm at most \sqrt N/(N-2)\to0.

Example

With a=0.25, Equation (14.2) gives 2 at x_0=0, 3.333 at x_0=0.2, and 7.143 at x_0=0.24, and a numerical integration of t^{2x_0}/w reproduces a/(a^2-x_0^2)=4, 11.111, 51.020. For the bump \phi of the previous example and z=0.1+3i, \abs{M\phi(z)}=0.2043, below the bound 0.8772.

Outside: with a=0.1, x_0=0.3, and \operatorname{bump}_1 the normalized bump on (0,1), the functions \phi_n have M\phi_n(0.3)=1 for every n, while \norm{\phi_n}_a=1.0526, 0.3872, 0.1425, 0.0193, 0.00035 for n=0,5,10,20,40. At the interior point z=0 their transforms 0.862, 0.192, 0.043, 0.0021, 5.3\times10^{-6} shrink with them, as continuity demands. On the edge x_0=a=0.1, the spread functions with N=4,16,64,256 have M\phi_N(a)=0.75, 0.9375, 0.9844, 0.9961 and norms 0.419, 0.241, 0.124, 0.062, close to N^{-1/2}.

Used in
  • Proposition 14.6: the jets at zeros inside the strip descend to the quotient.
  • Theorem 14.8 and Theorem 14.9: only those jets survive.
  • From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis: the absence of a zero outside the strip from the spectral side is what the endgame exploits.

The source also records a refinement for the edges with a positive Sobolev degree \sigma_0, where derivatives of order at most (\sigma_0-1)/2 at edge points become continuous; with \sigma_0=0 none do, in agreement with the edge computation above [1, Corollary 9.2.2.5(2), p. 414].

The failure outside the strip uses functions that escape toward t=\infty or t=0. Forbid one direction and that wall disappears. If every function is supported in [1/A,\infty) for a fixed A>1, the Cauchy-Schwarz integral becomes \int_{1/A}^1t^{2x_0+2a}\,\dd t/t+\int_1^\infty t^{2x_0-2a}\,\dd t/t, finite for every x_0<a, so on such functions evaluation is continuous on the whole half-plane left of the right edge. The source proves this as a Paley-Wiener theorem for Hardy-Sobolev spaces [1, Theorem 9.2.2.6 and Corollary 9.2.2.8, p. 415]. It matters for the next chapter. In the weighted picture the orbital functionals of Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces sit at the zeros of 1-p^{-(z+1/2)}, on the line \Re z=-\tfrac12 (our computation), which is outside the strip when a<\tfrac12. The source brings them into the coarse space with support conditions of this kind, its Paley-Wiener levels [1, p. 51, §7.3.2, p. 350], and Cutting the kernel along the primes works inside them.

14.4The quotient remembers only the strip#

Recall from Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions the space \mathcal V of weighted theta sums V_g(t)=t^{1/2}\Theta_g(t) (Definition 12.10), whose Mellin transforms are exactly the elements of AS(\CC) of the form \xi(z+\tfrac12) times an entire function (Theorem 12.11), and the divisor exact sequence: in S_E(\RR_{>0}), two functions are equal modulo \mathcal V exactly when they have the same jets at the points z=\rho-\tfrac12, the jth derivative for 0\le j<m_\rho at each zero (Theorem 12.13). That quotient was called \mathcal H; its counterpart in W_a gets the subscript a.

Definition 14.5 the strip quotient \mathcal H_a

The strip quotient is the Hilbert space

\mathcal H_a=W_a\big/\overline{\mathcal V},

where \overline{\mathcal V} is the closure in W_a of the weighted theta sums. Its elements are classes of elements of W_a modulo that closure, not functions. It is the source’s \mathcal H_{F,a,I} over \mathbb Q with Sobolev degree 0 [1, §10.2.2, p. 445, p. 13].

One half of the description follows at once from Theorem 14.4.

Proposition 14.6 The jets of the Mellin transform at zeros inside the strip are continuous on W_a and vanish on the closure of the theta sums, so they live on the quotient

Let \rho=\beta+i\gamma be a zero of \zeta with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a and 0\le j<m_\rho. Then \phi\mapsto(M\phi)^{(j)}(\rho-\tfrac12) is a continuous functional on W_a that vanishes on \overline{\mathcal V}, and so defines a continuous functional on \mathcal H_a.

Proof

The point \rho-\tfrac12 has real part \beta-\tfrac12\in(-a,a), so the functional is continuous by Theorem 14.4. On a weighted theta sum the Mellin transform is \xi(z+\tfrac12)h(z) with h entire, which vanishes to order m_\rho at z=\rho-\tfrac12, so the functional vanishes on \mathcal V, and by continuity on its closure.

For a zero outside the strip the same functional vanishes on \mathcal V but is not continuous, so it cannot pass to the closure, and nothing forces elements of \overline{\mathcal V} to keep the zero. The simplest case shows what happens instead: a forced zero outside the strip is no condition at all.

Lemma 14.7 In W_a every element is a multiple of z-z_0 when z_0 lies outside the closed strip, while inside the strip the multiples form a closed subspace of codimension one

Let z_0 satisfy \Re z_0>a and put k_{z_0}(t)=t^{-z_0}\mathbf 1_{t>1}. For every \phi\in W_a the function \psi=-A(k_{z_0})\phi lies in W_a, with

\norm\psi_a\le\frac{\sqrt2}{\Re z_0-a}\norm\phi_a,\qquad M\phi(z)=(z-z_0)\,M\psi(z)\quad(\lvert\Re z\rvert<a).

For \Re z_0<-a the same holds with \psi=A(k'_{z_0})\phi and k'_{z_0}(t)=t^{-z_0}\mathbf 1_{t<1}. For \lvert\Re z_0\rvert<a, by contrast, every multiple (z-z_0)M\psi vanishes at z_0, and these multiples lie in the kernel of the continuous functional \delta_{z_0}, a closed subspace of codimension one.

Proof

For \Re z<\Re z_0, Mk_{z_0}(z)=\int_1^\infty t^{z-z_0}\,\dd t/t=1/(z_0-z), and the Mellin transform of a convolution is the product of the transforms, so M\psi=M\phi/(z-z_0) on the strip. For \phi\in S_E the function A(k_{z_0})\phi is smooth, decays rapidly at 0, and behaves like t^{-z_0}M\phi(z_0) at \infty, so it lies in W_a. It is not in S_E, but the Plancherel identity in the proof of Proposition 14.3 applies to it all the same, because u\mapsto\psi(e^u)e^{\pm au} is integrable and square integrable. On the edges \lvert z-z_0\rvert\ge\Re z_0-a, so the edge integral of \psi is at most that of \phi divided by (\Re z_0-a)^2, and Equation (14.1) gives the bound, which extends to all of W_a by density. The case \Re z_0<-a is the mirror image, with Mk'_{z_0}(z)=\int_0^1t^{z-z_0}\,\dd t/t=1/(z-z_0) for \Re z>\Re z_0. The last sentence is Theorem 14.4.

The lemma and its proof are ours, as an illustration of the source’s mechanism. The test function t^{-z_0}\mathbf 1_{t>1} will reappear in From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis as the holomorphic family that turns the trace formula into a statement about \zeta'/\zeta. Dividing by a linear factor is the toy case. The theta sums are multiples of \xi(z+\tfrac12), which has infinitely many zeros, and dividing by all of them at once is not a bounded operation, so the full statement needs the source’s machinery.

Theorem 14.8

An element of W_a lies in the closure of the weighted theta sums exactly when the jets of its Mellin transform vanish at every zero inside the strip

[1, Theorem 10.2.2.1, p. 446; pp. 13, 31]
Statement

An element \phi\in W_a lies in \overline{\mathcal V} if and only if (M\phi)^{(j)}(\rho-\tfrac12)=0 for every zero \rho of \zeta with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a and every 0\le j<m_\rho. Equivalently, the functionals of Proposition 14.6, which are integration against the functions t^{\rho-1/2}(\log t)^j with the measure \dd t/t, are the coefficient functionals of a Markushevich basis of \mathcal H_a, and no zero outside the strip contributes a functional.

In plain terms

After completing in the strip norm and dividing by the theta sums, what is left is exactly the information about the zeros inside the strip, counted with multiplicity. A zero outside the strip, if there were one, would leave no mark on the quotient.

Why it is needed

The trace of convolution on \mathcal H_a is computed in the basis these functionals provide, so this theorem decides which zeros appear in the spectral side of the trace formula. It is why the Trace Formula of The local trace and the Trace Formula has a zero sum restricted to the strip while its prime side is Weil’s complete one.

Idea

Proposition 14.6 gives the strip jets as conditions on \overline{\mathcal V}. The content of the theorem is that there are no others, and Lemma 14.7 shows the mechanism: a factor of the Mellin transform whose zero lies outside the strip can be divided out inside W_a, so it imposes nothing after closure. A Markushevich basis is a biorthogonal system (x_m,f_m) whose vectors span a dense subspace and whose functionals separate points. It is weaker than a Schauder basis, since expansions need not converge, and it is what the source obtains in the Hilbert completions.

Proof sketch

[1, Theorem 10.2.2.1, p. 446; Theorem 10.2.1.1; Theorem 7.1.4.2, p. 326]

In the fine topology the dual of the quotient is spanned by all jets \delta^{(j)}_{\rho-1/2} (Theorem 7.1.4.2, the dual form of the divisor exact sequence). Passing to W_a, the continuous ones are those in the open strip (Theorem 14.4), and the source shows that the orthogonal of \overline{\mathcal V} in the dual of W_a is spanned by them and only them. The proof follows that of Theorem 10.2.1.1 (p. 440), with the Hardy-Sobolev estimates of Theorem 9.3.2.6, and uses the classical count of O(\log T) zeros in boxes of height 1 at height T (The zeros and the hypothesis). With a positive Sobolev degree, zeros on the edges also contribute, with multiplicity capped by \min\bigl(m_\rho,[(\sigma_0-1)/2]+1\bigr).

Used in
  • Theorem 14.9: the trace on \mathcal H_a in this basis.
  • Cutting the kernel along the primes: the spectral kernel is built from these basis vectors.

14.5The spectral trace#

Convolution by a test function preserves the theta sums and is bounded on W_a, so it acts on the quotient, and on the jets it acts by triangular matrices whose diagonal is the Mellin transform of \varphi.

Theorem 14.9

Convolution by \varphi acts on the strip quotient as a trace-class operator whose trace is the sum of M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) over the zeros inside the strip, with multiplicity

[1, pp. 13 to 14, 46 to 47 (Sobolev degree 0); Theorem 10.3.2.1, p. 453 (degree above 1)]
Statement

Let a>0 and \varphi smooth with compact support in \RR_{>0}. Then A(\varphi) is bounded on W_a, maps \overline{\mathcal V} into itself, and induces a trace-class operator on \mathcal H_a with

\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(A(\varphi)\big|_{\mathcal H_a}\bigr)=\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,M\varphi\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr),
(14.3)

the sum running over the zeros \rho=\beta+i\gamma of \zeta in the strip and converging absolutely.

In plain terms

Convolution amplifies each zero’s piece of information by the Mellin transform of the test function at that zero. Its trace adds these amplifications over the zeros the space can see, counting a double zero twice.

Why it is needed

This is the spectral side of the Trace Formula. Every later chapter of Part III computes the same trace a second way.

Idea

A jet of order m at z_0 is a vector (u(z_0),u'(z_0),\dots,u^{(m-1)}(z_0)). Convolution multiplies Mellin transforms by M\varphi, and by the Leibniz rule the jth derivative of M\varphi\cdot u at z_0 is M\varphi(z_0)u^{(j)}(z_0) plus lower derivatives of u. So A(\varphi) acts on each jet by a triangular m\times m matrix, a Jordan block, with M\varphi(z_0) on the diagonal, and its trace is m\,M\varphi(z_0).

Proof sketch

[1, Theorem 10.3.2.1, pp. 453 to 454; pp. 13 to 14]

Bounded. The weight e^{2a\abs{\log t}} is submultiplicative, e^{a\abs{\log x}}\le e^{a\abs{\log t}}e^{a\abs{\log(x/t)}}, so Minkowski’s inequality gives \norm{A(\varphi)\phi}_a\le\bigl(\int_0^\infty\abs{\varphi(t)}e^{a\abs{\log t}}\,\dd t/t\bigr)\norm\phi_a.

Invariant. A(\varphi)\bigl(t^{1/2}\Theta_g\bigr)=t^{1/2}A(t^{-1/2}\varphi)\Theta_g, and convolution maps theta sums to theta sums (as in Theorem 13.11), so \mathcal V is invariant, and so is its closure by continuity.

Trace. In the basis of Theorem 14.8 the matrix of A(\varphi) is block triangular with the Jordan blocks of the idea. The eigenvalues are absolutely summable: integrating by parts in u=\log t gives \abs{M\varphi(x+iy)}\le C_N(1+\abs y)^{-N} uniformly for \abs x\le a, and there are O(\log T) zeros with T\le\abs\gamma\le T+1. The source writes the operator as a trace-norm limit of finite-rank operators built from the basis and its dual and computes the trace as the sum of the diagonal entries. Which statement this card cites matters. The theorem in the source’s body, Theorem 10.3.2.1 (pp. 453 to 454), assumes a Sobolev degree above 1, and its trace then also contains the zeros on the two edges of the strip, with capped multiplicity. The statement at degree 0, with the open strip only and no edge terms, is the one the introduction and the letter give and use (pp. 13 to 14 and 46 to 47, where the author notes that degree 0 suffices for the paper); this page follows it.

Example

Suppose, as a schematic, that the strip contained a zero z_0=\rho-\tfrac12 of multiplicity 2. In the coordinates (u(z_0),u'(z_0)) convolution acts by

\begin{pmatrix}M\varphi(z_0)&0\\ M\varphi'(z_0)&M\varphi(z_0)\end{pmatrix},

because (M\varphi\cdot u)'(z_0)=M\varphi'(z_0)u(z_0)+M\varphi(z_0)u'(z_0). Its trace is 2M\varphi(z_0)=m_\rho M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12), and the off-diagonal entry, which carries the derivative of M\varphi, does not enter. (The zeros of \zeta computed so far are all simple; the example illustrates the algebra of multiplicity, not a known zero.)

Used in
  • Cutting the kernel along the primes: the diagonal mass of the geometric kernel equals minus this trace.
  • The local trace and the Trace Formula: the right side of the Trace Formula.
  • From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis: a zero outside the strip is absent from this sum.

14.6Why this is legitimate#

A reader who has followed this far may suspect a trick: choose a norm that hides the zeros you do not want, and then of course they disappear. Three points show that nothing of the kind is happening.

The first is that nothing about the zeros entered the choice. The norm \norm\cdot_a is defined by the weight \max(t^{2a},t^{-2a}), which knows nothing about \zeta: it is the same weight for every L-function and every number field, and a is any positive number. The source chose it, in its own account, by asking what the geometric computation needs, namely that evaluations of Mellin transforms on the imaginary line and all their derivatives be continuous, which takes “a little bit of interior” around that line [1, pp. 45 to 46]. The letter puts it bluntly: “the zeros play no role here” [1, p. 36].

The second is that the theorems of this chapter are true whatever the zeros are. Theorem 14.9 does not say that there are no zeros outside the strip. It says that if there were one, the operator on \mathcal H_a would not see it. The trace on \mathcal H_a is a number attached to an honest operator on an honest Hilbert space, and changing the space changes the number, just as the trace of a matrix depends on which subspace it acts on.

The third is where the price is paid. A trace formula equates two computations of the trace of one operator on one space. The spectral computation in W_a is easy and gives Equation (14.3). The geometric computation must now also be carried out inside W_a, with only the functionals that are continuous there, and nothing guarantees in advance that the answer will be the full prime side of Weil’s explicit formula. Meyer’s earlier degeneration from global to local used infinite Euler products, which converge only in fine topologies, and in the critical strip Mertens’ theorem blocks them [1, pp. 39 to 40]. Masullo’s answer is to remove one prime at a time with the orbital bases of Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces and to make the needed functionals continuous with support conditions, and that is the work of Cutting the kernel along the primes. If the geometric side in W_a comes out as Weil’s complete prime side, it knows every zero, while the spectral side knows only the strip, and From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis turns this mismatch into the conclusion that no zero lies outside the strip. The source’s slogan for this is that GRH “is a topological phenomenon” [1, §1.4.8, p. 31].

14.7Three topologies, three trace formulas#

The choice of topology is the only difference between three programs that share the divisor exact sequence of Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions.

Topology Which evaluations are continuous Zeros on the spectral side What the trace formula becomes
Fine: S_E, or Meyer’s bornologies at every point all zeros Weil’s explicit formula
Hardy-Sobolev W_a, a>0 (Masullo) inside the open strip \lvert\Re z\rvert<a zeros with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a the Trace Formula of The local trace and the Trace Formula
a=0: Connes’s Sobolev L^2 space at most low-order derivatives on the line, depending on the Sobolev degree zeros on the critical line no trace formula by this method

In the fine topology every jet is continuous, the quotient keeps every zero, and the trace of convolution is the zero side of Weil’s explicit formula. Meyer degenerated the global kernel to a local one with infinite Euler products, which forces such topologies, and his trace formula is therefore Weil’s explicit formula, a true statement with no information about where the zeros are [66] [1, pp. 32, 39].

At the other extreme, a=0 collapses the strip to the critical line. This is Connes’s setting, with the Sobolev degree equal to his \delta [1, §1.5.1, p. 32, p. 44]. Connes’s 1999 paper gives the zeros on the critical line as an absorption spectrum, while zeros off the line would appear only as resonances, and it reduces the Riemann hypothesis to the validity of a trace formula on the space of adele classes, in a version that no longer needs the parameter \delta [43]. The letter states that the degenerate case a=0 does not lead to a trace formula and traces the obstruction to the one point where the Euler factors of all primes share a zero, the repeated pole of Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces [1, pp. 36 to 37].

Between them, a>0 keeps enough interior around the critical line for the geometric side to be computed, and little enough of the plane that zeros outside the strip are invisible. Since a can be as small as we like, the strip can be made as thin as we like, which is what From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis needs.

14.8What changes in general#

For a number field F and a Hecke character \chi, \RR_{>0} is replaced by the idele class group C_F, and the weight is \max(\lvert g\rvert^{2a},\lvert g\rvert^{-2a}) in the idelic norm \lvert g\rvert, so the space decomposes into isotypes under the compact group C_F^1, one for each character of C_F^1, and on each the Mellin transform is a function on one component of the space of quasi-characters [1, §1.8.2.3, p. 44, §10.2.2, p. 445]. Everything in this chapter then holds isotype by isotype, with the zeros of L(s,\chi) in place of those of \zeta, so the trace is \sum N(\rho)\int_{C_F}\chi(g)\varphi(g)\lvert g\rvert^{\rho-1/2}\,\dd\mu(g) over the zeros with \lvert\Re\rho-\tfrac12\rvert<a [1, p. 53]. When \chi has \chi(\tau(t))=t^{ix_0} on a section \tau of the norm, the whole picture shifts vertically by x_0. The body of the source works with a positive Sobolev degree, at least 2[F:\mathbb Q] where the orbital functionals at the places above one prime require it, and then zeros on the edges of the strip contribute with capped multiplicity.

Recap

You now have the following, and where each is used.

  • A norm decides which linear measurements are continuous, and a coarser norm makes the closure of a subspace larger and the quotient smaller: the principle behind the whole of Route M.
  • The space W_a, with norm weighted by \max(t^{2a},t^{-2a}), whose Mellin picture is a Hardy space on the strip \lvert\Re z\rvert<a normed by its two edges: the space in which Cutting the kernel along the primes and The local trace and the Trace Formula compute.
  • Evaluation of the Mellin transform at z_0 is continuous exactly when \lvert\Re z_0\rvert<a, with norm \sqrt{a/(a^2-x_0^2)}, and explicit sequences show the failure on and beyond the edges: why zeros outside the strip leave the spectral side.
  • One-sided support restores continuity on one side: how the next chapter keeps the orbital functionals of Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces.
  • The strip quotient \mathcal H_a=W_a/\overline{\mathcal V}, described by the jets at the zeros inside the strip, and the spectral trace \sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12), computed through Jordan blocks: the right side of the Trace Formula in The local trace and the Trace Formula and the zero sum in From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis.
  • Why the choice is legitimate (the zeros play no role in it), where the price is paid (the geometric side in Cutting the kernel along the primes), and the contrast with Meyer’s fine topology, which gives back Weil’s explicit formula, and with Connes’s case a=0.
