Chapter 15

Cutting the kernel along the primes

Compute the trace of the convolution operator a second time, as the mass of a kernel on its diagonal, by cutting the kernel one prime at a time until only the places in a finite set S carry any mass.

Builds on 13. Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces, 14. Choosing the topology: what a strip can see

In plain terms

A trace can be computed in two ways: add up the eigenvalues, or add up the numbers on the diagonal of the matrix. Chapter 14 did the first and found only the zeros inside a strip. This chapter starts the second. It cuts the operator into pieces, one piece for each prime beyond a cutoff, and shows that every such piece has nothing on its diagonal, so that everything is concentrated on finitely many primes.

Chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see ended with a trace that sees too little. In the coarse space W_a, convolution by a test function \varphi descends to the quotient by the closed span of the weighted theta sums, and its trace there is \sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12), a sum over the zeros in the strip \lvert\Re z\rvert<a and over no others. That is a sum of eigenvalues. A trace has a second expression, the sum of the diagonal entries, and for an integral operator the diagonal entries become the values of its kernel k(x,x) on the diagonal. If we can compute that second expression inside the same space W_a and get the full prime side of Weil’s explicit formula, then chapter From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis has a comparison to make: Weil’s formula pairs the prime side with all the zeros, the new formula pairs the same prime side with the zeros in the strip, and the zeros outside the strip have nowhere to go. This chapter carries the diagonal computation to the point where only finitely many places are left, and chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula finishes it. The source calls the bases that make this possible “the crux of the matter” (p. 31), and the argument here is where they are used.

15.1The problem: a second computation of the same trace#

Recall the objects. A test function \varphi is smooth with compact support in (0,\infty), the operator A(\varphi) is multiplicative convolution, (A(\varphi)\psi)(x)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,\psi(x/t)\,\dd t/t, and on the Mellin side it multiplies by M\varphi(z)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)t^z\,\dd t/t. Throughout this chapter we follow the source’s standing assumption in the introduction (p. 15) that \varphi is supported strictly to the right of 1, and we fix a number Y>1 with

\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset(1,Y).
(15.1)

In particular \varphi(1)=0. The source extends the final formula to every \varphi with \varphi(1)=0 by a reflection and a continuity argument (p. 30), and chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula does that step.

Chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see gives the left side of the identity we are after. As there, write \overline{\mathcal V} for the closure in W_a of the space \mathcal V of weighted theta sums V_g(t)=t^{1/2}\Theta_g(t) and \mathcal H_a=W_a/\overline{\mathcal V} for the quotient. Write P^{\mathrm{geom}} for the orthogonal projection of W_a onto \overline{\mathcal V}, P^{\mathrm{spec}}=1-P^{\mathrm{geom}} for the projection onto its orthogonal complement (the source’s names, p. 456), and A_{\mathrm{spec}}(\varphi) for the operator that A(\varphi) induces on \mathcal H_a. Then

\Tr A_{\mathrm{spec}}(\varphi)=\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12).
(15.2)

The plan has four steps, one per section below. First we turn this trace into the mass of a kernel on the diagonal of \RR_{>0}\times\RR_{>0} and isolate the piece of the kernel that still has to be computed. Second we lift that piece to the ideles of chapter The adeles: all completions at once, where each prime has its own coordinate. Third we cut the lifted kernel along the primes beyond Y, one at a time, and identify each cut with the orbital quotient of chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces. Fourth we show that every cut has diagonal mass zero, so that only an S-local kernel is left, with S=\{\infty\}\cup\{p\le Y\}.

A common misreading

The whole computation happens inside W_a, the coarse space. Doing it in the fine topology of chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions is easy and gives Weil’s explicit formula with every zero, which proves nothing new. The difficulty, and the content of this chapter, is that every step must survive the coarse completion.

15.2Kernels and the diagonal on the positive reals#

For a square matrix B the trace has two expressions, \sum_iB_{ii}=\sum_i\lambda_i, the diagonal entries and the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity. An integral operator is the continuous version of a matrix, with the kernel in place of the entries.

Definition 15.1 Kernel and diagonal mass on the positive reals

A kernel is a measurable function k(x,y) on \RR_{>0}\times\RR_{>0}. It defines the operator (T\psi)(x)=\int_0^\infty k(x,y)\,\psi(y)\,\dd y/y, and we call k the kernel of T. When the restriction of k to the diagonal makes sense (see Making sense of a kernel on the diagonal), its diagonal mass is

\operatorname{mass}(k)=\int_0^\infty\tilde k(t,t)\,\frac{\dd t}{t}.

A kernel is a function of two variables, not an operator: different kernels that agree off a null set define the same operator, which is why the value on the diagonal, itself a null set, needs a definition.

The convolution operator has an explicit kernel. Substituting y=x/t in the definition of A(\varphi), so that t=x/y and \dd t/t becomes \dd y/y,

(A(\varphi)\psi)(x)=\int_0^\infty\varphi\!\left(\frac xy\right)\psi(y)\,\frac{\dd y}{y},
(15.3)

so the kernel of A(\varphi) is \varphi(x/y), the source’s \varphi(xy^{-1}) (p. 15). On the diagonal it equals \varphi(1) at every point. For our test functions \varphi(1)=0, so the kernel of A(\varphi) vanishes identically on the diagonal, and its diagonal mass is 0. In logarithmic coordinates u=\log x, v=\log y the kernel is \varphi(e^{u-v}), constant along every line parallel to the diagonal, a band whose position is set by the support of \varphi and which never touches the diagonal itself (Figure 15.1).

That number 0 is not a trace on all of \RR_{>0}, because A(\varphi) on the whole line has a continuous family of eigenfunctions x^{iy} and is not trace class. It becomes useful once the operator is split along an invariant subspace, and a finite example shows how.

ExampleA zero diagonal splits a trace into two equal and opposite halves

This analogy is ours. On \ZZ/4\ZZ take the convolution matrix C_{ij}=c_{i-j} with c=(c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3)=(0,1,2,0), the finite counterpart of the kernel \varphi(x/y) with \varphi(1)=0. Its diagonal is c_0=0, so \Tr C=0. Its eigenvectors are the characters v_k=(i^{jk})_j, the counterparts of t^z, with eigenvalues 3, -2-i, 1, and -2+i for k=0,1,2,3, which add to 0. The span U of v_0 and v_2 is invariant. The trace on U is 3+1=4, and the trace on the quotient by U is (-2-i)+(-2+i)=-4. Because the diagonal of C is zero, the trace on the subspace is minus the trace on the quotient. Replace U by the theta sums and the quotient by the zeros in the strip, and this is the identity of Theorem 15.3.

Spectral and geometric kernels#

The quotient trace Equation (15.2) comes with a kernel of its own. Chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see computed it with a basis of the quotient whose dual elements are the jets at the zeros in the strip. Lifting the basis elements to W_a and writing A(\varphi) as a limit of finite-rank operators, one per zero and jet order, gives a kernel built from the functions t^{\rho-1/2}(\log t)^m (p. 14).

Definition 15.2 Spectral kernel and geometric kernel

The spectral kernel k_{\mathrm{spec}}(x,y) is the kernel of A(\varphi)\circ P^{\mathrm{spec}} on W_a. It is the limit, in the trace norm and in L^2 against the weights of W_a, of explicit finite-rank kernels, one for each zero \rho with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a and each jet order m<m_\rho (pp. 14 to 15; Theorems 10.4.3.1, p. 466, and 10.4.3.5, p. 472). The geometric kernel is the difference

k_{\mathrm{geom}}(x,y)=\varphi(x/y)-k_{\mathrm{spec}}(x,y),

the kernel of A(\varphi)\circ P^{\mathrm{geom}} (p. 48; Definition 10.4.3.7, p. 473). It is a measurable function, not the kernel of a trace-class operator: A(\varphi)\circ P^{\mathrm{geom}} is neither trace class nor Hilbert-Schmidt (p. 48; Remark 12.1.1.4, p. 503).

On theta sums the geometric kernel acts as A(\varphi) itself, since P^{\mathrm{geom}} is the identity there (Theorem 10.4.3.6, p. 473). So k_{\mathrm{geom}} is the part of the convolution kernel that lives on the theta sums, the analog of C restricted to U in the example, and its diagonal mass is the trace that the zeros do not see.

Making sense of a kernel on the diagonal#

The diagonal of \RR_{>0}\times\RR_{>0} has measure zero, and k_{\mathrm{spec}} is only defined up to null sets, so k_{\mathrm{spec}}(t,t) has no meaning until we choose one. The source chooses it by averaging over small squares. In logarithmic coordinates, with B_\delta=[e^{-\delta},e^\delta],

\tilde k(t,t)=\lim_{\delta\to0}\frac1{(2\delta)^2}\int_{tB_\delta}\int_{tB_\delta}k(x,y)\,\frac{\dd x}{x}\,\frac{\dd y}{y},

which the source calls the smoothening (Definition 12.1.1.1, p. 498). For a continuous kernel such as \varphi(x/y) it returns the value \varphi(1) at every point. Two classical theorems, in versions for locally compact abelian groups, make it work for k_{\mathrm{spec}} (Theorems A.5.3.7 and A.5.4.1, p. 582, after Hewitt and Ross [67, Vol. II, Ch. XI, §44]). The diagonal is a null set, so Lebesgue’s theorem alone says nothing about it; it is applied to the factors a_i(x) and b_i(y) of a finite-rank kernel \sum_ia_i(x)b_i(y), whose smoothening on the diagonal is then \sum_ia_i(t)b_i(t) at almost every t. The Hardy-Littlewood maximal theorem controls all the averages at once by one integrable function, so that for a trace-norm limit of finite-rank kernels the smoothened diagonal still exists at almost every t, is the limit of the finite-rank diagonals, and integrates to the trace (Theorem 12.1.1.2, p. 499).

Theorem 15.3

The geometric kernel carries minus the spectral trace on its diagonal

[1, (1.8.3.6), p. 48; Theorem 12.1.1.3, p. 502]
Statement

Let a>0 and let \varphi be smooth with \operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset(1,Y). The smoothened diagonal \tilde k_{\mathrm{geom}}(t,t) exists for almost every t, it is integrable against \dd t/t, and

\operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}})=-\operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{spec}})=-\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12).
(15.4)
In plain terms

The convolution kernel is zero on its diagonal. Split it into the part that the zeros in the strip see and the part that lives on the theta sums: the two parts must have opposite diagonal masses, and the first one is the sum over the zeros in the strip.

Why it is needed

This identity, the source’s proto-trace formula, turns the remaining work into a computation of \operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}}) by any means other than its definition. Whatever that computation returns equals minus the zero sum over the strip. Without it there is no second expression to compare with the first.

Idea

This is the 4\times4 example in infinite dimensions: a kernel with zero diagonal, split along an invariant subspace, puts opposite traces on the subspace and on the quotient. The only new issue is that the pieces are measurable functions, and the diagonal has to be read by averaging.

Proof

The kernel \varphi(x/y) is continuous, so every point of the diagonal is regular for it and its smoothening there is \varphi(1)=0. Since k_{\mathrm{spec}} is a trace-norm limit of finite-rank kernels, its smoothening exists at almost every point of the diagonal by section Making sense of a kernel on the diagonal, so the smoothening of the difference k_{\mathrm{geom}} exists at those points too, and \tilde k_{\mathrm{geom}}(t,t)=\varphi(1)-\tilde k_{\mathrm{spec}}(t,t)=-\tilde k_{\mathrm{spec}}(t,t) almost everywhere (Theorem 12.1.1.3(1) and (3), pp. 502 to 503). Integrate against \dd t/t. The operator A(\varphi)\circ P^{\mathrm{spec}} is nuclear, k_{\mathrm{spec}} is a trace-norm limit of finite-rank kernels, and Theorem 12.1.1.2 (p. 499) says that for such a kernel the integral of the smoothened diagonal exists and equals the trace. That trace is the trace of A_{\mathrm{spec}}(\varphi) on the quotient, because A(\varphi) preserves the closure of the theta sums, and chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see evaluated it as Equation (15.2). Hence \operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}})=-\Tr A_{\mathrm{spec}}(\varphi), which is Equation (15.4).

Used in

Section What is left: the S-local kernel combines it with the vanishing of the slices, and chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula evaluates the left side.

Aside

The source’s body states these results with an extra Sobolev factor (1+\lvert\log t\rvert^2)^{\sigma_0/2} in the norm of W_a, with \sigma_0\ge3 in Definition 10.4.3.7 and Theorem 12.1.1.3. The introduction and the letter take \sigma_0=0 (p. 27), and we follow them. Nothing in the pictures of this chapter depends on \sigma_0, which only adds a slowly growing weight in \log t.

15.3Why the ideles#

We now have to compute \operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}}) another way, and the plan is to cut k_{\mathrm{geom}} along the primes. On \RR_{>0} there is nothing to cut with. A point of \RR_{>0} is a point of the idele class group C_\QQ\cong\RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times with its compact part forgotten, and a class contains ideles of every kind at a given prime p: if x has a unit at p, then px is in the same class and does not. “Being a unit at p” is a property of an idele, not of a class, and the source makes exactly this point: the restricted product structure of the ideles does not survive the quotient by \QQ^\times (p. 24).

On the ideles each prime has its own coordinate, and the theta sum already uses it. Recall from chapters The adeles: all completions at once and Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions that \Theta_g is the periodization of the adelic function f=g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} over \QQ^\times. At the idele \tau(t)=(t,1,1,\dots), with t at the real place and 1 at every prime,

\sum_{\xi\in\QQ^\times}f(\xi\,\tau(t))=\sum_{\xi\in\QQ^\times}g(\xi t)\prod_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}(\xi)=\sum_{n\ne0}g(nt)=\Theta_g(t),

because a rational number lies in every \ZZ_p exactly when it is an integer. Each factor \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}(\xi) is a separate condition on the coordinate at p. Replace one of them by \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times} and the sum keeps only the integers not divisible by p, which is D_p\Theta_g from chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions. On the ideles the operation “remove the prime p” is multiplication of the adelic function by an indicator, and a kernel can be multiplied by the same indicator.

To use this we need to move a kernel from C_\QQ to the ideles and back without changing its diagonal mass. Over \QQ the set

\mathcal D=\RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times\subset\AA^\times

is a fundamental domain for \QQ^\times: every idele is \xi d for exactly one \xi\in\QQ^\times and d\in\mathcal D, since \xi must clear every p-adic valuation and fix the sign at the real place. This is the source’s \tau(\RR_{>0})\cdot E^1_F (p. 24). The convolution kernel lifts as \tilde\varphi(xy^{-1}), where \tilde\varphi is a smooth compactly supported function on the ideles whose periodization \sum_\xi\tilde\varphi(\xi x) is \varphi(\lvert x\rvert), and the spectral kernel lifts with an indentation, a cutoff function whose \QQ^\times-average is 1, such as the indicator of \mathcal D (pp. 21 to 22). The difference is the lifted geometric kernel

K(x,y)=\tilde\varphi(xy^{-1})-\Psi(k_{\mathrm{spec}})(x,y),

a function on \AA^\times\times\AA^\times invariant under (x,y)\mapsto(\xi x,\xi y) for \xi\in\QQ^\times (p. 24). Here \Psi is the source’s \Psi^\Delta_{u_0}, the lift with the indentation u_0.

Proposition 15.4

The diagonal mass on the class group is a sum over the skewered diagonals of the ideles

[1, (1.3.1.12), p. 24; Proposition 12.2.2.2, p. 508]
Statement

With \mathcal D, K, and smoothenings as above,

\operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}})=\int_{\mathcal D}\sum_{\xi\in\QQ^\times}\tilde K(x,\xi x)\,\dd\mu(x),
(15.5)

the double integral converges absolutely, and its value depends neither on the lift \tilde\varphi nor on the indentation.

In plain terms

To add up a kernel on the diagonal of a quotient, add up the lifted kernel on every shifted copy of the diagonal, but only over one fundamental domain.

Why it is needed

After the lift, the indicator of “unit at p” is a function of the second variable y, and multiplying K by it is meaningful. Formula Equation (15.5) guarantees that cutting K into pieces and adding their skewered masses returns the mass we want.

Idea

The model case is a circle, and the analogy is ours. A kernel on \RR/\ZZ that is the periodization k(x,y)=\sum_nK(x,y+n) of a kernel on \RR has diagonal mass \int_0^1k(x,x)\,\dd x=\int_0^1\sum_{n\in\ZZ}K(x,x+n)\,\dd x, where [0,1) is a fundamental domain and x+n runs over the translates of x. Replace \RR by the ideles, \ZZ by \QQ^\times, and [0,1) by \mathcal D. For K(x,y)=h(x-y) the right side is \sum_nh(n), which by Poisson summation is \sum_m\hat h(m), the sum of the eigenvalues of convolution on the circle: the two ways of computing a trace meet again.

Proof sketch

[1, Proposition 12.2.2.2, p. 508; Proposition 12.2.2.4, p. 512]

Unfold the integral over C_\QQ=\AA^\times/\QQ^\times into an integral over \mathcal D and a sum over \QQ^\times, as for any discrete subgroup with a fundamental domain, and use the fact that smoothening on the ideles at a point equals smoothening on the quotient at its image (part (4) of the source’s list on p. 23). Absolute convergence of the double integral comes from integrability of the smoothened diagonal on the quotient, and Fubini then allows the sum and the integral to be taken in either order, which gives the four equal expressions (1.3.1.6) to (1.3.1.9) on p. 23.

Used in

Section The stratification is a sieve cuts K by indicators in the variable y, and Theorem Theorem 15.7 evaluates each piece in the form Equation (15.5).

15.4The stratification is a sieve#

Fix the finite set of places

S=\{\infty\}\cup\{p\le Y\},

and list the primes beyond Y in increasing order, p_1<p_2<p_3<\cdots. For Y=3 this is S=\{\infty,2,3\} and p_1=5, p_2=7, p_3=11. The plan is to remove p_1, then p_2, and so on, never touching the primes in S.

Definition 15.5 The divisorial stratification over the rationals

For j\ge0 the j-th stratum is the set of ideles that are units at the first j primes beyond Y,

\AA^\times_j=\{x\in\AA^\times:\ x_{p_i}\in\ZZ_{p_i}^\times\ \text{for}\ 1\le i\le j\},

and \alpha_j is its indicator function, with \alpha_0=1. The strata are open and closed, and they decrease, \AA^\times_0\supset\AA^\times_1\supset\AA^\times_2\supset\cdots. The set \AA^\times_{j-1}\setminus\AA^\times_j consists of the ideles that are units at p_1,\dots,p_{j-1} and not at p_j. A stratum is a subset of the ideles, not of C_\QQ: it is not stable under multiplication by \QQ^\times. Over \QQ the source’s primary stratification and its divisorial stratification coincide, because each prime has exactly one place above it (pp. 25 to 26; Section 11.3.1.1, p. 491).

The strata were chosen to match the theta sums. For an adelic function f=g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}, multiplying by \alpha_j changes the factor at each of p_1,\dots,p_j from \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_{p_i}} to \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_{p_i}}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_{p_i}^\times}=\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_{p_i}^\times} and leaves the rest alone (p. 26). We call what this does to the theta sum a sieve of Eratosthenes run on the theta sum. The name is our framing, not the source’s, and the next statement makes it precise.

Proposition 15.6

Restricting to the j-th stratum deletes the multiples of the first j primes beyond Y from the theta sum

[1, p. 26; Weil's identity, Theorem 3.4.1.1, p. 143]
Statement

Let g be even and Schwartz with g(0)=0 and \int_\RR g=0, and f=g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}. The periodization of \alpha_jf is the sieved theta sum

\Theta_g^{(j)}(t)=\sum_{\substack{n\ne0\\ p_1\nmid n,\dots,\,p_j\nmid n}}g(nt)=D_{p_j}\cdots D_{p_1}\Theta_g(t),
(15.6)

and its Mellin transform is

\int_0^\infty\Theta_g^{(j)}(t)\,t^s\,\frac{\dd t}{t}=\prod_{i=1}^j\bigl(1-p_i^{-s}\bigr)\cdot2\zeta(s)\,Mg(s),\qquad Mg(s)=\int_0^\infty g(t)\,t^s\,\frac{\dd t}{t}.

Consecutive sieved sums differ by the multiples of p_j: \Theta_g^{(j-1)}(t)-\Theta_g^{(j)}(t)=\Theta_g^{(j-1)}(p_jt).

In plain terms

Cutting the adelic function down to the j-th stratum is the same as crossing out, in the sum \sum_ng(nt), every n that some removed prime divides. On the Mellin side each crossing-out multiplies by one reciprocal Euler factor.

Why it is needed

It translates the stratification, which lives on the ideles, into operations on functions of one variable that chapters Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions and Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces already understand, and it tells us which quotient each cut of the kernel acts on.

Idea

The periodization evaluates f along the orbit \xi\,\tau(t), whose coordinate at p is the rational number \xi itself. The factor \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times}(\xi) asks that \xi be a p-adic unit, and for an integer n that means p\nmid n.

Proof

At the idele \tau(t) the periodization of \alpha_jf is \sum_{\xi\in\QQ^\times}g(\xi t)\prod_{i\le j}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_{p_i}^\times}(\xi)\prod_{p\ne p_1,\dots,p_j}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}(\xi). The product over all primes forces \xi\in\ZZ\setminus\{0\}, and for an integer \xi=n the condition n\in\ZZ_{p_i}^\times means p_i\nmid n. This gives the first expression in Equation (15.6). For the operator form, recall that D_p\psi(t)=\psi(t)-\psi(pt) on theta sums. For any set of conditions not involving p_j, the integers satisfying them and divisible by p_j are p_jn' with n' satisfying them, so \Theta_g^{(j-1)}(t)-\Theta_g^{(j)}(t)=\sum_{n'}g(p_jn't)=\Theta_g^{(j-1)}(p_jt), which says \Theta_g^{(j)}=D_{p_j}\Theta_g^{(j-1)} and also gives the last claim. Induction on j gives the second expression. For the Mellin transform, the substitution t\mapsto t/p gives \int_0^\infty\psi(pt)t^s\,\dd t/t=p^{-s}\int_0^\infty\psi(t)t^s\,\dd t/t, so each D_{p_i} multiplies by 1-p_i^{-s}, starting from 2\zeta(s)Mg(s) (chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions). In the source’s language, \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times} in place of \mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} multiplies the local zeta integral by the reciprocal Euler factor, which is Weil’s identity (Theorem 3.4.1.1, p. 143; pp. 25 and 49).

Example

Take Y=3 and g(x)=x^2\bigl(e^{-\pi x^2}-8e^{-4\pi x^2}\bigr). It is even, g(0)=0, and \int_\RR g=\tfrac1{2\pi}-\tfrac{8}{2\pi\cdot8}=0. From \int_0^\infty t^{s+1}e^{-\pi ct^2}\,\dd t=\tfrac12\Gamma(\tfrac s2+1)(\pi c)^{-s/2-1} one finds Mg(s)=\tfrac12\Gamma(\tfrac s2+1)\pi^{-s/2-1}(1-2^{1-s}), so 2\zeta(s)Mg(s)=\pi^{-s/2-1}\Gamma(\tfrac s2+1)\,\eta(s) with \eta the alternating series of chapter Zeta on the whole plane, an entire function. The first removal is p_1=5: cross out 5,10,15,\dots. The second is p_2=7: cross out 7,14,21,28,\dots among the survivors, so 35 was already gone. At t=0.1 the four sums are

\Theta_g(0.1)=0.000000,\quad\Theta_g^{(1)}(0.1)=-0.145345,\quad\Theta_g^{(2)}(0.1)=-0.347276,\quad\lim_j\Theta_g^{(j)}(0.1)=-0.418800,

where \Theta_g(0.1) is about 10^{-8} because theta sums with g(0)=\int g=0 decay fast as t\to0, and \Theta_g^{(1)}(0.1)=\Theta_g(0.1)-\Theta_g(0.5) is minus \Theta_g(0.5)=0.145345. At s=2 the Mellin transforms are \eta(2)\Gamma(2)\pi^{-2}=\tfrac1{12}, then (1-\tfrac1{25})\tfrac1{12}=\tfrac2{25}, then (1-\tfrac1{49})\tfrac2{25}=\tfrac{96}{1225}. We checked the first two against numerical Mellin integrals of the sums, at s=2 and at s=\tfrac12+3i, to eight digits.

Used in

The flag Equation (15.7) is built from these sums, and Proposition Proposition 15.8 studies their limit.

The flag of sieved theta sums and the slices#

Let U_j be the closure in W_a of the weighted sieved sums t^{1/2}\Theta_g^{(j)}(t), over all admissible g. Since every D_p multiplies the Mellin transform by a function of z and so does A(\varphi), they commute, and every U_j is invariant under A(\varphi). The spaces form a decreasing chain

U_0\supset U_1\supset U_2\supset\cdots,\qquad U_0=\overline{\mathcal V}.
(15.7)

On the Mellin side, in the variable z=s-\tfrac12, the elements of U_j have transforms \prod_{i\le j}(1-p_i^{-z-1/2})\,\xi(z+\tfrac12)\,h(z) with h entire of the class of chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions. Dividing by the common factor identifies the quotient U_{j-1}/U_j with functions h modulo multiples of 1-p_j^{-z-1/2}, which is the orbital quotient E_{p_j} of chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces, shifted by \tfrac12 because of the weight: functions on the circle \RR_{>0}/p_j^\ZZ of length \log p_j, with dual basis the evaluations at the zeros

z_m=-\tfrac12+\frac{2\pi i m}{\log p_j},\qquad m\in\ZZ,

of 1-p_j^{-z-1/2}. These zeros are simple. The source identifies the subquotient with the orbital quotient and its orbital Schauder basis on p. 27. That the theta quotient equals the quotient of all functions is the strong co-primality of chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces (Theorem 7.5.0.1, p. 374), and that the circle at p_j meets the earlier ones only at s=0 is the polar multiplicity theorem (Theorem 7.1.3.2, p. 324).

The slices of the kernel follow the flag. Define, on \AA^\times\times\AA^\times,

k_{p_j}(x,y)=\bigl(\alpha_{j-1}(y)-\alpha_j(y)\bigr)K(x,y),\qquad j\ge1,

the part of K whose second variable is a unit at p_1,\dots,p_{j-1} but not at p_j. The source writes the same difference in the other order, (\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k)K (p. 27; (11.3.1.4), p. 494); the sign is irrelevant for a mass that will turn out to be zero. Acting on the adelic function f, the cut kernel K\alpha_j(y) sees only \alpha_jf, so by Proposition 15.6 the slice k_{p_j} turns the sieved sum \Theta^{(j-1)}_g into A(\varphi) applied to the deleted multiples \Theta^{(j-1)}_g(p_jt). It kills U_j, whose elements have nothing left to delete at p_j, and on U_{j-1} its Mellin multiplier is M\varphi(z)\,p_j^{-z-1/2}. At the zeros z_m the factor p_j^{-z_m-1/2} equals 1, so on the quotient U_{j-1}/U_j the slice induces exactly the operator that A(\varphi) induces. This paragraph is our account, over \QQ, of the source’s description on pp. 26 to 27 and 50 to 51.

For a finite flag of invariant subspaces of a matrix, the trace is additive over the successive quotients, \Tr(B|_{U_0})=\sum_{j=1}^J\Tr(B\text{ on }U_{j-1}/U_j)+\Tr(B|_{U_J}), because the matrix is block upper triangular in a basis adapted to the flag. The telescoping identity \alpha_0=\sum_{j=1}^J(\alpha_{j-1}-\alpha_j)+\alpha_J is the kernel version of the same bookkeeping:

K=\sum_{j=1}^Jk_{p_j}+\alpha_J(y)K.
(15.8)

The analogy with block triangular matrices is ours. Two things remain: the mass of each slice, and the limit of \alpha_J(y)K as J\to\infty.

15.5Every slice beyond Y has zero mass#

The slice at p_j acts on the orbital quotient at p_j, and chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces computed traces there. The theorem below is that computation transported to the slice, with the weight t^{1/2} carried along.

Theorem 15.7

For a test function supported in (1,Y), every slice at a prime beyond Y has diagonal mass zero

[1, Theorem 11.3.2.1, p. 495]
Statement

Let a>0, let \varphi be smooth with \operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset(1,Y), and let p_j>Y. The slice k_{p_j} has diagonal mass, in the skewered form Equation (15.5),

\operatorname{mass}(k_{p_j})=\sum_{m\in\ZZ}M\varphi\Bigl(-\tfrac12+\frac{2\pi im}{\log p_j}\Bigr)=\log p_j\sum_{k\in\ZZ}p_j^{-k/2}\,\varphi(p_j^k),
(15.9)

and this number is 0.

In plain terms

Each slice is convolution on a circle of length \log p. Its trace is a sum of samples of \varphi at the powers of p, and when p is beyond the support of \varphi no power of p lands in the support.

Why it is needed

Every slice is a piece of \operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}}) that could have carried information about zeros outside the strip. Its vanishing is what concentrates the whole geometric side on the finitely many places in S, a cancellation of the kernel’s mass along the diagonal that the source singles out on p. 32.

Idea

On the quotient U_{j-1}/U_j the slice acts as A(\varphi) on functions on a circle, so its matrix in the exponential basis is diagonal with entries M\varphi(z_m). Poisson summation on the circle turns the sum of those entries into a sum over the points p^k of the dual lattice, the same computation as the toy circle of chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces.

Proof

We give the argument over \QQ step by step and name, at each step, where the source proves the functional-analytic part.

Steps
  1. The slice vanishes on U_j and induces on U_{j-1}/U_j the operator induced by A(\varphi) (The flag of sieved theta sums and the slices), so its trace is the trace of A(\varphi) on the orbital quotient at p_j, with dual basis the evaluations at the simple zeros z_m of 1-p_j^{-z-1/2}.
  2. In that basis A(\varphi) is diagonal, because M(A(\varphi)\psi)=M\varphi\cdot M\psi multiplies the functional “evaluate the Mellin transform at z_m” by M\varphi(z_m). So the trace of A(\varphi) on U_{j-1}/U_j is \sum_{m\in\ZZ}M\varphi(z_m).
  3. The sum converges absolutely. With u=\log t and h(u)=\varphi(e^u)e^{-u/2}, a smooth function with compact support, M\varphi(z_m)=\int_\RR h(u)e^{2\pi imu/\log p_j}\,\dd u=\hat h(-m/\log p_j), which decays faster than any power of m.
  4. Poisson summation for the lattice L\ZZ with L=\log p_j gives \sum_m\hat h(m/L)=L\sum_kh(kL), and h(k\log p_j)=p_j^{-k/2}\varphi(p_j^k), so \sum_{m\in\ZZ}M\varphi(z_m)=\log p_j\sum_{k\in\ZZ}p_j^{-k/2}\varphi(p_j^k).
  5. For k\ge1 the point p_j^k\ge p_j>Y, and for k\le0 the point p_j^k\le1. Neither lies in (1,Y), so every term vanishes and \operatorname{mass}(k_{p_j})=0.

Steps 2 to 5 are complete as written. Step 1 and the identification of the trace with the diagonal mass are where the source’s functional analysis is needed, because the points z_m lie on the line \Re z=-\tfrac12, outside the strip \lvert\Re z\rvert<a when a<\tfrac12, so evaluation there is not continuous on W_a (chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see). The source builds the orbital bases on the unweighted theta sums, where the points are s=2\pi im/\log p_j on the line \Re s=0: Theorem 11.2.0.2 (p. 485) gives a Markushevich basis of the orbital quotient with dual elements t^{\varepsilon} at the zeros \varepsilon of 1-p^{-s}, and Theorem 11.2.2.1 (p. 490) proves that A(\varphi) is nuclear there with trace \sum_\varepsilon M\varphi(\varepsilon). Both carry a Sobolev factor of degree at least 2, which makes evaluation on that line continuous (Remark 11.2.2.2, p. 491). The weight t^{1/2} is then carried through Paley-Wiener levels, closed subspaces defined by a support condition on Fourier transforms on which multiplication by t^a is continuous, whose union recovers the whole trace in the limit (Section 11.2.1, p. 487; Theorem 11.2.1.2, p. 488; p. 51). On those levels the slice is a trace-norm limit of the finite-rank kernels built from the basis, so its truncated diagonal mass is the trace of a nuclear operator (Theorem 12.1.1.2, p. 499; Proposition 12.2.2.2, p. 508), and the truncations are removed in the limit (proof of Theorem 11.3.2.1, pp. 495 to 496). The weighted evaluation points \varepsilon-\tfrac12 are the source’s own, in (11.3.2.5) on p. 496.

Example

Take p_j=5 and for \varphi the bump \varphi(t)=\operatorname{bump}\bigl((\log t-c)/r\bigr) of chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions, with \operatorname{bump}(x)=e^{-1/(1-x^2)} for \lvert x\rvert<1, which is supported on (e^{c-r},e^{c+r}). For \operatorname{supp}\varphi=(1.5,4) every sample 5^k misses the support and both sides of Equation (15.9) are 0; summing M\varphi(z_m) over \lvert m\rvert\le60 numerically leaves 6.5\times10^{-7}, the tail of the series. Widen the support to (1.5,6), which violates the hypothesis because 5\in(1.5,6): now the sum over m gives 0.0806542 and the right side gives \log5\cdot5^{-1/2}\varphi(5)=0.0806542, so the slice at 5 is no longer zero, as it should not be.

Used in

Corollary Corollary 15.9 adds the slices up, and chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula uses the result through the S-local kernel.

The source prints the right side of Equation (15.9) as \frac{\log q_v}{\mu_v(\mathcal O_v^\times)}\sum_k\varphi(\pi_v^k), which over \QQ is \log p\sum_k\varphi(p^k), the unweighted trace of chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces (Theorem 11.3.2.1, p. 495; pp. 19 and 52). In our notation we have carried the weight t^{1/2} of the source’s proof, its points \varepsilon_p-\tfrac12 in (11.3.2.5), through the Poisson step, which multiplies the k-th term by p^{-k/2}. Every term in either form contains the factor \varphi(p^k), so the vanishing is the same.

AsideThe slice is the prime’s own term in Weil’s formula

This observation is ours. For \varphi supported in (1,\infty) only k\ge1 contributes to Equation (15.9), and the slice mass is \sum_{k\ge1}\log p\cdot p^{-k/2}\varphi(p^k)=\sum_{k\ge1}\Lambda(p^k)(p^k)^{-1/2}\varphi(p^k), which is exactly the contribution of the prime p to the prime side \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2}\bigl(\varphi(n)+\varphi(1/n)\bigr) that the Trace Formula over \QQ shares with Weil’s explicit formula (chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula). The source reads the orbital traces as the local traces that Deninger anticipated (p. 33). So a slice vanishes exactly when its prime has nothing to contribute to the prime side, and cutting the slices away for p>Y removes nothing from the final formula.

15.6The shell structure: where the infinite limit is taken#

The telescoping identity Equation (15.8) holds for each finite J. To conclude, we need J\to\infty: the remnant \alpha_J(y)K should converge to a kernel that sees only the places in S, and the sum of the slice masses should converge to the mass of the slices. On the theta sums the limit is concrete. As J\to\infty the sieve deletes every integer with a prime factor beyond Y, and what is left is the sum over the Y-smooth integers, those whose prime factors are all at most Y. In adelic terms it is the S-local theta sum, the periodization of g\otimes\bigotimes_{p\le Y}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}\otimes\bigotimes_{p>Y}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times}. With a general S-local function f_S in place of g\otimes\bigotimes_{p\le Y}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} it is a sum over the S-units \pm\prod_{p\le Y}p^{e_p}, e_p\in\ZZ (p. 483).

The limit does not hold everywhere. The sieved sums \Theta^{(j)}_g decay rapidly as t\to0, like \Theta_g, but their limit does not: there are only on the order of (\log X)^{\pi(Y)} smooth integers below X, too few for the cancellation that Poisson summation forces in \Theta_g. The example of Proposition 15.6 shows it at t=0.05, where \Theta_g, \Theta^{(1)}_g, and \Theta^{(2)}_g are 0.000000, -0.000107, and -0.017364, while the limit is -0.710081. The source therefore takes the limit on shells \{t\ge1/R\} with R>0, which give its Chapter 11 its name (the source writes \Lambda for R; on this page \Lambda is von Mangoldt’s function).

Proposition 15.8

On every shell t\ge1/R, the sieved theta sums converge to the S-local theta sum

[1, Proposition 11.1.1.2, p. 476; Theorem 11.1.2.1, p. 480]
Statement

Let g be even and Schwartz, R>0, r\ge1, and w(t) a weight of at most polynomial growth in \log t, such as (1+\lvert\log t\rvert^2)^{\sigma_0/2}. Then

\Theta_g^{(j)}(t)\ \longrightarrow\ \sum_{\substack{n\ne0\\ p\mid n\Rightarrow p\le Y}}g(nt)\qquad(j\to\infty)

pointwise for every t>0, and in L^r\bigl([1/R,\infty),\,w(t)\,\dd t/t\bigr).

In plain terms

Removing the primes beyond Y one at a time makes the theta sums converge, on any region bounded away from t=0, to the sum over the integers built from the primes up to Y.

Why it is needed

It is the convergence that lets the infinitely many cuts add up: the remnant \alpha_J(y)K acts on theta sums through the sieved sums, and this proposition says that their limit is the S-local theta sum, so the remnant converges to a kernel that sees only S.

Idea

Each integer n is either eventually crossed out, if it has a prime factor beyond Y, or never crossed out. So the sums converge term by term, and one fixed summable majorant makes the convergence uniform enough.

Proof

Fix t>0. For each n\ge1 the indicator that n survives the first j removals is eventually constant in j: it is 1 forever if all prime factors of n are at most Y, and it becomes 0 once the least prime factor of n beyond Y has been removed. Every surviving term is bounded by \lvert g(nt)\rvert, and \sum_{n\ge1}\lvert g(nt)\rvert<\infty because g is Schwartz, so dominated convergence over n gives the pointwise limit. For the L^r limit we need one majorant in t. Every sieved sum and the limit are bounded by J(t)=2\sum_{n\ge1}\lvert g(nt)\rvert. Since g is Schwartz, \lvert g(x)\rvert\le C(1+x^2)^{-1}, so J(t)\le2C\sum_{n\ge1}(1+n^2t^2)^{-1}\le2C\bigl(1+\tfrac{\pi}{2t}\bigr), which is at most 2C(1+\pi R/2) on [1/R,\infty). For t\ge1 the bound \lvert g(x)\rvert\le C_N\lvert x\rvert^{-N-2} gives J(t)\le2C_N\zeta(N+2)\,t^{-N-2} for every N. So J^rw is integrable against \dd t/t on the shell, and dominated convergence in t gives the convergence in L^r. Near t=0 the bound J(t) grows like 1/t, and no single majorant works there, which is why the statement is restricted to shells. This is the source’s Proposition 11.1.1.2 (p. 476) specialized to \QQ, where its majorant J_F(\alpha) is our J and its fractional ideal is \ZZ.

Example

With Y=3, R=10, the function g of the earlier example, and w=1, the distance in L^2([0.1,20],\dd t/t) between \Theta^{(j)}_g and its limit, after removing all primes up to P, is 0.113 for P=5, 0.0187 for P=7, 1.3\times10^{-4} for P=13, 8\times10^{-8} for P=19, and below 10^{-12} from P=29 on: on this shell g(nt) is negligible once nt exceeds about 6.

Used in

Corollary Corollary 15.9 uses it to pass to the limit in Equation (15.8), and chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula starts from the S-local theta sums it produces.

The source’s Theorem 11.1.2.1 (p. 480) says more, in the completed space. For any order in which the places outside S are removed, the closed subspaces of truncated sieved theta sums decrease to a limit that does not depend on the order, each removal of a new prime shrinks the subspace strictly, and the limit is the closure of the span of the truncated S-local theta sums \mathbf 1_{t\ge1/R}\sum_\xi(f_S\otimes\bigotimes_{p\notin S}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p^\times})(\xi\,\cdot). Strictness comes from the orbital bases, which separate consecutive spaces, and the description of the limit uses the fact that the evaluation \hat\delta_0 at zero of the Fourier transform is discontinuous for the truncated norm. The passage from functions to diagonal masses is Proposition 12.2.2.4 (p. 512): for an increasing family of open subgroups G_J exhausting the ideles, here the ideles that are units at every prime beyond the J-th one, with each quotient G_{J+1}/G_J free of rank one, the part of the lifted kernel whose second variable lies outside the J-th subgroup has skewered mass tending to 0. Over \QQ the reason is the absolute convergence in Proposition 15.4: each term of the double integral eventually leaves that part, and dominated convergence does the rest.

15.7Why one prime at a time#

There is an obvious shortcut, and the source explains why it fails in a coarse topology. Remove all the primes beyond Y at once. On the Mellin side that is multiplication by the infinite product

\prod_{p>Y}\bigl(1-p^{-s}\bigr),

which turns 2\zeta(s)Mg(s) into 2Mg(s)\prod_{p\le Y}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}. This is Meyer’s route, as the source paraphrases it (pp. 32, 39): degenerate a global operator into an S-local one with operators that become infinite reciprocal Euler products, compute the S-local trace following Connes, and show that what was left behind contributes nothing. The product converges absolutely exactly where \sum_pp^{-\sigma}<\infty, that is for \sigma>1. At \sigma=1 Mertens’s theorem of chapter Euler's product: primes inside one function says that \sum_{p\le x}1/p grows like \log\log x [4], and inside the critical strip there is no absolute convergence at all. So Meyer’s operators converge only in topologies at least as fine as uniform convergence of the Mellin transforms on vertical strips in \Re s>1, and, through the functional equation, in \Re s<0 (p. 39). In such a fine topology every evaluation at every zero is continuous, every zero enters the spectral side, and the trace formula that comes out is Weil’s explicit formula again (pp. 32, 39). The source calls Mertens’s theorem “a herald for GRH” (p. 40): running into it means that the infinite product has to be avoided.

The source’s change is to take the steps one at a time and keep track of what each step loses (pp. 40 to 41). Each step is finite: one reciprocal Euler factor 1-p^{-s}, whose zeros are explicit and simple, so the lost piece U_{j-1}/U_j is a circle with an explicit basis, and its trace is computed exactly, as in Theorem 15.7. The only infinite limit is taken on the function side, in the sense of Proposition 15.8: pointwise and in L^r on shells, which the rapid decay of Schwartz functions provides with no Euler product in sight. The source describes this as a weaker, approximate form of Meyer’s Euler product convergence, asserted only on relatively compact regions, for which the bases compensate (pp. 32 to 33). The example makes the contrast concrete. The S-local theta sum \sum_{n\ Y\text{-smooth}}g(nt) is a perfectly good limit at each t>0, and its Mellin transform 2Mg(s)\prod_{p\le Y}(1-p^{-s})^{-1} converges for every \Re s>0, yet the multiplier \prod_{p>Y}(1-p^{-s}) that would produce it from 2\zeta(s)Mg(s) converges absolutely only for \Re s>1.

15.8What is left: the S-local kernel#

Let J\to\infty in Equation (15.8). The remnant \alpha_J(y)K converges to the source’s S-local kernel

k_S=\lim_{J\to\infty}\alpha_J(y)\,K(x,y),

which acts on theta sums through the S-local theta sums of Proposition 15.8. In the source’s terms, k_S is supported, in its effect on theta functions, on \AA_{\QQ,S}^\times\times\prod_{p>Y}\ZZ_p^\times in the variable y, is invariant under \prod_{p>Y}\ZZ_p^\times there, and factors through a kernel on \AA^\times_{\QQ,S}\times C_\QQ with the same diagonal mass, where \AA_{\QQ,S}=\RR\times\prod_{p\le Y}\QQ_p (pp. 16, 27, 52). It is a kernel about the finitely many completions in S, nothing more.

Corollary 15.9

Only the S-local kernel carries diagonal mass, and its mass is minus the zero sum over the strip

[1, pp. 16 and 52; proof of Theorem 12.5.1.1, p. 520]
Statement

Let a>0, \varphi smooth with \operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset(1,Y), and S=\{\infty\}\cup\{p\le Y\}. Then

\operatorname{mass}(k_S)=\operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}})=-\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12).
(15.10)
In plain terms

After every prime beyond Y has been cut away at no cost, the small piece of the kernel that knows only about the real numbers and the primes up to Y still carries the full diagonal mass, which is minus the sum over the zeros in the strip.

Why it is needed

It reduces the global problem to an S-local one. Computing \operatorname{mass}(k_S) is a problem about \RR\times\prod_{p\le Y}\QQ_p alone, which Connes solved, and the source describes this reduction as what the whole work is about (p. 16).

Idea

Telescoping, then vanishing of every slice, then the shell limit, then the proto-trace formula.

Proof

By Proposition 15.4 and linearity, the masses of the pieces in Equation (15.8) add up: \operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}})=\sum_{j=1}^J\operatorname{mass}(k_{p_j})+\operatorname{mass}(\alpha_JK) for every J. Each p_j exceeds Y, so every slice mass is 0 by Theorem 15.7, and \operatorname{mass}(\alpha_JK)=\operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}}) for every J. As J\to\infty, \operatorname{mass}(\alpha_JK)\to\operatorname{mass}(k_S) by the shell structure (Proposition 15.8; Theorem 11.1.2.1, p. 480) and Proposition 12.2.2.4 (p. 512). Hence \operatorname{mass}(k_S)=\operatorname{mass}(k_{\mathrm{geom}}), and Theorem 15.3 gives the value. The source states the result on pp. 16 and 52 and uses it in this form in the proof of Theorem 12.5.1.1 (p. 520).

Used in

Chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula computes \operatorname{mass}(k_S) with Connes’s S-local method, which is where the weight \tfrac12 becomes necessary, and turns Equation (15.10) into the Trace Formula. Chapter From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis uses the result.

Here is what chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula receives. The left side of Equation (15.10) is a diagonal mass on \AA^\times_{\QQ,S}, to be computed with the S-adelic Fourier transform as Connes did in 1998 [43] (Theorem 12.4.1.1, p. 514). It will come out as Weil’s local terms at \infty and at each p\le Y, minus the two pole terms M\varphi(\tfrac12)+M\varphi(-\tfrac12). The local terms at the primes p>Y vanish for our \varphi by the same argument as the slices, since they are also sums of samples \varphi(p^{\pm k}), so the result is Weil’s complete prime side. The right side has only the zeros in the strip. Every step leading here was done inside W_a, which is what the source means by “GRH is a topological phenomenon” (p. 31).

15.9What changes in general#

For a number field F and a unitary Hecke character \chi, the class group C_F has a compact part C_F^1, and the computation runs one isotype \chi|_{C_F^1} at a time. The set S must contain the archimedean places, the places where F or \chi ramifies, and enough places for \mathrm{Pic}(\mathcal O_{F,S})=1, so that every theta function has the form f_S\otimes\bigotimes_{v\notin S}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal O_v} (Fifth Structure Theorem, Theorem 6.2.1.1, p. 295; pp. 25, 48), and S is chosen so that the support of \varphi lies in (1/T,T) with T<N\mathfrak p_v for every finite v\notin S (proof of Theorem 12.5.1.1, p. 520). Several places can lie above one prime p. The source therefore removes whole fibers S_p at a time, the primary divisorial stratification (pp. 26, 49 to 50), so that each slice acts on the orbital quotient E_{S_p} with dual basis at the zeros of \prod_{v\mid p}L_v(\chi_v\lvert\cdot\rvert_v^s)^{-1}. These factors can share up to [F:\QQ] zeros, which is why the Sobolev degree is taken at least 2[F:\QQ] (Remark 11.2.2.2, p. 491; Theorem 7.1.3.2, p. 324). The slice mass becomes \sum_{v\mid p}\frac{\log q_v}{\mu_v(\mathcal O_v^\times)}\sum_k\varphi(\pi_v^k) in the source’s normalization, with twists by \chi(\pi_v) inside the exponential bases, and it vanishes for the same reason: q_v exceeds the support. The strata are still defined on the ideles \GL_1(\AA_F) and lost in C_F, and the lift uses the fundamental domain \tau(\RR_{>0})\cdot E_F^1 (p. 24).

Recap
  • The trace of chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see is minus the diagonal mass of the geometric kernel k_{\mathrm{geom}}=\varphi(x/y)-k_{\mathrm{spec}}, because the convolution kernel vanishes on the diagonal when \varphi(1)=0 (Theorem 15.3). Lebesgue differentiation defines the diagonal values, and the maximal theorem makes their integral equal the trace.
  • Lifted to the ideles with the fundamental domain \RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times, the diagonal mass becomes a sum over skewered diagonals (Proposition 15.4), and the kernel can be cut by the indicators \alpha_j of “unit at p_1,\dots,p_j”.
  • Cutting at p_j is the sieve step D_{p_j} on the theta sum, multiplication by 1-p_j^{-s} on the Mellin side (Proposition 15.6), and the slice acts on the orbital quotient at p_j.
  • Every slice at a prime beyond Y has mass \log p\sum_kp^{-k/2}\varphi(p^k)=0 (Theorem 15.7), the removals converge on shells (Proposition 15.8), and the S-local kernel carries the whole mass (Corollary 15.9). Chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula computes that mass, and chapter From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis compares the result with Weil’s explicit formula.
