Chapter 16

The local trace and the Trace Formula

After this chapter you can compute the S-local diagonal mass place by place, say why the weight has to be one half, state the Trace Formula over Q with its constants, and set it beside Weil’s explicit formula, from which it differs only in which zeros it counts.

Builds on 15. Cutting the kernel along the primes, 8. Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion

In plain terms

After the sieve of the previous chapter, everything that is left of the prime side lives at finitely many places: the real numbers and the primes up to the reach of the test function. This chapter computes that remnant. At each place the answer is one integral, and at a prime it can be done by hand and gives back the prime-power terms of the explicit formula. Put next to the spectral side, this is the Trace Formula: the complete prime sum of Weil equals the poles minus only those zeros that lie in a strip around the critical line, however thin the strip is.

Chapter Cutting the kernel along the primes ended with an equation whose right side is the spectral trace of chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see, minus the sum of M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) over the zeros in the strip \lvert\Re z\rvert<a, and whose left side is the diagonal mass of a kernel that sees only the places in a finite set S. Nothing about zeros is left to do. What remains is a computation with the primes p\le Y and the real place, and the source takes it from A. Connes, who did it in 1998 for a different purpose [1, §12.4, p. 514] [43]. We do it in three passes. First a single place, the real line, where the whole computation fits in a paragraph and shows where the shape 1/\lvert1-t\rvert comes from. Then the general S, where the additive Fourier transform turns a trace into a volume, and where the weight \tfrac12 is forced. Then the local terms by hand. The chapter ends with the Trace Formula over \QQ, checked against several hundred zeros, its general statement, and a line-by-line comparison with Weil’s explicit formula from chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion.

16.1Where the sieve left the calculation#

Fix the data that every statement in this chapter uses. The test function \varphi is smooth on \RR_{>0}, has compact support inside (1/Y,Y) for a real number Y>1, and satisfies \varphi(1)=0. The sieve of chapter Cutting the kernel along the primes was run under the source’s standing assumption that the support lies in (1,Y), to the right of 1. The local computations of this chapter do not care on which side of 1 the support lies, and the last step of the proof of Theorem 16.6 removes the assumption, as the source does. The finite set of places is S=\{\infty\}\cup\{p\le Y\}, the real place together with every prime up to Y. The strip has half-width a>0, and the coarse Hilbert space is the space W_a of chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see, in which only the zeros with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a survive in the quotient by the closure of the weighted theta sums.

In this setting chapter Cutting the kernel along the primes split the geometric kernel into the S-local remnant k_S and one orbital slice k_p for each prime p>Y, showed that each orbital slice has diagonal mass \log p\sum_kp^{-k/2}\varphi(p^k)=0 (Theorem 15.7), and proved that the geometric diagonal mass is minus the spectral trace of chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see (Theorem 15.3). Together these give

\int_0^\infty k_S(x,x)\,\frac{\dd x}{x}=-\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,M\varphi\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr),
(16.1)

which is Corollary 15.9 and the equation displayed at the top of the source’s §1.2.3 [1, p. 16], specialized to \QQ and the trivial character. The source is explicit that this reduction is the whole difficulty: once the calculation has been brought down to the S-local diagonal mass, it regards the problem as solved [1, p. 16]. The rest is a computation with finitely many places, none of which knows anything about zeros.

Two features of Equation (16.1) decide how the computation goes. The left side is an integral of a kernel along the diagonal, so we need the kernel k_S and not only the operator it represents. And the kernel is S-local, meaning that once it is lifted to the ideles it depends on the coordinates at the places of S only, and is invariant under the units \ZZ_p^\times at every prime outside S [1, p. 27]. So the natural home for the computation is the product of the completions at the places of S, and that is where we go next.

16.2The S-local stage#

The adeles of chapter The adeles: all completions at once keep one coordinate for every place. Keeping only the coordinates in S gives a ring of the same kind that is a finite product, and it carries an additive Fourier transform exactly as \RR does.

Definition 16.1 S-adeles, S-units, and the S-idele class group

The S-adeles are the finite product \AA_S=\RR\times\prod_{p\le Y}\QQ_p, a locally compact ring with componentwise operations, and the S-ideles are its units \AA_S^\times=\RR^\times\times\prod_{p\le Y}\QQ_p^\times, with the norm \lvert x\rvert_S=\lvert x_\infty\rvert\prod_{p\le Y}\lvert x_p\rvert_p. The S-units are the rational numbers \omega=\pm\prod_{p\le Y}p^{e_p} with integer exponents e_p of either sign, embedded diagonally in \AA_S^\times. They form a discrete subgroup, and the product formula of The adeles: all completions at once gives \lvert\omega\rvert_S=1. The quotient J_S=\AA_S^\times/\{S\text{-units}\} is the S-idele class group. It is a group, not a ring, and it is not the idele class group C_\QQ of The adeles: all completions at once, although for our test functions the two give the same integrals.

Every class in J_S has a representative whose coordinate at each p\le Y is a unit, because multiplying by p^{e_p} moves x_p into \ZZ_p^\times, and multiplying by \pm1 makes x_\infty positive. So J_S\cong\RR_{>0}\times\prod_{p\le Y}\ZZ_p^\times, with the norm as the projection to \RR_{>0}, which is the S-local copy of C_\QQ\cong\RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times. A function of the norm alone, such as our \varphi, is a function on J_S that ignores the compact factor.

Definition 16.2 The additive and multiplicative measures on the S-adeles

The additive measure \nu_S on \AA_S is the product of \dd x on \RR and the Haar measure \dd x_p on each \QQ_p with \int_{\ZZ_p}\dd x_p=1. It is self-dual for the character \mathbf e_S(x)=\mathbf e_\infty(x_\infty)\prod_{p\le Y}\mathbf e_p(x_p) of The adeles: all completions at once, so the Fourier transform \mathcal F_Sf(y)=\int_{\AA_S}f(x)\,\mathbf e_S(xy)\,\dd\nu_S(x) is inverted by the same formula with \mathbf e_S(-xy). The multiplicative measure \mu_S on \AA_S^\times is the product of \dd x/\lvert x\rvert on \RR^\times and \dd^\times x_p on each \QQ_p^\times, normalized by \int_{\ZZ_p^\times}\dd^\times x_p=1 as in The adeles: all completions at once. The two are related by

\dd\mu_S(x)=c_S\,\frac{\dd\nu_S(x)}{\lvert x\rvert_S},\qquad c_S=\prod_{p\le Y}\frac{p}{p-1}.
(16.2)

The relation Equation (16.2) is the source’s (12.4.1.17) [1, p. 518], and it is the place-by-place identity Equation (11.5) multiplied out. For Y=8 the places are \infty,2,3,5,7, the S-units are \pm2^{e_2}3^{e_3}5^{e_5}7^{e_7}, and c_S=2\cdot\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac54\cdot\tfrac76=4.375. For 1<Y<2 there is no prime in S, so \AA_S=\RR, the S-units are \pm1, J_S=\RR^\times/\{\pm1\}\cong\RR_{>0}, and c_S=1.

The functions on which the S-local operator acts are S-local theta sums. A Schwartz-Bruhat function f on \AA_S is summed over the S-units, \sum_\omega f(\omega x), and weighted by \lvert x\rvert_S^{1/2}, the S-local version of the weighted theta sums t^{1/2}\Theta_g(t) of chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions [1, pp. 16, 514 to 515]. For f=g\otimes\bigotimes_{p\le Y}\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p} and x=(t,1,\dots,1), only the S-units that are integers at every p\le Y survive, so the sum is \sum_n\bigl(g(nt)+g(-nt)\bigr) over the positive integers n with no prime factor above Y. This is what the sieve of chapter Cutting the kernel along the primes leaves of \Theta_g(t)=\sum_{n\ne0}g(nt) after every prime beyond Y has been removed. For Y<2 it is the single pair g(t)+g(-t).

16.3One place first: the trace of a dilation#

Take 1<Y<2, so that S=\{\infty\} and the support of \varphi lies in (1/2,2). Then no prime power meets the support, the prime side of everything below is empty, and the S-local space is made of even functions on \RR: g(t)+g(-t) is all that an S-local theta sum can be. The operator is convolution by \varphi acting on \lvert x\rvert^{1/2} times such functions, which after dividing out the weight reads

(A g)(x)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(y)\,y^{-1/2}\,g\Bigl(\frac xy\Bigr)\,\frac{\dd y}{y},
(16.3)

a superposition of the dilations (U_yg)(x)=g(x/y) with weights \varphi(y)y^{-1/2}. A trace of A is therefore a superposition of traces of dilations, and a dilation of the line has a trace that can be computed once the infinite volume of the line is cut off. Cut it off in space, by restricting to \lvert x\rvert\le R, and in frequency, by keeping only the Fourier modes with \lvert\eta\rvert\le R'. (The source writes \lambda,\lambda' for the two cutoffs; on this page \lambda is the period of the toy circle.)

Proposition 16.3 Cut off in space and in frequency, the dilation by y of the line has trace tending to \lvert y\rvert/\lvert1-y\rvert, its fixed-point weight [43]

For y\in\RR^\times, y\ne1, let T=P_RU_y\hat P_{R'}, where \hat P_{R'}g=\mathcal F^{-1}(\mathbf 1_{\lvert\eta\rvert\le R'}\,\mathcal Fg) keeps the frequencies up to R' and P_R multiplies by \mathbf 1_{\lvert x\rvert\le R}. The kernel K of T is continuous and, with c=y^{-1}-1,

\int_\RR K(x,x)\,\dd x=\frac{2}{\pi\lvert c\rvert}\,\mathrm{Si}\bigl(2\pi\lvert c\rvert RR'\bigr)\ \longrightarrow\ \frac1{\lvert c\rvert}=\frac{\lvert y\rvert}{\lvert1-y\rvert}\qquad(RR'\to\infty),
(16.4)

where \mathrm{Si}(v)=\int_0^v\sin w\,\dd w/w tends to \pi/2. For y=1 the same integral is 4RR'.

Proof

The kernel of \hat P_{R'} is k(w,v)=\int_{-R'}^{R'}e^{2\pi i(w-v)\eta}\,\dd\eta, since \mathcal F^{-1}(\mathbf 1\cdot\mathcal Fg)(w)=\int_{\lvert\eta\rvert\le R'}e^{2\pi iw\eta}\int g(v)e^{-2\pi iv\eta}\,\dd v\,\dd\eta. Composing with U_y and P_R gives K(x,v)=\mathbf 1_{\lvert x\rvert\le R}\,k(x/y,v), so on the diagonal

\int_\RR K(x,x)\,\dd x=\int_{-R}^{R}\int_{-R'}^{R'}e^{2\pi icx\eta}\,\dd\eta\,\dd x=\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{\sin(2\pi cR'x)}{\pi cx}\,\dd x=\frac{2}{\pi\lvert c\rvert}\,\mathrm{Si}\bigl(2\pi\lvert c\rvert RR'\bigr).

For y=1, c=0 and the integrand is 1 on a box of area 4RR'.

The limit has a geometric meaning, and it is the one Connes emphasized [43]. The map x\mapsto x/y has one fixed point on the line, x=0, and near it the map is linear with derivative 1/y. The classical fixed-point formula of Atiyah and Bott weights an isolated fixed point by 1/\lvert1-(\text{derivative})\rvert, which here is 1/\lvert1-y^{-1}\rvert=\lvert y\rvert/\lvert1-y\rvert. The cutoffs are what make the trace of an operator on an infinite-dimensional space a finite number, and the proposition says that in the limit the answer is the fixed-point weight and nothing else. At y=1 every point is fixed, and the trace is the area 4RR' of the box in the plane of position and frequency, which grows without bound. This is the only place where the cutoffs leave a trace, and it is multiplied by \varphi(1).

For a number, take y=\tfrac13, so c=2 and the limit is \tfrac12. At RR'=1, 10, and 1000 the trace Equation (16.4) is 0.47497, 0.49747, and 0.49997. For y=\tfrac23, where c=\tfrac12 and the limit is 2, the values are 2.35796, 1.95955, and 1.99959, the overshoot at RR'=1 being the familiar Gibbs bump of \mathrm{Si}.

Now restrict to even functions. The projection onto even functions is \tfrac12(1+U_{-1}), and U_yU_{-1}=U_{-y}, so the trace of P_RU_y\hat P_{R'} on even functions is the average of Equation (16.4) at y and at -y. For y>0 the second fixed point weight is 1/\lvert1+y^{-1}\rvert=y/(1+y). Feeding this into the superposition Equation (16.3) and letting RR'\to\infty, the trace of A on even functions tends to

\int_0^\infty\varphi(y)\,y^{-1/2}\cdot\frac12\Bigl(\frac{y}{\lvert1-y\rvert}+\frac{y}{1+y}\Bigr)\frac{\dd y}{y}=\frac12\int_0^\infty\varphi(y)\,y^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac1{\lvert1-y\rvert}+\frac1{1+y}\Bigr)\frac{\dd y}{y}.
(16.5)

The exchange of the limit and the integral is legitimate because \lvert\varphi(y)\rvert\le C\lvert1-y\rvert near y=1 (this is where \varphi(1)=0 enters) while the trace at y is at most a constant times 1/\lvert c\rvert, so the integrand is bounded uniformly in RR'. The right side of Equation (16.5) is the archimedean term of Weil’s explicit formula, with its factor \tfrac12 and its companion term 1/(1+y). Both come from the evenness: \tfrac12 is the averaging over \pm1, and 1/(1+y) is the fixed point of the dilation composed with the reflection x\mapsto-x.

One more step turns this into a trace formula. The functions that build theta sums satisfy two linear conditions, g(0)=0 and \int_\RR g=0 (chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions), so the operator that the kernel k_S represents acts on a subspace of codimension two, and its trace is the trace on all even functions minus the trace on the two-dimensional piece that the conditions remove. That piece is spanned by the two functionals g\mapsto g(0) and g\mapsto\int g, and A multiplies each by a number,

(Ag)(0)=\int_0^\infty\varphi(y)y^{-1/2}\,\frac{\dd y}{y}\;g(0)=M\varphi(-\tfrac12)\,g(0),\qquad\int_\RR Ag=\int_0^\infty\varphi(y)y^{1/2}\,\frac{\dd y}{y}\int_\RR g=M\varphi(\tfrac12)\int_\RR g.

So the trace on the subspace is Equation (16.5) minus M\varphi(\tfrac12)+M\varphi(-\tfrac12). This is exactly how the source’s proof of the Trace Formula uses the S-local computation: the diagonal mass of k_S is the left side of (12.5.1.1) with the two pole terms subtracted [1, p. 520]. The identification of the two pole terms with the functionals g(0) and \int g is our gloss on that line. Combined with Equation (16.1) it gives, for every \varphi supported in (1,2), and then by the extension in Step 6 of the proof of Theorem 16.6 for every \varphi supported in (\tfrac12,2) with \varphi(1)=0,

\frac12\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac1{\lvert1-t\rvert}+\frac1{1+t}\Bigr)\frac{\dd t}{t}=M\varphi(\tfrac12)+M\varphi(-\tfrac12)-\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,M\varphi\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr),
(16.6)

the Trace Formula for test functions too short to reach any prime. Section Both sides in numbers checks it with numbers.

16.4All the places of S: Connes’s computation#

With primes in S the same idea works with \AA_S in place of \RR, and the source carries it out in the form Connes gave it [1, Theorem 12.4.1.1, pp. 514 to 519] [43]. Two things change. The dilation by an S-idele y acts on all coordinates at once, so a fixed point must be found in a product, and the space of S-local theta sums is a quotient by the S-units, so the dilations by y and by \omega y for an S-unit \omega are the same operator. Connes’s geometric picture of the answer is that the fixed points of this action on \AA_S modulo S-units are the classes with exactly one vanishing coordinate, one family for each place v\in S, and that each family contributes the fixed-point weight of its place integrated against \varphi [43]. These are the periodic orbits of length \log p and the fixed point at infinity that chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces met as the supports of dual basis vectors. The source’s proof does not count fixed points, though. It turns the trace into a volume.

Theorem 16.4

The S-local diagonal mass is the sum over the places of S of Weil’s local principal values, plus \varphi(1) times the logarithm of the cutoffs

[43]
Statement

Let \varphi be smooth with compact support in \RR_{>0}, viewed as a function on J_S through the norm, and let k^{\mathrm{PW}}_{S,\varphi,R,R'} be the kernel of the S-local operator truncated in space at \lvert x\rvert_S\le R and in S-adelic frequency at R'. With the measures of Definition 16.2, and as R,R'\to\infty,

\int_{J_S}k^{\mathrm{PW}}_{S,\varphi,R,R'}(x,x)\,\dd\mu_S(x)=\frac12\int'_{\RR^\times}\frac{\varphi(y)\lvert y\rvert^{1/2}}{\lvert1-y\rvert}\frac{\dd y}{\lvert y\rvert}+\sum_{p\le Y}\log p\int'_{\QQ_p^\times}\frac{\varphi(y)\lvert y\rvert_p^{1/2}}{\lvert1-y\rvert_p}\,\dd^\times y+\varphi(1)\log(RR')+o(1).
(16.7)

Here \varphi(y) for y\in\QQ_v^\times means \varphi at the norm of y, and \int' is Weil’s principal value, which for \varphi(1)=0 is the ordinary absolutely convergent integral.

In plain terms

Once the operator is cut off in space and in frequency, its trace is a sum of one integral for each place of S, plus a term that grows with the cutoffs. That growing term is multiplied by \varphi(1), so it disappears for the test functions of this route.

Why it is needed

This is the whole content of the left side of Equation (16.1). The sieve reduced the infinitely many primes to the finitely many in S, and this theorem evaluates what is left as Weil’s local terms, which is what makes the geometric side of the new formula identical to the prime side of the old one.

Idea

Write the trace as an integral over the diagonal with respect to the additive measure, apply Parseval for the S-adelic Fourier transform, and change variables w=xu in the product of position and frequency. The integral over x becomes the multiplicative volume of the annulus \{\lvert w\rvert_S/R'\le\lvert x\rvert_S\le R\} in J_S, which is \log(RR')-\log\lvert w\rvert_S. The constant \log(RR') produces the \varphi(1) term. The logarithm \log\lvert w\rvert_S=\sum_{v\in S}\log\lvert w_v\rvert_v splits into places, and the Fourier transform of \log\lvert\cdot\rvert_v is the distribution that defines Weil’s principal value at v.

Proof sketch

[1, Theorem 12.4.1.1, pp. 514 to 519]

Lift. Choose \tilde\varphi smooth with compact support on \AA_S^\times with \sum_\omega\tilde\varphi(\omega y)=\varphi(y), the sum over S-units, which exists because the S-units are discrete ((12.4.1.4), p. 515). The operator to trace is f\mapsto\int\tilde\varphi(y)\lvert y\rvert_S^{-1/2}f(y^{-1}x)\,\dd\mu_S(y) on Schwartz-Bruhat functions f on \AA_S, the S-local form of Equation (16.3), with Schwartz kernel \int\lvert y\rvert_S^{-1/2}\tilde\varphi(y)\,\delta(v-y^{-1}x)\,\dd\mu_S(y) ((12.4.1.5) to (12.4.1.7), p. 516).

Truncate. Multiply by a smoothed \mathbf 1_{\lvert x\rvert_S\le R} on the left and by the Fourier cutoff \mathcal F_S^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\lvert\eta\rvert_S\le R'}\mathcal F_S on the right, whose kernel is a convolution kernel ((12.4.1.8) to (12.4.1.10), p. 517).

Parseval. Integrate the kernel along the diagonal, shifted by each S-unit, with respect to \nu_S, and apply Parseval in the second variable. After the substitution y\omega-1=z and the relation Equation (16.2) the inner integral becomes c_S\,\hat\eta_\omega(xu) for an explicit compactly supported \eta_\omega built from \lvert y\rvert_S^{1/2}\tilde\varphi(y^{-1}) ((12.4.1.11) to (12.4.1.21), pp. 517 to 518).

Volume. The remaining double integral over \lvert x\rvert_S\le R and \lvert u\rvert_S\le R' is rewritten with w=xu. The product \dd\nu_S(x)\,\dd\nu_S(u) becomes \dd\nu_S(x)/\lvert x\rvert_S\otimes\dd\nu_S(w), and c_S\,\dd\nu_S(x)/\lvert x\rvert_S=\dd\mu_S(x), so the x-integral is the multiplicative volume of an annulus, \log(RR')-\log\lvert w\rvert_S ((12.4.1.22) to (12.4.1.24), p. 518).

Connes’s lemma. Summing over S-units, the \log(RR') part gives \varphi(1)\log(RR'), and the \log\lvert w\rvert_S part gives Weil’s principal value at each place, by Connes’s computation together with the source’s Lemmas B.4.4.3, B.4.4.5, and B.4.3.2 on the Fourier transform of \log\lvert\cdot\rvert_v. The result has \varphi(y^{-1}), and the local terms are unchanged under y\mapsto y^{-1}, which gives Equation (16.7) with \varphi(y) (p. 519) [43].

Used in
  • Theorem 16.6, which adds the pole terms and combines with Equation (16.1).
  • Section Why the weight is one half, which reads the weight \tfrac12 off the volume step.

The truncations in the statement are the source’s Paley-Wiener levels, subspaces cut out by a support condition on Fourier transforms on which multiplication by \lvert x\rvert^{a} is continuous. Over \QQ they can be read as the two cutoffs of Proposition 16.3, and we do not need more about them [1, p. 51]. The normalization factor 1/\mu_{S,1}(J_S^1) of the source’s statement is 1 here, because the compact part \prod_{p\le Y}\ZZ_p^\times of J_S has volume 1 in our measure.

16.5Why the weight is one half#

The theta sums of chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions were weighted by t^{1/2} before the strip topology was applied, and chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see measured the strip from the line \Re z=0, that is from \Re s=\tfrac12. The source carries the exponent of the weight as a parameter w>0 through the earlier steps, with the zeros then sitting at z=\rho-w and the strip centered on \Re s=w, and it locates the one step that needs w=\tfrac12 in the S-local computation, explaining it in a sentence about measures [1, pp. 16, 52].

The step is the volume step of Theorem 16.4. The trace that Parseval computes is an integral along the diagonal against the additive measure \nu_S, because Fourier analysis on \AA_S lives on the additive group. The diagonal mass that Equation (16.1) needs is an integral against the multiplicative measure \mu_S, because the kernel k_S lives on the idele class group. In the source’s words, the product \lvert x\rvert_S^{w}\lvert y\rvert_S^{w} that appears in the kernel becomes \lvert x\rvert_S^{2w} on the diagonal, and \lvert x\rvert_S^{2w}\,\dd\mu_S is a multiple of \dd\nu_S exactly when 2w=1, by Equation (16.2). Only then does the additive trace equal the multiplicative diagonal mass, and only then does the x-integral in the volume step become the volume of an annulus. The source draws the conclusion in one line: “This forces the 1/2 in the very statement of GRH” [1, p. 16]. It adds that Connes had expected the S-adelic Fourier transform to play exactly this role.

On \RR the statement is an identity anyone can check. The map g\mapsto\lvert x\rvert^{w}g sends functions on the line to functions on \RR^\times, and

\int_{\RR^\times}\bigl\lvert\,\lvert x\rvert^{w}g(x)\bigr\rvert^2\,\frac{\dd x}{\lvert x\rvert}=\int_\RR\lvert g(x)\rvert^2\,\lvert x\rvert^{2w-1}\,\dd x,
(16.8)

which equals \int\lvert g\rvert^2\,\dd x for every g exactly when w=\tfrac12. So g\mapsto\lvert x\rvert^{1/2}g is the unique power weight that is a unitary map from L^2(\RR,\dd x), where the Fourier transform is unitary by Plancherel, to L^2(\RR^\times,\dd x/\lvert x\rvert), where dilations act. The same identity at a prime holds up to the constant p/(p-1). It is the same fact that chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion recorded as the reason the critical line is special for the Mellin transform: square integrability against \dd x is measured on \Re s=\tfrac12 and nowhere else.

The weight is also visible in the answer. The local factor of Equation (16.7) is \lvert y\rvert^{1/2}/\lvert1-y\rvert, and under y\mapsto y^{-1} it becomes \lvert y\rvert^{-1/2}/\lvert1-y^{-1}\rvert=\lvert y\rvert^{1/2}/\lvert1-y\rvert again. The last line of the source’s proof uses exactly this invariance to replace \varphi(y^{-1}) by \varphi(y) [1, p. 519]. With the weight \lvert y\rvert^{-w} in the operator, the fixed-point weight of Proposition 16.3 would give \lvert y\rvert^{1-w}/\lvert1-y\rvert, whose image under inversion is \lvert y\rvert^{w}/\lvert1-y\rvert, and the two agree only at w=\tfrac12. The symmetry y\leftrightarrow y^{-1} of the local terms is the symmetry z\leftrightarrow-z of the functional equation, seen at one place.

Aside

A consistency check that is ours. Suppose a version of the Trace Formula held with the weight w in place of \tfrac12. Its zero side would run over the zeros with \lvert\beta-w\rvert<a, and the argument of chapter From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis would show that every zero has \beta\le w, and with the functional equation \beta\ge1-w. For w<\tfrac12 these two bounds contradict each other, while the zero \tfrac12+14.1347\,i exists, so no such formula can hold. For w>\tfrac12 the bounds say only that the zeros lie in 1-w\le\beta\le w, a zero-free region that is weaker than the hypothesis and, for w\ge1, already known. The weight \tfrac12 is the only one at which the method can give the hypothesis, and the S-local computation is the step that selects it.

16.6The local terms by hand#

With \varphi(1)=0 every term of Equation (16.7) is an ordinary integral, and each can be computed for a function of the norm.

Lemma 16.5 At a prime p, the local term is \log p\sum_{m\ge1}p^{-m/2}\bigl(\varphi(p^m)+\varphi(p^{-m})\bigr) [1, Lemma B.4.4.3, p. 620; §1.4.1, p. 28]

For \varphi smooth with compact support in \RR_{>0} and \varphi(1)=0,

\log p\int_{\QQ_p^\times}\frac{\varphi(\lvert y\rvert_p)\,\lvert y\rvert_p^{1/2}}{\lvert1-y\rvert_p}\,\dd^\times y=\log p\sum_{m\ge1}p^{-m/2}\bigl(\varphi(p^m)+\varphi(p^{-m})\bigr).
(16.9)
Proof

Split \QQ_p^\times into the shells p^m\ZZ_p^\times of Equation (11.4), each of multiplicative volume 1. On the unit shell m=0 the norm is 1, so the integrand is \varphi(1)\cdot\lvert1-y\rvert_p^{-1}=0 there, and the singularity of 1/\lvert1-y\rvert_p at y=1 never matters. This is the reason the principal value reduces to an ordinary integral, which the source states as Lemma B.4.4.3. On a shell with m\ge1 the element y lies in p\ZZ_p, so 1-y is a unit and \lvert1-y\rvert_p=1, while \lvert y\rvert_p=p^{-m}. The integrand is the constant \varphi(p^{-m})p^{-m/2}. On a shell with m=-k\le-1, \lvert y\rvert_p=p^{k} and the ultrametric inequality gives \lvert1-y\rvert_p=\lvert y\rvert_p=p^{k}, so the integrand is the constant \varphi(p^{k})p^{k/2}p^{-k}=\varphi(p^{k})p^{-k/2}. Summing the shells gives Equation (16.9). Only finitely many terms are nonzero, those with p^m<Y.

Summed over the primes, the local terms are the familiar prime sum,

\sum_p\log p\sum_{m\ge1}p^{-m/2}\bigl(\varphi(p^m)+\varphi(p^{-m})\bigr)=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}\bigl(\varphi(n)+\varphi(1/n)\bigr),
(16.10)

because \Lambda(p^m)=\log p. The primes p>Y contribute nothing to it, which is the same vanishing that killed the orbital slices of chapter Cutting the kernel along the primes, now seen in the formula. The factor \log p in front is the length of the circle of chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces: in the source’s general statement it appears as \log q_v/\mu_v(\mathcal O_v^\times), the ratio that turns any Haar measure into the canonical measure on \QQ_p^\times, in which the annulus 1\le\lvert x\rvert<T has volume \log T+O(1) [1, Remark B.4.4.2, p. 620].

At the real place the integral is over \RR^\times with \dd y/\lvert y\rvert. For a function of the norm the negative half-line contributes \varphi(t)t^{1/2}/(1+t) at y=-t, so

\frac12\int_{\RR^\times}\frac{\varphi(\lvert y\rvert)\lvert y\rvert^{1/2}}{\lvert1-y\rvert}\frac{\dd y}{\lvert y\rvert}=\frac12\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac1{\lvert1-t\rvert}+\frac1{1+t}\Bigr)\frac{\dd t}{t},
(16.11)

the term already found in Equation (16.5). The constants need care, because the source states them for a general number field with its own measures, and because Weil’s principal value at infinity carries constants \log2\pi+\gamma_{\mathrm E} when \varphi(1)\ne0. We checked three things. The source’s Theorem B.4.4.7 has the real place with coefficient 1/M_v=\tfrac12 and the measure \mu_v=\dd y/\lvert y\rvert, whose canonical normalization is \mu_v/2 [1, Remark B.4.4.2, p. 620, and Theorem B.4.4.7, p. 623], which matches the \tfrac12 of the Trace Formula. Weil’s principal value at the real place is defined through the Fourier transform of \log\lvert x\rvert, and its constant terms all multiply f(0), where f(x)=\varphi(1+x)\lvert1+x\rvert^{-1/2}, so f(0)=\varphi(1)=0 removes them and leaves the integral Equation (16.11) [1, (B.4.3.13), p. 619, and (B.4.4.2), p. 620]. Finally, numerically, Equation (16.11) agrees with the Gamma-function form of the archimedean term,

\frac12\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac1{\lvert1-t\rvert}+\frac1{1+t}\Bigr)\frac{\dd t}{t}=-\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}M\varphi(ir)\,\Re\frac{\Gamma'}{\Gamma}\Bigl(\frac14+\frac{ir}2\Bigr)\dd r\qquad(\varphi(1)=0,\ \varphi\text{ real}),
(16.12)

to ten digits for both test functions of section Both sides in numbers: 0.4404763838 on both sides for the first, and 0.0412165516 for the second.

16.7The Trace Formula over Q#

Everything is now in place, and the main result of Part III over \QQ follows by adding up.

Theorem 16.6

For every test function vanishing at 1 and every strip half-width a>0, Weil’s prime sum plus the archimedean term equals the two pole terms minus the zeros in the strip

[1, Theorem 12.5.1.1, p. 519; §1.4.1, p. 28]
Statement

Let \varphi be smooth with compact support in \RR_{>0} and \varphi(1)=0, and let a>0. Then

\frac12\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac1{\lvert1-t\rvert}+\frac1{1+t}\Bigr)\frac{\dd t}{t}+\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}\bigl(\varphi(n)+\varphi(1/n)\bigr)=M\varphi(\tfrac12)+M\varphi(-\tfrac12)-\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,M\varphi\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr),
(16.13)

where the last sum runs over the nontrivial zeros \rho=\beta+i\gamma of \zeta in the open strip, counted with multiplicity, and converges absolutely.

In plain terms

Weigh the prime powers and their reciprocals by a test function that vanishes at 1, add a smooth term that comes from the real numbers, and you get two simple numbers from the pole of zeta, minus one number for each zero that lies close to the critical line. How close is up to you: the formula holds for every width of the strip, and the zeros outside it simply do not appear.

Why it is needed

The left side is the prime side of Weil’s explicit formula, the side that knows every zero, because the explicit formula holds with all zeros on its right. The right side knows only the zeros in the strip. Chapter From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis turns this mismatch into the hypothesis.

Idea

Compute one diagonal mass two ways inside the coarse space W_a. Spectrally it is minus the zeros in the strip (chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see). Geometrically, the sieve leaves only the places of S (chapter Cutting the kernel along the primes), the S-local trace is a sum of fixed-point weights computed by Fourier analysis on \AA_S (Theorem 16.4), and two linear conditions on theta sums subtract the pole terms.

Proof

Suppose first that \operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset(1,Y), and put S=\{\infty\}\cup\{p\le Y\}. Step 6 removes this assumption.

Step 1, reduction. By chapter Cutting the kernel along the primes, the geometric kernel is k_S+\sum_{p>Y}k_p with \int k_p(x,x)\,\dd x/x=0 for every p>Y (Theorem 15.7), and the geometric diagonal mass is minus the spectral trace of chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see (Theorem 15.3). This is Equation (16.1) [1, proof of Theorem 12.5.1.1, p. 520, using Theorems 11.3.2.1 and 10.4.2.8].

Step 2, the S-local trace. By Theorem 16.4 with \varphi(1)=0, the cutoff term vanishes and the S-local trace on all Schwartz-Bruhat functions tends to the sum of the local terms at the places of S.

Step 3, the pole terms. The theta sums are built from functions with the two conditions f(0)=0 and \hat f(0)=0, which over \QQ are g(0)=0 and \int g=0. The source’s proof records that the diagonal mass of k_S is the sum of the local terms minus M\varphi(\tfrac12)+M\varphi(-\tfrac12) (p. 520). In our gloss of section One place first: the trace of a dilation, these are the eigenvalues of the operator on the two functionals the conditions remove.

Step 4, local terms. By Lemma 16.5 and Equation (16.10) the finite places give the prime sum, and by Equation (16.11) the real place gives the archimedean term. Primes p>Y add zeros to the prime sum, so it may be written over all n\ge2.

Step 5, assembly. Steps 2 to 4 say that the left side of Equation (16.1) is the left side of Equation (16.13) minus the two pole terms. Setting this equal to minus the strip sum and moving the pole terms across gives Equation (16.13).

Step 6, the support. The source performs the trace calculation for \varphi supported in [1+\varepsilon,\infty), extends it to \varphi supported in (0,1-\varepsilon], and then to every \varphi with \varphi(1)=0 by continuity [1, §1.4.6, p. 30]. Over \QQ both extensions can be checked directly, and the following is our account of them. Put \varphi^\vee(t)=\varphi(1/t). The archimedean term and the prime sum of Equation (16.13) do not change when \varphi is replaced by \varphi^\vee, the two pole terms trade places because M\varphi^\vee(z)=M\varphi(-z), and the zero sum is unchanged because M\varphi^\vee(\rho-\tfrac12)=M\varphi\bigl((1-\rho)-\tfrac12\bigr) and \rho\mapsto1-\rho permutes the zeros in the strip with their multiplicities (chapter Zeta on the whole plane). So the formula for \varphi supported in (0,1) follows from the formula for \varphi^\vee. For a general \varphi with \varphi(1)=0, let \psi_\varepsilon(t)=\psi(\log t/\varepsilon) with \psi smooth, equal to 1 near 0, and supported in (-1,1). Then \varphi(1-\psi_\varepsilon) is a sum of a function supported in (1,\infty) and one supported in (0,1), and every term of the formula for \varphi\psi_\varepsilon tends to 0 as \varepsilon\to0: no prime power lies in its support once \varepsilon<\log2, the archimedean term is at most a constant times \varepsilon because \lvert\varphi(t)\rvert\le C\lvert\log t\rvert near 1, the pole terms are O(\varepsilon^2), and in u=\log t two integrations by parts give \lvert M(\varphi\psi_\varepsilon)(\rho-\tfrac12)\rvert\le C\min(\varepsilon^2,\lvert\gamma\rvert^{-2}), whose sum over the zeros is O(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)) by the count of chapter The zeros and the hypothesis. Absolute convergence of the strip sum is the source’s Lemma B.4.4.9 (p. 624); over \QQ it follows from \lvert M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12)\rvert\le C_k(1+\lvert\gamma\rvert)^{-k} (integration by parts in u=\log t, uniformly for \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert\le\tfrac12) and the count N(T)=O(T\log T) of chapter The zeros and the hypothesis.

Example

For Y=8 and \varphi(e^u)=u(1+u)\operatorname{bump}(u/\log8) with \operatorname{bump}(x)=e^{-1/(1-x^2)} on \lvert x\rvert<1, the prime powers in the support are 2,3,4,5,7, the left side is 0.4404763838+1.0652276403=1.5057040241, the pole terms are 1.0852426053+0.4149972171=1.5002398224, and the zero sum is -0.0054642016, so the right side is 1.5057040241. Section Both sides in numbers gives the details and says what this check does and does not show.

Used in
  • From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis: the endgame feeds a holomorphic family of test functions into Equation (16.13), and the shorter route subtracts it from Weil’s formula.
  • Section Beside Weil’s explicit formula: the side-by-side comparison with chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion.

There is no Lean block here: the formalization behind this page belongs to the other route, and the source of this route is the monograph alone.

16.8The general statement#

The source states the Trace Formula for every number field and every test function on the idele class group, all characters at once.

Theorem 16.7 Trace Formula on the idele class group of a number field [1, Theorem 12.5.1.1, p. 519]

Let F be a number field and \varphi a smooth compactly supported function on the idele class group C_F with \varphi(C_F^1)=0. Then

\begin{aligned} &\sum_{v\ \mathrm{real}}\frac12\int'_{F_v^\times}\frac{\varphi(y)\lvert y\rvert_v^{1/2}}{\lvert1-y\rvert_v}\,\dd\mu_v(y)+\sum_{v\ \mathrm{complex}}\frac1{2\pi}\int'_{F_v^\times}\frac{\varphi(y)\lvert y\rvert_v^{1/2}}{\lvert1-y\rvert_v}\,\dd\mu_v(y)+\sum_{v\ \mathrm{finite}}\frac{\log q_v}{\mu_v(\mathcal O_v^\times)}\int'_{F_v^\times}\frac{\varphi(y)\lvert y\rvert_v^{1/2}}{\lvert1-y\rvert_v}\,\dd\mu_v(y)\\ &\qquad=M\varphi(\lvert\cdot\rvert^{1/2})+M\varphi(\lvert\cdot\rvert^{-1/2})-\sum_{c}m_c\,M\varphi(c\,\lvert\cdot\rvert^{-1/2}), \end{aligned}

where M\varphi(c)=\int_{C_F}\varphi\,c\,\dd\bar\mu for a quasi-character c of C_F, and the last sum runs over the zeros c of the Hecke L-functions of F in the interior of the strip \Re c\in\tfrac12+[-a,a], with multiplicity m_c.

The dictionary to Equation (16.13) is short. Over \QQ there is one real place and no complex place, the finite places are the primes with q_v=p, and with \mu_p(\ZZ_p^\times)=1 the finite term is Equation (16.9). A test function on C_\QQ\cong\RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times that is invariant under \hat\ZZ^\times is a function of t=\lvert y\rvert, the condition \varphi(C_\QQ^1)=0 is \varphi(1)=0, and only the trivial character of \hat\ZZ^\times has nonzero Mellin transform against it, so the zeros c are \lvert\cdot\rvert^{\rho} for the zeros \rho of \zeta and M\varphi(c\lvert\cdot\rvert^{-1/2})=M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) once \hat\ZZ^\times has volume 1. The source writes N(c) for the multiplicity and g_v for the variable, and states the strip as \sigma(c)\in\tfrac12+I with I=[-\alpha,\alpha] in Chapter 12 and [-a,a] in Chapter 1 [1, pp. 28, 519]. Test functions that transform by a character \bar\chi of C_F^1 pick out the zeros of L(s,\chi), and the finite term becomes \log q_v\sum_{m\ge1}q_v^{-m/2}\bigl(\chi(\pi_v^m)\varphi(q_v^m)+\bar\chi(\pi_v^m)\varphi(q_v^{-m})\bigr) [1, §1.4.1, p. 28], which is the form used in chapter From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis for general L-functions.

16.9Both sides in numbers#

A formula of this kind can be tested, and the test shows something real, but less than the theorem. Take the bump \operatorname{bump}(x)=e^{-1/(1-x^2)} for \lvert x\rvert<1 and 0 otherwise, as in chapter Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions, and \varphi(t)=u(1+u)\operatorname{bump}(u/\log Y) with u=\log t. This is smooth, supported in (1/Y,Y), vanishes at t=1, and is not symmetric under t\mapsto1/t, so both \varphi(n) and \varphi(1/n) enter. We computed every term of Equation (16.13) for Y=8 and for Y=2: the integrals by Gauss-Legendre quadrature with the interval split at t=1, and the zero sum from the first 1,500 zeros of \zeta, whose ordinates were computed with mpmath and checked against zetazero at five indices.

For Y=8 the prime terms are, at n=2,3,4,5,7,

0.1529009,\quad0.3824281,\quad0.2201944,\quad0.3079172,\quad0.0017869,

from the values \varphi(2)=0.3810122 and \varphi(\tfrac12)=-0.0690517, \varphi(3)=0.5758691 and \varphi(\tfrac13)=0.0270597, and so on. Their sum is 1.0652276403, the archimedean term Equation (16.11) is 0.4404763838, and the left side is 1.5057040241. On the right, M\varphi(\tfrac12)=1.0852426053 and M\varphi(-\tfrac12)=0.4149972171. The zero sum, with each pair \pm\gamma contributing 2\Re M\varphi(i\gamma), settles quickly:

zeros used zero sum left side minus right side
1 pair -0.0062873666 -8.2\times10^{-4}
10 pairs -0.0054637958 4.1\times10^{-7}
100 pairs -0.0054642018 -1.3\times10^{-10}
500 pairs -0.0054642016 below 10^{-12}
1,500 pairs -0.0054642016 below 10^{-12}

For Y=2 there is no prime term, as in section One place first: the trace of a dilation, and Equation (16.6) reads 0.0412165516=0.0356193861+0.0120833266-0.0064861611, with a difference of 10^{-15} at 1,500 pairs. The zero sum converges fast because \varphi is smooth, so M\varphi(i\gamma) decays faster than any power of \gamma.

What this shows is that the two sides agree for these test functions when the zero side is evaluated with the first 1,500 zeros. All of these zeros lie on the critical line, as every computed zero does, so every one of them is inside the strip for every a>0, and the computation cannot tell Equation (16.13) apart from Weil’s explicit formula, which sums over all zeros. What the theorem adds is exactly what no computation of this kind can see: the identity holds for every admissible \varphi, and with the zero sum restricted to the strip \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a for every a>0, whatever zeros there are, including zeros far beyond any computed height. The content of the theorem is a statement about zeros that no one has computed.

16.10Beside Weil’s explicit formula#

Chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion proved Weil’s explicit formula Theorem 8.5 in the normalization of Bombieri, with a test function f on (0,\infty), the transform \mathcal Mf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(x)x^s\,\dd x/x, and the local terms W_p and W_\infty of Definition 8.3. This part centers everything at s=\tfrac12, and the conversion between the two is exact. Set

\varphi(t)=t^{1/2}f(t),\qquad\text{so that}\qquad M\varphi(z)=\mathcal Mf\bigl(z+\tfrac12\bigr),
(16.14)

and the zeros, poles, and local terms translate one by one. A zero \rho gives \mathcal Mf(\rho)=M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12). The poles give \mathcal Mf(0)+\mathcal Mf(1)=M\varphi(-\tfrac12)+M\varphi(\tfrac12). At a prime, W_p(f)=\log p\sum_{k\ge1}\bigl(f(p^k)+p^{-k}f(p^{-k})\bigr)=\log p\sum_{k\ge1}p^{-k/2}\bigl(\varphi(p^k)+\varphi(p^{-k})\bigr), which is Equation (16.9). At infinity, \varphi(1)=f(1), and when this vanishes

W_\infty(f)=\int_1^\infty\Bigl(f(x)+\frac{f(1/x)}{x}\Bigr)\frac{\dd x}{x-x^{-1}}=\frac12\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac1{\lvert1-t\rvert}+\frac1{1+t}\Bigr)\frac{\dd t}{t},
(16.15)

as one sees by splitting the right side at t=1. Since \varphi(t)t^{1/2}/t=f(t), the right side is \int_1^\infty f(t)\,\frac{t\,\dd t}{t^2-1}+\int_0^1f(t)\,\frac{\dd t}{1-t^2}. The first piece is \int_1^\infty f(x)\,\dd x/(x-x^{-1}), and the substitution t=1/x turns the second into \int_1^\infty f(1/x)\,\dd x/(x^2-1)=\int_1^\infty x^{-1}f(1/x)\,\dd x/(x-x^{-1}). The constant (\log4\pi+\gamma_{\mathrm E})f(1) and the subtraction 2x^{-1}f(1) of Equation (8.3) vanish with f(1). With Equation (16.14), Weil’s formula \sum_\rho\mathcal Mf(\rho)=\mathcal Mf(0)+\mathcal Mf(1)-\sum_pW_p(f)-W_\infty(f) becomes, for \varphi(1)=0,

\frac12\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,t^{1/2}\Bigl(\frac1{\lvert1-t\rvert}+\frac1{1+t}\Bigr)\frac{\dd t}{t}+\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}\bigl(\varphi(n)+\varphi(1/n)\bigr)=M\varphi(\tfrac12)+M\varphi(-\tfrac12)-\sum_{\text{all }\rho}m_\rho\,M\varphi\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr).
(16.16)

This is also the source’s idelic form of the explicit formula, Theorem B.4.4.7, specialized to \QQ [1, p. 623] [35]. The numbers of section Both sides in numbers check Equation (16.16) as much as they check Equation (16.13), and the Gamma form Equation (16.12) is W_\infty(f) written through the factor \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2) from which chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion derives it.

Side by side, the two formulas are:

Weil’s explicit formula Equation (16.16) Trace Formula Equation (16.13)
test functions every \varphi in C_c^\infty(\RR_{>0}) (with extra constants if \varphi(1)\ne0) \varphi(1)=0
archimedean term \tfrac12\int\varphi\,t^{1/2}\bigl(\lvert1-t\rvert^{-1}+(1+t)^{-1}\bigr)\dd t/t the same
prime side \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2}(\varphi(n)+\varphi(1/n)) the same
pole terms M\varphi(\tfrac12)+M\varphi(-\tfrac12) the same
zero side every nontrivial zero only the zeros with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a, for any a>0
where the zeros come from contour shift past every pole of \zeta'/\zeta point evaluations that are continuous on W_a
proved by complex analysis of \zeta traces on theta sums in a coarse topology

The left sides agree term for term. The source makes the same observation: the side made of places and poles is identical to that of the explicit formula, while the side made of zeros is not [1, p. 36]. Subtracting one formula from the other leaves the sum of M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) over the zeros outside the strip, set equal to zero, for every \varphi with \varphi(1)=0. Chapter From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis shows that this forces the set of such zeros to be empty.

A common misreading

The Trace Formula is not the explicit formula with some terms dropped by hand. Both identities are true at once, for the same \varphi and the same left side. If a zero \rho_0 with \lvert\beta_0-\tfrac12\rvert\ge a existed, Equation (16.16) would contain its term and Equation (16.13) would not, and the only way both could hold for every admissible \varphi is that the terms of all such zeros cancel. The next chapter shows they cannot.

16.11What changes in general#

For a number field F the S-local computation runs on \AA_{F,S}=\prod_{v\in S}F_v, and three things change. The set S must contain the archimedean places, the places that ramify over \QQ, the places where the character ramifies, and enough places that the ring of S-integers has trivial class group, \mathrm{Pic}(\mathcal O_{F,S})=1, so that every idele class has a representative that is a unit at every place outside S, and a test function invariant under those units is a function on the S-idele class group J_{F,S} [1, Theorem 12.4.1.1 and proof of Theorem 12.5.1.1, pp. 514, 520]. The archimedean places come in two kinds: a real place contributes with the factor \tfrac12 as over \QQ, and a complex place with \frac1{2\pi}, where 2\pi is the volume of the unit circle of \CC^\times in its measure, and the fixed point of a dilation of \CC has the weight 1/\lvert1-y\rvert_v with \lvert\cdot\rvert_v the square of the usual absolute value. At a finite place the local term is \log q_v/\mu_v(\mathcal O_v^\times) times the local integral, and for a test function of weight \bar\chi it is \log q_v\sum_{m\ge1}q_v^{-m/2}\bigl(\chi(\pi_v^m)\varphi(q_v^m)+\bar\chi(\pi_v^m)\varphi(q_v^{-m})\bigr). The pole terms appear only for the isotype of the trivial character on C_F^1 [1, §1.4.1, p. 28], and the normalization of the global Mellin transform gives C_F^1 volume 1, which is how the source’s Theorem B.4.4.7 divides by \mu_1(C_F^1) (p. 623). The weight is \tfrac12 for the same reason in every case: \lvert x\rvert_{F,S}\,\dd\mu_S is a constant times the additive measure \dd\nu_S, and no other power is [1, p. 16].

Symbol What it is Kind Where it lives

\omega an S-unit \pm\prod_{p\le Y}p^{e_p} rational number Definition 16.1
J_S S-idele class group, \cong\RR_{>0}\times\prod_{p\le Y}\ZZ_p^\times locally compact group Definition 16.1

Recap
  • Chapter Cutting the kernel along the primes reduced the geometric side to the S-local diagonal mass Equation (16.1), with S the real place and the primes up to Y.
  • On one place the trace of a dilation, cut off in space and frequency, is the fixed-point weight \lvert y\rvert/\lvert1-y\rvert (Proposition 16.3). Averaging over \pm1 gives the archimedean term with its \tfrac12 and its 1/(1+t), and the two conditions on theta sums subtract the pole terms.
  • On all of S, Connes’s computation Theorem 16.4 turns the trace into the volume \log(RR')-\log\lvert w\rvert_S and splits it into Weil’s local terms, place by place.
  • The weight \tfrac12 is the one power for which \lvert x\rvert^{2w}\,\dd\mu_S is the additive measure, which is the source’s explanation of the \tfrac12 in the hypothesis (section Why the weight is one half).
  • At a prime the local term is \log p\sum_{m\ge1}p^{-m/2}(\varphi(p^m)+\varphi(p^{-m})) (Lemma 16.5), and the archimedean constants agree with the source’s Theorem B.4.4.7 and with the Gamma form.
  • The Trace Formula over \QQ Theorem 16.6 has Weil’s left side and only the zeros of the strip on the right. It checks to better than 10^{-12} against 1,500 zeros, and its content lies beyond any such check. Chapter From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis uses the difference from Equation (16.16).
