Chapter 17

From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis

After this chapter you can derive the Riemann Hypothesis from the Trace Formula in two ways, say why Weil’s positivity is never used, explain in what sense the hypothesis becomes a statement about topology, and retrace Route M as one chain from the adeles to the end.

Builds on 16. The local trace and the Trace Formula

In plain terms

Feed the Trace Formula a family of test functions that turns its prime side into the logarithmic derivative of zeta. That function has a pole at every zero of zeta, while the other side of the formula only has poles at the zeros inside the strip. A zero outside the strip would be a pole with nowhere to come from, so there is none, and since the strip can be as thin as we like, every zero lies on the critical line.

Chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula proved an identity whose left side is Weil’s complete prime sum and whose right side counts only the zeros with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a. This chapter draws the consequence. The source does it in its introduction and in a letter to P. Sarnak, with a holomorphic family of test functions, a mollifier, and Montel’s theorem [1, §§1.4.2 to 1.4.5, pp. 28 to 30, and §§1.8.4.2 to 1.8.5.1, pp. 53 to 55]. We give that argument with each limit named and located, in a form over \QQ in which every limit converges without passing to a subsequence. Then we give a shorter route of our own, which subtracts the Trace Formula from Weil’s explicit formula and needs neither the prime sum nor the archimedean term. After the proof come three things the source says about it: that positivity is never used, that the hypothesis appears as a topological phenomenon, and that the method does not reach function fields, where chapters The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields and Stepanov's proof proved the hypothesis by a different mechanism. The chapter ends with Route M on one page.

17.1The family that turns primes into a logarithmic derivative#

The prime side of the Trace Formula is \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2}\bigl(\varphi(n)+\varphi(1/n)\bigr). Chapter Euler's product: primes inside one function showed that \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-s}=-\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s) for \Re s>1, so a test function that equals t^{-z} on the integers n\ge2 and vanishes on their reciprocals turns the prime side into -\zeta'/\zeta(z+\tfrac12), a function with a pole at every zero of \zeta. The source’s family does exactly this [1, §1.4.2, p. 28].

Definition 17.1 The holomorphic family

For z\in\CC let \varphi_z(t)=t^{-z} for t>1, \varphi_z(t)=0 for 0<t<1, and \varphi_z(1)=\tfrac12. It is a family of functions on \RR_{>0} that depends holomorphically on z at each fixed t. It is not a test function in the sense of chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula: it jumps at t=1, its value there is not 0, and it does not have compact support.

Its Mellin transform is a single pole. For \Re z>\Re w,

M\varphi_z(w)=\int_1^\infty t^{w-z}\,\frac{\dd t}{t}=\frac1{z-w}.
(17.1)

So the pole terms of the Trace Formula become M\varphi_z(\tfrac12)+M\varphi_z(-\tfrac12)=\frac1{z-1/2}+\frac1{z+1/2}, a zero \rho contributes \frac1{z-(\rho-1/2)}, and the prime side becomes \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2-z}=-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(z+\tfrac12) for \Re z>\tfrac12. If Equation (16.13) could be applied to \varphi_z as it stands, it would read

(\text{archimedean term})-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}\bigl(z+\tfrac12\bigr)=\frac1{z-\frac12}+\frac1{z+\frac12}-\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}\frac{m_\rho}{z-(\rho-\frac12)},
(17.2)

with an archimedean term that is holomorphic in a half-plane. The left side has a pole at z=\rho-\tfrac12 for every zero \rho, with residue -m_\rho, because -\zeta'/\zeta has residue -m at a zero of order m. The right side has poles only at the zeros in the strip. A zero with \beta-\tfrac12>a would put a pole on the left at a point where the right side is holomorphic. That is the whole idea, and the rest of this section and the next make it a proof by replacing \varphi_z with honest test functions and controlling the limits.

The same equation with the sum over all zeros is the classical partial-fraction expansion of -\zeta'/\zeta that comes from Hadamard’s product for \xi (chapter The zeros and the hypothesis), and in that form it says nothing about where the zeros are. Every pole on the left is matched by a term on the right. The Trace Formula breaks the matching by removing the terms of the zeros outside the strip from the right side while leaving the left side, built from primes, untouched.

17.2The source’s argument, limit by limit#

The source makes Equation (17.2) honest in eight steps, tied to the numbered paragraphs of its introduction [1, pp. 28 to 30]. We follow them for \QQ and the trivial character, writing \varphi for a function of the norm. Step 2 contains a bound that fails as stated; the warning after the list says what goes wrong, and Theorem 17.2 gives a version over \QQ that does not need it.

  1. Smoothed truncations (§1.4.2, pp. 28 to 29). Let J_\varepsilon be a mollifier on \RR_{>0} (the source’s \rho_\varepsilon; on this page \rho is a zero) and h a smooth bump with values in [0,1] supported in (1,\infty), and put \varphi_{h,\varepsilon,z}=h\cdot(J_\varepsilon*\varphi_z). Each \varphi_{h,\varepsilon,z} is smooth, compactly supported in (1,\infty), so it vanishes at 1, and it is a legitimate test function for Theorem 16.6. As \varepsilon\to0 and h increases to \mathbf 1_{(1,\infty)}, \varphi_{h,\varepsilon,z}(t)\to\varphi_z(t) for every t\ne1.
  2. Archimedean term, by Montel’s theorem (§1.4.3, p. 29). Fix a compact set K in the half-plane \Re z>a whose interior meets \Re z>1. The archimedean integrals are holomorphic in z, and the source asserts that they are bounded on K by one constant independent of h and \varepsilon. Granting that, by Montel’s theorem a sequence of (\varepsilon,h) can be extracted along which they converge uniformly on compact discs inside K, and the limit is holomorphic [15, Ch. 8].
  3. Zero sum (§1.4.3, p. 29, by the same reasoning as step 2). The sums \sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho M\varphi_{h,\varepsilon,z}(\rho-\tfrac12) converge to a function holomorphic for z in the interior of K off the strip. Each term tends to 1/(z-(\rho-\tfrac12)) by Equation (17.1), which is holomorphic in \Re z>a because \Re(\rho-\tfrac12)<a.
  4. Prime sum (§1.4.4, p. 29). Since \varphi_{h,\varepsilon,z} vanishes on (0,1], all the terms \varphi(1/n) are 0, and \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2}\varphi_{h,\varepsilon,z}(n) tends to \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2-z}=-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(z+\tfrac12) uniformly on compact subsets of \Re z>1. (The source writes the limit as L_f'/L_f; for \zeta the prime sum is -\zeta'/\zeta, and we use that sign throughout.)
  5. Assembly (§1.4.5, p. 29). On the interior of K, -\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(z+\tfrac12) equals \frac1{z-1/2}+\frac1{z+1/2} minus a function holomorphic on \Re z>a minus a function holomorphic on the interior of K. The source singles this out as the main consequence of the Trace Formula, from which everything else follows.
  6. Continuation (p. 30). Since K was any compact set of this kind, -\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(z+\tfrac12)-\frac1{z-1/2}-\frac1{z+1/2} is holomorphic on \Re z>a, first on \Re z>1 and then by analytic continuation on all of \Re z>a. So \zeta'/\zeta(s) has no pole in \Re s>\tfrac12+a other than s=1.
  7. Shrinking the strip (p. 30). The half-width a>0 is arbitrary, so \zeta'/\zeta(s) is holomorphic on \Re s>\tfrac12 except at s=1, and \zeta has no zero with \Re s>\tfrac12.
  8. Reflection (p. 30). The functional equation \xi(s)=\xi(1-s) of chapter Zeta on the whole plane sends a zero \rho to the zero 1-\rho, so there is no zero with \Re s<\tfrac12 either.

The contradiction at the heart of step 6 can be stated exactly. Suppose \zeta(\rho_0)=0 with \beta_0>\tfrac12, and choose 0<a<\beta_0-\tfrac12. Then z_0=\rho_0-\tfrac12 lies in \Re z>a, and -\zeta'/\zeta(z+\tfrac12) has a pole at z_0 with residue -m_{\rho_0}\ne0. But the Trace Formula with this a expresses the same function near z_0 as a sum of terms that are each holomorphic at z_0: the archimedean limit, the two pole terms at \pm\tfrac12, and the terms m_\rho/(z-(\rho-\tfrac12)) of the zeros in the strip, none of which sits at z_0. The zero \rho_0 is absent from the right side because of the topology of chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see, and present on the left because the left side is Weil’s prime sum, which has a pole at every zero.

A common misreading

The bound in step 2 fails as stated, and this is the one place where we depart from the source. If h increases to \mathbf 1_{(1,\infty)}, the left end 1+\delta of its support tends to 1, and just to the right of that end J_\varepsilon*\varphi_z is close to a number between \tfrac12 and 1, not to 0. The archimedean integral \tfrac12\int\varphi\,t^{1/2}\lvert1-t\rvert^{-1}\,\dd t/t then contains a piece comparable to \int_{1+\delta}^2\dd t/(t-1)=\log(1/\delta), so it is unbounded as \delta\to0. The prime sum and the pole terms stay bounded, so the Trace Formula forces the zero sum to diverge at the same rate with the opposite sign. The growing part comes from t near 1, where t^{-z} is close to 1, so to leading order it does not depend on z, and one could move it from the archimedean term to the zero sum. That rescues Montel’s theorem for the archimedean term, but step 3 then has to show that the renormalized zero sum tends to a function holomorphic on all of \Re z>a, and this is no longer a statement about single terms: the termwise limit \sum m_\rho/(z-(\rho-\tfrac12)) does not converge absolutely, because \sum_\rho1/\lvert\rho\rvert diverges. The source’s text gives no argument for this step. Over \QQ the difficulty disappears with a fixed cutoff: no prime power lies strictly between 1 and 2, so the test functions can vanish on (0,\tfrac32] for good without changing the prime side, and then every limit converges outright. That is the version we prove next, and section What changes in general notes that the same choice works over every number field.

Theorem 17.2

Every nontrivial zero of \zeta has real part one half

[1, §§1.4.2 to 1.4.5, pp. 28 to 30]
Statement

Every nontrivial zero \rho=\beta+i\gamma of \zeta has \beta=\tfrac12.

In plain terms

Choose test functions that turn the prime side of the Trace Formula into the logarithmic derivative of zeta. Then the formula expresses that function, which has a pole at every zero, as a sum of pieces whose only poles are at the zeros inside a strip around the critical line. So there are no zeros outside the strip, and the strip can be as thin as we like.

Why it is needed

This is the theorem the whole of Part III is for. Every earlier chapter of the route contributes one ingredient of Equation (16.13), and this chapter only reads it off.

Idea

Use the family h_0(t)\,t^{-z}, where h_0 is 0 near 1 and 1 from t=2 on. Since no prime power lies in (1,2), the prime side is exactly the Dirichlet series of -\zeta'/\zeta(z+\tfrac12), and every other term converges to an explicit function whose poles we can list. The identity then continues analytically from \Re z>\tfrac12 to \Re z>a, where the two sides have different poles unless no zero lies to the right of the strip.

Proof

Setup (our choice over \QQ). Fix a fixed cutoff h_0, smooth on \RR_{>0} with h_0=0 on (0,\tfrac32] and h_0=1 on [2,\infty), and \kappa smooth with \kappa=1 on (0,1] and \kappa=0 on [2,\infty). Put b(u)=\frac{\dd}{\dd u}h_0(e^u), a smooth function supported in [\log\tfrac32,\log2] with \int_\RR b=1, and

\tilde b(w)=\int_\RR b(u)\,e^{-wu}\,\dd u,\qquad H(w)=\frac{\tilde b(w)}{w}.
(17.3)

\tilde b is entire with \tilde b(0)=1, and integrating by parts k times shows \lvert\tilde b(w)\rvert\le C_{k,B}(1+\lvert\Im w\rvert)^{-k} for \lvert\Re w\rvert\le B. So H is meromorphic on \CC with one simple pole, at w=0, of residue 1, and decays rapidly on vertical strips. For \Re w>0 one integration by parts gives H(w)=\int_1^\infty h_0(t)\,t^{-w}\,\dd t/t. Fix a\in(0,\tfrac12).

Step 1, test functions. For R\ge2 and z\in\CC let \varphi_{R,z}(t)=h_0(t)\,\kappa(t/R)\,t^{-z}. It is smooth with compact support in [\tfrac32,2R]\subset(1,\infty), so \varphi_{R,z}(1)=0, and Theorem 16.6 applies to it; it even satisfies the standing assumption \operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset(1,Y) of chapter Cutting the kernel along the primes with Y=2R+1. It is complex valued, and the Trace Formula holds for complex \varphi because both sides are linear in \varphi and it holds for the real and imaginary parts.

Step 2, prime side. For n\ge2, h_0(n)=1 and \varphi_{R,z}(1/n)=0, so the prime side is \sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2-z}\kappa(n/R). For \Re z>\tfrac12 the series converges absolutely, and by dominated convergence it tends to -\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(z+\tfrac12) as R\to\infty. This is the source’s limit of §1.4.4 without the mollifier.

Step 3, pole terms. M\varphi_{R,z}(\pm\tfrac12)=\int h_0(t)\kappa(t/R)t^{\pm1/2-z}\,\dd t/t tends to H(z\mp\tfrac12) for \Re z>\tfrac12.

Step 4, archimedean term. It tends to

E_\infty(z)=\frac12\int_{3/2}^\infty h_0(t)\,t^{1/2-z}\Bigl(\frac1{t-1}+\frac1{t+1}\Bigr)\frac{\dd t}{t},

which converges absolutely and is holomorphic for \Re z>-\tfrac12, because the integrand vanishes near t=1 and is O(t^{-\Re z-3/2}) at infinity. This replaces the source’s Montel step: with h_0 fixed near t=1 no subsequence is needed.

Step 5, zero sum. Write u=\log t and v=\rho-\tfrac12-z. Then M\varphi_{R,z}(\rho-\tfrac12)=\int G_R(u)e^{vu}\,\dd u with G_R(u)=h_0(e^u)\kappa(e^u/R). For z in a compact set Q\subset\{\Re z>a\} and \rho in the strip, \Re v\le-\delta<0 for some \delta=\delta(Q). Two integrations by parts in u, with no boundary terms since G_R has compact support, give \lvert M\varphi_{R,z}(\rho-\tfrac12)\rvert\le\lvert v\rvert^{-2}\int\lvert G_R''(u)\rvert e^{-\delta u}\,\dd u, where \lvert v\rvert\ge\max(\delta,\lvert\gamma-\Im z\rvert)\ge c_Q(1+\lvert\gamma\rvert), and the last integral is bounded independently of R because G_R'' is bounded uniformly in R and supported in [\log\tfrac32,\log2]\cup[\log R,\log2R]. Each term converges, uniformly on Q: the difference between M\varphi_{R,z}(\rho-\tfrac12) and its limit \int_1^\infty h_0(t)\,t^{v}\,\dd t/t=H(-v) is at most \int_R^\infty t^{-\delta}\,\dd t/t=R^{-\delta}/\delta. Since \sum_\rho m_\rho(1+\lvert\gamma\rvert)^{-2}<\infty by the count N(T)=O(T\log T) of chapter The zeros and the hypothesis, dominated convergence gives, uniformly on Q,

\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,M\varphi_{R,z}\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr)\ \longrightarrow\ Z_a(z)=\sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho\,H\bigl(z-(\rho-\tfrac12)\bigr),

a function holomorphic on \Re z>a, since each term is and the convergence is locally uniform. This is the limit of the zero sum in §1.4.3 of the source.

Step 6, the identity. Letting R\to\infty in Equation (16.13) for \Re z>\tfrac12,

E_\infty(z)-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}\bigl(z+\tfrac12\bigr)=H\bigl(z-\tfrac12\bigr)+H\bigl(z+\tfrac12\bigr)-Z_a(z).
(17.4)

This is the source’s (1.8.5.1) over \QQ.

Step 7, continuation. Put F(z)=-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(z+\tfrac12)-\frac{\tilde b(z-1/2)}{z-1/2}. It is meromorphic on \CC, and the pole of -\zeta'/\zeta(s) at s=1 with residue 1 is canceled at z=\tfrac12 because \tilde b(0)=1. By Equation (17.4), on \Re z>\tfrac12,

F(z)=H\bigl(z+\tfrac12\bigr)-Z_a(z)-E_\infty(z),

and the right side is holomorphic on the connected half-plane \Re z>a, because the only pole of H(z+\tfrac12) is at z=-\tfrac12. By uniqueness of analytic continuation, F is holomorphic on \Re z>a.

Step 8, no zero right of the strip. If \zeta(\rho_0)=0 with \beta_0>\tfrac12+a, then -\zeta'/\zeta(z+\tfrac12) has a pole at z_0=\rho_0-\tfrac12 with residue -m_{\rho_0}\ne0, and \tilde b(z-\tfrac12)/(z-\tfrac12) is holomorphic there since z_0\ne\tfrac12. So F has a pole in \Re z>a, which Step 7 excludes. Hence every zero has \beta\le\tfrac12+a. A zero exactly on the edge, \beta=\tfrac12+a, contributes no term to Z_a and gives a point z_0 on the line \Re z=a, outside the region where Step 7 applies, so this a says nothing about it, but every smaller a excludes it. Since a\in(0,\tfrac12) was arbitrary, \beta\le\tfrac12.

Step 9, reflection. The zeros are symmetric under \rho\mapsto1-\rho by the functional equation (Zeta on the whole plane), so \beta\ge\tfrac12 as well, and \beta=\tfrac12.

Example

The identity Equation (17.4) can be checked with numbers, with the known zeros, all on the line, standing in for the strip. Take h_0(e^u)=S\bigl((u-\log\tfrac32)/\log\tfrac43\bigr) with the smooth step S(x)=e^{-1/x}/(e^{-1/x}+e^{-1/(1-x)}) on (0,1). At z=2, -\zeta'/\zeta(\tfrac52)=0.2887406856, while H(\tfrac32)=0.29319455, H(\tfrac52)=0.10201852, and E_\infty(2)=0.12741720, so the zero sum must be -0.0209448, and the first 500 pairs of zeros give it to 5\times10^{-12}. Rewritten as -\zeta'/\zeta(z+\tfrac12)=H(z-\tfrac12)+H(z+\tfrac12)-Z_a(z)-E_\infty(z), the identity can also be tested where the Dirichlet series diverges and the left side means its continuation. At z=0.25+3i, -\zeta'/\zeta(0.75+3i)=-0.3392087731+0.0433329351\,i, and the right side agrees to 10^{-11} with 500 pairs. At z=0.05+14i, near the first zero at z=14.1347\,i, -\zeta'/\zeta(0.55+14i)=-2.0236013-6.4357089\,i, the right side agrees to 10^{-11}, and the first pair alone already gives -1.93-6.51\,i. (Computed with mpmath and Gauss-Legendre quadrature from the first 1,500 zeros.)

Used in
  • Section Route M in one page: the last link of the chain.

17.3A shorter route: subtract Weil’s formula#

The argument above computes the prime sum, the archimedean term, and the pole terms for a family of test functions, only to watch them cancel against the left side of an identity. Chapter The local trace and the Trace Formula already noted that Weil’s explicit formula Equation (16.16) has the same left side as the Trace Formula, term for term. Subtracting one from the other removes every term built from primes, places, and poles at once, and leaves a statement about the zeros alone. This is our compression of the endgame, suggested by the source’s own plan for its Chapter 13, whose first section is titled “Recollections on the Explicit Formulas” [1, p. 522]. We checked each step, including the convergence of the zero sums and the zeros on the edges of the strip.

Proposition 17.3

For each a>0 the zeros with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert\ge a contribute a Mellin sum of zero to every admissible test function, and therefore there are none

[1, Theorem 12.5.1.1, p. 519; Theorem B.4.4.7, p. 623; Lemma B.4.4.9, p. 624]
Statement

Let a>0 and let Z^{\mathrm{off}}_a be the set of nontrivial zeros \rho of \zeta with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert\ge a. Then:

  1. For every \varphi smooth with compact support in \RR_{>0} and \varphi(1)=0,
\sum_{\rho\in Z^{\mathrm{off}}_a}m_\rho\,M\varphi\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12\bigr)=0,
(17.5)

with the sum absolutely convergent. 2. Z^{\mathrm{off}}_a is empty.

In plain terms

Weil’s formula and the Trace Formula have the same left side, so their right sides are equal. Weil’s right side has every zero, and the Trace Formula’s has only the zeros in the strip, so the zeros outside the strip add up to zero against every test function. A single family of test functions turns that sum into a function with a pole at each such zero, and a function that is identically zero has no poles.

Why it is needed

It isolates the one fact that the new trace formula contributes, a statement about the off-strip zeros alone, and shows that this fact already contains the hypothesis. A reader who has the explicit formula from chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion sees the endgame as one subtraction.

Idea

After subtraction the prime side is gone, so the family need not produce \zeta'/\zeta. It only needs Mellin transforms with a pole, which a test function that is t^{-z} out to infinity provides.

Proof

Step 1, the two formulas. Weil’s explicit formula Equation (16.16) holds for every \varphi in question with the zero sum over all nontrivial zeros, absolutely convergent [1, Theorem B.4.4.7, p. 623]. The Trace Formula Equation (16.13) holds for the same \varphi with the zero sum over the open strip \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a. With the Sobolev degree 0 that the source uses for the endgame, the strip is open and there are no edge terms [1, p. 13]: a zero with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert=a appears in Weil’s sum and not in the Trace Formula, so it belongs to Z^{\mathrm{off}}_a.

Step 2, convergence. Every subsum of the zero sum converges absolutely. The source proves this for any set of zeros [1, Lemma B.4.4.9, p. 624]. Over \QQ it is direct: in u=\log t, M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12)=\int\varphi(e^u)e^{(\rho-1/2)u}\,\dd u, two integrations by parts bound it by C(1+\lvert\gamma\rvert)^{-2} uniformly for 0\le\beta\le1, and \sum_\rho m_\rho(1+\lvert\gamma\rvert)^{-2}<\infty by N(T)=O(T\log T).

Step 3, subtraction. The left sides of the two formulas are identical, so the right sides are equal. The pole terms cancel, and by Step 2 the zero sums can be subtracted term by term, which leaves Equation (17.5). This proves part 1.

Step 4, a family. Take h_0, \kappa, \tilde b, and H as in the proof of Theorem 17.2, and apply Equation (17.5) to \varphi_{R,z}(t)=h_0(t)\kappa(t/R)t^{-z}. For \Re z>\tfrac12 every \rho has \Re\bigl(\rho-\tfrac12-z\bigr)<0, and the integration by parts of Step 5 of that proof bounds \lvert M\varphi_{R,z}(\rho-\tfrac12)\rvert by C(1+\lvert\gamma\rvert)^{-2} uniformly in R. Letting R\to\infty,

\Delta(z)=\sum_{\rho\in Z^{\mathrm{off}}_a}m_\rho\,H\bigl(z-(\rho-\tfrac12)\bigr)=\sum_{\rho\in Z^{\mathrm{off}}_a}m_\rho\,\frac{\tilde b(z-\rho+\frac12)}{z-\rho+\frac12}=0\qquad(\Re z>\tfrac12).

Step 5, continuation. For z in a compact set Q\subset\CC, the real parts of z-\rho+\tfrac12 are bounded, so \lvert\tilde b(z-\rho+\tfrac12)\rvert\le C_Q(1+\lvert\gamma\rvert)^{-2}, and the series for \Delta converges absolutely and uniformly on Q once the finitely many terms with \rho-\tfrac12 in or near Q are set aside. So \Delta is meromorphic on \CC, and its poles are the points \rho-\tfrac12 with \rho\in Z^{\mathrm{off}}_a. At such a point only one term is singular, with residue m_\rho\tilde b(0)=m_\rho\ge1, so the pole is really there. But \Delta=0 on the open set \Re z>\tfrac12, hence on all of \CC minus its poles, which is connected, and a function that is identically zero near a point cannot have a pole there. So Z^{\mathrm{off}}_a is empty, which is part 2.

Step 6, conclusion. Since a>0 is arbitrary, every nontrivial zero has \beta=\tfrac12.

Used in
  • Section Route M in one page, as the alternative last link.

Three remarks place this shortcut. First, it uses less than the source’s argument: no mollifier, no Montel, no limit of the prime sum, no archimedean term, and no separate appeal to the functional equation, because the zeros on both sides of the line are in Z^{\mathrm{off}}_a and Weil’s formula already contains the functional equation. What it uses instead is Weil’s explicit formula for the same test functions, a classical theorem with a separate proof [35], which the source also proves in its own normalization. Second, the two routes are the same mathematics seen from two sides: in the source’s argument the prime sum stands in for “all zeros” through the poles of -\zeta'/\zeta, and in ours Weil’s formula says so outright. Third, any family whose Mellin transforms have a pole that can be moved to an arbitrary point would serve; we use h_0(t)t^{-z} because it shows the poles directly through Equation (17.3) and is already at hand from Theorem 17.2.

17.4Why positivity is never used#

Chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion reduced the hypothesis to an inequality: by Weil’s criterion Theorem 8.9, the hypothesis holds exactly when W(f*\tilde f)\ge0 for every test function f. Route A, in Part IV, is built on an inequality: its note speaks of the positivity of W on particular test functions, and its formal proof establishes a one-sided upper bound on a smoothed sum over primes (The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros). Route M proves no inequality at all, and the source stresses in a paragraph of its own that Weil’s criterion is not used [1, §1.4.6, p. 30], and explains elsewhere why it could not be [1, p. 35]. The body of the draft is not consistent with its introduction on this point: a later subsection on multiplicities, whose footnote says it needs correcting, calls the main theorem on zeros a consequence of the Trace Formula “combined with the Positivity Criterion” [1, §14.1.2, p. 528], and p. 533 says the same. This page follows the introduction, whose endgame is the one given in this chapter and uses no positivity.

The reason is structural, and over \QQ it is one line. The Trace Formula needs \varphi(1)=0. Weil’s criterion is about the functions f*\tilde f, which in chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion satisfy (f*\tilde f)(x)=\int_0^\infty f(xy)\overline{f(y)}\,\dd y. Translated to this part’s normalization by Equation (16.14), the function is \varphi(t)=t^{1/2}(f*\tilde f)(t), and

\varphi(1)=(f*\tilde f)(1)=\int_0^\infty\lvert f(y)\rvert^2\,\dd y,

which is positive unless f=0. So the only function of Weil’s form to which the Trace Formula applies is 0 [1, p. 35]. The source adds that the condition \varphi(C_F^1)=0 cannot be removed before the hypothesis is proved: the Trace Formula does hold for every test function once all zeros are known to be on the line, but only a posteriori [1, p. 30].

The contrast with chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion is between a quadratic form and a linear identity. Weil’s criterion asks for a sign of \sum_\rho M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) on a cone of test functions, and an off-line zero would show up as a negative value. The Trace Formula asks for nothing of the sort: it is an equality, and an off-line zero would show up as a term present in one formula and absent from another. The source compares the avoidance of positivity to Deligne’s proof of the Weil conjectures, which went through families instead of the positivity of an intersection pairing [1, pp. 30, 35]. In the same comparison, the input that plays the role of Deligne’s non-vanishing on the edge of the critical strip is the non-vanishing of \zeta on \Re s=1 from chapter The zeros and the hypothesis, which the route uses to pass from S-local to global statements [1, §1.4.7, pp. 30 to 31].

17.5The hypothesis as a statement about topology#

The source titles one paragraph of its introduction “GRH is a topological phenomenon” [1, §1.4.8, p. 31]. The proof above shows what this means. Two trace formulas have the same geometric side, because in each of the topologies involved the geometric side comes out as Weil’s sum over the places. They differ in their spectral sides, because the spectral side is the trace on functions modulo theta sums, and which zeros survive in that quotient depends on which point evaluations M\phi\mapsto M\phi(\rho-\tfrac12) are continuous. In a fine topology, the one in which R. Meyer had earlier computed the trace by infinite Euler products, every evaluation is continuous, every zero survives, and the trace formula is Weil’s explicit formula [1, p. 32]. In the coarse Hilbert space W_a of chapter Choosing the topology: what a strip can see, only the evaluations inside the strip are continuous, and only those zeros survive. The geometric side is the same in both. So the zeros outside the strip have to contribute nothing in the fine topology too, and the two proofs above show that this means there are none.

The source insists on the order of the logic. The topology is not chosen by looking at zeros: the norms with weight \max(t^{2a},t^{-2a}) are chosen by asking what the computation of the geometric side truly needs [1, p. 36], and the orbital bases and the S-local cutoffs have to live in the completed space. The source says that the zeros are never an input to any construction, that they stay passive, and that they are casualties of the topology of the normed space [1, pp. 35 to 36]. The degenerate case a=0, the line itself, no longer leads to a trace formula [1, p. 36], which is why the endgame works with strips of positive width that shrink, and never with the line.

Read this way, the hypothesis is the statement that the coarse topology loses nothing. A zero off the line would be a functional that the fine topology sees and every thin strip does not, and the Trace Formula says that the geometric side cannot tell the two topologies apart. The source compares the shrinking of the strip to Deligne’s tensor-power trick, which enlarges a zero-free region step by step [1, p. 31].

17.6Why the method stops at function fields#

For a curve C over a finite field \FF_q, chapter The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields stated the hypothesis as the bound \lvert N_n-q^n-1\rvert\le2g\,q^{n/2}, and chapter Stepanov's proof proved it by Stepanov’s method: an auxiliary function that vanishes to high order at every rational point, a degree count, and the Frobenius map, which turns the points over \FF_{q^n} into the fixed points of an algebraic map. The source asks whether its own method gives a second proof there, and answers no [1, §14.2, pp. 534 to 536].

The reason is in the Euler product. For a function field the local factors are (1-\lvert k(x)\rvert^{-s})^{-1} over the closed points x of the curve, and every residue field size \lvert k(x)\rvert is a power q^{d} of q. So every reciprocal factor 1-q^{-ds} vanishes at all the points s=2\pi ik/\log q, k\in\ZZ, and the factors share infinitely many zeros. Over \QQ, chapter Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces showed that 1-p^{-s} and 1-p'^{-s} share only s=0 for distinct primes, because the logarithms of primes are linearly independent over \QQ (Theorem 13.12). That fact is what lets the orbital quotients of different primes be cut one at a time without interfering. Over a function field the overlaps would have to be corrected by test functions whose Mellin transforms vanish to unbounded order at a point, and the only such holomorphic function is 0. The source concludes that the topology which makes the computation possible there is not normable, and that the resulting trace formula would give back Weil’s explicit formula and nothing more, as R. Meyer’s representation-theoretic proof of the explicit formula does [1, p. 535].

The geometry of the plane changes too. Over a function field the Mellin variable lives on q^{-s}, so the vertical strips of this route become annuli of finite area, and the components of the space of quasi-characters are not simply connected [1, p. 33]. The source’s broader reasons for “yes” over number fields and “no” over function fields are the archimedean place, which gives the function spaces their analysis, the solenoid quotients built from it, and the linear independence of the \log p [1, pp. 33 to 35].

So the two settings trade places. For curves over \FF_q the hypothesis has a proof, by Weil and in Stepanov’s elementary form, whose engine is Frobenius, an operator the integers lack, as chapter Stepanov's proof emphasized at its end. Over \QQ, Route M gets its proof from the very features a function field lacks: an archimedean place and primes whose logarithms do not line up. Route A, in Part IV, takes the other path and looks for a substitute for Stepanov’s mechanism over \ZZ.

17.7What changes in general#

For a number field F and a unitary Hecke character \chi the endgame is the same with three changes [1, pp. 28 to 30, 53 to 55]. The test functions transform by \bar\chi on C_F^1, and the family is \chi\cdot(\varphi_{h,\varepsilon,z}\circ\lvert\cdot\rvert_F), so the prime side becomes \sum_v\log q_v\sum_{m\ge1}\chi(\pi_v^m)q_v^{-m/2-mz}, the logarithmic derivative of the finite part L_f(z+\tfrac12,\chi) of the Hecke L-function, up to sign. The fixed cutoff of Theorem 17.2 can replace the source’s family here too, which is our observation: the norm q_v of every prime ideal is at least 2, so no q_v^m lies in (1,2), the prime side is unchanged by h_0, and the archimedean integrals, real and complex, see the test function only where \lvert y\rvert_v\ge\tfrac32, away from the singularity at y=1. The pole terms are present only when \chi is trivial on C_F^1, which the source records with \delta\in\{0,1\} in (1.4.5) and (1.8.5.1). And the reflection uses the functional equation of the completed Hecke L-function from Tate’s thesis [63]. The conclusion is that L(s,\chi) has no zero with \Re s\ne\tfrac12, for every number field and every unitary Hecke character. The source does not normalize characters to be unitary in the strong sense, so for a character with \chi(\tau(t))=t^{ix_0} the point of symmetry on the line sits at s=\tfrac12-ix_0; the line itself is still \Re s=\tfrac12 [1, p. 529]. The analytic inputs beyond the Trace Formula are classical in every case: non-vanishing and polynomial growth of 1/L_f on \Re s=1, the convexity bound, the count of zeros up to height T, and horizontal segments on which 1/L_f grows polynomially [1, pp. 30 to 31].

17.8Route M in one page#

The whole route, for \zeta over \QQ, is a chain of ten links. Each names the chapter where it is explained and the source’s location.

  1. Adeles (The adeles: all completions at once). Every completion of \QQ at once: \RR and the \QQ_p, the adeles \AA and ideles, and the idele class group C_\QQ\cong\RR_{>0}\times\hat\ZZ^\times, on which a function of the norm is a function on \RR_{>0} [1, App. A.1].
  2. Theta sums and zeta (Tate's thesis as theta and zeta: functions modulo theta functions). \Theta_g(t)=\sum_{n\ne0}g(nt) is the adelic theta function of g\otimes\bigotimes_p\mathbf 1_{\ZZ_p}, its symmetry is Poisson summation, and its Mellin transform is 2\zeta(s)Mg(s). Weighted by t^{1/2} and with g(0)=0=\int g, the theta sums V_g=t^{1/2}\Theta_g have Mellin transforms \xi(z+\tfrac12) times entire functions, a function in S_E(\RR_{>0}) is such a sum exactly when the jets of its Mellin transform at the points \rho-\tfrac12 vanish, and convolution by \varphi acts on those jets with eigenvalues M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) [1, pp. 13, 45, Theorem 6.3.2.1].
  3. Primes as circles (Primes as circles: orbital bases and their traces). Deleting the multiples of p from a theta sum multiplies its Mellin transform by 1-p^{-s}, and the quotient is the space of functions on a circle of length \log p, where the trace of convolution is \log p\sum_k\varphi(p^k), which is 0 when p is beyond the support of \varphi. Different primes do not interfere [1, Ch. 7].
  4. The strip topology (Choosing the topology: what a strip can see). In the Hilbert space W_a, evaluation of Mellin transforms is continuous exactly inside the strip \lvert\Re z\rvert<a, so the quotient by the closure of the theta sums keeps only the zeros with \lvert\beta-\tfrac12\rvert<a, and the spectral trace is \sum_{\lvert\beta-1/2\rvert<a}m_\rho M\varphi(\rho-\tfrac12) [1, Ch. 9 and 10].
  5. The kernel and its diagonal (Cutting the kernel along the primes). The kernel \varphi(x/y) splits into spectral and geometric parts, and the diagonal mass of the geometric part is minus the spectral trace [1, §12.1].
  6. The sieve (Cutting the kernel along the primes). Lifted to the ideles, the geometric kernel is cut along the strata “unit at the first k primes”, each slice acts on an orbital quotient, and every slice for p>Y has trace 0. What remains is an S-local kernel [1, Ch. 11].
  7. The S-local trace (The local trace and the Trace Formula). By Connes’s computation, the S-local diagonal mass is the sum of Weil’s local terms at the places of S, with the weight \tfrac12 forced by the match between additive and multiplicative measures [1, Theorem 12.4.1.1, p. 514].
  8. The Trace Formula (The local trace and the Trace Formula). Weil’s prime sum plus the archimedean term equals the pole terms minus the zeros in the strip, for every test function with \varphi(1)=0 and every a>0 [1, Theorem 12.5.1.1, p. 519].
  9. The endgame (From the Trace Formula to the hypothesis). The family h_0(t)t^{-z} turns the prime side into -\zeta'/\zeta(z+\tfrac12), which has a pole at every zero, while the other side has poles only in the strip; or, in our shorter route, subtracting the Trace Formula from Weil’s formula leaves the off-strip zeros summing to zero against every test function, which forces them to be absent [1, pp. 28 to 30].
  10. The conclusion. No zero lies outside any strip of positive width around the critical line, so every nontrivial zero of \zeta has real part \tfrac12, and the same chain proves the hypothesis for every Hecke L-function of every number field.

Classical results enter at four points: Weil’s explicit formula (Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion) for the left side and for the shorter route, the functional equation (Zeta on the whole plane) for the reflection, the count of zeros and the absence of zeros on \Re s=1 (The zeros and the hypothesis) for convergence and for passing from S-local to global, and Montel’s theorem in the source’s form of the endgame.

Recap
  • The family t^{-z}\mathbf 1_{t>1} turns the prime side into -\zeta'/\zeta(z+\tfrac12), with a pole at every zero; the Trace Formula gives the same function poles only at the zeros in the strip (Equation (17.2)).
  • The source’s endgame runs through smoothed truncations, Montel’s theorem, the limit of the prime sum, analytic continuation, a\to0, and the functional equation (pp. 28 to 30). Over \QQ, a truncation that stays fixed near t=1 makes every limit converge outright, and Theorem 17.2 proves the hypothesis.
  • Our shorter route Proposition 17.3 subtracts the Trace Formula from Weil’s explicit formula: the off-strip zeros sum to zero against every test function, and the family h_0(t)t^{-z} shows that this forces them to be absent.
  • Positivity is never used, and cannot be, because Weil’s functions f*\tilde f never vanish at 1. The proof is an identity compared with an identity.
  • The hypothesis appears as a statement about topology: the geometric side cannot tell a thin strip from the whole plane, so the zeros outside every strip are absent.
  • The method does not reach function fields, where the Euler factors share infinitely many zeros, and where chapters The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields and Stepanov's proof proved the hypothesis with Frobenius instead.
  • Route M is the ten-link chain of section Route M in one page. Part IV follows Route A, which rests on a one-sided inequality where Route M uses none.

Part IVRoute two: Stepanov's method over the integers

Chapter 18

Stepanov over the integers: the plan and the map of the formal proof

After this chapter you can state exactly what the second proof of 2026 establishes, say in Stepanov’s terms what its author says the idea is, follow the toy identity of the note’s footnote as far as it can be made rigorous, place every node of the formal proof’s spine with its Lean declaration and its chapter, and tell which of the note’s twenty steps the code contains.

Builds on 10. Stepanov's proof, 8. Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion, 7. What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations

In plain terms

The second proof of 2026 comes as a four-page note and a very large proof checked by a computer. The note says that the argument copies the one that settled the finite-field case, where a cleverly built function vanishes many times at every point being counted, and that the hard part over the whole numbers, making something vanish many times, is done by a chain of about the square root of X transformations between spaces of automorphic forms. This chapter states what was proved, retells the idea in the note’s own words, and draws a map of the formal proof so that the next six chapters can be read as tours of its regions.

Chapter Stepanov's proof ended with a list of what Stepanov’s proof used and the integers lack, and the second item on that list is the one this part of the page is about: over a finite field an auxiliary function could be made to vanish to order p^\mu at every rational point for free, because p-th powers are invisible to derivatives, while over \ZZ every derivation is zero and there is nothing to count multiplicity with (section What the proof used). The proof released by Levent Alpoge with Claude on 2026-11-20 offers a substitute for that missing derivative, and it proves the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalization to all Dirichlet L-functions with it [2]. Its sources are unusual. The note is four pages long and gives the idea in a few sentences, a footnote, and a timeline of twenty steps that its author calls rough, while the formal proof is a Lean 4 tree of 175,187 files with no comments at all [3]. This page’s account of that tree rests on our reading of five regions of it, each unfolded into ordinary mathematics: the assembly and the analytic endgame from Main down to the zero-free statement, the theta-integral assembly and its unitary-group inputs, the theta lifts with the Galois-representation side and the integrality bookkeeping, the cohomological window VWin with base change, and the published inputs. This chapter puts those readings together into a map. It says what the code proves, what the note says the idea is, how far the toy identity of the note’s footnote can be followed, how the formal proof is laid out, which of the note’s steps the code contains, and what chapters The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros to What the proof stands on will and will not unfold.

18.1What the formal proof proves#

Everything the formal proof establishes is stated in one file of twelve lines, Main.lean, and every other file of the tree is there to make those five lines check. The theorems use Mathlib’s definitions of \zeta, of Dirichlet characters, and of their L-functions, together with four propositions written out in a second short file, Statements.lean [3]. Here are both files, verbatim except for their import lines.

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := rhOfAll

theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re : RiemannZetaZerosOnLine := rhOfAll

theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re : DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf := allChi

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re : DirichletLZerosOnLine := claimAll.2.1

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive : PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine := critAll

def RiemannZetaZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

def DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

def DirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

def PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
    ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

Read in ordinary mathematics, with L(s,\chi) the analytic continuation of \sum_n\chi(n)n^{-s} from chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations, the five theorems say the following.

  1. riemannHypothesis is the Riemann Hypothesis in Mathlib’s own definition: every zero s of \zeta that is not one of -2,-4,-6,\dots and is not s=1 has real part \tfrac12. The exclusion of s=1 is there only because Mathlib gives \zeta a value at its pole, and it removes nothing.
  2. riemannZeta_eq_zero_re is the same statement written out in Statements.lean. Main.lean gives the same proof term rhOfAll for both, so the two must agree up to unfolding of definitions.
  3. LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re says that for every modulus N\ge1, every Dirichlet character \chi modulo N, primitive or not, and every s with \Re s>\tfrac12, the value L(s,\chi) is not zero, except at the single point s=1 when \chi is the principal character. This is the half-plane form of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis of Definition 7.8.
  4. LFunction_eq_zero_re says that every zero of every L(s,\chi) in the open strip 0<\Re s<1 has real part \tfrac12. For an imprimitive \chi the extra zeros contributed by the missing Euler factors lie on \Re s=0, outside the strip.
  5. LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive is the same for primitive characters only, a special case of the fourth.

All five rest on the third, which the code also calls UpperTheory.EveryCharacter, and chapter The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros proves the short functional-equation arguments that pass from it to the others.

Theorem 18.1

Every nontrivial zero of \zeta and of every Dirichlet L-function lies on the critical line

[3]
Statement

Every zero of \zeta other than the trivial zeros -2,-4,-6,\dots has real part \tfrac12. For every Dirichlet character \chi modulo N\ge1, L(s,\chi)\ne0 whenever \Re s>\tfrac12, except at s=1 for the principal character, and every zero of L(s,\chi) with 0<\Re s<1 has real part \tfrac12.

In plain terms

The Riemann Hypothesis holds, and so does its generalization to every L-function of a Dirichlet character.

Why it is needed

This is the theorem Part IV explains. Its reach, the zeta function and every Dirichlet L-function, fixes what the rest of the proof has to deliver.

Idea

Show that no L-function of a primitive character has a zero with real part above \tfrac12+9\varepsilon, for every small \varepsilon>0, by bounding from above, on long windows of scales, the smoothed prime sum S(X) of chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations with its main term removed, twisted by the powers of the character and combined. The bound is one-sided: the code proves an upper bound on these sums and never states the positivity of Weil’s functional of which the note speaks. The bound comes from a chain of about \sqrt x theta lifts between definite unitary groups and from a bound on certain Galois cohomology groups. The functional equation then gives the line.

Proof sketch

[3, Main.lean and the spine of section ra-map]

The section The map of the formal proof lays out the chain of declarations from Main.lean down to the three named inputs, and chapters The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros to What the proof stands on take the links in turn. A text search of the tree finds no sorry and no axiom. This repository indexed and searched the tree and did not build it, so whether the five theorems rest only on Lean’s foundations and Mathlib is what a build would certify; chapter What the proof stands on says what a build would add.

In Lean

riemannHypothesis in Main.lean

The five theorems take no hypotheses and are the only statements in Main.lean.

Used in

The endgame The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros derives the five statements from the half-plane statement, and every later chapter of Part IV explains one region of its proof.

The reach of the proof is the zeta function and all Dirichlet L-functions. As our remark, not the code’s, this also gives the hypothesis for the Dedekind zeta function of every abelian number field, because such a function is a product of Dirichlet L-functions, but the code states nothing about number fields or Hecke characters in general. The note goes no further either, and says of the extended hypothesis of Definition 7.11 only “I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too” [2]. Route M of Part III already reaches every Hecke L-function of every number field, so on this page the two proofs share the Riemann Hypothesis and the Dirichlet case, and only the first reaches the extended hypothesis (section What changes in general).

18.2The idea in the author’s words#

The note gives the idea in four sentences and asks the reader to take the Lean code as the full account [2]. We quote them sparingly and set each against chapter Stepanov's proof, because the vocabulary of that chapter, auxiliary function, order of vanishing, degree budget, is the one the note uses.

A descendant of Stepanov’s#

The note says of its argument that it “is a descendant of Stepanov’s”, and it names the feature that makes the descent hard: Stepanov’s argument “uses a divisor involving multiplicity” [2]. In chapter Stepanov's proof that divisor was the zero set of an auxiliary function F that vanished to order at least p^\mu=\sqrt q at every rational point but one, while its pole order at the remaining point stayed below a budget fixed by the Riemann and Roch count. The proof was then the inequality of Theorem 10.2 in disguise, since zeros of order at least m at N points cost mN units of degree, so that N\le D/m.

What multiplicity bought, and why the integers do not sell it#

Multiplicity bought the whole gain. With multiplicity one, the same count only shows that the number of points is at most the degree of an auxiliary function, which gives nothing better than the trivial bound, while with multiplicity \sqrt q each point uses up \sqrt q units of the degree budget and the count becomes the bound q+(2g+1)\sqrt q of Theorem 10.9. And multiplicity was free in characteristic p, because a p^\mu-th power that vanishes at a point vanishes there to order p^\mu (lemma Lemma 10.6).

Over the integers the note puts the obstacle in one phrase, saying that multiplicity is hard to find, “corresponding to something like differentiating whole numbers” [2]. Chapter Stepanov's proof made this precise. A derivation \delta\colon\ZZ\to\ZZ with \delta(ab)=a\,\delta(b)+b\,\delta(a) has \delta(1)=2\delta(1), so \delta(1)=0 and then \delta(n)=n\,\delta(1)=0 for every n. There is no derivative to make an integer vanish twice. What does exist is divisibility: an integer that is divisible by p^m behaves, for counting purposes, like a function that vanishes to order m at the point p, and a nonzero integer that is divisible by p^e must be at least p^e in size, which is the integer form of the degree budget (the determinant method of section What the proof used).

So for something else to play the role of the derivative, it has to do three things that p-th powers did for Stepanov. It has to manufacture high divisibility automatically, without solving for it point by point. It has to do so for many primes at once, the analogue of many rational points. And the object it acts on has to be nonzero and of controlled size, so that a product formula or a lattice count can play the degree budget. In our reading, the formal proof does all three. Divisibility is measured \ell-adically, prime by prime and lift by lift, with a valuation bound on jets of powers of determinants (ThmP, which bounds the valuation of some jet in every window of orders), and the degree budget on the spine is the product formula for a nonzero algebraic number, which says that it cannot be divisible by more prime powers than its archimedean size allows (norm_height_bound); both are in chapter Multiplicity without derivatives: a chain of length about the square root. The code names neither D nor multiplicity.

A chain of theta lifts#

The note’s answer to what plays the derivative is the sentence its author singles out. The “simple, new, Fourier-analytic ideas” of a toy setting led to “chaining theta lifts”, so that the same tricks would recur “in a natively automorphic manner”, and for the von Mangoldt sum of length X the suggested length of the chain, “in view of each mimicking multiplicity, was \sqrt X”, followed by the aside “And yet, what else could it be?” [2]. The timeline’s step 8 says the same in formulas: iterated theta lifts U(X_0)\to U(X_1)\to\dots\to U(X_m) between totally definite unitary groups, each sending a form \pi to \pi\boxplus\mu_j[t], win “multiplicity m” [2].

A theta lift is a map that carries an automorphic form on one group to an automorphic form on another, by integrating it against a theta function built from a Weil representation. On a totally definite unitary group, one whose Hermitian form is positive definite at every real place, an automorphic form of fixed level is a function on a finite set of lattice classes, so a theta lift between two such groups is a finite matrix and a chain of m lifts is a product of m matrices (chapter Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices). The code builds such a chain at each scale x and fixes its length in the declaration GlobalTheory.EX.RankVal [3].

def RankVal (s : Scale) (R : Ranks) : Prop :=
  (s.x ^ (2 + 8 * s.eps) ≤ (R.n : ℝ) ∧ (R.n : ℝ) ≤ 2 * s.x ^ (2 + 8 * s.eps)) ∧
  (Real.sqrt (s.x * s.delta1) ≤ (R.m : ℝ) ∧ (R.m : ℝ) ≤ 2 * Real.sqrt (s.x * s.delta1)) ∧
  (s.x ^ (9 / 2 + 10 * s.eps) ≤ (R.k : ℝ) ∧ (R.k : ℝ) ≤ 2 * s.x ^ (9 / 2 + 10 * s.eps)) ∧
  R.r + R.t = 8 * R.f * R.r + 4 + TOv s * nWv R s

With \delta_1=x^{-\varepsilon/8} (Scale.delta1), the second line says \sqrt{x^{1-\varepsilon/8}}\le m\le2\sqrt{x^{1-\varepsilon/8}}, so m is between x^{1/2-\varepsilon/16} and twice that. The code has no variable named after the note’s X. Taking X to be this scale x, which is also the scale at which the endgame bounds its sums, makes m the note’s square root with an \varepsilon of room, and that identification is our reading. The same datum also carries a much longer length, about x\,e^{x^\varepsilon} (chapter Multiplicity without derivatives: a chain of length about the square root), and the code does not say which length the note means.

Why the square root? The note’s aside suggests the author found it inevitable, and the code does not say. One comparison with chapter Stepanov's proof is ours and is offered only as an analogy. In Bombieri’s form of Stepanov’s proof the multiplicity at each rational point is p^\mu=\sqrt q, the square root of the size of the field whose points are counted, and the resulting error term is of size \sqrt q. Here the chain length, which the note says mimics multiplicity, is the square root of the scale x at which primes are counted, and the target is an error of size x^{1/2+9\varepsilon}. In both cases the multiplicity is matched to the error the proof is aiming at.

The turning point of the discovery, by the note’s account, was “multiplicity 2 on O(2,n) via the ‘natively-automorphic’ determinant”, found by analogy with “the definite sign of the left-hand side of qN=M^k+R” in the toy setting, after which more theta lifts won more multiplicity [2]. That identity is the subject of the next section.

18.3The toy setting#

The note says that the author had been “combining two quite different ideas present in a toy setting”, one of them new, and that the new ideas were Fourier-analytic [2]. Elsewhere it calls one result of that setting a “qN=M^k+R sign-only proof of Weil and Deligne”, and footnote 3 describes it in a single dense paragraph [2]. Weil’s theorem is the Riemann Hypothesis for curves of chapter The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields, and Deligne’s is its extension to varieties of every dimension [48] [52]. This section is our reconstruction of the footnote, and everything in it is our reading unless it is quoted. We take the simplest instance, prove what can be proved at the level of this page, check it with numbers, and stop where the footnote’s meaning cannot be pinned down.

The sum of the footnote#

In this section, as in chapters The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields and Stepanov's proof, q is the size of a finite field, and we take it to be an odd prime so that additive characters are plain exponentials. The letters k, t, h, M, N, and R are the note’s, used here only inside this section, so k is not the Tate twist of chapter The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology, t is not an imaginary part, h is not a test function, and N is not a zero count. For a\in\FF_q write e_q(a)=e^{2\pi i a/q}, an additive character of \FF_q, which is well defined because a is an integer modulo q. Fix a positive integer k and a real weight t\colon\FF_q\to\RR, and let

Q_k(x)=x_1x_2+x_2x_3+\dots+x_{k-1}x_k ,\qquad x=(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in\FF_q^k ,
(18.1)

the quadric the note writes, which we call the path quadric because its terms follow the edges of a path through the k coordinates. The footnote’s sum is

\Sigma=\sum_{h\in\FF_q}\ \sum_{x\in\FF_q^k} t(x_1)\cdots t(x_k)\, e_q\big(h\,Q_k(x)\big).
(18.2)

It is a finite sum of q^{k+1} terms. The footnote does not say what t is. We take for t the simplest function whose sum M=\sum_x t(x) is a quantity that Weil’s theorem bounds. With f(x)=x^3+x+1, the curve of chapters The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields and Stepanov's proof, let t(x) be the Legendre symbol of f(x) modulo q, that is 1 if f(x) is a nonzero square, -1 if it is a nonsquare, and 0 if f(x)=0. Each x gives 1+t(x) affine points on y^2=f(x), so with the point at infinity N_1=q+1+M, and by Equation (9.9) with n=1,

M=\sum_{x\in\FF_q}t(x)=N_1-q-1=-(\alpha_1+\alpha_2),
(18.3)

minus the sum of the two inverse roots. Weil’s theorem says \lvert M\rvert\le2\sqrt q. Over \FF_{101} chapter Stepanov's proof found N_1=105, so M=3.

Summing over h first#

The footnote’s instruction is to “sum over h first for the left-hand side” [2]. The inner sum over h is a geometric series in e_q(Q_k(x)), and the orthogonality of additive characters evaluates it,

\sum_{h\in\FF_q}e_q(h a)=\begin{cases} q, & a=0,\\ 0, & a\ne0,\end{cases}

because for a\ne0 the number e_q(a) is a q-th root of unity different from 1 and the sum of its powers is (e_q(a)^q-1)/(e_q(a)-1)=0. Putting a=Q_k(x) keeps exactly the points of the quadric,

\Sigma=q\,N,\qquad N=\sum_{x\in\FF_q^k,\ Q_k(x)=0} t(x_1)\cdots t(x_k).
(18.4)

So N counts the solutions of x_1x_2+\dots+x_{k-1}x_k=0 over \FF_q, each weighted by the product of the weights of its coordinates. With t\equiv1 it is the number of points of the quadric. For even k the path quadric is a nondegenerate quadratic form in k variables (the determinant of the adjacency matrix of a path with an even number of vertices is \pm1) of the split type, and the standard count gives q^{k-1}+q^{k/2}-q^{k/2-1} points [45, ch. 6]. We checked this formula by direct count for q\in\{5,7,11,13\} and k\in\{2,4,6\}.

Expanding the other way#

The other way to evaluate \Sigma is to keep h outside. For each h write

S_h=\sum_{x\in\FF_q^k}t(x_1)\cdots t(x_k)\,e_q\big(h\,Q_k(x)\big),

so that \Sigma=\sum_h S_h. The term h=0 has no exponential and factors as M^k, which is what the footnote calls the “zero-mode” [2]. The rest is the remainder R=\sum_{h\ne0}S_h, and comparing with Equation (18.4) gives the identity of the note’s step 3,

q\,N = M^k + R .
(18.5)

The footnote says that R has “square-root-quality” by “iterating Parseval k times” [2]. Parseval’s identity on \FF_q says that for h\ne0 and any v\colon\FF_q\to\CC,

\sum_{y\in\FF_q}\Big\lvert\sum_{x\in\FF_q}v(x)\,e_q(hxy)\Big\rvert^2=q\sum_{x\in\FF_q}\lvert v(x)\rvert^2 ,
(18.6)

which follows by expanding the square and applying orthogonality in y. The path structure of Q_k is what lets it be iterated: e_q(hQ_k(x)) is a product of factors e_q(hx_jx_{j+1}), one per edge, so S_h is a chain in which each coordinate meets only its two neighbours.

Proposition 18.2

For every real weight bounded by 1, the weighted count of the path quadric satisfies qN=M^k+R with \lvert R\rvert\le(q-1)\,q^{(k-1)/2} times the sum of the squared weights

Statement

Let q be an odd prime, k\ge2, and t\colon\FF_q\to\RR with \lvert t\rvert\le1. With M, N, R, and S_h as above, qN=M^k+R, and for every h\ne0

\lvert S_h\rvert\le q^{(k-1)/2}\sum_{x\in\FF_q}t(x)^2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \lvert R\rvert\le(q-1)\,q^{(k-1)/2}\sum_{x\in\FF_q}t(x)^2\le(q-1)\,q^{(k+1)/2}.
(18.7)
In plain terms

The weighted count of solutions of the path quadric, times q, is the k-th power of the plain sum of the weights plus a remainder, and the remainder is controlled by Parseval’s identity alone, with no knowledge of how the weights cancel.

Why it is needed

This is the part of the footnote’s “sign-only” argument that can be proved at the level of this page. It shows how the size of R comes from Fourier analysis on the path, with no Gauss sum and no algebraic geometry, which matches the footnote’s phrase “Gauss sum cancellation replaced by iterated Parseval” [2].

Idea

Cut the path at one edge. The two halves are vectors whose lengths grow by at most \sqrt q per edge, by Parseval, and the cut edge pairs them through one more Fourier transform, so Cauchy and Schwarz finish.

Proof

The identity is Equation (18.5). For the bound fix h\ne0 and define vectors on \FF_q from the left end and from the right end of the path,

v_1=t,\quad v_{j+1}(y)=t(y)\sum_{x}v_j(x)\,e_q(hxy);\qquad u_1=t,\quad u_{j+1}(x)=t(x)\sum_{y}e_q(hxy)\,u_j(y).
Steps
  1. Unfolding the definitions, the chain splits at the edge between coordinates a and a+1 for any 1\le a\le k-1, and with b=k-a,
S_h=\sum_{x,y\in\FF_q}v_a(x)\,e_q(hxy)\,u_b(y).
  1. Since \lvert t\rvert\le1, Parseval Equation (18.6) gives \lVert v_{j+1}\rVert_2\le\big\lVert\sum_x v_j(x)e_q(hx\,\cdot)\big\rVert_2=\sqrt q\,\lVert v_j\rVert_2, and the same for u, so
\lVert v_a\rVert_2\le q^{(a-1)/2}\lVert t\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert u_b\rVert_2\le q^{(b-1)/2}\lVert t\rVert_2 .
  1. Cauchy and Schwarz in x, then Parseval once more for the inner sum over y, give
\lvert S_h\rvert\le\lVert v_a\rVert_2\,\sqrt q\,\lVert u_b\rVert_2\le q^{(k-1)/2}\lVert t\rVert_2^2 .
  1. Summing over the q-1 values h\ne0 and using \lVert t\rVert_2^2=\sum_x t(x)^2\le q gives
\lvert R\rvert\le(q-1)\,q^{(k-1)/2}\lVert t\rVert_2^2\le(q-1)\,q^{(k+1)/2}.

The proof applies Parseval k-1 times and Cauchy and Schwarz once. The footnote says k times, and we take the difference to be bookkeeping.

Example

For t\equiv1 everything is explicit. Then M=q, N is the point count of Equation (18.4), and for even k the identity reads q\big(q^{k-1}+q^{k/2}-q^{k/2-1}\big)=q^k+(q-1)q^{k/2}. So every S_h with h\ne0 equals q^{k/2}, the square root of the zero mode S_0=q^k, and R=(q-1)q^{k/2}. For q=5 and k=4 that is 725=625+100. The bound Equation (18.7) gives \lvert S_h\rvert\le q^{(k+1)/2}, worse than the truth by \sqrt q, because Parseval does not see the Gauss sum. Our reading of the footnote’s “up to an inch or so” is this loss of a fixed power of q, which becomes negligible after a k-th root.

Used in

The sign question of section What a sign would give, and where we stop and the figure Figure 18.2.

Worked numbers for k = 2 and k = 4#

For k=2 the quadric x_1x_2=0 is the union of the two coordinate axes, so N=2t(0)M-t(0)^2 exactly, and with the Legendre weight t(0) is the symbol of f(0)=1, which is 1. Over \FF_{101} this gives N=2\cdot3-1=5, and the identity reads 101\cdot5=505=9+496, so M^2=9 and R=496. The Parseval bound for this R is 100\cdot101^{1/2}\cdot101\approx1.015\times10^5, and the largest single \lvert S_h\rvert is 248.8 against its bound 101^{3/2}\approx1015. The case k=2 carries no information, since the identity is the trivial count of the two axes, and the first case with content is k=4.

For k=4 we computed N exactly with integer arithmetic by a recursion along the path, which tracks the last coordinate and the partial value of Q_4 modulo q, and computed each S_h separately in floating point. The identity Equation (18.5) held to rounding in every case. The table lists the Legendre weight of y^2=x^3+x+1 for six primes. The column “bound” is (q-1)q^{3/2}\sum_xt(x)^2 from Equation (18.7).

q M N qN M^4 R bound
5 3 21 105 81 24 224
7 -3 53 371 81 290 778
11 2 -72 -792 16 -808 3,648
13 4 4 52 256 -204 6,750
37 10 -76 -2{,}812 10,000 -12{,}812 291,681
101 3 -1{,}675 -169{,}175 81 -169{,}256 1.025\times10^7

Two things are visible. The remainder is far inside its Parseval bound, and in fact \lvert R\rvert is within a factor of three of q^{(k+1)/2} in every row (at q=101 it is 1.65 times 101^{5/2}), which is what square-root quality relative to the q^{k+1} terms of \Sigma would predict. And the sign of qN changes from prime to prime, positive for q=5, 7, and 13, negative for q=11, 37, and 101.

What a sign would give, and where we stop#

The footnote’s claim is about that sign. Summing over h first, it says, “Bertini gives a definite sign from middle cohomology, one off the one on M^k”, and on the other side M^k is the zero mode and R has square-root quality, with “opposite signs meaning no cancellation of inverse roots, QED” [2]. The deduction that such a sign would allow is elementary, and we give it as our reading. Suppose that for some even k the left side had the sign opposite to M^k\ge0, that is qN\le0. Then Equation (18.5) and Equation (18.7) give

M^k=qN-R\le-R\le\lvert R\rvert\le(q-1)\,q^{(k+1)/2}<q^{(k+3)/2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad\lvert M\rvert<q^{\frac12+\frac{3}{2k}} .
(18.8)

The exponent tends to \tfrac12 as k grows. Applied over every extension \FF_{q^n}, where by Equation (18.3) the sum becomes -(\alpha_1^n+\alpha_2^n), a bound \lvert\alpha_1^n+\alpha_2^n\rvert\le C\,q^{n(1/2+3/(2k))} for all n forces \lvert\alpha_i\rvert\le q^{1/2+3/(2k)} by the argument of Lemma 9.7, and letting k grow gives \lvert\alpha_i\rvert\le\sqrt q. A definite sign on one side and square-root quality on the other would therefore prove Weil’s theorem for this curve with no geometry beyond the sign, which is our reading of “sign-only”.

The plain sum Equation (18.2) does not have that sign, and the table already shows it changing. More is true, and it is a theorem rather than an observation. Over \FF_{37} the Legendre weight has M=10, larger than \sqrt{37}\approx6.08 though within Weil’s 2\sqrt{37}\approx12.2, and \sum_xt(x)^2=36 because f has one root modulo 37. For every even k\ge12 the zero mode beats the Parseval bound, 10^k>36\cdot36\cdot37^{(k-1)/2}, so Equation (18.5) forces qN>0, the same sign as M^k. At k=12 the exact values are qN=1{,}007{,}583{,}904{,}577 against M^{12}=10^{12} and the bound 5.47\times10^{11}. If the plain sum had the opposite sign for every even k, the argument above would prove \lvert M\rvert\le\sqrt q over every field, which is false here. So the definite sign of the footnote is not a property of the plain sum. It needs the ingredients the footnote names and does not explain, coefficients on the quadric (“with e.g. quadric coefficients too”), Bertini’s theorem, and the middle cohomology of the resulting variety, and a cohomological sign of that kind is beyond what this page can reconstruct or check. We stop here. The footnote also says to “vectorize to go up dimensions” and traces the path quadric to a reciprocity law for normalized Gauss sums that live on a cover of \mathrm{GL}_2, and we do not reconstruct those remarks either.

Is the identity in the code?#

We searched the index of the Lean tree for the identity, by the names and statements that would carry it: quadrics, Parseval, products of additive characters, path-shaped sums x_i\,x_{i+1}, and the names Deligne, Katz, Bertini, and Gabber, with special attention to Development/WeilBound and to the inventory’s section on the toy setting. The weighted sum Equation (18.2), the identity Equation (18.5), and any sign argument for it do not occur. The nearest statements are an unweighted count of a quadric by the same orthogonality step, GlobalTheory.CompanionTheory.SW.QuadricCount.count_mul_card, and the square-root count of a nondegenerate quadric in an even number of variables, quadric_count_even, both in CompanionTheory/SpectralGeometry/LocalGlobalProofs/AdelicAnalysis/FiniteFieldQuadraticFormPointCount.lean [3].

theorem count_mul_card (ψ : AddChar k ℂ) (hψ : ψ ≠ 1) (B : Matrix ι ι k) (s : k) :
    (Nat.card {x : ι → k // quadForm B x = s} : ℂ) * (Fintype.card k : ℂ) =
      ∑ t : k, ψ (-(t * s)) * ∑ x, ψ (t * quadForm B x)

The second is proved through Gauss sums, not iterated Parseval. Both are in the import closure of Main, and we did not check whether the final theorem uses them. The absence is what one would expect, since the toy setting is a finite-field model and the formal proof works over the integers.

18.4The map of the formal proof#

The formal proof is a chain of named propositions. Many large theorems in the tree take their inputs as explicit hypotheses named after the statements they need, and a separate theorem proves each such statement, so the proof reads as a tree of propositions whose leaves are closed one by one [3]. Following that tree down from Main.lean, every link has been read in at least one of those five regions, and the spine has nine nodes. The table gives each node in one sentence of ordinary mathematics, its Lean declaration, and the chapter that explains it. Declarations in UpperTheory live under Development/AutomorphicArithmetic, and those in Formalism.HC under Formalism/SharpRestriction/RamificationFrobenius/TotientGaloisClasses.

Read from the bottom up, the half-plane statement follows from the Galois input Row0b alone, once local Langlands for \mathrm{GL}_n (recTExists, also proved in the tree) is supplied. Row0b enters twice. It fills the literature record that builds the automorphic construction of node 6, and through vwin_of_row it proves the cohomological window of node 8. Row0b itself is proved as galoisLocalGlobalStrong_recParameter from two statements, TLiftK, which says that theta lifts exist between totally definite unitary groups in a stable range of ranks, and GeoOne, which finds Galois representations in the cohomology of varieties with Hecke correspondences. So the three inputs named in the code are Row0b, TLiftK with GeoOne, and VWin, and all three are proved. Our reading of the theta lifts adds a fact that shapes the next chapters. TLiftK is used once, to raise an even rank to an odd one on the Galois side, and the m-fold chain of the note’s step 8 does not go through it but through the chain operators of the automorphic construction (chainOp, ColumnChain).

The endgame meets these inputs through three statements, which chapter The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros states as one interface (Theorem 19.13). If Green’s parametrization of the cuspidal characters of \mathrm{GL}_d(\FF_g) holds, if the window statement VWinAt ψ 401 holds for every primitive \psi, and if a record of type HypsAlt with the condition DefiniteSideCondition exists, then every primitive L-function is zero-free on \Re s>\tfrac12 (UpperTheory.Top.zero_free_all_of_green_v_win). The record has about 45 proof fields, and it is where the automorphic construction of node 6 is packed.

The tree has 175,187 Lean files with 17,374,215 lines, about 1.03 GB of text, and 1,061,425 declarations, of which 784,092 are theorems [3]. Every file is reachable from Main through imports, within at most 43 import steps, and the tree contains no comments, no sorry, and no axiom (chapter What the proof stands on). Being imported is not the same as being used, though. Tracing the declarations the final theorem actually cites finds statements that are imported and proved but not used, such as a weak form of Vandiver’s conjecture over \QQ, and statements that are imported and never proved, such as a Behrend-type bound, and the table of section The note’s twenty steps against the code keeps track of that difference.

18.5The note’s twenty steps against the code#

The note’s timeline was compiled by Claude “after a thorough search”, and its author warns in a footnote that where Claude was the expert he is “sort of paraphrasing” a summary, and that “the Lean should suffice to clarify everything” [2]. The table checks the timeline against the code. Its rows follow the logical order of the page’s reading of the note, grouped as the toy setting (steps 1, 3, 2), the positivity frame over the integers (4, 6, 5, 7), multiplicity from theta lifts (8, 12, 9, 10, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18), and the arithmetic residue (11, 19, 17, 20). A step is located when a declaration states essentially the step, partly located when the area and tools are there but the step itself is not identified or is used only in part, and not found otherwise. Where our readings of different regions disagreed, the table reconciles them and says so.

Three facts bound everything in the table. The names Stepanov, Guinand, Bost, and Vandiver occur nowhere in the code, neither in declaration names nor in file paths. The code never states that Weil’s functional W of Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion is nonnegative on any test function, and the positivity it uses on the spine is an upper bound on a smoothed sum over primes. And the tree has no comments. So wherever the table connects the note’s wording to a declaration, the connection is our reading, made from the shape of the statements, and it is marked as such where it is not a direct match.

The count is eight steps located, eight partly located, and four not found. The pattern is informative. The steps about theta lifts, periods, masses, the tower, and the cohomology groups are in the code with recognizable names, while the steps about Weil’s functional, determinants, and positivity are not, and we find in their place an upper bound on a smoothed prime sum and a rank condition on a map of periods. The toy identity of step 3 is a finite-field model and is not formalized. Steps 14 and 15, the barrier at 2/3 and the gluing across characters, are the note’s account of the hardest part of the discovery, and we did not find them; chapter Paying for the chain: integrality, Galois representations, and the count that is bounded names candidates only.

18.6How to read Part IV#

Part IV has three kinds of sentence about this proof. The first is what the note says, quoted and cited as the note. The second is what the code states, given with its Lean declaration and file and cited as the Lean code; a statement the code proves is proved, and the page does not hedge it. The third is our reading: every link between the first two kinds, every mechanism inferred from the shape of a statement, every special case worked out for the page, and every analogy, and each such passage says so where it starts. In this chapter the comparisons with Stepanov’s proof in section The idea in the author’s words, the reconstruction of the toy identity in section The toy setting, the identification of the note’s X with the scale x, and the pairing of the note’s steps with declarations in section The note’s twenty steps against the code are our reading.

A region of the code is unfolded when we have opened its definitions down to statements of ordinary mathematics and checked the translation against the text. The endgame of chapter The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros is unfolded completely and proved on the page. The definitions behind the theta chain, the window, and the Galois input are unfolded far enough to state what they say, and chapters Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices to The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology explain each mechanism in its smallest case with numbers. Some parts were left as statements, and the chapters name them rather than fill them with a plausible story. Among them are the meaning of most of the roughly 45 fields of the record HypsAlt and of DefiniteSideCondition, the proof (TopG) that the record yields data tied to the chain on windows, how the chain’s divisibility and integrality (ThmP, DGam, chain_ge, PeriodClassSumWeyl, and the exponents of LeafDepthGood) feed the divisibility inequality DIV of the record SizeData₂, from which chapter Paying for the chain: integrality, Galois representations, and the count that is bounded follows the count to the bound on G_r, the identification of the chain’s kernel ColumnChain.unf with theta coefficients between lattice classes, the plus-part bounds of the window, LemmaK, and the proof of base change. Chapter What the proof stands on tabulates these gaps region by region. Where a chapter relies on one of these, it says in one sentence that the formal proof establishes it in a named declaration and that the page states it without unfolding its proof.

Recap
  • The formal proof proves the Riemann Hypothesis in Mathlib’s definition and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for every Dirichlet L-function, in five theorems of Main.lean with no hypotheses (Theorem 18.1). Route M of Part III reaches further, to every Hecke L-function.
  • The note’s idea is Stepanov’s: multiplicity against a degree budget. The integers have no derivative, and the note’s substitute is a chain of about \sqrt X theta lifts, each mimicking one unit of multiplicity, which the code fixes as \sqrt{x^{1-\varepsilon/8}}\le m\le2\sqrt{x^{1-\varepsilon/8}} in RankVal (section A chain of theta lifts).
  • The toy identity qN=M^k+R holds for every weight by orthogonality, and Parseval alone bounds R by (q-1)q^{(k-1)/2}\sum t^2 (Proposition 18.2). A definite opposite sign would give Weil’s bound, but the plain sum has no such sign, and the footnote’s cohomological sign is beyond this page (section What a sign would give, and where we stop). The identity is not in the code.
  • The spine runs from Main.lean through the half-plane statement and a windowed Landau endgame to an inequality on windows, which rests on the automorphic construction and the cohomological window, and through them on Row0b, TLiftK with GeoOne, and VWin, all proved (section The map of the formal proof).
  • Of the note’s twenty steps, eight are located, eight partly located, and four not found. The code never states positivity of Weil’s functional and never names Stepanov, Guinand, Bost, or Vandiver (section The note’s twenty steps against the code).
  • Chapter The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros starts at the top of the spine and proves the endgame in full.
