Chapter 19

The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros

Follow the formal proof from an upper bound on a smoothed prime sum, known only on sparse windows of scales, to the absence of zeros to the right of one half, and from there to the five theorems of Main.lean.

Builds on 7. What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations, 18. Stepanov over the integers: the plan and the map of the formal proof

In plain terms

Every zero of an L-function to the right of the critical line would leave a wave in the primes that grows faster than the square root, and the waves of such zeros always rise above any square-root-sized ceiling somewhere. So it is enough to show that one smoothed count of primes never rises far above its expected value, and it is even enough to show this only on long stretches that recur, with gaps between them. This chapter proves that implication completely, with elementary analysis, and then proves that it gives the Riemann Hypothesis and its version for every Dirichlet L-function.

Everything else in Part IV, the definite unitary groups, the chain of theta lifts, the Galois representations, the bound in Galois cohomology, is spent to produce one inequality: an upper bound x^{1/2+9\varepsilon} on a combination of smoothed prime sums at the scales x of certain windows. Here we take that inequality as given, show how the code turns it into zero-freeness to the right of \tfrac12 and then into the five theorems of Main.lean, and reconstruct the one new piece of analysis, the windows, as a complete proof. The chapter ends with the inequality stated as the contract the next four chapters must honor.

19.1The question this chapter answers#

Stepanov’s proof in chapter Stepanov's proof ended in two moves. The auxiliary function gave a bound on point counts, \abs{N_n - q^n - 1} \le C q^{n/2}, and then Lemma 9.7 turned the bound into the location of the zeros: the generating function \sum_n (q^n + 1 - N_n)u^n converges on a disc whose radius is set by the bound, so no pole can sit inside it. The warning after that lemma made a point that returns here: the poles are weighted by positive multiplicities, so none can hide behind another.

Over the integers the point count becomes a smoothed count of prime powers with its main term removed, combined with the same sums twisted by the powers of one character. The bound becomes an upper bound x^{1/2+9\varepsilon}, on one side only. The disc of convergence becomes a half-plane where a Laplace transform is analytic, and the positive multiplicities become positive weights. One feature has no counterpart over a finite field: the bound is known only on windows [Y, Y^{3/2}] of scales, for Y tending to infinity, and not between them. The auxiliary function and its multiplicity, which produce the bound, are chapters Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices to The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology; this chapter is the analogue of From the bounds to the zeros.

What the note says is cited as [2]; what the code states is cited as [3] and quoted only in lean blocks, with paths relative to the formalization’s src folder; what we worked out ourselves is marked “ours” or “our reading” where it starts.

19.2From one half-plane to five theorems#

We begin at the top, because it is short and shows which statement the analysis must deliver.

In the Lean formalization riemannHypothesis in Main.lean

The five final theorems, and the four propositions of Statements.lean that they prove, verbatim.

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := rhOfAll
theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re : RiemannZetaZerosOnLine := rhOfAll
theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re : DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf := allChi
theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re : DirichletLZerosOnLine := claimAll.2.1
theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive : PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine := critAll

def RiemannZetaZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

def DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

def DirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

def PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
    ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

The first two say, once in Mathlib’s wording and once spelled out, that every zero of \zeta other than -2, -4, -6, \dots has real part \tfrac12 (s = 1 is excluded only because Mathlib gives \zeta a value at its pole). The third says L(s,\chi) \ne 0 for \Re s > \tfrac12, for every Dirichlet character of every modulus except at the pole of a principal character; the fourth and fifth say that zeros in the open strip lie on the critical line, for all \chi and for primitive \chi. Here L(s,\chi) is Mathlib’s continuation of \sum \chi(n) n^{-s} (Definition 7.6).

All five follow from one statement about primitive characters. A primitive character, recall from Proposition 7.7, is one not induced from a smaller modulus; the trivial character modulo 1 counts as primitive, and its L-function is \zeta.

In the Lean formalization Formalism.HC.ZeroFreeAll in Formalism/SharpRestriction/RamificationFrobenius/TotientGaloisClasses/ExplicitFormulaErrorOfHostConditions.lean

The zero-free statement for primitive characters; PChar packages a primitive character with its conductor.

def PChar.ZeroFreeAbove (ψ : PChar) (θ : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ s : ℂ, θ < s.re → DirichletCharacter.LFunction ψ.χ s ≠ 0

def ZeroFreeOn (Q : PChar → Prop) : Prop := ∀ ψ : PChar, Q ψ → ψ.ZeroFreeAbove (1 / 2)

def ZeroFreeAll : Prop := ZeroFreeOn fun _ => True
Theorem 19.1

If no primitive Dirichlet L-function vanishes to the right of one half, then all five theorems of Main.lean hold

Statement

Assume that L(s,\chi) \ne 0 for every primitive Dirichlet character \chi (including the trivial character modulo 1) and every s with \Re s > \tfrac12. Then:

  1. for every Dirichlet character \chi modulo any N \ge 1 and every s with \Re s > \tfrac12, L(s,\chi) \ne 0 unless \chi is principal and s = 1;
  2. every zero s \ne 1 of \zeta other than -2, -4, -6, \dots has real part \tfrac12 (the point s = 1 is excluded only because Mathlib gives \zeta a value there);
  3. every zero of every L(s,\chi) with 0 < \Re s < 1 has real part \tfrac12, and in particular so does every such zero for primitive \chi.
In plain terms

Once the primitive L-functions are known to have no zero to the right of the critical line, the rest is bookkeeping: imprimitive L-functions differ from primitive ones by factors that never vanish there, and the mirror symmetry s \leftrightarrow 1 - s carries the zero-free half-plane to the left half of the strip.

Why it is needed

It isolates the one statement that needs new mathematics; the whole of Part IV aims at its hypothesis.

Idea

Three classical moves. Euler factors 1 - \chi^*(p)p^{-s} have absolute value at least 1 - p^{-\Re s} > 0. The functional equation of \zeta, or of a completed primitive L-function, sends a zero at s to a zero at 1 - s (for the conjugate character). The gamma factors that appear in the functional equation never vanish where they are used.

Proof
Steps
  1. Imprimitive characters (UpperTheory.Top.imprimitive). Let \chi be a character modulo N and \chi^* the primitive character inducing it, of conductor N^* \mid N. Mathlib’s LFunction_changeLevel gives, whenever \chi^* \ne 1 or s \ne 1,
L(s,\chi) = L(s,\chi^*) \prod_{p \mid N} \bigl(1 - \chi^*(p)\,p^{-s}\bigr).

For \Re s > 0 each factor is nonzero, because \abs{\chi^*(p)p^{-s}} \le p^{-\Re s} < 1. For \Re s > \tfrac12 the first factor is nonzero by hypothesis. If \chi \ne 1 then \chi^* \ne 1, so the only excluded case is \chi principal and s = 1. This is statement 1, which is LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re and the proposition the code calls UpperTheory.EveryCharacter.

L(s,\chi) \ne 0 \quad (\Re s > \tfrac12,\ \chi \ne 1 \text{ or } s \ne 1).
  1. The zeta function (Formalism.VW.rh_of_every, Formalism.VW.rh_of_right). Statement 1 with N = 1 and \chi = 1, together with Mathlib’s LFunction_modOne_eq (L(s, 1) = \zeta(s) modulo 1), gives \zeta(s) \ne 0 for \Re s > \tfrac12, s \ne 1. Now let \zeta(s) = 0 with \Re s < \tfrac12 and s not a trivial zero. Then s \ne 0, since \zeta(0) = -\tfrac12. Mathlib’s functional equation riemannZeta_one_sub, applied at 1 - s, reads
\zeta(s) = 2(2\pi)^{-(1-s)}\,\Gamma(1-s)\cos\Bigl(\frac{\pi(1-s)}{2}\Bigr)\zeta(1-s).

The Gamma function has no zeros, and the cosine vanishes only when 1 - s = 2k+1 for an integer k, that is s = -2k: k < 0 contradicts \Re s < \tfrac12, k = 0 is s = 0, and k \ge 1 is a trivial zero. So \zeta(1-s) = 0 with \Re(1-s) > \tfrac12 and 1 - s \ne 1, which contradicts the first sentence. With \Re s = \tfrac12 remaining, this is statement 2, the theorems riemannHypothesis and riemannZeta_eq_zero_re.

\zeta(s) = 0,\ s \notin \{-2,-4,\dots\},\ s \ne 1 \implies \Re s = \tfrac12.
  1. The strip (Claim.strip, Formalism.VW.critLine). Let L(s,\chi) = 0 with 0 < \Re s < \tfrac12. By the factorization of step 1 and the nonvanishing of Euler factors for \Re s > 0, L(s,\chi^*) = 0 (Claim.prim_zero). Mathlib writes L(s,\chi^*) = \Lambda(s,\chi^*)/\Gamma_\chi(s) with \Lambda the completed L-function and \Gamma_\chi(s) equal to \Gamma_\RR(s) or \Gamma_\RR(s+1) by parity, where \Gamma_\RR(s) = \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2); it is nonzero for \Re s > 0, so \Lambda(s,\chi^*) = 0. The functional equation of the completed L-function of a primitive character (Mathlib’s IsPrimitive.completedLFunction_one_sub, the statement of Proposition 7.7) makes \Lambda(1-s, \overline{\chi^*}) a constant multiple of \Lambda(s,\chi^*), hence zero, and dividing by the nonzero gamma factor at 1 - s gives L(1-s, \overline{\chi^*}) = 0 (Claim.prim_reflect). But \overline{\chi^*} is primitive and \Re(1-s) > \tfrac12, which contradicts the hypothesis. Zeros with \tfrac12 < \Re s < 1 are excluded by step 1. This is LFunction_eq_zero_re, and critLine runs the same argument without the passage to \chi^* for the primitive version.
L(s,\chi) = 0,\ 0 < \Re s < 1 \implies \Re s = \tfrac12.

19.3The smoothed sum is pure zero noise#

The object at the center of the endgame is the smoothed sum of chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations with its main term removed. For real X \ge 1,

G_0(X) = S(X) - X\log X + (1+\gamma_E)X,\qquad S(X) = \sum_{n \le X}\Lambda(n)\Bigl(\frac Xn - 1\Bigr).
(19.1)

It is a real number for each X, continuous in X, and it is not a count: it is a count minus its expected size. Subtracting the main term from Equation (7.4) leaves only the zeros, the constant \log 2\pi, and a tail that dies like X^{-2}:

G_0(X) = \log 2\pi - \sum_\rho \frac{X^\rho}{\rho(\rho-1)} - \sum_{k \ge 1}\frac{X^{-2k}}{2k(2k+1)}.
(19.2)

This is the note’s step 5 exactly: “definitively switch to” \sum_{n \le X}\Lambda(n)(X/n-1)_+ - X\log X + (1+\gamma)X [2], where the note writes \gamma for Euler’s constant, which this page calls \gamma_E. The code defines the same function twice, as Formalism.Gz and as An.G, and proves them equal (GzEq.lean in Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/PrimitiveCosets).

In the Lean formalization Formalism.Gz in Formalism/StatementOC.lean

The smoothed sum and the function G_0.

def Sz (x : ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊, Λ n * (x / n - 1)

def Gz (x : ℝ) : ℝ := Sz x - x * Real.log x + (1 + Real.eulerMascheroniConstant) * x

The same construction works for a character. Its main term is different: a nonprincipal L(s,\chi) has no pole at s = 1, so the twisted sum has no term X\log X, but it does have a linear term, and the code removes it.

Definition 19.2 The twisted smoothed sum with its linear term removed

For a Dirichlet character \chi \ne 1 and real X \ge 1,

g_\chi(X) = \sum_{n \le X}\Lambda(n)\chi(n)\Bigl(\frac Xn - 1\Bigr) + X\,\frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi).
(19.3)

It is a complex number in general and real when \chi is real. It is not \psi(X,\chi) of chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations, and its correction term X\,L'(1,\chi)/L(1,\chi) is a constant times X, with L(1,\chi) \ne 0 by Dirichlet’s theorem. For the trivial character modulo 1 the code uses G_0 in its place (An.gChi, Deduction.Gchi).

In the Lean formalization Formalism.HC.An.gChi in Formalism/SharpRestriction/RamificationFrobenius/TotientGaloisClasses/Analytic.lean

The code’s g_\chi; abelian₂ n is ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt n.

def logDerivativeAtOne {N : ℕ} [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) : ℂ :=
  deriv (DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ) 1 / DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ 1

def gChi {N : ℕ} [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (y : ℝ) : ℂ :=
  if χ = 1 then ((G y : ℝ) : ℂ) else sumLamChi χ y + (y : ℂ) * logDerivativeAtOne χ

The next statement and its proof are ours: the code never writes an explicit formula for g_\chi, and uses only its transform, in poleData below. We include it because it shows that g_\chi is, like G_0, nothing but the waves of the zeros.

Proposition 19.3

For a primitive character, the twisted smoothed sum with its linear term removed is a constant, at most a logarithm, and an absolutely convergent sum over zeros

Statement

Let \chi be a primitive character modulo q > 1 with parity a \in \{0,1\}. For \Re s > 1,

\int_1^\infty g_\chi(y)\,y^{-s-1}\,\dd y = \frac{-\frac{L'}{L}(s,\chi)}{s(s-1)} + \frac{\frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi)}{s-1},
(19.4)

and for X > 1, with \rho running over the nontrivial zeros of L(s,\chi) with multiplicity,

g_\chi(X) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{L'}{L}(0,\chi) - \displaystyle\sum_\rho \frac{X^\rho}{\rho(\rho-1)} - \sum_{k \ge 0}\frac{X^{-2k-1}}{(2k+1)(2k+2)} & (a = 1),\\[3ex] \log X + 1 - C_\chi - \displaystyle\sum_\rho \frac{X^\rho}{\rho(\rho-1)} - \sum_{k \ge 1}\frac{X^{-2k}}{2k(2k+1)} & (a = 0), \end{cases}
(19.5)

where C_\chi is the constant term of -\frac{L'}{L}(s,\chi) at its simple pole s = 0.

In plain terms

Twisting by a character changes only the bookkeeping near s = 0 and s = 1. After the linear term is removed, what is left is a constant, a slowly growing \log X for even characters, and one wave X^\rho/(\rho(\rho-1)) for each zero.

Why it is needed

The endgame reads G_0 and every g_\chi through the poles of their transforms; these are exactly the zeros, with residue -1/(\rho(\rho-1)) per zero, once the linear term removes the pole at s = 1.

Idea

Repeat the proof of Theorem 7.4 with -\frac{L'}{L}(s,\chi) in place of -\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s). The pole at s = 1 is now simple and comes only from the kernel 1/(s(s-1)), with residue -X\frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi), which the correction cancels. At s = 0 the kernel’s pole meets either a regular value (odd \chi) or the trivial zero at 0 (even \chi), which produces \log X.

Proof
Show the proof

The transform follows from \int_n^\infty (y/n - 1)y^{-s-1}\,\dd y = n^{-s}/(s(s-1)), summed against \Lambda(n)\chi(n), whose Dirichlet series is -\frac{L'}{L}(s,\chi) by Definition 7.6, together with \int_1^\infty y\cdot y^{-s-1}\,\dd y = 1/(s-1). Mellin inversion then writes the twisted sum as \frac1{2\pi i}\int_{(c)}(-\frac{L'}{L}(s,\chi))X^s\,\dd s/(s(s-1)) for c > 1, an absolutely convergent integral, and we shift the line to the left exactly as in Theorem 7.4, collecting residues.

Steps
  1. At s = 1, L(1,\chi) \ne 0, so the only pole is the kernel’s, with residue -X\frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi). Adding X\frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi) removes it.
  2. At a nontrivial zero \rho of multiplicity m_\rho, -\frac{L'}{L} has residue -m_\rho, so the contribution is -m_\rho X^\rho/(\rho(\rho-1)).
  3. At s = 0 for odd \chi, L(0,\chi) \ne 0 and the kernel has residue X^0/(0 - 1) = -1, so the contribution is \frac{L'}{L}(0,\chi). At the trivial zeros s = -2k-1, k \ge 0, the residue of -\frac{L'}{L} is -1 and the kernel is X^{-2k-1}/((2k+1)(2k+2)).
  4. For even \chi, L(s,\chi) has a simple trivial zero at 0, so -\frac{L'}{L}(s,\chi) = -1/s + B_\chi + O(s), while X^s/(s-1) = -1 - s(\log X + 1) + O(s^2). The product with 1/s has residue \log X + 1 - B_\chi. The other trivial zeros s = -2k, k \ge 1, give -X^{-2k}/(2k(2k+1)) as for \zeta.

The horizontal and left integrals vanish in the limit by the bounds for L'/L in Davenport [6], as for \zeta, and the sum over \rho converges absolutely because the number of zeros up to height T is O(T\log qT).

Example

For \chi_4, the odd character modulo 4, mpmath gives L(0,\chi_4) = \tfrac12, and numerical differentiation gives \frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi_4) = 0.2456096 and \frac{L'}{L}(0,\chi_4) = 0.7831888. We found the 92 zeros of L(s,\chi_4) with 0 < \gamma < 160 as sign changes of the completed function on the critical line (the first are 6.020949, 10.243770, 12.988098, matching chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations, and the count matches the formula \frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{4T}{2\pi e} = 92.3). Summing a sieve of \Lambda up to 2\times10^7 gives the left column; the right columns use Equation (19.5) truncated to the first 10 or 92 zero pairs.

X g_{\chi_4}(X) from primes 10 pairs 92 pairs
10 0.790212 0.789319 0.790685
10^2 0.047769 0.076091 0.043453
10^3 -0.516934 -0.482469 -0.513997
10^4 6.995268 6.635104 7.064647
10^6 -18.850393 -17.313096 -18.694840

Including the zeros up to height 160 instead of the first ten shrinks the error by a factor between 2 (at X = 10, where both errors are below 10^{-3}) and 12, as a truncated absolutely convergent sum should; what remains is the contribution of the zeros above height 160, which grows with X. The same check for G_0 with the first 1000 zero pairs of \zeta (from mpmath) gives agreement to 4\times10^{-6} at X = 10 and 4\times10^{-3} at X = 10^6, where G_0(10^6) = 11.040436.

The even case carries the constant 1 - C_\chi, which comes from the double pole at s = 0, so we tested it on two real even characters. For the quadratic character modulo 5, C_\chi = -L''(0,\chi)/(2L'(0,\chi)) = 0.0220247 and \frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi) = 0.8276795; with its 98 zeros of height below 160, Equation (19.5) gives 3.095068 at X = 10 and 7.367647 at X = 10^3, against 3.095318 and 7.375421 from the primes. For the character \chi(n) = (2/n) modulo 8, C_\chi = 0.2964638, and with 110 zeros the formula gives 3.104367 and 4.570891 against 3.104313 and 4.574974. A wrong constant, such as -1 - C_\chi, would be off by 2.

Used in

The transform Equation (19.4) is the input to the pole computation of Lemma 19.8.

19.4Which way a zero pushes#

By Equation (19.2) a zero \rho = \beta + i\gamma adds the wave -X^\rho/(\rho(\rho-1)), of size X^\beta/\abs{\rho(\rho-1)}, to G_0. If every \beta = \tfrac12 the waves together are at most c_0\sqrt X, c_0 = 0.0461914 (Equation (7.5)); a zero with \beta > \tfrac12 adds a wave growing like X^\beta. Since the proof’s bound is an upper bound only, the direction of the wave matters. Take the smallest examples.

A real zero \beta \in (0,1). Then \rho(\rho-1) = \beta(\beta - 1) < 0, so the wave is +X^\beta/(\beta(1-\beta)), positive at every X. A hypothetical real zero at \beta = 0.8 adds 6.25\,X^{0.8}. It pushes G_0 up and never down, so any upper bound G_0(X) \le CX^\alpha with \alpha < 0.8 fails for large X.

A complex pair \rho = 0.8 \pm 14i. Together they add 2\Re\bigl(-X^\rho/(\rho(\rho-1))\bigr) = 0.010186\,X^{0.8}\cos(14\log X + \phi) for a fixed phase \phi. This wave swings both ways, but its crests come once every 2\pi/14 = 0.449 units of \log X, and at a crest it equals 0.010186\,X^{0.8}. It passes X^{0.6} once X^{0.2} > 98.2, that is for X > 9.1\times10^9, and from then on every crest breaks the bound. The small amplitude only delays the crossing.

So an upper bound sees every kind of off-line zero: real zeros push up everywhere, and complex zeros push up at their crests. Compare the unsmoothed count: in von Mangoldt’s formula \psi(x) - x = -\sum_\rho x^\rho/\rho + \dots a real zero contributes -x^\beta/\beta < 0, a push down, which an upper bound on \psi(x) - x cannot see. The kernel 1/(s(s-1)) of the smoothing is negative on (0,1), and that flips the sign. This is why the endgame works with G_0 and not with \psi.

A common misreading

“One-sided” does not refer to one side of the critical line. It means that G(X) \le CX^\alpha bounds the function from above and says nothing about how negative it becomes; the argument below never uses a lower bound.

19.5Landau’s theorem, the classical form#

For a bound that holds at every large X, the step from a one-sided bound to a zero-free half-plane is a theorem of Landau from 1905 [68]. Its content is that positivity forbids cancellation in a transform, so the transform converges until it meets a singularity on the real axis.

Theorem 19.4

A Mellin integral of a nonnegative function is analytic to the right of its abscissa of convergence and singular at that real point

[68]
Statement

Let H be measurable on [1,\infty), bounded on bounded intervals, and H(x) \ge 0 for x \ge x_0. Let \sigma_c be the infimum of the real \sigma for which F(\sigma) = \int_1^\infty H(x)\,x^{-\sigma-1}\,\dd x converges (the abscissa of convergence), and suppose \sigma_c < \infty. Then F(s) is analytic for \Re s > \sigma_c, and if \sigma_c > -\infty, F has no analytic continuation to any disc around the real point \sigma_c.

In plain terms

If you average a function that is eventually nonnegative against x^{-s}, the average converges until the first point on the real axis where the continued function breaks down. No cancellation can carry it past that point.

Why it is needed

It is the classical engine, formalized as Formalism.landauEq (Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/LandauEq.lean) and used in the unwindowed endgame landau_entire, off the path from Main. The windowed theorem replaces it.

Idea

Expand F in a Taylor series at a real point \sigma_1 > \sigma_c. Its coefficients are \int H(x)(\log x)^k x^{-\sigma_1-1}\,\dd x/k!, which are nonnegative. If F were analytic on a disc around \sigma_c, the series would converge at a real point \sigma_2 < \sigma_c, and with nonnegative terms one may exchange the sum and the integral, which shows that the integral itself converges at \sigma_2, a contradiction.

Proof sketch

[14, ch. 15]

For \sigma_2 < \sigma_c < \sigma_1 with F analytic on a disc around \sigma_c containing \sigma_2, the series F(\sigma_2) = \sum_k \frac{(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^k}{k!}\int_1^\infty H(x)(\log x)^k x^{-\sigma_1-1}\,\dd x converges, and Tonelli’s theorem turns this double sum of nonnegative terms into \int_1^\infty H(x)x^{-\sigma_2-1}\,\dd x < \infty [14, ch. 15].

Used in

Corollary 19.5 applies it, and Theorem 19.7 replaces it with a version that needs positivity only on windows.

Applied to a smoothed prime sum with an allowance subtracted, it gives the classical consequence. We state it for G_0 and for \psi to show the role of the sign; both are classical, and the proof is our arrangement.

Corollary 19.5

A one-sided bound on the prime sums at every large X excludes zeros to the right of its exponent

[14]
Statement

Let 0 < \alpha < 1.

  1. If G_0(X) \le CX^\alpha for all X \ge X_0, then \zeta(s) \ne 0 for \Re s > \alpha.
  2. If \psi(x) - x \ge -Cx^\alpha for all x \ge x_0, then \zeta(s) \ne 0 for \Re s > \alpha. The same conclusion follows from \psi(x) - x \le Cx^\alpha, but only because \zeta has no real zero in (0,1).
In plain terms

A smoothed count that never runs far ahead of its expected value, or an unsmoothed count that never falls far behind it, leaves no room for a zero to the right of the allowance’s exponent.

Why it is needed

This is the unwindowed endgame, which the proof would use if its bound held at every scale (Why windows, and what they cost explains why it does not).

Idea

The allowance minus the function is nonnegative. Its transform has a pole at \alpha and one at each zero; at a real zero the residue’s sign would drive the transform to -\infty, which a nonnegative integrand forbids, and Landau’s theorem does the rest.

Proof

Part 1. Since G_0 is bounded on [1, X_0], after enlarging C we may assume H(x) = Cx^\alpha - G_0(x) \ge 0 for all x \ge 1. By Theorem 7.4's transform \int_1^\infty S(x)x^{-s-1}\,\dd x = -\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)/(s(s-1)) and the transform (s-1)^{-2} - (1+\gamma_E)(s-1)^{-1} of the main term, for \Re s > 1

F(s) = \int_1^\infty H(x)x^{-s-1}\,\dd x = \frac{C}{s-\alpha} - \Phi_0(s),\qquad \Phi_0(s) = \frac{-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)}{s(s-1)} - \frac{1}{(s-1)^2} + \frac{1+\gamma_E}{s-1}.

The Laurent expansions -\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s) = \frac1{s-1} - \gamma_E + O(s-1) and \frac{1}{s(s-1)} = \frac{1}{s-1} - 1 + O(s-1) show that \Phi_0 is regular at s = 1, so on \Re s > 0 its only poles are the zeros \rho of \zeta, each with residue -m_\rho/(\rho(\rho-1)). On the real half-line (\alpha, \infty), then, F is analytic except at real zeros. If \beta were the largest real zero above \alpha, Landau’s theorem would make \beta = \sigma_c, and as \sigma \downarrow \beta, F(\sigma) \approx -\frac{m_\beta}{\beta(1-\beta)}\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma - \beta} \to -\infty, impossible for an integral of a nonnegative function. So there is no real zero above \alpha, F is analytic on (\alpha,\infty), Landau’s theorem gives \sigma_c \le \alpha, F is analytic on \Re s > \alpha, and so is \Phi_0, which leaves no room for a zero there.

Part 2. By Equation (7.2), H(x) = \psi(x) - x + Cx^\alpha \ge 0 has transform F(s) = \frac{C}{s-\alpha} + \frac1s\bigl(-\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s) - \frac{s}{s-1}\bigr), and a real zero \beta > \alpha gives F(\sigma) \approx -\frac{m_\beta}{\beta(\sigma - \beta)} \to -\infty, so part 1’s argument applies. For the upper bound the residue changes sign, and real zeros must be excluded by the separate fact \zeta(\sigma) < 0 on (0,1) (The four mirror images of a zero).

In Lean

Formalism.zetaLandau in Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaLandau.lean

The single-function form for G_0, the proposition Formalism.ZetaLandau of Formalism/StatementU.lean, proved as Formalism.zetaLandau; it accepts a bound on either side (s_0 = \pm1), the lower side being usable because \zeta has no real zero in (0,1), as in part 2. The family form is Formalism.HC.Landau.landau_family in .../TotientGaloisClasses/Landau.lean. Neither is on the path from Main.

def ZetaLandau : Prop :=
  ∀ s₀ : ℝ, (s₀ = 1 ∨ s₀ = -1) → ∀ θ : ℝ, 0 < θ → θ < 1 →
  (∃ C x₀ : ℝ, ∀ x : ℝ, x₀ ≤ x → s₀ * Gz x ≤ C * x ^ θ) →
  ∀ s : ℂ, θ < s.re → riemannZeta s ≠ 0
Used in

The windowed theorem Theorem 19.7 has the same conclusion as part 1, from a hypothesis on windows only.

The allowance Cx^\alpha enters only through the pole C/(s - \alpha) of its transform. That is the whole role of the exponent: a pole at \alpha is harmless, and a pole to its right is not.

19.6Why windows, and what they cost#

The proof does not deliver a bound at every large x. It delivers, for each primitive character and each small \varepsilon, a bound

G_r(x) \le x^{1/2 + 9\varepsilon}\qquad\text{for every large } x \text{ in a window } [Y, Y^{3/2}],
(19.6)

for a sequence of Y tending to infinity, and nothing between the windows. (G_r is the combination of Definition 19.11; for now read it as G_0.) The reason is upstream. The bound comes from a construction at the scale x whose arithmetic input, the code’s VWin, bounds certain Galois cohomology groups of abelian number fields cut out of cyclotomic fields only for x in windows [Y, Y^2] found by a pigeonhole over finitely many exceptional twists (chapter The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology). The code cuts windows [Z, Z^{3/2}] out of those (winPairs), hence the exponent \tfrac32. Between windows the proof knows nothing about G_r.

In the Lean formalization Formalism.HC.HasWindows in Formalism/SharpRestriction/RamificationFrobenius/TotientGaloisClasses/Window.lean

A set of reals has windows of exponent la when it contains [Y, Y^{\mathtt{la}}] for arbitrarily large Y; on the spine la is \tfrac32.

def HasWindows (S : Set ℝ) (la : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ y : ℝ, ∃ Y : ℝ, y ≤ Y ∧ ∀ x : ℝ, Y ≤ x → x ≤ Y ^ la → x ∈ S

Landau’s classical argument cannot use such a bound: its transform integrates Cx^\alpha - G(x) over all of [1,\infty), and between windows that difference may be negative.

For a single zero the windows are enough. In u = \log x a window [Y, Y^{3/2}] is [U, \tfrac32 U] with U = \log Y, of length \tfrac12 U, growing with Y. The wave of a pair \beta \pm i\gamma, divided by the allowance e^{\alpha u}, is A e^{(\beta - \alpha)u}\cos(\gamma u + \phi), with a crest every 2\pi/\gamma units of u. Once \tfrac12 U > 2\pi/\gamma every window contains a crest, and once A e^{(\beta-\alpha)U} exceeds the rest, that crest breaks the bound inside the window. For \gamma = 14 a window starting at Y = 10^{10}, of length 11.5, contains about 25 crests.

With infinitely many zeros the waves might conspire to stay low exactly on the windows. Ruling that out needs a tool that reads G on one window only and still sees the poles of the transform. The code’s tool is the sequence of Taylor coefficients of the Laplace transform at a real point.

19.7The windowed one-sided Landau theorem#

This section is the reconstruction the chapter promised. The code proves it in 28 of the 32 files of the folder Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/DedekindLFunctions/LandauTheorems; the other four (ChCore, ChTop, ChBalance, mertensUpper) are not part of this argument. We follow the code’s argument step by step and name the declaration at each step. Where a step is ours (an explanation, a choice of words, a numerical check), we say so.

The theorem is stated for a finite family of characters with positive weights, because that is how the code uses it.

Definition 19.6 A weighted family of characters and its combined sum

A weighted family is a finite list of Dirichlet characters \chi_1, \dots, \chi_n, each either the trivial character modulo 1 or nontrivial (of any modulus), with weights a_1, \dots, a_n > 0. Write G_\chi = G_0 when \chi is trivial modulo 1 and G_\chi = g_\chi otherwise (the code’s Gchi). The combined sum is the real-valued function

G(y) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,\Re\,G_{\chi_i}(y)\qquad(y \ge 1).
(19.7)

It is not a count of primes with positive weights in general, since \Re\chi_i(n) can be negative; what is positive is each weight a_i on a whole sum.

In the Lean formalization Deduction.CharFamily in Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/DedekindLFunctions/CharFamily.lean

The family, its combined sum Gm, and the zero-free conclusion.

structure CharFamily where
  ι : Type
  [fin : Fintype ι]
  N : ι → ℕ
  [nz : ∀ i, NeZero (N i)]
  χ : ∀ i, DirichletCharacter ℂ (N i)
  a : ι → ℝ
  a_pos : ∀ i, 0 < a i
  adm : ∀ i, N i = 1 ∨ χ i ≠ 1

def Gm (F : CharFamily) (y : ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i, F.a i * (Gchi (F.χ i) y).re

def ZeroFree (F : CharFamily) (θ : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i, ∀ s : ℂ, θ < s.re → DirichletCharacter.LFunction (F.χ i) s ≠ 0
Theorem 19.7

An upper bound C\,y^\alpha on windows [Y,Y^{1+\delta}] for arbitrarily large Y excludes every zero of the family to the right of \alpha

Statement

Let G be the combined sum of a weighted family (\chi_i, a_i). Let 0 < \alpha < 1, \delta > 0, and C \in \RR. Suppose that for every Y_0 there is Y \ge Y_0 with

G(y) \le C\,y^\alpha\qquad\text{for all } y \in [Y, Y^{1+\delta}].
(19.8)

Then L(s,\chi_i) \ne 0 for every i and every s with \Re s > \alpha.

In plain terms

If a positively weighted combination of smoothed prime sums stays below a ceiling y^\alpha on stretches [Y, Y^{1+\delta}] that recur as far out as we like, then none of its L-functions has a zero to the right of \alpha. Nothing is assumed between the stretches, or about how negative the combination becomes.

Why it is needed

This is where the hypothesis is forced. Upstream produces the bound Equation (19.6) only on windows, and without a windowed form of Landau’s theorem that bound would prove nothing.

Idea

Pass to the logarithmic scale and take the Laplace transform \Phi. Its Taylor coefficients at a real point \sigma are integrals of G against Gamma kernels u^k e^{-\sigma u}/k!, which for a well chosen k put almost all their mass on one window. On the window the one-sided bound controls the coefficients, through the identity \abs t + t = 2\max(t,0), at the rate (\sigma - \alpha)^{-k}. A zero to the right of \alpha is a pole of \Phi closer than \sigma - \alpha to some point of the line \Re s = \sigma, and a pole at distance d makes the coefficients grow like d^{-k}. The two rates are incompatible.

Proof

The proof assembles the five lemmas of the subsections below, in the order of the code’s lemmaL and landau_window. Let \mathsf G(u) = G(e^u) and let \Phi be its Laplace transform (Lemma 19.8); let \mathcal Z be the set of its poles. Suppose some L(s_0,\chi_i) = 0 with \Re s_0 > \alpha.

Steps
  1. Mathlib’s nonvanishing of Dirichlet L-functions on \Re s \ge 1 (charFamily_LFunction_ne_zero_of_one_le_re) gives \Re s_0 < 1, so s_0 \in \mathcal Z by Lemma 19.8.
s_0 \in \mathcal Z,\qquad \alpha < \Re s_0 < 1.
  1. The hypothesis Equation (19.8) gives, through windowHyp_of_rpow and windowHypU_of_windowHyp, for every \nu > 0 arbitrarily large U = \log Y with \mathsf G(u) \le R(u) = \abs C e^{\alpha u} on [U, (1+\delta)U] and \int_U^{(1+\delta)U} R(u)e^{-\alpha u}\,\dd u = \abs C\delta U \le e^{\nu U}.
\int_U^{(1+\delta)U} R(u)\,e^{-\alpha u}\,\dd u \le e^{\nu U}.
  1. Lemma 19.9 turns this into an upper bound for the coefficients: there are \sigma > 2 and C_2 such that for every \nu > 0 there are arbitrarily large U and k \ge U with, for all real \gamma,
\abs{b_k(\sigma + i\gamma)} + b_k(\sigma) \le C_2\,e^{\nu U}(\sigma - \alpha)^{-k}.
  1. Every pole has real part below 1 < \sigma (landau_pole_re_le gives at most 2 in general), so Lemma 19.10 applies and turns the pole s_0 into a lower bound: there are \gamma, C_3 > 0, C_4 \ge 0, and 0 < d < d' \le \sigma - \alpha such that for every k,
\abs{b_k(\sigma + i\gamma)} + b_k(\sigma) \ge C_3\,d^{-k} - C_4\,d'^{-k}.
  1. Combining steps 3 and 4 and multiplying by d^k: C_3 \le C_4(d/d')^k + C_2 e^{\nu U}(d/(\sigma-\alpha))^k \le (C_4 + C_2)\,e^{\nu k}(d/d')^k, using U \le k and d' \le \sigma - \alpha. Choose \nu = \tfrac12\log(d'/d) > 0 in step 3. Then the right side is (C_4 + C_2)(d/d')^{k/2}, which tends to 0 as U, and with it k, tends to infinity (landau_growth_contra, landau_window_contra). This contradicts C_3 > 0.
C_3 \le (C_4 + C_2)\Bigl(\frac{d}{d'}\Bigr)^{k/2} \to 0.

So no L(s,\chi_i) vanishes for \Re s > \alpha. The order of choices matters and is the code’s: \sigma and C_2 are fixed by step 3 before any zero is considered, d and d' are then fixed by the poles near the line \Re s = \sigma, and only then is \nu chosen; step 3 holds for every \nu.

theorem zeroFree_of_rpow_window (F : CharFamily) {θ δ C : ℝ} (hθ : 0 < θ) (hθ1 : θ < 1) (hδ : 0 < δ)

Used in

Theorem 19.12 applies it with \delta = \tfrac12 and C = 1 to the cyclic combination G_r of Definition 19.11.

We did not find this windowed form in the standard references: their statements of Landau’s theorem, and of its uses for oscillation of error terms, assume a one-sided bound at every large x [14, ch. 15]. The literature on oscillation theorems also has results that locate sign changes in bounded ranges of scales, and we have not compared them with this one. As stated here, with its Taylor-coefficient proof, the windowed form is the code’s.

The Laplace transform and its poles#

On the logarithmic scale u = \log y, put \mathsf G(u) = G(e^u) for u \ge 0 (the code’s gm), and let

\Phi(s) = \int_0^\infty \mathsf G(u)\,e^{-su}\,\dd u = \int_1^\infty G(y)\,y^{-s-1}\,\dd y.
(19.9)

This is the Laplace transform of \mathsf G, which is the Mellin transform of chapter What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations written in u; it is the code’s Φ, and not the function \Phi(s) of chapter Zeta on the whole plane. The code uses only a crude size bound, \abs{\mathsf G(u)} \le C_0e^{2u} for u \ge 0 (Gchi_growth), so the integral converges absolutely for \Re s > 2. Everything about \Phi that the proof uses is packaged in one structure.

In the Lean formalization Deduction.PoleData in Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/DedekindLFunctions/LandauZeroFreeCriterion.lean

The properties of \Phi used by the argument: measurability, the growth bound, the Laplace formula for \Re s > 2, continuation to \Re s > 0 off the set Z, isolation of Z, and a simple pole at each point of Z, with a positive real residue at real points.

structure PoleData (g : ℝ → ℝ) (Φ : ℂ → ℂ) (Z : Set ℂ) : Prop where
  meas : Measurable g
  growth : ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ u : ℝ, 0 ≤ u → |g u| ≤ C * Real.exp (2 * u)
  laplace : ∀ s : ℂ, 2 < s.re → Φ s = ∫ u in Ioi (0 : ℝ), (g u : ℂ) * cexp (-s * u)
  pos : ∀ ρ ∈ Z, 0 < ρ.re
  diff : DifferentiableOn ℂ Φ ({s : ℂ | 0 < s.re} \ Z)
  iso : ∀ z : ℂ, 0 < z.re → ∀ᶠ w in 𝓝[≠] z, w ∉ Z
  pole : ∀ ρ ∈ Z, ∃ c : ℂ, c ≠ 0 ∧ (ρ.im = 0 → 0 < c.re ∧ c.im = 0) ∧
    ∃ h : ℂ → ℂ, AnalyticAt ℂ h ρ ∧ ∀ᶠ s in 𝓝[≠] ρ, Φ s = c / (s - ρ) + h s
Lemma 19.8

The transform of a positively weighted family is analytic on \Re s>0 except for simple poles at the zeros, with a positive residue at every real zero

Statement

For a weighted family, \Phi continues analytically to \{\Re s > 0\} minus the set

\mathcal Z = \{\rho : \Re\rho > 0,\ L(\rho,\chi_i) = 0 \text{ or } L(\bar\rho,\chi_i) = 0 \text{ for some } i\},

which has no accumulation point in \Re s > 0. At each \rho \in \mathcal Z it has a simple pole with residue

c_\rho = -\frac{w_\rho}{\rho(\rho-1)},\qquad w_\rho = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{a_i}{2}\Bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{s=\rho}L(s,\chi_i) + \operatorname{ord}_{s=\rho}L(s,\overline{\chi_i})\Bigr) > 0.
(19.10)

In particular c_\rho \ne 0, and c_\rho > 0 when \rho is real.

In plain terms

The transform has a pole at every zero of every L-function in the family and nowhere else to the right of the imaginary axis, with strength the total weighted multiplicity, positive because every weight is.

Why it is needed

Poles are what the coefficients detect, and the sign at a real pole is what makes a one-sided bound enough; with mixed weights, zeros could cancel or a real pole could carry a negative residue.

Idea

Take the real part of g_\chi as \tfrac12(g_\chi + g_{\bar\chi}), which holds because \overline{g_\chi(y)} = g_{\bar\chi}(y). Each piece has the transform Equation (19.4) (or \Phi_0 for \zeta), whose only poles in \Re s > 0 are the zeros, with residue -\operatorname{ord}/(\rho(\rho-1)), because the main term cancels the pole at s = 1. Add with the weights a_i/2.

Proof

For each \chi of the family the code builds the continuation in poleData_char from an abstract lemma, poleData_abstract, applied to P(s) = (s-1)\zeta(s) for the trivial character and to P(s) = L(s,\chi) otherwise: the function -\bigl(P'(s)/P(s) - s P'(1)/P(1)\bigr)/(s(s-1)), plus the term 1/s for \zeta only, which matches its main term, is analytic wherever s \ne 0 and P(s) \ne 0, including s = 1, and has a simple pole of residue -m_\rho/(\rho(\rho-1)) at a zero of order m_\rho \ge 1 (logDeriv_local gives the local form of P'/P). For \zeta the value P'(1) = \gamma_E comes from Mathlib’s tendsto_riemannZeta_sub_one_div, which is how (1+\gamma_E)X enters. The identity \overline{g_\chi(y)} = g_{\bar\chi}(y) is Gchi_conj, and \overline{L(\bar s,\chi)} = L(s,\bar\chi) is in LFunctionConj.lean. Then poleData defines \Phi = \sum_i \frac{a_i}{2}(\Phi_{\chi_i} + \Phi_{\bar\chi_i}), so the residues add to Equation (19.10), and positivity of w_\rho is the single inequality 0 < \frac{a_{i_0}}{2}(\operatorname{ord} + \operatorname{ord}) for an index i_0 at which \rho is a zero, plus nonnegativity of the other terms. For real \rho \in (0,1), \rho(\rho-1) < 0, so c_\rho = w_\rho/(\rho(1-\rho)) > 0. We read the statements of these declarations and the assembly in poleData (poleData.lean, 404 lines); the residue computation is classical and is the one in the proof of Proposition 19.3.

theorem poleData (F : CharFamily) : ∃ Φ : ℂ → ℂ, PoleData (gm F) Φ (zeroSet F), where gm F u = Gm F (Real.exp u) and zeroSet F is the set \mathcal Z.

Used in

The residue enters the lower bound Lemma 19.10; its positivity at real points is used in case (a) there.

Now the coefficients. For a point z with \Re z > 2 define

b_k(z) = \frac{(-1)^k\,\Phi^{(k)}(z)}{k!},\qquad\text{so that}\qquad \Phi(z - w) = \sum_{k \ge 0} b_k(z)\,w^k
(19.11)

near w = 0: they are the Taylor coefficients of \Phi expanded leftward from z, toward the poles. Differentiating under the integral (iteratedDeriv_laplace, legitimate because of the growth bound) gives the formula the argument runs on, landau_coeff:

b_k(z) = \int_0^\infty \mathsf G(u)\,\frac{u^k e^{-zu}}{k!}\,\dd u\qquad(\Re z > 2).
(19.12)

Write z = \sigma + i\gamma. The kernel is K_k(u)e^{-i\gamma u} with

K_k(u) = \frac{u^k\,e^{-\sigma u}}{k!} \ge 0.
(19.13)

The kernel is a window#

The kernel K_k is, up to the factor \sigma^{k+1}, the Gamma probability density with shape k+1 and rate \sigma: its total mass is \int_0^\infty K_k = \sigma^{-(k+1)} (kernel_integral), its mean is (k+1)/\sigma, and its standard deviation is \sqrt{k+1}/\sigma. So when k is large it lives on a stretch of relative width about 1/\sqrt k around u = k/\sigma. Choosing k proportional to \sigma U puts it on the window [U, (1+\delta)U]. This is the mechanism that lets the argument read \mathsf G on one window only.

Two estimates make this precise, and both are in the code.

On the window, the kernel is at most a pure exponential. For every a > 0 and u \ge 0,

\frac{u^k e^{-au}}{k!} \le a^{-k},
(19.14)

because (au)^k/k! \le e^{au} (one term of the exponential series). This is landau_kernel_max. With a = \sigma - \alpha it gives K_k(u) \le (\sigma - \alpha)^{-k}e^{-\alpha u}, so the kernel, against the allowance e^{\alpha u}, costs at most (\sigma - \alpha)^{-k} per unit length.

Off the window, the kernel is exponentially smaller. The tail lemma landau_tails says: for every \delta > 0 there are \sigma > 2 and C_1 such that for every U \ge 1 there is an integer k \ge U with

\int_{(0,\infty)\setminus[U,(1+\delta)U]} \frac{u^k e^{-(\sigma-2)u}}{k!}\,\dd u \le C_1\,\sigma^{-k}.
(19.15)

The exponent \sigma - 2 instead of \sigma absorbs the crude growth e^{2u} of \mathsf G. The code’s choices are \lambda = 2 + 6/\delta, \kappa = \lambda(1+\delta) (the code’s M), \sigma = \kappa (2 + \lambda), and k = \lceil (1 + \delta/2)\sigma U\rceil, which puts the kernel’s mean at about (1 + \delta/2)U, the midpoint of the window.

ProofProof of the tail bound, following landau_tails

Write \sigma' = \sigma - 2 and V = (1+\delta)U. For u outside [U,V] one of the exponents \lambda(u - V), \lambda(U - u) is nonnegative, so 1 \le e^{\lambda(u - V)} + e^{\lambda(U - u)} (landau_tails_chernoff; this is a Chernoff bound [69]). Multiplying the kernel by this and integrating exactly with kernel_integral,

\text{tail} \le e^{-\lambda V}(\sigma' - \lambda)^{-(k+1)} + e^{\lambda U}(\sigma' + \lambda)^{-(k+1)}.

To compare each term with \sigma^{-k} the code uses (\sigma/a)^k \le e^{k(\sigma - a)/a} for a > 0 (from 1 + t \le e^t) in landau_tails_pow. The arithmetic, which we checked by hand, rests on two identities that follow from the choices: (1 + \delta/2)(2 + \lambda) = \kappa - 1 and (1 + \delta/2)(\lambda - 2) = \lambda + 1. For the first term, \sigma - (\sigma' - \lambda) = 2 + \lambda and \sigma' - \lambda = (\kappa -1)(2+\lambda), so it is at most \exp\bigl(-\lambda V + k/(\kappa -1)\bigr)\,\sigma^{-k}/(\sigma'-\lambda); since k \le (1+\delta/2)\sigma U + 1 = \kappa (\kappa -1)U + 1 and \lambda V = MU, the exponent is at most 1/(\kappa -1) \le 1. For the second term, the exponent is \lambda U - k(\lambda - 2)/(\sigma' + \lambda), which is at most 0 because k(\lambda - 2) \ge (\lambda + 1)\sigma U \ge \lambda(\sigma' + \lambda)U, the last step being \lambda^2 - 2\lambda \le \sigma. Hence C_1 = e/(\sigma - 2 - \lambda) + 1/(\sigma - 2 + \lambda) works, and k \ge (1 + \delta/2)\sigma U \ge U.

Example

On the spine \delta = \tfrac12, so \lambda = 14, \kappa = 21, \sigma = 336, k = \lceil 420\,U\rceil, and C_1 = 0.011368. With mpmath’s incomplete Gamma function: at U = 1, k = 420, the kernel u^k e^{-334u}/k! has mean 1.2605, standard deviation 0.061, and a fraction 1.1\times10^{-4} of its mass outside [1, 1.5]; the tail integral is 3.6\times10^{-1067}, below C_1\sigma^{-k} = 9.8\times10^{-1064} and far below the window rate (\sigma - 0.6)^{-k} = 1.8\times10^{-1061}. At U = 10 the fraction outside is 3.0\times10^{-32}. The large \sigma is what narrows the kernel: at U = 10 with k = \lceil 1.25\sigma U\rceil, the fraction outside [10, 15] is 0.28 for \sigma = 2.5, 0.027 for \sigma = 10, and 1.5\times10^{-6} for \sigma = 50.

Aside

Our reading: \sigma^{k+1}b_k(\sigma) is the Gamma-kernel average of \mathsf G around u = k/\sigma, and its limit as k, \sigma \to \infty with k/\sigma = u fixed is \mathsf G(u), the Post and Widder inversion formula for the Laplace transform [70] [71]. The code never takes the limit and uses only the concentration estimates above. The reading explains the choice of instrument: Taylor coefficients at a real point can be localized on the u-axis, and they are also what a pole controls.

The one-sided inequality#

Here the one-sidedness enters, through one line of algebra. For real t, \abs t + t = 2\max(t, 0).

Lemma 19.9

On a window where the sum is below its ceiling, the absolute value of a Taylor coefficient off the axis plus the real coefficient on the axis is at most the ceiling’s cost

Statement

Suppose \abs{\mathsf G(u)} \le C_0e^{2u} for u \ge 0, let \sigma, C_1 be as in Equation (19.15), and let 0 < \alpha < 1. If \mathsf G \le R on [U, (1+\delta)U] with R \ge 0 there, then for the k \ge U of Equation (19.15) and every real \gamma,

\abs{b_k(\sigma + i\gamma)} + b_k(\sigma) \le \frac{2}{(\sigma-\alpha)^k}\int_U^{(1+\delta)U} R(u)\,e^{-\alpha u}\,\dd u + \frac{2C_0C_1}{\sigma^k}.
(19.16)
In plain terms

The size of a coefficient at any height plus the real coefficient on the axis sees only where the function is positive. On the window that part is below the ceiling, and off the window the kernel is negligible.

Why it is needed

It is the only use of the hypothesis, and the windowed replacement for the nonnegativity of Cx^\alpha - G(x) in Landau’s proof.

Idea

Since \mathsf G and K_k are real, b_k(\sigma) = \int\mathsf G K_k, and \abs{b_k(\sigma + i\gamma)} \le \int\abs{\mathsf G}K_k because \abs{e^{-i\gamma u}} = 1. Adding, the integrand becomes (\abs{\mathsf G} + \mathsf G)K_k = 2\max(\mathsf G, 0)K_k.

Proof

By Equation (19.12) and the two remarks of the idea,

\abs{b_k(\sigma + i\gamma)} + b_k(\sigma) \le \int_0^\infty \bigl(\abs{\mathsf G(u)} + \mathsf G(u)\bigr)K_k(u)\,\dd u.

Split the integral at the window. On [U,(1+\delta)U], \abs{\mathsf G} + \mathsf G = 2\max(\mathsf G,0) \le 2R because \mathsf G \le R and R \ge 0, and K_k(u) \le (\sigma - \alpha)^{-k}e^{-\alpha u} by Equation (19.14) with a = \sigma - \alpha; this gives the first term. Off the window, \abs{\mathsf G} + \mathsf G \le 2\abs{\mathsf G} \le 2C_0e^{2u} and e^{2u}K_k(u) = u^ke^{-(\sigma-2)u}/k!, whose integral there is at most C_1\sigma^{-k} by Equation (19.15); this gives the second term. The code’s statement, landau_window_ineq, is this inequality before the tail bound is inserted, and landau_window_key combines it with landau_tails and the window hypothesis.

theorem landau_window_key {g : ℝ → ℝ} {Φ : ℂ → ℂ} {Z : Set ℂ} (hP : PoleData g Φ Z) {θ δ : ℝ}

    ∃ σ : ℝ, 2 < σ ∧ ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ η : ℝ, 0 < η → ∀ U₀ : ℝ, ∃ U : ℝ, U₀ ≤ U ∧ ∃ k : ℕ, U ≤ k ∧ ∀ γ : ℝ,
      ‖(-1) ^ k * iteratedDeriv k Φ ((σ : ℂ) + γ * I) / (k.factorial : ℂ)‖ +
        ((-1) ^ k * iteratedDeriv k Φ (σ : ℂ) / (k.factorial : ℂ)).re ≤
        C * Real.exp (η * U) / (σ - θ) ^ k
Used in

Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 19.7, with R(u) = \abs C e^{\alpha u}, so that the window integral is \abs C\delta U \le e^{\nu U} for large U, and \sigma^{-k} \le e^{\nu U}(\sigma - \alpha)^{-k}; together the constant is C_2 = 2 + 2C_0C_1 in the code’s normalization.

What a pole does to the coefficients#

The other side of the comparison is complex analysis. If \Phi has a simple pole c/(s - \rho) near z and is otherwise analytic on a disc around z, then the pole term contributes c\,(z - \rho)^{-k-1} to b_k(z), exactly, since (-1)^k\frac{\dd^k}{\dd s^k}(s - \rho)^{-1}/k! = (s-\rho)^{-k-1}, and the analytic remainder contributes at most B\,d'^{-k} for any d' smaller than a radius on which it is analytic, by the Cauchy estimates [15]. This is landau_pole_asym and landau_cauchy. So the nearest pole sets the growth rate of the coefficients: distance d means growth d^{-k}.

The difficulty is the word “nearest”: if the pole nearest to the real point \sigma is complex, b_k(\sigma) collects rotating phases from a conjugate pair and can be small. The code handles this with a dichotomy.

Lemma 19.10

A pole of the transform to the right of \alpha forces the off-axis plus on-axis coefficient to grow faster than (\sigma-\alpha)^{-k}

Statement

Let \Phi satisfy the properties of Lemma 19.8, let \sigma > 2 exceed the real part of every pole, and suppose some \rho_0 \in \mathcal Z has \Re\rho_0 > \alpha. Then there are a real \gamma, constants C_3 > 0 and C_4 \ge 0, and radii 0 < d < d' \le \sigma - \alpha such that for every k \ge 0

\abs{b_k(\sigma + i\gamma)} + b_k(\sigma) \ge C_3\,d^{-k} - C_4\,d'^{-k}.
(19.17)
In plain terms

A zero to the right of \alpha is a pole of the transform closer than \sigma - \alpha to some point of the line \Re s = \sigma. At that point the coefficients grow at the rate set by the pole, and the coefficient on the real axis cannot cancel this growth.

Why it is needed

It is the lower bound that the window bound Lemma 19.9 contradicts. It uses the residue’s sign exactly once, for a real pole.

Idea

Look at the poles in the closed disc of radius \sigma - \alpha about \sigma; there are finitely many (landau_finite). Either the pole nearest to \sigma is real and nothing else is as close, and then b_k(\sigma) itself grows with the positive residue; or some pole is horizontally closer to the line \Re s = \sigma than any pole is to \sigma, and then a point \sigma + i\gamma at its height has it as unique nearest pole, while b_k(\sigma) stays small because \sigma is farther from every pole.

Proof

landau_dichotomy splits into two cases.

(a) The nearest pole is real. Every pole \rho satisfies \sigma - \Re\rho \ge D, where D is the distance from \sigma to the nearest pole \rho_s. Then D = \abs{\sigma - \rho_s} \ge \sigma - \Re\rho_s \ge D, so \rho_s = \beta is real (eq_ofReal_sub_of_dist_le_of_le_sub_re), and D = \sigma - \beta < \sigma - \alpha because \rho_0 has \sigma - \Re\rho_0 < \sigma - \alpha. By finiteness there is r > \sigma - \beta with no other pole within r of \sigma. Take \gamma = 0, d = \sigma - \beta, and d' \in (d, \min(r, \sigma-\alpha)). By the pole expansion, \abs{b_k(\sigma) - c_\beta(\sigma - \beta)^{-k-1}} \le C_4\,d'^{-k}, and c_\beta is real and positive by Lemma 19.8. So, using only \abs{b_k(\sigma)} \ge 0 (as the code does), \abs{b_k(\sigma)} + b_k(\sigma) \ge c_\beta d^{-k-1} - C_4\,d'^{-k}, and we take C_3 = c_\beta/d.

(b) Some pole is horizontally closer. Otherwise there are D \le \sigma - \alpha with no pole within D of \sigma and a pole \rho_1 with \sigma - \Re\rho_1 < D. landau_nearest picks \gamma close to \Im\rho_1 and outside the finitely many heights at which two poles of the relevant disc are equidistant from \sigma + i\gamma (landau_nearest_equi). Then z = \sigma + i\gamma has a unique nearest pole \rho, at distance d = \abs{z - \rho} < D, and no other pole within some r \in (d, D]. With d' = (d + r)/2, the pole expansion gives \abs{b_k(z)} \ge \abs{c_\rho}\,d^{-k-1} - C_4\,d'^{-k}, and since \Phi is analytic on the disc of radius D > d' about \sigma, the Cauchy estimate gives \abs{b_k(\sigma)} \le C_4'\,d'^{-k}. So \abs{b_k(z)} + b_k(\sigma) \ge \abs{c_\rho}d^{-k-1} - (C_4 + C_4')d'^{-k}, and we take C_3 = \abs{c_\rho}/d, which is positive because c_\rho \ne 0.

In both cases d < d' \le \sigma - \alpha.

theorem landau_window {g : ℝ → ℝ} {Φ : ℂ → ℂ} {Z : Set ℂ} (hP : PoleData g Φ Z) {θ δ : ℝ}
    (hθ : 0 < θ) (hθ1 : θ < 1) (hδ : 0 < δ) (hW : WindowHypU g θ δ) : ∀ ρ ∈ Z, ρ.re ≤ θ
Used in

A common misreading

The sign of the residue is used only in case (a), and there it is essential. If a real pole had a negative residue, then b_k(\sigma) \approx -\abs{c_\beta}d^{-k-1} would be negative, and since b_k(\sigma) is real, \abs{b_k(\sigma)} + b_k(\sigma) = 0: the functional would see nothing. This is the same fact as in Which way a zero pushes, that an upper bound sees a real zero because a real zero pushes G_0 up, now in the language of transforms. The explanation of why the code splits into two cases, and the description of case (b) as the case where the real point is “farther from every pole”, are ours.

19.8The mechanism in numbers#

We tested each step on the real primes, with one hypothetical zero added. The computation is ours; it uses a sieve of \Lambda up to 2\times10^7, the first 1000 zero pairs of \zeta from mpmath, and Simpson’s rule on u \in [0, \log(2\times10^7)] with step 10^{-4}.

ExampleThe coefficient formula, from primes and from zeros

Take \mathsf G(u) = G_0(e^u) and \sigma = 2.5. The transform has the closed form \Phi_0(s) of Corollary 19.5, and mpmath gives \Phi_0(2.5) = 0.6840302. The integral Equation (19.12) computed from the primes gives b_0(2.5) = 0.6840302. Integrating Equation (19.2) term by term gives a second formula,

b_k(z) = \frac{\log 2\pi}{z^{k+1}} - \sum_\rho \frac{1}{\rho(\rho-1)(z - \rho)^{k+1}} - \sum_{m \ge 1}\frac{1}{2m(2m+1)(z + 2m)^{k+1}},
(19.18)

in which every zero is visibly a pole with residue -1/(\rho(\rho-1)). The two sides agree:

ExampleA hypothetical zero, detected

Now add the wave of a hypothetical pair \rho^* = 0.8 \pm 14i to \mathsf G, take \alpha = 0.6, \sigma = 2.5, and z = 2.5 + 14i. The hypothetical pole is at distance \abs{z - \rho^*} = 1.7 from z, closer than \sigma - \alpha = 1.9, while the nearest true zero, \tfrac12 + 14.1347i, is at distance 2.0045, farther than 1.9. The prime-side integral sees the added wave: at k = 5 it gives b_5(z) = (2.81563 + 0.39126i)\times10^{-4}, 3.7 times the size of the value without the wave, and agrees with Equation (19.18) plus the two extra poles to a relative error below 10^{-7}. The table shows the functional of Lemma 19.9 measured in units of the window bound’s rate, \mathcal N_k = (\sigma - \alpha)^k\bigl(\abs{b_k(z)} + b_k(\sigma)\bigr), from Equation (19.18):

k 0 10 20 40 80 160 320
\mathcal N_k, true zeros only 0.796 0.0487 3.89\times10^{-3} 3.05\times10^{-4} 3.44\times10^{-5} 4.74\times10^{-7} 9.0\times10^{-11}
\mathcal N_k, with \rho^* 0.796 0.0575 0.0309 0.256 21.9 1.60\times10^{5} 8.59\times10^{12}

Without the hypothetical zero, \mathcal N_k decays, eventually like (1.9/2.0045)^k, as the window bound allows. With it, \mathcal N_k grows like (1.9/1.7)^k = 1.118^k from k \approx 20 on, and from k = 40 on it agrees to within 0.2\% with the pole term alone, \abs{c^*}1.9^k/1.7^{k+1} with \abs{c^*} = 1/\abs{\rho^*(\rho^*-1)} = 0.005093. No constant in front of the window bound can survive this growth, which is the contradiction of step 5. The moderate \sigma = 2.5 is our choice for visibility; the code’s \sigma = 336 gives the same picture with a slower rate per step, (335.4/335.2)^k, over far more steps, k = 420U.

19.9One character at a time: the combination G_r#

The code does not apply the windowed theorem to \zeta alone, nor to one L-function at a time. It applies it, for each primitive character \chi, to a combination over the cyclic group that \chi generates.

Definition 19.11 The cyclic combination

Let \chi be a primitive Dirichlet character of order r (the smallest r \ge 1 with \chi^r = 1). For 1 \le j \le r-1 let (\chi^j)^* be the primitive character inducing \chi^j; the r characters (\chi^0)^* = 1, (\chi^1)^*, \dots, (\chi^{r-1})^* are distinct. The cyclic combination is the real-valued function

G_r(X) = G_0(X) + \frac{1}{3r+1}\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}\Re\,g_{(\chi^j)^*}(X).
(19.19)

It is the combined sum Equation (19.7) of the weighted family with weight 1 on the trivial character modulo 1 and weight 1/(3r+1) on each (\chi^j)^*, j \ne 0. For r = 1 (\chi trivial) it is G_0. It depends on \chi through the group it generates, and the code calls this bookkeeping object the cyclic level of \chi.

In the Lean formalization Formalism.HC.Level.Gm in Formalism/SharpRestriction/RamificationFrobenius/TotientGaloisClasses/ExplicitFormulaErrorOfHostConditions.lean

The weights and the combination. Level.cyc ψ is Level.ofSub (Subgroup.zpowers ψ.χ), whose KEPT is the image of the cyclic group under “primitive character inducing”, whose exceptional slot psK is none, and whose o is the order of the group. With psK = none, every weight wt is 1/(3o+1).

def Nt : Finset PChar := Λ.KEPT.erase PChar.one

def wt (ψ : PChar) : ℝ := if Λ.psK = some ψ then 1 else (3 * (Λ.o : ℝ) + 1)⁻¹

def Gm (y : ℝ) : ℝ := Formalism.Gz y + ∑ ψ ∈ Λ.Nt, Λ.wt ψ * (An.gChi ψ.χ y).re

We confirmed the weights in the code: 1 on G_0 (the term Formalism.Gz y, outside the sum) and (3r+1)^{-1} on every other kept character, since on the spine the exceptional slot is always empty. The code’s level_family (Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/PrimitiveCosets/LevelFamily.lean) shows that every such level is a weighted family in the sense of Definition 19.6, with the same sum and the same zero-free conclusion, and formB then applies the windowed theorem.

Why positive weights let one inequality control every L-function at once. By Lemma 19.8, the transform of G_r has at each \rho the residue -w_\rho/(\rho(\rho-1)) with

w_\rho = \operatorname{ord}_{s=\rho}\zeta(s) + \frac{1}{3r+1}\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}\operatorname{ord}_{s=\rho}L\bigl(s,(\chi^j)^*\bigr),

since the set \{(\chi^j)^*\} is closed under conjugation and the halves in Equation (19.10) recombine. Every term is nonnegative, so w_\rho > 0 as soon as any one of the r functions vanishes at \rho: one inequality on G_r excludes the zeros of all of them, and none can hide behind another. With mixed signs, in G_0 - g_\chi say, a common zero of \zeta and L(s,\chi) of equal order would leave no pole, and a real zero of L(s,\chi) alone would leave a negative residue that Lemma 19.10 cannot see. This is the integer counterpart of the warning after Lemma 9.7. Why the code uses the whole cyclic group with these weights is decided upstream, where exactly these characters are “kept” in a finite abelian group (chapter Paying for the chain: integrality, Galois representations, and the count that is bounded); on the endgame side any positive weights would do.

ExampleThe weights as a count

For n coprime to the modulus of \chi, (\chi^j)^*(n) = \chi^j(n), and \sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\chi^j(n) = r if \chi(n) = 1 and 0 otherwise. So, apart from the powers of the finitely many primes dividing the modulus, the prime-power part of G_r is \sum_{n \le X}\Lambda(n)\,w(n)\,(X/n - 1) with

w(n) = 1 + \frac{r\,\mathbf 1[\chi(n) = 1] - 1}{3r+1} = r\cdot\begin{cases}\dfrac{4}{3r+1} & \chi(n) = 1,\\[2ex] \dfrac{3}{3r+1} & \chi(n) \ne 1,\end{cases}

taking the real parts. For \chi_4 (r = 2) the weights are 8/7 on n \equiv 1 \bmod 4 and 6/7 on n \equiv 3 \bmod 4; for a character of order 4 modulo 5 they are 16/13 on n \equiv 1 \bmod 5 and 12/13 on the other classes. Our reading: the numbers 4/(3r+1) and 3/(3r+1), one of the first and r-1 of the second, add to 1, and they are exactly the coset proportions (4 \text{ or } 3)/(3o+1) that the code’s Frame.lam prescribes upstream, which fits the view that this weighting is what makes an averaged finite-group sum reproduce G_r (chapter Paying for the chain: integrality, Galois representations, and the count that is bounded). For \chi_4 at X = 10^6, G_0 = 11.0404 and g_{\chi_4} = -18.8504, so G_2 = 11.0404 - 18.8504/7 = 8.3475, against \sqrt{X} = 1000.

19.10The contract: from x^{1/2+9\varepsilon} on windows to the half-plane#

The windowed theorem needs a fixed exponent \alpha. The proof supplies a family of bounds, one for each small \varepsilon, with exponent \tfrac12 + 9\varepsilon, and the code turns the family into the half-plane in one step, with no iteration.

Theorem 19.12

If for every small \varepsilon the cyclic combination is at most x^{1/2+9\varepsilon} on windows [Y,Y^{3/2}], then neither \zeta nor any L(s,\chi^j) vanishes to the right of one half

Statement

Let \chi be a primitive character of order r. Suppose there is \varepsilon_1 > 0 such that for every \varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_1) there are a threshold x_1 and a set of scales containing windows [Y, Y^{3/2}] for arbitrarily large Y, with

G_r(x) \le x^{1/2 + 9\varepsilon}\qquad\text{for every scale } x \ge x_1 \text{ in the set.}
(19.20)

Then \zeta(s) \ne 0 and L(s, (\chi^j)^*) \ne 0 for every j and every s with \Re s > \tfrac12.

In plain terms

A bound slightly worse than the square root, on long recurring stretches of scales, for every degree of “slightly”, is exactly as good as the Riemann Hypothesis for the characters involved.

Why it is needed

Applied to every primitive \chi, which is one of its own (\chi^j)^*, it gives ZeroFreeAll, the hypothesis of Theorem 19.1.

Idea

Given a target point s with \Re s > \tfrac12, choose \varepsilon so small that \tfrac12 + 9\varepsilon is below \Re s with room to spare, and apply the windowed theorem once with that exponent.

Proof

This follows level_of_tiedWin. Let \Re s > \tfrac12 and \Delta = \min(\Re s - \tfrac12, \tfrac12) > 0. Choose \varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_1) with 9\varepsilon \le \Delta/2 (exists_small_eps), and put \alpha = \tfrac12 + \Delta/2, so that \tfrac12 < \alpha < 1 and \alpha < \Re s. For x \ge \max(x_1, 1) in the set, G_r(x) \le x^{1/2+9\varepsilon} \le x^\alpha. So the set \{x : G_r(x) \le x^\alpha\} has windows of exponent \tfrac32 (HasWindows.mono), and Theorem 19.7 with \delta = \tfrac12, C = 1, and the family of Definition 19.11 (this is formB via level_family and zeroFree_of_rpow_window) gives L(s', (\chi^j)^*) \ne 0 for all \Re s' > \alpha, in particular at s.

In Lean

theorem level_of_tiedWin {Λ : Level} {la : ℝ} (h112 : ChebyshevInequalityOnWindows @core @Tied Λ) (hB : Λ.FormBAt la)
    (h : ChebyshevInequalityAtWindowScale @core @Tied la Λ) : Λ.ZeroFreeLevel

Theorem 19.13 states where the hypothesis comes from.

There is no bootstrap here: each half-plane \Re s > \tfrac12 + \Delta/2 comes directly from one \varepsilon. The note’s step 4 ends with “bootstrap!!” [2], and on the path from Main nothing in this region iterates a weaker zero-free region into a stronger one, so we cannot say where the bootstrap lives in the code.

The scale dictionary is short. The window [Y, Y^{3/2}] is [U, \tfrac32U] in u = \log x, the allowance is x^{1/2+9\varepsilon}, and the Taylor index is k = \lceil 420\,U\rceil, proportional to \log Y. At that k a zero at \beta > \alpha wins by a factor of roughly ((\sigma - \alpha)/(\sigma - \beta))^k \approx e^{1.25(\beta - \alpha)U}, so the contradiction appears once \log Y is a large multiple of 1/(\beta - \alpha).

19.11What the rest of Part IV must supply#

Everything above is unconditional analysis. What remains is the hypothesis of Theorem 19.12, for every primitive \chi. The page names three inputs for the whole of Part IV, the inputs of UpperTheory.EveryCharacter as the code has them (MainConclusion.lean): Row0b, Galois representations attached to the automorphic representations that the chain uses (chapter Paying for the chain: integrality, Galois representations, and the count that is bounded); TLiftK with GeoOne, from which the tree proves Row0b (galoisLocalGlobalStrong_recParameter); and VWin, the bound on Galois cohomology on windows of scales, which the tree proves from Row0b (vwin_of_row, chapter The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology). The endgame meets them one level down, through a theorem whose three hypotheses are cut differently: Green, VWin, and a HypsAlt record. On the way from the three inputs the tree proves Green (green_of_regular) and the HypsAlt record (nonempty_hyps_definite_side_of_closed_bound), in every_character_of_theta_integrals_local_matching, so the card below states the interface at that level. We describe Green and HypsAlt only as far as we unfolded them; chapters Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices to The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology open the construction further, and chapter What the proof stands on traces the inputs to published theorems.

Theorem 19.13

From Green, VWin, and the HypsAlt record, every cyclic combination is at most x^{1/2+9\varepsilon} on windows [Y,Y^{3/2}], and every Dirichlet L-function is zero-free to the right of one half

Statement

Assume (i) GlobalTheory.GLq.Green, (ii) UpperTheory.Top.VWin, and (iii) that a record of type HypsAlt (Closed · LinkN) DefiniteSideCondition exists. Then for every primitive Dirichlet character \chi of order r there is \varepsilon_1 > 0 such that for every \varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_1) there is a family of data at scales x whose set of scales has windows [Y, Y^{3/2}] for arbitrarily large Y, and

G_r(x) \le x^{1/2 + 9\varepsilon}\qquad\text{at every large scale } x \text{ of the family.}
(19.21)

Consequently ZeroFreeAll holds, and with it the five theorems of Main.lean.

In plain terms

The rest of the proof is a machine that, given a primitive character and a small \varepsilon, finds long recurring stretches of scales on which the cyclic combination is at most x^{1/2+9\varepsilon}, and this chapter showed that such a machine proves the hypothesis for every Dirichlet L-function.

Why it is needed

The inequality Equation (19.21), with its exponent, windows, and quantifiers, is exactly what chapters Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices to The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology must produce.

Idea

The code splits the inequality in two: for each small \varepsilon a family exists whose scales have windows and whose data are “tied” there (from Green, VWin, and HypsAlt), and tied data at a scale x force G_r(x) \le x^{1/2+9\varepsilon} (a finite-group explicit formula).

Proof

The code’s route, step by step (zero_free_all_of_green_v_win and zeroFreeAll_of_topG); the last two steps are where this chapter’s proofs take over.

Steps
  1. Hosts on windows (UpperTheory.Top.supplyChi). From VWinAt ψ 401 the code builds, for every \varepsilon < 1/52, “hosts” at all scales of some windows of exponent \tfrac32 satisfying the requirement GChi ψ: the explicit-formula conditions EAtH for the cyclic level with constant 4, and the cohomology bound VVle. VWin asks, for each primitive character and certain abelian CM fields E built from it, that the sum, over all primes \ell and all Tate twists of \QQ_\ell/\ZZ_\ell below x^{401}, of \log\#\text{Sha}^1 of E with those coefficients be at most \exp(x^\varepsilon/2), at every scale x of a window [Y, Y^2] (chapter The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology defines these groups). (The code writes this as the \ZZ_\ell-length of each group times \log\ell, which is the logarithm of its order.) This is the input of chapter The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology.

AsideHow this matches the note’s step 6, in our reading

The note’s step 6 reads “W(\mathbb 1_{(0,1]} + (\sim X^\eta)\,\mathbb 1_{(0,1/X]}) \ge 0 gives > 1-\eta” [2], with W Weil’s functional of Definition 8.4. On the path from Main the code states no positivity of Weil’s functional and uses no indicator test functions; it proves the upper bound Equation (19.21) with an allowance. Our reading of the correspondence: for f = \mathbf 1_{(0,1]}, chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion found f * \tilde f = \min(1, 1/x) with transform 1/(s(1-s)), which is minus the smoothing kernel 1/(s(s-1)). The function \min(1, X/x) has transform X^s/(s(1-s)), so the zero side of W there is \sum_\rho X^\rho/(\rho(1-\rho)), which by Equation (19.2) is G_0(X) - \log 2\pi up to the trivial-zero tail (the prime side needs the regularization chapter Weil's explicit formula and the positivity criterion mentions, because the transform has poles at 0 and 1). So W on indicator-built functions, scaled to X, speaks about G_0(X). The note’s test function is a sum of two indicators rather than such a convolution, and in it the piece of size about X^\eta plays the allowance, whose transform C/(s-\alpha) has its pole at \alpha and so limits the conclusion to \Re s > \alpha, as “> 1 - \eta” limits the note’s. On this reading the note’s 1 - \eta corresponds to the code’s \tfrac12 + 9\varepsilon. Both are inequalities about primes with no zero in them, as in Theorem 8.9.

Recap
  • The five theorems of Main.lean follow from ZeroFreeAll, by Euler factors and the functional equation (Theorem 19.1).
  • G_0 and g_\chi are a constant, at most \log X, and one wave -X^\rho/(\rho(\rho-1)) per zero (Proposition 19.3); real zeros push up and complex zeros have crests, so an upper bound sees every off-line zero (Which way a zero pushes).
  • Landau’s theorem turns a one-sided bound at every large X into a zero-free half-plane (Corollary 19.5); the proof’s bound holds only on windows, because its cohomological input does (Why windows, and what they cost).
  • The windowed theorem (Theorem 19.7) uses Taylor coefficients of the Laplace transform: Gamma kernels localize them on a window (The kernel is a window), \abs t + t = 2\max(t,0) bounds them there by (\sigma-\alpha)^{-k} (Lemma 19.9), and a zero right of \alpha makes them grow like d^{-k}, d < \sigma - \alpha (Lemma 19.10), with positive weights making every residue count (Lemma 19.8).
  • Applied to G_r for each primitive \chi, a bound x^{1/2+9\varepsilon} on windows for every small \varepsilon gives the half-plane (Theorem 19.12). That bound, Equation (19.21), is what chapters Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices to The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology supply, through Green, VWin, and HypsAlt (Theorem 19.13), from the three inputs Row0b, TLiftK with GeoOne, and VWin.
