21.4Reading a form as a number: periods#

After m lifts the chain holds a form on U(X_m), a function on a finite set of classes with values in a vector space. To be compared with an integer budget it must become a number, and the standard way is a period: restrict the form to a smaller group and integrate it against a form there. The rule that decides when such an integral can be nonzero is the branching rule.

Restriction from U(k) to U(k-1)#

An irreducible representation of the compact unitary group U(k) is determined by its highest weight, a non-increasing sequence of integers \lambda = (\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_k). Restricting it to U(k-1), embedded as the matrices that fix the last basis vector, gives a representation of the smaller group, which breaks into irreducibles.

Theorem 21.5

Restricting an irreducible representation of U(k) to U(k-1) contains each irreducible exactly once if its weight interlaces and not at all otherwise

[86]
Statement

The restriction of the irreducible representation of U(k) with highest weight \lambda to U(k-1) is the direct sum, each with multiplicity one, of the irreducible representations with highest weights \mu = (\mu_1\ge\dots\ge\mu_{k-1}) satisfying

\lambda_1 \ge \mu_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \mu_2 \ge \dots \ge \mu_{k-1} \ge \lambda_k .
(21.9)

Every other \mu occurs with multiplicity zero.

In plain terms

When a big symmetry group shrinks by one dimension, each irreducible piece of the small group appears once or not at all, and the test is whether its weights sit between the big group’s weights.

Why it is needed

A period pairs the restriction of a form on the big group with a form on the small one. The branching rule says when the pairing can be nonzero (multiplicity one) and when it must vanish (multiplicity zero), which is the “values 0, 1” of the note’s step 7.

Idea

Characters of U(k) are Schur polynomials, and setting the last variable to 1 expands s_\lambda(x_1,\dots,x_{k-1},1) as the sum of s_\mu(x_1,\dots,x_{k-1}) over interlacing \mu. Iterating down to U(1) gives a basis indexed by triangular arrays of interlacing rows, the Gelfand and Tsetlin patterns.

Proof sketch

[86, ch. 8]

The branching law for U(k) \downarrow U(k-1) goes back to Weyl and is proved in Goodman and Wallach’s chapter on branching laws, by the character identity in the idea.

Example

Take k = 3 and \lambda = (2,1,0), the adjoint representation twisted by the determinant, of dimension 8 by Weyl’s formula \prod_{i<j}(\lambda_i - \lambda_j + j - i)/(j-i) = 2\cdot2\cdot2. The interlacing \mu = (\mu_1, \mu_2) satisfy 2 \ge \mu_1 \ge 1 \ge \mu_2 \ge 0, so they are (2,1), (2,0), (1,1), (1,0), of dimensions \mu_1 - \mu_2 + 1 = 2, 3, 1, 2. These add up to 8, and we checked the identity s_{(2,1,0)}(x_1,x_2,1) = s_{(2,1)} + s_{(2,0)} + s_{(1,1)} + s_{(1,0)} with sympy. The weight (3,0) fails 2 \ge \mu_1 and the weight (2,2) fails 1 \ge \mu_2, so each occurs zero times.

Used in

It explains the interlacing condition of Definition 21.7 and the reading of step 7 in The note’s step 7 and the rank condition.

The code writes the interlacing in a shifted form. A Harish-Chandra parameter is the highest weight plus half the sum of the positive roots, which for U(k) adds \tfrac{k+1}{2} - i to \lambda_i. Write u_i = \lambda_i + \tfrac{k+1}2 - i for U(k) and v_i = \mu_i + \tfrac k2 - i for U(k-1). Since \lambda_i,\mu_i are integers, \lambda_i \ge \mu_i holds exactly when u_i > v_i, and \mu_i\ge\lambda_{i+1} exactly when v_i > u_{i+1}, so weak interlacing of weights is strict interlacing of parameters, and every difference u_i - v_j lies in \ZZ + \tfrac12. For \lambda = (2,1,0) the parameter is u = (3, 1, -1), and \mu = (2,0) gives v = (\tfrac52, -\tfrac12), with 3 > \tfrac52 > 1 > -\tfrac12 > -1. This computation is ours. Since the shift is half-integral on a group of even rank and integral on one of odd rank, it also explains why the code’s u (on a group of even rank k) are half-integers, its v (on a group of odd rank) are integers, and its inequalities are strict.

Bessel periods#

The automorphic counterpart of the branching rule is a period. Let V be a Hermitian space and W \subset V a nondegenerate subspace whose orthogonal complement has odd dimension 2r+1 and is split as far as possible. The Bessel subgroup is U(W)\ltimes N, with N a unipotent group built from a flag in the complement and carrying a character \psi.

Definition 21.6 Bessel period

For an automorphic form \varphi on U(V) and an automorphic form \phi on U(W), the Bessel period is the number

\mathcal P(\varphi,\phi) = \int_{[U(W)]}\int_{[N]} \varphi(nh)\,\overline{\phi(h)}\,\overline{\psi(n)}\,\dd n\,\dd h ,

where [G] denotes the quotient of the adelic points of G by its rational points. When \dim V = \dim W + 1 the group N is trivial and \mathcal P is the integral of \varphi\,\overline\phi over [U(W)]. It is a number attached to a pair of forms, not a form, and it is linear in \varphi.

Gan, Gross, and Prasad organized these periods for all classical groups [87]. Locally, for \dim V = \dim W + 1, the space of U(W)-equivariant functionals from an irreducible representation of U(V) to one of U(W) has dimension at most one, a theorem of Aizenbud, Gourevitch, Rallis, and Schiffmann over p-adic fields and of Sun and Zhu over the reals [88] [89], and Gan, Gross, and Prasad reduce the general Bessel case over p-adic fields to this one [87]. That is the local form of “multiplicity 0 or 1”. For a definite group with \dim V - \dim W = 1 the period is a finite sum \sum_c w(c)\,\varphi(\iota c)\,\overline{\phi(c)} over classes of W, with \iota sending a class of W to one of V. The splitting X_m = X'\oplus\langle z\rangle of Definition 21.2 is of this kind, and as our reading, the period map of the datum restricts the last form of the chain to U(X') and pairs it there.

The code states the archimedean half of the rule precisely, for discrete series of a real unitary group of rank 2r + k + 1 restricted to the subgroup of rank k.

Definition 21.7 The code’s interlacing condition and the local Bessel nonvanishing

Let u \in \RR^k, v \in \RR^{k-1}, and b \in \RR^{2r+2}. The interlacing condition is

v_i < u_i \ \text{and}\ u_{i+1} < v_i \quad (0 \le i \le k-2), \qquad -b_0 < u_{k-1},
(21.10)

that is, u_0 > v_0 > u_1 > \dots > v_{k-2} > u_{k-1} > -b_0. The half-integrality condition asks that every u_i - \lambda_s lie in \ZZ + \tfrac12, where \lambda = (v_0,\dots,v_{k-2},-b_0,\dots,-b_{2r+1}). The proposition BesselPeriodGGP states: for even k \ge 2, if u and \lambda are Harish-Chandra parameters satisfying both conditions, \sigma is a discrete series representation with parameter \lambda of the real unitary group of rank 2r+k+1 (with the signature fixed by the code’s sign pattern), w a unit vector in its lowest K-type, and \pi the finite-dimensional representation of the subgroup U_W with parameter u, then for some group elements g, g_0

\int_{U_W\times N}\big\langle\sigma(g_0)w,\ \sigma(hn)\sigma(g)w\big\rangle\,\overline{\psi(n)}\;\pi(h)^{-1}\,\dd(h,n) \ne 0 .

It is a statement about one real place: a matrix coefficient of \sigma integrated over the Bessel subgroup is a nonzero operator.

In the Lean formalization PI.BesselPeriodGGP.BesselPeriodGGP in Formalism/PeriodIntegrals/BesselPeriodGGP.lean

InterlacingCondition and HalfIntegralDifference are defined in the same file, and the only statement that mentions BesselPeriodGGP is GlobalTheory.BesselPeriodCompare.besselPeriod_iff, which proves it equivalent to BesselPeriodNeZero. We did not find where either is proved, so we state the proposition and claim no more.

def InterlacingCondition (k r : ℕ) (u : Fin k → ℝ) (v : Fin (k - 1) → ℝ) (b : Fin (2 * r + 2) → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ i : Fin (k - 1), v i < u ⟨i.val, by have := i.isLt; omega⟩ ∧
      u ⟨i.val + 1, by have := i.isLt; omega⟩ < v i) ∧
    ∀ h : 0 < k, -b ⟨0, by omega⟩ < u ⟨k - 1, by omega⟩
Example

The code checks that its smallest instance satisfies the hypotheses of BesselPeriodGGP, in Formalism.L2.SG.LitS.besselNV_numeric_example: k = 2, r = 0, u = (\tfrac32, -\tfrac12), v = (1), b = (1, 10^{11}). Interlacing reads \tfrac32 > 1 > -\tfrac12 > -1, and the differences u_i - \lambda_s with \lambda = (1, -1, -10^{11}) are all half-integers. Here the subgroup U_W has rank 2 and u = (\tfrac32,-\tfrac12) is the highest weight (1,0) shifted by (\tfrac12,-\tfrac12), the standard representation, while \lambda = (1,-1,-10^{11}) is the parameter of a discrete series of a real unitary group of rank 3. Two of its entries interlace with u and the third sits far below everything. Note that the roles are the reverse of Theorem 21.5. There the k weights of the larger group enclose the k-1 weights of the smaller one. Here the k entries of u, the parameter of the smaller group U_W, enclose the k-1 entries of v, which belong to the parameter of the larger group.

The code also states local multiplicity one, Formalism.L2.SG.LitS.BesselMultOne (any two Bessel functionals on the same pair are linearly dependent), and derives it in besselMultOne_of_uniq from a uniqueness statement we did not follow.

The note’s step 7 and the rank condition#

Step 7 of the note reads “determinants for W(\cdot)'s containing the desired periods, indeed GGP periods”, with “values 0, 1 meaning interlacing weights, or up to m non-interlacing ones” [2]. In our reading the code realizes it as follows. The datum’s Harish-Chandra data HCParam consist of an interlacing block u_0 > v_0 > \dots > v_{k-2} > u_{k-1} and m further pairs (b_j, e_j), one per lift, separated by gaps of at least (c+3)/2, and interlace_of derives InterlacingCondition for them. The block is where the multiplicity is 0 or 1, and the m pairs beyond it are the “up to m non-interlacing” weights.

We found no declaration that computes a determinant whose entries are Bessel periods. What the code states is a rank condition on the linear map whose matrix entries are those periods.

Definition 21.8 The period map and the rank condition

Let M_{\rm ram} be the space of forms, inside a fixed finite-dimensional space of forms on the first class set, that are ramified at the auxiliary prime P, meaning killed by the sum of the action of \FF_P^\times at each of the 2n chosen places, and let d_u = \dim M_{\rm ram}. The period map \mathcal P_C (the code’s PhiC) sends \varphi \in M_{\rm ram} to the linear functional F \mapsto \operatorname{period}\big(\operatorname{low}(\operatorname{ev}_z(\mathrm{col}\,\varphi)), F\big), where \mathrm{col} is the chain Definition 21.3 and \operatorname{ev}_z, the lowering map \operatorname{low}, and the pairing are linear maps fixed by the datum. The rank condition \mathrm{RKC} is

d_u < 2\operatorname{rank}\mathcal P_C, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad 2\dim\ker\mathcal P_C < d_u .
(21.11)

It says that the periods of the lifted forms detect more than half of the ramified forms. It is a statement about the rank of a linear map, not about the value of a determinant.

def PhiC : A.Mram →ₗ[ℂ] Module.Dual ℂ P.Mt := P.period ∘ₗ PsiC C A P
def rkC : ℕ := Module.finrank ℂ (LinearMap.range (PhiC C A P))
def RKC : Prop := A.du < 2 * rkC C A P
In the Lean formalization GlobalTheory.Core.Rk.RKC in Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Definitions/LatticeFrames/FiniteDimensionalMram.lean

rkc_iff_ker proves the equivalence in Equation (21.11), two examples record that \mathcal P_C = 0 violates the condition and an injective \mathcal P_C satisfies it when d_u > 0, and PhiC_apply identifies \mathcal P_C with the column periods PeriodMap.PtilCol.

As our reading, a rank lower bound is the statement that some maximal minor of the matrix of \mathcal P_C, a determinant of periods, is nonzero, which is how the note’s “determinants for W(\cdot)'s containing the desired periods” and RKC say the same thing. Where RKC is proved for the datum was not traced.

21.5The seesaw: two orders of summation#

A period of the m-fold lift is a sum over the top class set of a form that was itself built by m sums. A seesaw identity, in Kudla’s sense, compares two dual pairs that share one theta kernel and rearranges those sums so that the period can be computed one level at a time [85]. On finite sets it is nothing but the statement that a finite sum can be taken in either order.

Take two finite class sets, \mathcal C with weights w(a) and \mathcal C' with weights w(b), two kernels K_1, K_2\colon \mathcal C\times\mathcal C'\to\CC, and two forms u_1, u_2 on \mathcal C. Lift each form to \mathcal C' by Equation (21.7), \theta_i(b) = \sum_a w(a)u_i(a)K_i(a,b), and take the inner product on \mathcal C'. The result is the sum of the three-index array

A(a, a', b) = w(a)\,w(a')\,w(b)\;u_1(a)\,K_1(a,b)\;\overline{u_2(a')\,K_2(a',b)}
(21.12)

over all (a, a', b). Contracting a and a' first gives \langle\theta_1,\theta_2\rangle_{\mathcal C'} = \sum_b w(b)\theta_1(b)\overline{\theta_2(b)}, an inner product of lifts on the big side. Contracting b first gives \sum_{a,a'} w(a)w(a')\,u_1(a)\overline{u_2(a')}\,G(a,a') with G(a,a') = \sum_b w(b)K_1(a,b)\overline{K_2(a',b)}, a pairing of the original forms against a kernel on the small side. The two contractions agree.

Example

Let \mathcal C have two classes with weights (\tfrac12,\tfrac16) and \mathcal C' three classes with weights (\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac1{12}). These are toy numbers, not a real genus. Take

K_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\3&1&1\end{pmatrix},\quad K_2 = \begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\1&1&4\end{pmatrix},\quad u_1 = (1,-1),\quad u_2 = (2,1).

The lifts are \theta_1 = (0, \tfrac56, -\tfrac16) and \theta_2 = (\tfrac{13}6, \tfrac16, \tfrac53), and \langle\theta_1,\theta_2\rangle_{\mathcal C'} = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac56\cdot\tfrac16 - \tfrac1{12}\cdot\tfrac16\cdot\tfrac53 = \tfrac5{108}. In the other order, G = \begin{pmatrix}\tfrac12 & \tfrac54\\ \tfrac{19}{12}&\tfrac{19}{12}\end{pmatrix}, and \sum_{a,a'}w(a)w(a')u_1(a)u_2(a')G(a,a') = \tfrac14 + \tfrac5{48} - \tfrac{19}{72} - \tfrac{19}{432} = \tfrac{5}{108}. The common denominator of the weights is 6, and 6\theta_1 = (0,5,-1) and 6\theta_2 = (13,1,10) are integral, which is the integrality of Definition 21.3 for one step.

The code states a finite form for lattice classes, LatSeeSaw in Formalism/ThetaLiftIndependence/Statement.lean (lifting f along a kernel and pairing with g equals pairing f with the lift of g along the conjugate kernel), but no statement uses it. The version the proof uses is analytic.

Theorem 21.9

The inner product of two theta lifts equals a double integral of the starting forms against the inner product of the kernels

[3]
Statement

Let V and V' be Hermitian spaces of the datum, with Haar measures on U(V)(\AA) and U(V')(\AA). Let K_1, K_2\colon U(V)(\AA)\times U(V')(\AA)\to\CC be continuous, left invariant under U(V) of the rationals in the first variable, square-integrable on [U(V')] in the second, and of moderate growth, and let u_1, u_2 be rapidly decreasing on [U(V)]. Then the lifts \theta_i(h) = \int_{[U(V)]}K_i(g,h)\,u_i(g)\,\dd g are square-integrable on [U(V')], and

\langle\theta_1,\theta_2\rangle_{[U(V')]} = \iint_{[U(V)]^2}\big\langle K_1(q_1,\cdot),K_2(q_2,\cdot)\big\rangle_{[U(V')]}\,u_1(q_1)\,\overline{u_2(q_2)}\;\dd q_1\,\dd q_2 .
(21.13)
In plain terms

Lifting two forms and comparing them upstairs gives the same number as comparing their kernels upstairs first and then integrating the forms downstairs.

Why it is needed

It is the analytic step of every seesaw argument in the proof, the step that lets a period of a lifted form be rewritten as an integral over the smaller group, where it can be computed.

Idea

The left side is the integral of the array Equation (21.12) over three variables, first over q_1 and q_2 and then over h. The right side integrates over h first. Fubini’s theorem allows the exchange once the absolute integral converges, which is what rapid decrease of u_i and moderate growth of K_i provide.

Proof

On finite class sets the identity is the exchange of two finite sums shown above. In general the integrand \abs{K_1(q_1,h)K_2(q_2,h)u_1(q_1)u_2(q_2)} is integrable on [U(V)]^2\times[U(V')]: by Cauchy and Schwarz in h the inner integral is at most \lVert K_1(q_1,\cdot)\rVert\,\lVert K_2(q_2,\cdot)\rVert, which grows moderately in q_1, q_2, and the rapid decrease of u_1, u_2 makes the outer integral finite. Fubini’s theorem then exchanges the order. The formal proof is GlobalTheory.Core.Rk.Seesaw.seesaw_fubini, which we did not read line by line.

Theorem 21.10

The Bessel period of the m-fold lift is an iterated integral, one level at a time, of an explicit unfolded integrand

[3]
Statement

For the datum’s chain of length m, with theta functions at every step, a continuous automorphic form F on the space the chain starts from, a continuous automorphic form \varphi on the subgroup of the Bessel level where it ends, and the rapid-decrease conditions Rapid along the chain, the Bessel period of the lifted form against \varphi satisfies

\mathrm{Iter}\big(\mathrm{colPer}(F,\varphi),\ \mathcal P(\mathrm{down}\,F,\varphi)\big),

that is, \mathcal P(\mathrm{down}\,F,\varphi) equals the iterated integral, step by step down the chain, of the explicit integrand \mathrm{colPer}.

In plain terms

The number read off the last form of the chain can be computed one level at a time, instead of building the whole lifted form first.

Why it is needed

Without it the period of a form built by m lifts is an integral of m nested integrals, with no control level by level.

Idea

Apply the seesaw Theorem 21.9 at the top step to move the pairing with \varphi one level down, where \varphi is replaced by its theta transform (the code’s hand, built from handBF and handFB). Repeat m times.

Proof sketch

[3]

iter_colPer is obtained from iter_chain and chain_Q_eq, which identifies the chain’s unfolded integrand Chain.Q with colPer through Q_eq_colPer, and the unfoldings themselves are GlobalTheory.Unf.unfoldings_of_chain. The integrand colPer and the functional besPer were not opened, so we state the shape of the identity and do not unfold it.

The note’s step 12, discussed next, and, as our reading, the periods of the period map Definition 21.8.

The note’s step 12, headed “Seesaw”, says that the period of the iterated lift is “a Bessel period independent of the Hecke characters” and names Rallis [2]. The first half is Theorem 21.10. For the second half we found no theorem stating independence of the Hecke characters \mu_j. The nearest statements make the dependence explicit instead. The global identity ThetaIntegralsAgree (its clauses StepBeta and StepAlpha, in Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/BlockTheory/DivisorBase/WeilTensorModels.lean) says that adding one hyperbolic plane on either side of a tower multiplies a theta-integral constant by one partial Hecke L-value and explicit Gauss-sum factors, times a constant independent of the characters, and D7.perCol_tie equates the twisted period columns with periods of the twisted chain.

21.6The sizes#

The chain must be compared with a budget, so the sizes of its pieces must be known: how many classes there are, how large a lifted form is, how large the normalizing periods are, and how divisible the derivative-like quantities are. The note’s step 9 names the tools, “Chowla-Selberg, Weyl, and Siegel mass” [2].

Siegel’s mass formula as a ratio#

The mass of a genus of definite lattices is \sum_L 1/\abs{\operatorname{Aut}L} over class representatives, the total weight of the class set on which forms live. Siegel’s mass formula computes it as a product of local densities [75], and for Hermitian lattices over CM fields exact forms are in Gan, Hanke, and Yu [90]. The code uses it as a ratio between consecutive ranks.

Theorem 21.11 The mass of the standard Hermitian lattice of rank M divided by that of rank M-1 is an explicit factorial times an L-value [3]

Let E be a CM field unramified over its totally real subfield E^+ at all finite primes (the code writes K), n_E = [E^+:\QQ], v_E = \abs{d_E}^{1/(2n_E)}/2 with d_E the discriminant of E, and I_M the lattice with an orthonormal basis of size M. For M \ge 3,

\frac{\operatorname{mass}(I_M)}{\operatorname{mass}(I_{M-1})} = \frac{\big((M-1)!\,(v_E/\pi)^M\big)^{n_E}}{\sqrt{(2v_E)^{n_E}}}\;L_E(M),
(21.14)

where L_E(M) = \prod_\mathfrak p e_\mathfrak p over the maximal ideals of \mathcal O_E, with e_\mathfrak p = (1 - (-1)^M N\mathfrak p^{-M/2})^{-1} when \mathfrak p is stable under conjugation and e_\mathfrak p = (1 - N\mathfrak p^{-M})^{-1/2} otherwise.

Proof sketch [75]

The mass is a product of local densities times archimedean volumes [90]. Adding one dimension changes the archimedean volume by a \Gamma(M)-type factor, which gives (M-1)! and the powers of \pi, and changes each local density by one Euler factor, which together give L_E(M). This account and the following identification are our reading: comparing Euler factors, L_E(M) is the Hecke L-function of E^+ at M of the character \chi_{E/E^+}^M, with \chi_{E/E^+} the quadratic character of E/E^+.

In the Lean formalization GlobalTheory.Mass.siegelMassRatio_holds in Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/FlagMeasures/SiegelMassRatioUnimodularDefinite.lean

Proves SiegelMassRatio of Formalism/HermitianLattices/StatementMass.lean, a hypothesis of 58 statements by our count, while MassTelescope, the product of the ratios over a range of ranks, is used by none.

Each extra dimension multiplies the symmetry-weighted number of classes by a factorial, a power of the discriminant, and an L-value, and the chain adds c+1 dimensions at each of its m steps. The class count of the first space, \abs{\mathcal C_0} = \operatorname{mass}_I(N_0)\cdot\mathrm{idx}\cdot(P^{N_0}-1)^{2n}, is the condition ClassNumberFormula₂, which level_rank_of_trivial_stabilisers uses to compute the dimension of the space of forms on \mathcal C_0.

The Rallis inner product formula#

A theta lift can vanish, and the chain needs its size. The Rallis inner product formula computes the inner product of two theta lifts of cusp forms as an integral of the forms against a Siegel Eisenstein series on the doubled group [91]. In the later language of the doubling method of Piatetski-Shapiro and Rallis this is a doubling zeta integral, which factors as a value of a standard L-function times local factors.

Theorem 21.12 The inner product of two theta lifts of cusp forms is a doubling zeta integral of the forms [3]

Let V and V' be Hermitian spaces of the datum with \operatorname{rank}V < \operatorname{rank}V' \le 2\operatorname{rank}V, and V' anisotropic or \operatorname{rank}V + (\text{Witt index of }V') < \operatorname{rank}V'. For cusp forms f_1, f_2 in an irreducible cuspidal representation of U(V) whose lifts vanish to every smaller space of the Witt tower of V' (the spaces obtained from V' by removing hyperbolic planes), and theta functions \Xi_1, \Xi_2, the lifts converge and are square-integrable, and

\frac{1}{\operatorname{vol}[U(V')]}\,\big\langle\theta(f_1,\Xi_1),\theta(f_2,\Xi_2)\big\rangle = Z\big(s_0, f_1, f_2, \Xi(\delta(\Xi_1,\Xi_2))\big),

the doubling zeta integral at the Siegel and Weil point s_0.

Proof sketch [91]

Expand the inner product of two theta integrals, exchange the order of integration, and recognize the inner integral as a Siegel Eisenstein series on the doubled group by the Siegel and Weil formula. Rallis did this for orthogonal and symplectic groups, and the statement above is the code’s version for unitary groups in the convergent range. Regularized versions for unitary groups followed from Kudla and Rallis and later authors [92]. In the tree the formula is proved as rallis_of_dm from the doubling method, the Siegel and Weil formula, and convergence of theta integrals.

In the Lean formalization GlobalTheory.Published.RallisInnerProductConvergent in Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/PublishedTheorems/TwistedTraceFormula/LowerLiftsZeroOfWittIdxEqZero.lean

The field RallisInnerProductConvergent of the record of published theorems states the formula with the hypotheses above, and the definite-side records use it as the isometry seeIso : SEEIso, so that norms of lifts are known multiples of norms of the original forms.

Chowla and Selberg#

The Chowla and Selberg formula expresses the periods of an elliptic curve with complex multiplication by an imaginary quadratic field through values of the Gamma function, and its logarithmic form is the Kronecker limit formula averaged over the class group [93]. The tree proves it in the form chowla_selberg_eta (in Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/HomogeneousIdeals/DedekindZetaEqSumRealEisenstein.lean): for an imaginary quadratic field of discriminant -d with class number h, character \chi, and one CM point \tau_c in the upper half-plane for each ideal class c,

\frac1h\sum_c \log\big(4\pi\,\Im\tau_c\,\abs{\eta(\tau_c)}^4\big) = \gamma_E + \log\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt d} - \frac{L'(1,\chi)}{L(1,\chi)},
(21.15)

with \eta Dedekind’s eta function. For d = 7, with h = 1 and \tau = (-1+\sqrt{-7})/2, both sides equal 1.42650196679, and for d = 23, with h = 3 and \tau = (-1+\sqrt{-23})/2, (\mp1+\sqrt{-23})/4, both equal 1.26946657138 (we computed both with mpmath). The datum uses the right side as a normalizing period: SizeData₂.logOm is \gamma_E + \log(2\pi/\mathrm{rd}_E) - \Re\,L'/L(1,\chi_{\mathsf d}) with \mathrm{rd}_E the root discriminant of E and \chi_{\mathsf d} the quadratic character modulo the datum’s auxiliary prime \mathsf d (the code’s d, with \sqrt{-\mathsf d} \in E), and the quantity MAIN adds, over the indices t of the datum, m(a_T\log a_T - a_T - a_T\log\Omega) - a_T\log P. As our reading, this is the logarithmic size of m copies of an a_T-th derivative normalized by \Omega^{a_T}, set against P^{a_T}, the bookkeeping of the note’s “D^a\theta(0)/\Omega^a”.

Divisibility as multiplicity: the odd-level series#

The note’s step 2 is the stand-in for differentiation: “D^p \equiv 0 on a CM curve for p inert in K”, with D an invariant derivation, and D^a\theta(0)/\Omega^a is divisible by p^{a/p + a/p^3 + \cdots - O(\log a)} [2]. Our reading of the integrality bookkeeping located its arithmetic engine in the declaration ThmP, whose constants are the odd-level series

\gamma_\ell = \sum_{k\ \mathrm{odd}}\ell^{-k} = \frac{\ell}{\ell^2-1}, \qquad \rho_\ell = \sum_{k\ \mathrm{even},\,k\ge2}\ell^{-k} = \frac{1}{\ell^2-1}, \qquad \gamma_\ell + \rho_\ell = \frac1{\ell-1},
(21.16)

stated and proved as Formalism.IncomingBounds.Constants (in Formalism/IncomingBounds/IncomingBound.lean, proved as constants).

\ell \gamma_\ell \rho_\ell \gamma_\ell+\rho_\ell = \frac1{\ell-1} \frac1\ell + \frac1{\ell^3} + \frac1{\ell^5}+\frac1{\ell^7}
2 2/3 = 0.6667 1/3 1 0.6641
3 3/8 = 0.375 1/8 1/2 0.37494
5 5/24 = 0.20833 1/24 1/4 0.2083328

The note’s exponent is a/p + a/p^3 + \cdots = a\gamma_p, minus O(\log a). Legendre’s formula v_p(a!) = \sum_{k\ge1}\lfloor a/p^k\rfloor \approx a/(p-1) shows where it sits, as the odd levels a\gamma_p of a budget whose even levels are a\rho_p. For a = 1000 and p = 5 the terms \lfloor 1000/5^k\rfloor are 200, 40, 8, 1, so v_5(1000!) = 249, the odd levels give 200 + 8 = 208 against 1000\gamma_5 = 208.33, and the even levels give 41 against 1000\rho_5 = 41.67. The note’s exponent keeps the odd levels only.

Fix n_0 \ge 1 and two n_0\times n_0 matrices of variables, X_L and X_R. For a polynomial Q and a power series g in these variables, the jet Q(\partial)g(0) applies the differential operator with the coefficients of Q to g at the origin. For a prime \ell, an odd i, and e(\ell,i) = 1 + \ell\sum_{0\le s<(i-1)/2}\ell^{2s}, set

h = -\ell^{-e(\ell,i)}\sum_{b,c}X_L(b,c)^{\ell^i}X_R(b,c) + h_1, \qquad J(y) = \big[\det(\partial_L)^{\ell^iy}\det(\partial_R)^{y}\,e^{h}\big](0),
(21.17)

with h_1 a power series satisfying a weight condition. Only \ell^i-th powers of the left variables enter, and they come with an explicit negative power of \ell. As our reading, this is the analog of the note’s “D^p\equiv0”: in characteristic p a derivation kills p-th powers, and here the \ell^i-th powers are what the left determinant operator sees.

Theorem 21.13

In every window of length S_0 there is an order y at which the jet J(y) is divisible by at most the predicted power of \ell

[3]
Statement

Let C be a field of characteristic 0 with an additive valuation v such that v(\ell) = 1, where \ell \ge 5 is prime, let i be odd, 1 \le n_1, n_0 \le n_1, and let h_1 satisfy the weight condition v(\text{coefficient of } X^\alpha) + \deg_L(\alpha)(r_1 - \delta) + \deg_R(\alpha)(r_2 - \delta) \ge \frac1{\ell-1} for every monomial X^\alpha, with r_1 = \rho_\ell + \tfrac1{2\ell^i}, r_2 = \rho_\ell + \tfrac12, \delta = \tfrac1{8\ell^i}, and have every nonzero monomial of degree at least 1 in X_R. If n_0 \ge 1, then for every Y_0 there is an integer y with Y_0 \le y < Y_0 + S_0, where S_0 = \lceil 64n_0^2(i + 3 + 3\log_\ell(n_0+1))\rceil, such that

v\big(J(y)\big) \le n_0\,y\,\big((\ell^i+1)\gamma_\ell - 1\big) + n_1(\log_\ell n_1 + 1).
(21.18)

If n_0 = 0 then J(y) = 1 for every y.

In plain terms

The derivative-like quantities J(y) are not more divisible by \ell than the formula predicts, at least once in every stretch of orders of a fixed length.

Why it is needed

An upper bound on a valuation is a statement that the quantity is not zero and not too divisible. As our reading, it plays the role of Lemma 10.7 in Stepanov’s argument: without it, the quantity that carries the multiplicity could vanish identically and bound nothing.

Idea

Expand J(y) exactly as a binomial-type sum (-\ell^{-e})^{n_0y}\,\mathrm{cap}(n_0, \ell^iy)\sum_s\binom ys a_s, using the Cayley identity \det(\partial)\det^{s+1} = (s+1)\cdots(s+n_0)\det^s to compute the derivatives of powers of determinants. Legendre’s formula gives the valuation of the factorial product \mathrm{cap}. The coefficients a_s have valuation growing like s/8, and a Newton-polygon argument finds, in every window of length S_0, a y at which the binomial sum has valuation at most 0.

Proof sketch

[3]

ThmP is proved by GlobalTheory.OddBlock.WindowValuationBound.main and exported as GlobalTheory.OddBlock.windowBound, both in Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/UnramifiedDepth/SumEqOfIsHomogeneous.lean. The proof starts from the exact expansion GlobalTheory.OddBlock.BinomialValue.main, then uses a Newton-polygon step, Legendre’s formula for v_\ell(N!), and a Capelli bound, and the file of the statement also defines the corresponding propositions CoefficientExpansionLambda, P7, F2, F3, and CayleyId. We state the theorem and its mechanism and do not unfold the Newton-polygon step.

Example

Take n_0 = n_1 = 1 and h_1 = 0, which satisfies both conditions. Then h = -\ell^{-e}X_L^{\ell^i}X_R, and only the term h^y/y! of e^h contains X_L^{\ell^iy}X_R^y, so

J(y) = (\ell^iy)!\,y!\cdot\frac{(-\ell^{-e})^y}{y!} = (-\ell^{-e})^{y}\,(\ell^iy)!,

which we also checked by direct differentiation for \ell = 5, i = 1, y = 1, 2 (values -24 and 145{,}152). By Legendre, v_\ell(J(y)) = \frac{\ell^iy - s_\ell(y)}{\ell-1} - e\,y, with s_\ell(y) the sum of the base-\ell digits of y. For \ell = 5 and i = 3, e = 6 and the slope of Equation (21.18) is (126)\tfrac5{24} - 1 = 25.25. The valuations for y = 1, \dots, 6 are 25, 50, 75, 100, 126, 151, against 25.25y = 25.25, 50.5, 75.75, 101, 126.25, 151.5. For i = 1 the slope is (\ell+1)\gamma_\ell - 1 = \tfrac1{\ell-1}, and v_\ell(J(y)) = v_\ell(y!) exactly. In this case the bound holds at every y, not only once per window.

Now compare with the note. Write a = \ell^iy for the order of the left derivatives, the note’s a and not the scale a = x\,b of The scale dictionary. The main term of Equation (21.18) is

n_0 y\big((\ell^i+1)\gamma_\ell - 1\big) = n_0\big(a\gamma_\ell - y(1-\gamma_\ell)\big) = n_0\Big(\frac a\ell + \frac a{\ell^3} + \cdots\Big) - n_0(1-\gamma_\ell)\frac{a}{\ell^i},

so up to a correction of relative size \ell^{-i} it is the note’s exponent a/p + a/p^3 + \cdots with p = \ell, times n_0. In the example above, a = 125 and y = 1 give a\gamma_5 = 26.04, and the correction 1-\gamma_5 = 0.79 brings it to 25.25. The note’s step 2 asserts a lower bound on divisibility, while ThmP is an upper bound. A lower bound of the same shape is in the tree, GlobalTheory.T.determinantPairing_quotient_valuation_lower_bound, and we did not trace which of the two feeds the per-lift exponents e_0(w,j).

Here is our reading of how this relates to multiplicity. Over the integers the counterpart of “vanishes to order m at p” is “divisible by p^m”, as What the proof used noted, and by the note’s step 2 the divisible quantities are jets, derivatives of a theta function at a CM point divided by a period. Each of the m lifts contributes its own exponents, one per place and per lift (the e_0(w,j) of LeafDepthGood), which is the sense in which the lifts are, in the note’s words, “each mimicking multiplicity”. The definition vonMangoldtClassSum of How long the chain is adds, for each lift and each prime p, the odd levels a_T/p^i minus at least 1 per level, which has the form of the note’s a/p + a/p^3 + \cdots - O(\log a) with a = a_T.

21.7The closing ledger#

The chain provides multiplicity, about x^{1/2-\varepsilon/16} lifts, each contributing exponents e_0(w,j) at each place, with ThmP bounding the valuations of the jets from above in every window of orders. It provides numbers, the periods of the lifted forms, computable level by level (Theorem 21.10), detecting more than half of the ramified forms (RKC), and algebraic with denominators controlled by stabilizer orders (PeriodClassSumWeyl). And it comes with a budget, Theorem 21.1, by which a nonzero algebraic number cannot carry more divisibility than its archimedean size allows.

The chain costs size. The ranks reach about x^{399+58\varepsilon}, the class sets grow by the mass ratios Equation (21.14) at each added dimension, the auxiliary prime has \log P \gtrsim x^{1/2+15\varepsilon/16} wherever TuGe holds, the norms of the lifts are fixed by the Rallis formula, and MAIN charges m\,a_T\log\Omega for the Chowla and Selberg period. The note’s step 14 says that a precise count of the cost of each lift showed “one would stop at 2/3 a priori” without a further idea [2]. We found no declaration matching that count, and the page does not reconstruct it.

Chapter Paying for the chain: integrality, Galois representations, and the count that is bounded takes the chain from here, with the Galois representations of automorphic forms over CM fields and the count of inert prime powers that the chain bounds through a record of divisibility and slope inequalities (its SizeData₂, with the divisibility inequality DIV), which its finite-group explicit formula turns into a bound on the combination G_r of smoothed prime sums. How the chain’s divisibility and integrality (ThmP, DGam, chain_ge, PeriodClassSumWeyl, and the exponents of LeafDepthGood) feed the divisibility inequality DIV of that record was not traced, in this chapter, in Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices, or in Paying for the chain: integrality, Galois representations, and the count that is bounded. Chapter The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros consumes that bound, G_r(X) \le X^{1/2+9\varepsilon} on windows of scales [Y, Y^{3/2}], which forbids zeros to the right of \tfrac12 + 9\varepsilon. The scale x of Definition 21.4 is the scale of those windows, with the same \varepsilon.

Chapter 22

Paying for the chain: integrality, Galois representations, and the count that is bounded

After this chapter you can say what a Galois representation attached to an automorphic form is, state the theorem Row0b that the formal proof re-proves and the five steps by which it does so, and follow how a weighted count of inert prime powers, bounded by the chain of theta lifts, becomes the one-sided bound on G_r that the endgame consumes.

Builds on 21. Multiplicity without derivatives: a chain of length about the square root, 19. The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros

In plain terms

Over a finite field, Frobenius ties each point of a curve to an equation, and the count of points is bounded by an auxiliary function. Over the integers the proof needs two substitutes. The first is a Galois representation, which lets every prime act as a Frobenius on a vector space built from an automorphic form, and the proof builds these representations from scratch. The second is a count of primes of a special kind, which the chain of theta lifts bounds from above, and which a finite version of the explicit formula turns into the bound on prime sums that rules out zeros.

In Stepanov’s proof, as Stepanov's proof gave it, an auxiliary function that vanishes to order m at every rational point is played against a degree budget, so the count of rational points is bounded from above (Theorem 10.9), twisted counts over a Galois cover give the bound from below (Theorem 10.12), and Frobenius makes “rational point” an equation. Chapters Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices and Multiplicity without derivatives: a chain of length about the square root built the integer substitute for the auxiliary function, a chain of totally definite Hermitian spaces X_0,\dots,X_m of ranks N_0+j(c+1), with m about \sqrt x and no inclusion of one space in the next in the code’s record Spaces, and The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros showed what the chain must deliver, an upper bound G_r(x)\le x^{1/2+9\varepsilon} on windows of scales. In our reading, the rational points become prime powers inert in an auxiliary abelian field, counted with the ramp weight of the smoothed sum, the vanishing to order m becomes divisibility of the m-fold lift, the degree budget becomes an inequality between slopes of lattices, the Galois trick becomes orthogonality of characters on a finite abelian group, and Frobenius returns through the Galois representations attached to automorphic forms. The first half of the chapter explains those representations and the theorem Row0b that supplies them, and the second half follows the count from the chain to G_r.

22.1Frobenius comes back: Galois representations#

The integers have no Frobenius, as What the proof used recorded: the only ring endomorphism of \ZZ is the identity. A prime p does have a Frobenius in a different sense, as an element of a Galois group, and a Galois representation is the device that lets that element act on a vector space, where it has eigenvalues and a trace.

Definition 22.1 Galois representation

Let K be a number field with algebraic closure \overline K, and let \ell be a prime. An \ell-adic Galois representation of K of dimension n is a continuous homomorphism \varrho\colon\Gal(\overline K/K)\to\GL_n(\overline{\QQ}_\ell). It is unramified at a prime \mathfrak p of K when it is trivial on the inertia groups above \mathfrak p. Then the Frobenius elements above \mathfrak p, which form one conjugacy class \Frob_{\mathfrak p}, have a well-defined characteristic polynomial \det(X-\varrho(\Frob_{\mathfrak p})). It is a homomorphism into matrices, not a number attached to a prime and not an automorphic form, although the point of this section is that the two kinds of object determine each other’s numbers.

The smallest example has dimension one. \Gal(\overline\QQ/\QQ) acts on the \ell^n-th roots of unity by \zeta\mapsto\zeta^{c} for a unit c modulo \ell^n, and letting n grow gives the cyclotomic character \chi_{\mathrm{cyc}}\colon\Gal(\overline\QQ/\QQ)\to\ZZ_\ell^\times. For p\ne\ell the Frobenius at p raises these roots of unity to the power p, since it does so modulo a prime above p and they stay distinct modulo p. So

\chi_{\mathrm{cyc}}(\Frob_p)=p .
(22.1)

For \ell=5 and p=2, Frobenius sends a primitive fifth root of unity \zeta to \zeta^2, then \zeta^4, \zeta^3, and back to \zeta, so it has order 4, the order of 2 in (\ZZ/5\ZZ)^\times, and its trace is the prime itself.

The next example has dimension two and is the one The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields already met. For an elliptic curve E over \FF_q and a prime \ell\nmid q, the points of order dividing \ell^k form a group E[\ell^k]\cong(\ZZ/\ell^k)^2, and Frobenius acts on it by a 2\times2 matrix whose trace is congruent to a=q+1-\#E(\FF_q) modulo \ell^k (section Frobenius, the operator behind the zeros). The limit over k is the Tate module T_\ell E\cong\ZZ_\ell^2, on which Frobenius has characteristic polynomial X^2-aX+q exactly [53, ch. III and V].

Example

Take E\colon y^2=x^3+x+1 over \FF_5, the curve of The world where it was already true: curves over finite fields, with \#E(\FF_5)=9 and a=-3, so the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius is X^2+3X+5.

  • Modulo 2 it is X^2+X+1. The points of order 2 are (e_i,0) with e_i the roots of x^3+x+1, which has no root in \FF_5 (its values at 0,\dots,4 are 1,3,1,1,4), so Frobenius permutes the three roots cyclically. In the basis P_1=(e_1,0), P_2=(e_2,0), with P_1+P_2=(e_3,0), it sends P_1\mapsto P_2\mapsto P_1+P_2, the matrix \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix} with trace 1\equiv-3 and determinant -1\equiv5 modulo 2.
  • Modulo 3 it is X^2-1=(X-1)(X+1), so Frobenius fixes one line of E[3] and negates another. The fixed line is E(\FF_5)[3]: by direct computation E(\FF_5) is cyclic of order 9, with two points of order 3 and six of order 9.

The same integer -3 is seen through every \ell at once, as a trace modulo \ell^k for every k.

For an elliptic curve over \QQ the action of \Gal(\overline\QQ/\QQ) on T_\ell E is a two-dimensional \ell-adic Galois representation, unramified at every prime p of good reduction with p\ne\ell, and the Frobenius at such a p acts through the reduction modulo p, so its trace is a_p=p+1-\#E(\FF_p) [53, ch. VII]. The theorem that connects this to automorphic forms says that these traces are also the Hecke eigenvalues of a modular form, and that, conversely, modular forms produce Galois representations.

Theorem 22.2

A weight-two newform has a Galois representation whose Frobenius traces are its Hecke eigenvalues

[94]
Statement

Let f=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nq^n be a normalized cuspidal newform of weight 2 for \Gamma_0(N) with rational coefficients. There is an elliptic curve E_f over \QQ such that for every prime p\nmid N

a_p=p+1-\#E_f(\FF_p),
(22.2)

and so for every prime \ell the representation on T_\ell E_f is unramified at every p\nmid N\ell with \Tr\varrho(\Frob_p)=a_p and \det\varrho(\Frob_p)=p. For newforms of weight k\ge2 for \Gamma_0(N) with arbitrary coefficients, Deligne constructed an \ell-adic representation with the same property, trace a_p and determinant p^{k-1}.

In plain terms

A modular form is a list of numbers a_p, one for each prime. There is a geometric object, an elliptic curve in the simplest case, whose number of points modulo p is p+1-a_p, and a Galois group acting on it in which the Frobenius at p has trace a_p.

Why it is needed

Row0b below is the generalization of this theorem from \GL_2 over \QQ to \GL_n over CM fields, and this case shows what its clauses say before they are stated in full.

Idea

The Jacobian of the modular curve X_0(N) carries the Hecke operators as endomorphisms, and modulo p the operator T_p becomes Frobenius plus its dual, the Verschiebung (the Eichler and Shimura congruence relation). So on the Tate module the trace of Frobenius is the eigenvalue of T_p, and f cuts an elliptic curve out of the Jacobian.

Proof sketch

[94, ch. 8 and 9]

The congruence relation is due to Eichler and Shimura and is proved in Diamond and Shurman’s book, which also constructs the Galois representations of weight two [94, ch. 8]. Deligne’s construction for higher weight uses the étale cohomology of Kuga and Sato varieties [95].

Example

The eigenform f=q\prod_{n\ge1}(1-q^n)^2(1-q^{11n})^2 of level 11 and the curve y^2+y=x^3-x^2 give, by expanding the product and by counting points modulo p,

p 2 3 5 7 13 17 19 23
a_p from the q-expansion -2 -1 1 -2 4 -2 0 -1
p+1-\#E(\FF_p) -2 -1 1 -2 4 -2 0 -1

At p=2 the Frobenius eigenvalues are the roots of X^2+2X+2, namely -1\pm i, of absolute value \sqrt2, which is the Riemann Hypothesis of Theorem 9.6 for the curve modulo 2.

Used in

The language of this card is the language of Theorem 22.3.

The roots of X^2-a_pX+p are the Satake parameters of f at p, up to normalization. For an automorphic representation \pi of \GL_n unramified at a place w, the Satake parameters are n nonzero complex numbers that record all its Hecke eigenvalues at w. The code’s algSat multiplies the unitary Satake parameters by q_w^{(n-1)/2}, with q_w the size of the residue field, and its FrobEig says that \varrho is unramified at w and that for a Frobenius element \sigma at w,

\det\bigl(X-\varrho(\sigma^{-1})\bigr)=\prod_{\alpha}\Bigl(X-q_w^{(n-1)/2}\alpha\Bigr),
(22.3)

the product over the Satake parameters \alpha [3]. The inverse \sigma^{-1} is the geometric Frobenius, the usual convention for Galois representations found in étale cohomology.

22.2The theorem Row0b#

The formal proof needs the generalization of Theorem 22.2 to automorphic representations of \GL_n over a CM field. A CM field is a totally imaginary quadratic extension E of a totally real field E^+, such as \QQ(i) over \QQ, and complex conjugation c is then a well-defined automorphism of E. The theorem is stated in the code as a proposition named Row0b, and it is proved there.

The record PropsB has six fields, cont, ss, away, weights, weights_conj, and above, and Rc is instantiated to recT, the local parametrization whose laws What the proof stands on states. The card translates every clause. We write n for the code’s rank a and \varrho for its representation r, because the page reserves r for the order of a character. Theorem 22.3

Every regular algebraic polarized cuspidal representation of \GL_n over a CM field has an \ell-adic Galois representation whose Frobenius data are its local data

[96]
Statement

Let E be a CM field with maximal totally real subfield E^+ and algebraic closure \overline E, let \ell be a prime, \iota\colon\overline\QQ_\ell\to\CC a field isomorphism, and n\ge1. Let \pi be a cuspidal automorphic representation of \GL_n(\AA_E) that is regular algebraic, and \chi a Hecke character of E^+ such that (\pi,\chi) is a polarized pair: \chi_v(-1)=(-1)^n at every real place v of E^+ (sign), and \pi twisted by (\chi\circ N_{E/E^+})^{-1} is paired with \pi through complex conjugation, the code’s form of “the dual of \pi is its complex conjugate up to the twist by \chi\circ N_{E/E^+}” (dual). Then there are a representation \varrho\colon\Gal(\overline E/E)\to\GL_n(\overline\QQ_\ell), an integer w_0, and for each embedding \tau\colon E\to\overline\QQ_\ell a multiset \mathrm{HT}_\tau of n integers, such that:

  1. (cont, ss) \varrho is continuous and semisimple.
  2. (weights) \mathrm{HT}_\tau=\{\tfrac{n-1}2-z\}, as z runs over the infinitesimal character of \pi at the complex place \iota\circ\tau.
  3. (weights_conj) \mathrm{HT}_{\tau\circ c}=w_0-\mathrm{HT}_\tau.
  4. (away) At every finite place w\nmid\ell, and for every local parametrization \mathrm{rec} that satisfies the laws of recT, the Weil and Deligne representation of \varrho restricted to a decomposition group at w has the dimension of \mathrm{rec}(\pi_w), the parameter attached to the normalized local component (dim). It equals \mathrm{rec}(\pi_w) whenever \mathrm{rec}(\pi_w) is trivial on commutators of the Weil group and has zero monodromy (tor). When E_w\cong\QQ_g for a prime g>16n^2 (or n=1), and \mathrm{rec}(\pi_w) has zero monodromy, is trivial on wild inertia (characteristic polynomial (X-1)^n there), and at a tame generator of inertia has no repeated eigenvalue other than (q_w-1)-th roots of unity, the representation of \varrho has zero monodromy and the same characteristic polynomial as \mathrm{rec}(\pi_w) at every element of inertia (tame0).
  5. (above) For every choice of the \ell-adic period data over which the code quantifies (LocPrime, LocAinf, LocTied), the following holds at every place w\mid\ell. Where \pi_w is spherical, \varrho restricted to a decomposition group is crystalline and de Rham with Hodge and Tate weights \mathrm{HT} (crys). Under either set of hypotheses of item 4 on \mathrm{rec}(\pi_w) (with g>16n^2 read for the rank n), it is potentially semistable and de Rham with the same weights, and its Weil and Deligne representation, built by Fontaine’s functor, relates to \mathrm{rec}(\pi_w) as in item 4 (nice).
In plain terms

For a large class of automorphic representations over CM fields there is a Galois representation whose Frobenius eigenvalues at almost every prime are the representation’s local data, whose behavior above \ell is set by the weights at infinity, and whose behavior at the remaining primes matches the local data in a weakened, explicit sense.

Why it is needed

The proof uses it twice. It is the input of the cohomological window bound VWin of The arithmetic residue: a window in Galois cohomology, and it fills two fields of the record of published statements that the theta-integral assembly consumes. Without it neither input exists (What the Galois representations are used for).

Idea

At a place w where \pi_w is unramified, \mathrm{rec}(\pi_w) is an unramified representation of the Weil group, which factors through the abelian quotient by inertia, so it is trivial on commutators and has zero monodromy. Item 4 then says that the local Galois representation equals \mathrm{rec}(\pi_w), and in our reading of how the laws of recT combine, that is the statement that the Frobenius eigenvalues are the Satake parameters, as in Equation (22.3). Items 2 and 3 are the higher-dimensional form of “the determinant is p^{k-1}”: the weights at infinity of \pi become Hodge and Tate weights, and the polarization makes them symmetric about w_0/2. The tame clause with g>16n^2 is the weakening: at ramified places compatibility is promised only in the listed cases.

Proof sketch

[96]

The existence of \varrho with items 1 to 4 at unramified places and item 5 at spherical places is due to work of Clozel, Kottwitz, Harris and Taylor, Shin, and Chenevier and Harris, among others [97; 98]. The form for polarized pairs follows Barnet-Lamb, Gee, Geraghty, and Taylor [96], and compatibility at ramified places is in the direction of Caraiani’s theorem [99]. The code obtains Row0b from a stronger Row0 of the same shape, with no size condition on g, by forgetting that condition (Row0.row0b), and it proves Row0 from scratch, as the next section describes.

The folder ZetaCharacterDivisibility below is about divisibility of polynomials, and the congruences of CongruenceOddLevel are used to construct Galois representations, not to bound the chain. 22.3How the formal proof builds them#

The assembly of Row0b sits in one file, IntegralStructures/Development.lean, and it reads as a five-step recipe. Before the steps, the classical recipe they follow.

Aside

Background. A standard way to construct the Galois representation of an automorphic form that does not appear in the cohomology of any variety is by congruences and limits. One finds forms f_k that do appear in cohomology and whose Hecke eigenvalues are congruent to those of f modulo \ell^k, takes their Galois representations, and passes to the limit k\to\infty through their traces, which converge \ell-adically. Wiles used this for ordinary forms through Hida families, with two-dimensional pseudo-representations to turn a limit of traces into a Galois representation [100], and Taylor extended pseudo-representations to every dimension and applied the method to Siegel forms of low weight [101]. A second standard device changes the rank: when the forms of rank n are not reachable, one adds characters to reach a rank where they are and removes the characters afterwards. Chenevier and Harris complete the construction for \GL_n over CM fields along these lines [98]. The formal proof follows both devices, with theta lifts between totally definite unitary groups in the role of the rank change.

The formal proof works on totally definite unitary groups, where, as Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices showed, an automorphic form is a vector of numbers indexed by finitely many lattice classes, so that congruences are congruences between vectors of integers. Its five steps are geometry for forms of a special type and odd rank (GeoOne), division of a large representation down to the right dimension (DivAll), congruences to every form of odd rank (CongFinOdd), an \ell-adic limit (LimFinOdd), and two theta lifts for even rank (TLiftK). Then rest passes to Row0 by local and global compatibility at spherical and Iwahori levels, and Row0.row0b weakens Row0 to Row0b. Each step below gets its declaration and a paragraph that says what was and was not read.

Step 1: geometry#

For a form U of odd rank and of a special type at an auxiliary \ell-adic place, GeoOne gives a semisimple \varrho^{\mathrm{big}}, usually of dimension larger than n, whose Frobenius eigenvalues at almost every usable place include the Satake parameters of U, with crystalline versions at the \ell-adic places whose crystalline Frobenius has a characteristic polynomial dividing a power of the Satake polynomial. It is proved as geometric_realization_of_weight_one, from a record Steps of seventeen lemmas, a record KSAll, and a statement PlanEx, and its one named published input is the holomorphic Lefschetz formula of Atiyah and Bott, which the tree proves. The representation is a piece of the étale cohomology of a variety Z with Hecke correspondences: HTower is a scheme Z with pairs of maps Y_g\rightrightarrows Z, and Nice asks that Z be smooth and projective and the maps finite étale, so that the Lefschetz formula computes Hodge numbers of the pieces from fixed points. Which variety Z is was not unfolded: a Plan attaches to U a prime p, a datum Datum p, a group HTGroup p, and a tower, and a lemma is named kodaira_spencer_of_weight_one, but we did not identify Z. Step 2: division#

DivAll takes one representation with the properties VBase and returns \varrho of dimension n with IsDivRep: on a dense open set of Frobenius elements, \det(X-\varrho(\sigma^{-1})) is the product of X-b over the normalized Satake parameters b, as in Equation (22.3). The proof divAll_holds combines a determinant character (DetEx), its divisibility (DivDet), a division lemma (DivOne), uniqueness (DivUniq), and a seed for the crystalline Frobenius (PhiSeed). The clause PhiKilled asks that the characteristic polynomial of the crystalline Frobenius of \varrho^{\mathrm{big}} divide a power of the Satake polynomial, and Inside r ρ says that \varrho embeds in \varrho^{\mathrm{big}} through an intertwining matrix of rank n. In a small example of ours, a five-dimensional \varrho^{\mathrm{big}} with Frobenius polynomial (X^2+2X+2)^2(X-1) at p=2 and a form with Satake polynomial X^2+2X+2 would give the two-dimensional piece with that polynomial.

A common misreading

The divisibility of the note’s steps 2, 9, and 10 is the divisibility of numbers by powers of a prime, the integer form of vanishing to high order. The divisibility of ZetaCharacterDivisibility is the divisibility of one polynomial by another, the algebraic form of “this representation contains that one”. The two are unrelated in the code, and only the first is the multiplicity of Stepanov’s argument.

Step 3: congruences#

CongFinOdd is the odd-rank instance of CongUW4. For U of odd rank and two auxiliary \ell-adic places it gives a level and nonzero constants such that the system \theta_U of Hecke eigenvalues of U, extended by weighted powers of Satake parameters at the \ell-adic places, satisfies PolyApprox: it lies in the \ell-adic closure of the polynomial expressions in eigenvalue systems of forms U' of the special type TyEll, with the same level and weight away from the auxiliary places. The type TyEll asks for a vector on which a pro-\ell subgroup at an auxiliary place acts through a character of order \ell^m, chosen so that every representation containing it is supercuspidal there. In the finite picture of Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices a congruence is concrete. If the integer matrix T=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&0\end{pmatrix} stands in for a Hecke operator on a genus with two classes, then f=(1,1) has Tf=3f and f'=(2,-3) has Tf'=-2f'. Modulo 5, f'\equiv2f and -2\equiv3, and this is forced: \lambda'f'=Tf'\equiv2Tf=2\lambda f\equiv\lambda f', and an entry of f' is a unit modulo 5. The classical instance is Ramanujan’s congruence \tau(p)\equiv1+p^{11}\pmod{691} between \Delta and an Eisenstein series, for instance \tau(2)=-24\equiv2049 modulo 691 [102]. Step 4: the \ell-adic limit#

LimFinOdd is the conclusion of SeedFinOdd for every form of odd rank: an n-dimensional \varrho with FrobEig at every usable place away from \ell, crystalline and de Rham at the other \ell-adic places, and with crystalline Frobenius data approximated \ell-adically by crystalline representations (JointApprox). It is proved in one line, limWU4_of _ _ _ _ h h', in a folder named TraceLimits. An \ell-adic limit is a limit in the topology in which \ell^k is small: 1,3,7,15,\dots,2^k-1 converges 2-adically to -1, because the differences 2^k tend to 0. Eigenvalue systems that agree modulo higher and higher powers of \ell converge in the same way, and so do the characteristic polynomials of their Galois representations, coefficient by coefficient. That the code passes to the limit through traces, as pseudo-representations do, is our inference from the folder name and the shape of LimWU4, and the proof of limWU4_of was not unfolded.

Step 5: the single use of TLiftK#

TLiftK, the existence of theta lifts between totally definite unitary groups that Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices and Multiplicity without derivatives: a chain of length about the square root discuss, enters this region exactly once, in twoUpOK_of_steps. For even n and an automorphic U on the unitary group in n variables over a CM field E of the kind TwoUpAll allows (E unramified over E^+ at every finite place, [E^+:\QQ] even), the code takes d_0 from TLiftK, sets t=2(d_0+n)+1, which is odd so that n+t is odd, chooses two families \psi_1=(\psi_{1,1},\dots,\psi_{1,t}) and \psi_2 of Hecke characters of E with no character in common, and lifts U twice to the unitary group in n+t variables. The record IsUp describes each lift U_i: it is automorphic, its weights move by an explicit rule, and at every split place w where everything is unramified its Satake parameters, normalized by algSat as in Equation (22.3) (for rank n+t on the left and rank n on the right), are

\operatorname{algSat}_w(U_i)=\kappa(w)^{-1}\cdot\operatorname{algSat}_w(U)\ \cup\ \{\psi_{i,1}(w),\dots,\psi_{i,t}(w)\},
(22.4)

as multisets, with \kappa a fixed algebraic Hecke character. By step 4 each U_i, of odd rank, has a Galois representation \varrho_{U_i}, which contains \varrho_U\otimes\kappa^{-1} and t characters. Because no character occurs in both families, the part common to \varrho_{U_1} and \varrho_{U_2} is \varrho_U\otimes\kappa^{-1}, and the code’s Subtract turns this into the representation of U. The statement rowDef_of_odd records the logic: even rank from odd rank, through Subtract and TwoUpAll.

Example

Take n=2 with the Satake parameters \{-1+i,\,-1-i\} of the level 11 form at p=2, ignore the twist \kappa, and take t=3 for the picture (the code’s t=2(d_0+2)+1 is larger) with character values \{2,3,5\} for the first lift and \{7,11,13\} for the second at the same place. The two odd-rank representations have Frobenius eigenvalues \{-1+i,-1-i,2,3,5\} and \{-1+i,-1-i,7,11,13\}, and the common part is \{-1+i,-1-i\}, as it should be. If the second family reused the value 5, the common part would be \{-1+i,-1-i,5\}, three-dimensional, and the subtraction could not tell the form’s part from a character. This is why TwoUp demands \psi_{1,i}\ne\psi_{2,j} for all i,j. The numbers 2,3,5,7,11,13 are placeholders of ours, not values of actual Hecke characters.

Our reading of the window VWin found that the plus part of those groups, where Vandiver’s conjecture speaks, is bounded through automorphy of Galois representations, and that Row0b and the base change statement BaseChangeIsobaricN enter there. We confirmed the calls in VwinOfRow.lean and did not follow the plus-part argument.

We followed them, by names and fields only, into a package of automorphy and Galois cohomology statements that supplies the theta-integral assembly with a hypothesis that certain representations are not endoscopic (NonEndoscopicHypothesesAlt).

The digests support no use of Row0b for integrality or for congruences in the chain. The congruences of CongFinOdd are between forms on one unitary group and serve to build Galois representations, not the note’s step 18 “congruences between lifts and forms”, and TLiftK is used only inside the construction of Row0b, so the m-fold chain does not go through it [3].

22.5The count that is bounded#

We now turn from what the chain stands on to what it delivers. Chapter The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros needs, for each primitive character of order r, an upper bound on

G_r(X)=G_0(X)+\frac1{3r+1}\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}\Re\,g_{(\chi^j)^*}(X)

at every scale in windows [Y,Y^{3/2}]. A smoothed prime sum cannot be bounded above by looking at it, because its size is decided by the zeros. The formal proof bounds a different quantity, a count of prime powers of a special kind, and converts. In Stepanov’s terms, and as our reading, this count plays the part of the number of rational points, the quantity that the auxiliary construction bounds from above.

The smallest case: primes inert in \QQ(i)#

An odd prime p is inert in \QQ(i) when p\equiv3\pmod4, that is, when \chi_4(p)=-1 for the character \chi_4 of What the hypothesis says about primes, and its generalizations, and split when p\equiv1\pmod4. By Dirichlet’s theorem about half of the odd primes are inert. Up to 1000 there are 167 odd primes, 87 inert against 83.5 expected, and up to 10{,}000 there are 1228, with 619 inert against 614. The excess is the zero noise of L(s,\chi_4), and the smoothed version makes this exact in a worked case of ours, before the code’s general statement.

Count, with the ramp weight of the smoothed sum and with weight 2, the odd prime powers n=p^i with \chi_4(n)=-1, which are the powers p^i with p\equiv3\pmod4 and i odd:

A_4(X)=\sum_{\substack{n\le X\\ n\ \text{odd},\ \chi_4(n)=-1}}2\Lambda(n)\Bigl(\frac Xn-1\Bigr).
(22.5)

For odd n, 2\cdot\mathbf 1[\chi_4(n)=-1]=1-\chi_4(n), the orthogonality of the two characters modulo 4 (Equation (7.6)). Summing against \Lambda(n)(X/n-1) over odd n gives A_4(X)=S(X)-B_2(X)-\sum_{n\le X}\chi_4(n)\Lambda(n)(X/n-1), where B_2(X)=\sum_{2^k\le X}\log2\,(X/2^k-1) removes the powers of 2. Write S(X)=X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X+G_0(X) as in The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros, and \sum_n\chi_4(n)\Lambda(n)(X/n-1)=g_{\chi_4}(X)-X\frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi_4) by the definition of g_\chi. With the expected size

M_4(X)=X\log X-(1+\gamma_E)X-X\log2+X\,\frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi_4),

the count’s excess over its expected size is

A_4(X)-M_4(X)=G_0(X)-g_{\chi_4}(X)-\bigl(B_2(X)-X\log2\bigr).
(22.6)

The last term is O(\log X), because B_2(X)=X\log2\,(1-2^{-K})-K\log2 with K=\lfloor\log_2X\rfloor. The constant is \frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi_4)=\gamma_E+2\log2+3\log\pi-4\log\Gamma(\tfrac14)=0.2456096, which we checked against a numerical derivative of L(s,\chi_4).

Example

Both sides of Equation (22.6), computed independently, the left from the inert prime powers alone and the right from all prime powers and the character sum, with mpmath at 30 digits:

X A_4(X) M_4(X) A_4-M_4 G_0(X) g_{\chi_4}(X) B_2(X)-X\log2 right side
100 264.9575 258.0417 6.9158 1.7217 0.0478 -5.2419 6.9158
1000 4892.6420 4883.0020 9.6400 1.5309 -0.5169 -7.5921 9.6400
10000 71860.4822 71855.8711 4.6111 1.7493 6.9953 -9.8570 4.6111

The count is about X\log X in size and its excess is a handful, of the size of the zero noise G_0 and g_{\chi_4} and of the logarithm from the prime 2. An upper bound on the count of the form A_4(X)\le M_4(X)+X^{\theta} is therefore the same as an upper bound G_0(X)-g_{\chi_4}(X)\le X^\theta+O(\log X).

The toy shows both the mechanism and its difficulty. The count controls a combination of smoothed sums, the one picked out by orthogonality on the group \Gal(\QQ(i)/\QQ), and the combination carries the character \chi_4 with a minus sign. Landau’s argument of The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros needs positive weights, so in the toy a bound on the count bounds G_0 from above only if \lvert g_{\chi_4}\rvert is already known to be small. The formal proof meets this difficulty in its general form, and in our reading resolves it in two ways that the next sections confirm in the code: it averages over a large finite group so that the characters it wants appear with positive weights, and it chooses the auxiliary field so that the characters that keep an uncontrolled sign are twists by Jacobi symbols of huge auxiliary primes, for which a square-root bound is available by averaging (Characters that get their bound for free).

The general count in the code#

The code’s count lives on a finite abelian group \mathcal G=(\ZZ/2\ZZ)^2\times A, where A is the frame group of Definition 21.4 (the code writes E0 × H, with H the frame group), supplied with the chain data at each scale. The subgroup \Phi\subset\mathcal G of elements whose first coordinate is 0 has index 2 (InPhi, PhiSet), the character \chi_C that is -1 off \Phi is the code’s chC, and a record ArithData assigns to every prime p a Frobenius element f_p\in\mathcal G and an inertia subgroup, together with two auxiliary primes \mathsf q_1 and \mathsf d. A prime p\ne2,\mathsf q_1,\mathsf d is inert (IsInert) when f_p\notin\Phi. This \mathcal G is not the genus of Forms you can hold: definite unitary groups and theta lifts as matrices, and this \Phi is a subgroup, not the function \Phi(s) of Zeta on the whole plane. On the spine the record is not abstract. The host’s arith builds it by class field theory (cftData, in RamificationTwoAndConjugationAtQAndD.lean) from the host’s CM field E, with \mathsf q_1 the host’s prime \mathsf q and f_p the image of p under the Artin map, and the identifications HostRaw.gal and Comparison₂.toE make \mathcal G the Galois group of E over \QQ, the group \{\pm1\}^2\times A of Definition 21.4. Under them \Phi is the subgroup that fixes \sqrt{-\mathsf d} (inPhi_iff), \chi_C is the quadratic character of \QQ(\sqrt{-\mathsf d}), and a prime is inert exactly when it is inert in \QQ(\sqrt{-\mathsf d}). The hypotheses HostFacts (unramified outside 2,\mathsf q_1,\mathsf d, ramified at \mathsf d with inertia of order two) and the field ReadsKept, in which the values of kept Dirichlet characters at n are computed from the group through primVal, are the abstract record’s form of the same facts.

For a scale a>0, an element t\in A, a positive weight function \mathsf w on \Phi, and a cutoff N, the count is

\mathrm{ASK}=\sum_{\substack{p\le N\\ p\ \text{inert}}}2\log p\sum_{\substack{1\le i\le N\\ i f_p\notin\Phi}}\Bigl(\frac a{p^i}-\mathsf w\bigl(\text{partner}_t(i f_p)\bigr)\Bigr)_+\ +\ \log\mathsf d\cdot(\text{the same sum at the ramified prime }\mathsf d),
(22.7)

where \text{partner}_t(g)=g+((1,1),0)+((0,0),t) is a bijection from the complement of \Phi onto \Phi (PartnerBij). It is the toy count Equation (22.5) with two changes: the ramp (a/p^i-\mathsf w)_+ has a cutoff that depends, through \mathsf w, on where the Frobenius of p^i sits in the group, and the weight 2\log p appears with the same factor 2. The expected size is

\mathrm{MAIN}=a\Bigl(\log a-1-\gamma_E+\mathrm{ld}(\chi_C)-\frac1{\lvert\Phi\rvert}\sum_{\rho\in\Phi}\log\mathsf w(\rho)\Bigr),

where \mathrm{ld}, the code’s ell, assigns to each character of \mathcal G a complex number, which for the characters that come from Dirichlet characters is \frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi) (a clause of TieArith in ChainTied). For each character \psi of \mathcal G the code forms the smoothed sum GPsi, which is G_0(y) for \psi trivial and \sum_{n\le y}\Lambda(n)\,\mathrm{primVal}(\psi,n)(y/n-1)+y\,\mathrm{ld}(\psi) otherwise, the sum g_\chi of the Dirichlet character \chi that \psi defines through the Frobenius map.

Theorem 22.5

The excess of the inert count over its expected size is an exact combination of smoothed prime sums over the characters of the auxiliary group

[3]
Statement

Assume HostFactsS D S. For every a>0, every t\in A, every weight \mathsf w>0 on \Phi, and every cutoff N with a/\mathsf w(\rho)\le N for all \rho\in\Phi,

\mathrm{ASK}-\mathrm{MAIN}=\frac1{\lvert\Phi\rvert}\sum_{g\notin\Phi}\ \sum_{\psi\in\widehat{\mathcal G}}\overline{\psi(g)}\ \mathsf w\bigl(\text{partner}_t(g)\bigr)\ \mathrm{GPsi}\Bigl(\psi,\frac{a}{\mathsf w(\text{partner}_t(g))}\Bigr),
(22.8)

where \widehat{\mathcal G} is the group of characters of \mathcal G. The right side is the code’s De.

In plain terms

Counting prime powers whose Frobenius lands in a given part of a finite group, with the ramp weight, gives its expected size plus a sum of smoothed prime sums, one for each character of the group, each rescaled to its own cutoff.

Why it is needed

It is the bridge from an arithmetic count, which the chain can bound, to the smoothed sums g_\chi that Landau’s argument reads. Without it an upper bound on the count would say nothing about zeros.

Idea

Orthogonality of characters writes the indicator of “Frobenius of p^i equals g” as \frac1{\lvert\Phi\rvert}\sum_\psi\overline{\psi(g)}\psi(f_{p^i}), up to the factor 2 that matches the 2\log p, at unramified primes (OrthoUnram) and as an average over the inertia coset at ramified ones (OrthoRam). Summing over g\notin\Phi and i rewrites the count as a sum over characters of twisted smoothed sums with cutoffs a/\mathsf w. Each twisted sum is its GPsi minus its main term, and the main terms add up, by ColourSum, to MAIN, because only the trivial character and \chi_C survive the sum over g\notin\Phi.

Proof
Show the proof

The code proves the identity as Deduction.ch_balance (DedekindLFunctions/LandauTheorems/ChBalance.lean, line 200). It first applies askExp, the proved instance of AskExpansion, which states

\mathrm{ASK}=\frac1{\lvert\Phi\rvert}\sum_{g\notin\Phi}\sum_\psi\overline{\psi(g)}\sum_{n\le N}\Lambda(n)\,\mathrm{primVal}(\psi,n)\Bigl(\frac an-\mathsf w(\text{partner}_t(g))\Bigr)_+ ,

with lemmas for the unramified primes, the split primes 2 and \mathsf q_1, and the ramified prime \mathsf d. With \mathsf w_g=\mathsf w(\text{partner}_t(g)), the identity \sum_n\Lambda(n)(a/n-\mathsf w_g)_+=\mathsf w_g\sum_{n\le a/\mathsf w_g}\Lambda(n)\bigl(\frac{a/\mathsf w_g}n-1\bigr) turns each inner sum into \mathsf w_g\cdot\mathrm{GPsi}(\psi,a/\mathsf w_g) plus a main term (sum_cut, inner_eq), and ColourSum, which says that \sum_{g\notin\Phi}\overline{\psi(g)} is \lvert\Phi\rvert, -\lvert\Phi\rvert, or 0 as \psi is trivial, \chi_C, or neither, adds the main terms up to MAIN. We read the statement and the top level of the proof, and the lemmas by their statements.

Example

For \mathcal G=\Gal(\QQ(i)/\QQ) of order 2, \mathsf w\equiv1, and the prime 2 removed by hand, the identity becomes Equation (22.6), which the table above checks. This specialization is ours: in the code the smallest group is (\ZZ/2\ZZ)^2 and the prime 2 splits.

22.6From the count to G_r#

The identity Equation (22.8) holds for one value of t and one weight \mathsf w. The chain supplies an upper bound on the excess \mathrm{ASK}-\Re\,\mathrm{MAIN} summed over a set \mathcal T\subseteq A of values of t (the code’s TT, whose elements we call shifts) and over the m steps j of the chain, each with its own weight \mathsf w_j. The code calls this sum the gap,

\mathrm{gapA}(u_0)=\sum_{t\in \mathcal T}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Bigl(\mathrm{ASK}\bigl(a_t,t,\mathsf w_{u_0,j}\bigr)-\Re\,\mathrm{MAIN}\bigl(a_t,\mathsf w_{u_0,j}\bigr)\Bigr),

with one gap for each element u_0 of a subgroup A_0\subseteq A (the code’s Frame.A0), and it turns gaps into a bound on G_r in the theorem core_gm.

Theorem 22.6

A small gap between the inert count and its expected size, at a scale x, bounds G_r(x) by x^{1/2+O(\varepsilon)}

[3]
Statement

For every level \mathsf L, every e_D,e_L,K,c_{HH},e_K,C, and every \varepsilon>0 there is x_1 such that for every x\ge x_1, every frame \varphi with a host satisfying the axioms HostAx, and every finite set \mathcal T in the frame’s group, if the host satisfies the explicit-formula conditions EAtH with constant C at x and the chain conditions CoreAtH with constants e_D,e_L,K,c_{HH},e_K at x, then

G_{\mathsf L}(x)\le x^{1/2+(e_D+e_L+7)\varepsilon}.

For the cyclic level of a primitive character \chi of order r, G_{\mathsf L} is the function G_r of The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros.

In plain terms

If, at a scale x, the weighted count of inert prime powers never exceeds its expected size by much, and the characters that are not kept are already known to be small, then the combination of smoothed prime sums that Landau’s argument needs is at most x^{1/2} times a small power of x.

Why it is needed

This is the one-sided bound that The last mile: a one-sided bound on windows forbids zeros consumes at each scale of each window. It is the last place where the chain of theta lifts enters the proof.

Idea

Apply Theorem 22.5 to every t, every step j, and every coset representative u_0, and add. Averaging over u_0\in A_0 is orthogonality on the subgroup A_0: it kills every character that is not trivial on A_0 and multiplies the rest by \lvert A_0\rvert. Among the survivors, the kept characters, those that come from the cyclic group of \chi, appear with weight 1 for the trivial character and \frac1{3r+1} for the others, because the set \mathcal T meets each coset of A_0 in that proportion. The remaining survivors are bounded in absolute value by x^{1/2+\varepsilon}, and the gap is bounded by the chain. What is left is G_r(x) against a power of x. In our reading this is Bombieri’s twisted count of Theorem 10.12 turned around. There, upper bounds for all twists but one bound the last one from below, and here an upper bound on one count, together with bounds on every twist that is not kept, bounds the kept combination from above.

Proof
Show the proof

We read the proofs of core_gm, ch_core, core, and ch_top in full and the statements of the lemmas they call. The argument has five moves.

  1. core_gm (PrimitiveCosets/CoreGm.lean) unpacks CoreAtH into a data record Dd, the arithmetic data, a set T_2, sizes a_t, weights \mathsf w, and the identification IdentU of the record’s abstract fields Dd.ASK and Dd.Main with the arithmetic ASK and MAIN, and it applies Deduction.ch_core with C=e_D+e_L+3, the weight \frac1{3r+1}, the kept set keptA at the level, and the character conditions charsA.
  2. The gap hypothesis of ch_core comes from ch_top (LandauTheorems/ChTop.lean), which uses IdentU and ch_top_main_eq to write \mathrm{gapA}(u)=\mathrm{Dd.ASK}(u)-\mathrm{Dd.Main}(u), then each_unit_bound_statement to bound this by \mathrm{ErrX5at}(u) from the record SizeData₂ of Where the chain’s divisibility is paid, and finally ErrWindows and BNBoundsU to bound \mathrm{ErrX5at}(u) by x^{C_{\mathrm{Err}}\varepsilon} times the bracket, with C_{\mathrm{Err}}\le e_D+e_L+3.
  3. The lemma core (LandauTheorems/ChCore.lean, line 283) adds Theorem 22.5 over t and j, moves each term to the common scale a_t/b at a cost 2b/x (th_le), and averages over u_0\in A_0, where sum_A keeps exactly the characters trivial on A_0. It bounds \lvert \mathcal T\rvert\,m\,b\,\frac{\delta_2}{2}\,Y by \mathrm{Err}+2\lvert \mathcal T\rvert mb/x for any Y below the averaged character sum.
  4. The lemma one_char bounds the character sum from below one character at a time: G_0 for the trivial character, \frac1{3r+1}\Re\,\mathrm{GPsi} for a kept one up to the equidistribution error of CharsA, and -\lVert\mathrm{GPsi}\rVert for an unkept one. Taking Y=\mathrm{GmA}-\mathrm{SigA}-4x^{1/2+\varepsilon} and proposition_size_bound gives the conclusion of ch_core, \mathrm{GmA}(x)\le x^{1/2+(C+3)\varepsilon}+\mathrm{SigA}(x).
  5. core_gm finishes with gmA_eq, which identifies the frame sum GmA with G_{\mathsf L}, and sigA_le, which bounds the unkept part by 4r\,x^{1/2+\varepsilon} using the bounded characters of EAtH, so that G_{\mathsf L}(x)\le(1+4r)\,x^{1/2+(e_D+e_L+6)\varepsilon}, which is at most x^{1/2+(e_D+e_L+7)\varepsilon} once x^\varepsilon\ge1+4r.

Moves 1 to 4 are confirmed in the code. In move 5 we confirmed the calls, and the statements of gmA_eq and sigA_le are as our reading of the endgame gives them.

22.7Characters that get their bound for free#

The unkept characters of Theorem 22.6 need \lvert g_\chi(y)\rvert\le y^{1/2+\varepsilon} before the argument starts, and that is a statement of the strength of the hypothesis itself. The code arranges that every such character is a twist \xi\cdot(\cdot/\mathsf q)^i(\cdot/\mathsf d)^j with (i,j)\ne(0,0), where \xi is a character of the modulus M of \chi and (\cdot/\mathsf q), (\cdot/\mathsf d) are Jacobi symbols of two auxiliary primes (boundedTw, CharacterBoxes/BoundedTw.lean), and it supplies the bound for these twists through PairGood.
